notes.explains: White's hypermodern opening (b3) aims to lure Black's pawns forward and later attack them. Black responds by occupying the center with e5 and d5, building a strong pawn chain.
notes.teaches: Against hypermodern openings, the classical response is to seize the center with pawns and develop pieces, punishing any violation of opening principles.
notes.plans: Black will complete development, then launch a kingside attack using the open h-file after the pawn sacrifice on h5.

notes.explains: White has castled kingside but neglected queenside development. Black, despite not being fully developed, senses the opportunity to attack because White's king is exposed and the h-file can be opened.
notes.teaches: When the opponent violates opening principles (e.g., moving the same piece multiple times, neglecting development), you should complete your own development and then look for an immediate attack.
notes.plans: Play h5 to open the h-file, then castle queenside to bring the rook into the attack.

notes.explains: After the pawn sacrifice on h5 and the exchange on h4, Black has a rook on h8 and queen on h4, with White's king on g1. Black now plays Qh6, sacrificing the rook to maintain the attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, sacrificing material to keep the initiative can be decisive. The rook sacrifice on h1 is not necessary to take; instead, the queen invades with mate threats.
notes.plans: Play Qh6, threatening Qxh2#. White's only defense is Rf1, but then g3 opens lines for Black's pieces to deliver mate or win back the rook.

notes.explains: White pushes pawns on the queenside, but this creates weaknesses. Black's knight retreats to d7, keeping it centralized and flexible.
notes.teaches: Pawn advances can create permanent weaknesses. Here, White's b4-b5 leaves a backward pawn on c3 and weakens the queenside. Black should target these weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black can now plan to attack the c3 pawn with Rc8, or switch to a kingside attack. The knight on d7 can later go to c4 or e5.

notes.explains: Black occupies the semi-open c-file with Rc8, targeting the backward pawn on c3. This ties White's rook to its defense.
notes.teaches: A semi-open file is a strategic asset. Occupying it with a rook pressures the pawn and restricts the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: Continue to pressure c3. If White defends with Rc1, Black can consider switching to a kingside attack, as White's pieces are tied down.

notes.explains: Black maneuvers the queen to h5, targeting the knight on h3 and preparing a kingside attack. White must respond with Kg2 to support the knight.
notes.teaches: Switching the attack from queenside to kingside is a common strategic shift. The queen on h5 creates threats and forces White to defend passively.
notes.plans: After Kg2, Black can look for ways to exploit the trapped bishop on f4 or create further weaknesses. The knight on h3 is a target.

notes.explains: Black plays Bc5, attacking the knight on a3 and preparing Nc4. This threatens to trap the bishop on f4 and create chaos.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are poorly coordinated, look for ways to exploit their lack of mobility. Here, Bc5 forces a favorable exchange or wins material.
notes.plans: After the knight moves, play Nc4, attacking the queen and threatening e5 or g5 to trap the bishop. This should win material.

notes.explains: Black plays d4, an interference tactic that breaks the connection between White's queen and bishop. This wins material.
notes.teaches: Interference tactics can disrupt the opponent's coordination. Here, d4 blocks the queen's defense of the bishop, allowing Black to capture it.
notes.plans: After d4, Black will win the bishop on e3 or the knight on h3, leading to a decisive material advantage.

notes.explains: Black wins a pawn after a tactical sequence. The knight on d4 is captured, and Black's bishop on d4 is active.
notes.teaches: Tactics often flow from a development advantage. Here, the central break leads to a winning pawn grab.
notes.plans: Black is up a pawn and has a strong position. Continue to develop and consolidate.

notes.explains: Black captures on e4 with the knight, forking the queen and rook. This wins the exchange.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for tactical finishes. The fork here is decisive.
notes.plans: After Nxe4, Black will win the rook. The game is effectively over.

notes.explains: Black correctly plays Qd7 to cover the diagonal and then trades bishops. White puts the knight on e2 to keep the f-pawn free for a future f4-f5 break.
notes.teaches: In the French Advance, Ne2 (instead of Nf3) keeps the f-pawn unobstructed, enabling a kingside pawn storm after castling.
notes.plans: Castle, then prepare f4 to break open the kingside.

notes.explains: Black plays h5, creating a weakness on g5. White should not play h4; instead, let Black push h4 and then fix the pawn with h3.
notes.teaches: When your opponent weakens their kingside with h5, do not automatically play h4. Wait for them to play h4, then fix the pawn with h3; the h4 pawn often becomes a target.
notes.plans: Occupy g5 with Bg5, then develop Nd2 and later Nf3 to attack the h4 pawn.

notes.explains: White places the bishop on g5, occupying the weak square created by h5.
notes.teaches: Occupy weak squares immediately; here g5 is a permanent outpost for the bishop.
notes.plans: Develop Nd2, then Nf3, targeting the h4 pawn after Black plays h4.

notes.explains: Black plays g6, creating a new weakness on f6. White's bishop on g5 now has a permanent home.
notes.teaches: Every pawn move creates weaknesses; g6 weakens the dark squares, especially f6.
notes.plans: Keep the bishop on g5, bring the knight to f3, and later consider taking on f5 when the time is right.

notes.explains: White plays a3, preparing b4 to challenge Black's c5 pawn. This is a typical French Advance idea: force the c5 pawn to decide its fate.
notes.teaches: In the French Advance, a3-b4 is a standard way to put pressure on Black's queenside and open lines if Black captures on d4.
notes.plans: Play b4, and if Black takes on d4, open the c-file with Rc1 and double rooks. If Black pushes c4, White's d4 pawn is safe and White can focus on the kingside.

notes.explains: Black captures on d4, opening the c-file. White plays h3 to prevent ...Ng4, which would kick the bishop from f6.
notes.teaches: Prophylaxis: stop your opponent's threats before they happen. Here h3 prevents ...Ng4 and keeps the bishop on f6 as a 'bone in Black's throat'.
notes.plans: Play Rc1, double rooks on the c-file, and then switch to the kingside attack.

notes.explains: White uses Qd2 to prepare Rc1 with tempo (attacking the knight on h6). After Black retreats to f5, White seizes the c-file.
notes.teaches: Use threats to gain tempi for important moves. Here Qd2 forces the knight to f5, then Rc1 grabs the open file.
notes.plans: Double rooks on the c-file, then switch to the kingside with Qh6 or other attacking moves.

notes.explains: Black trades knights on g3, and White recaptures with the f-pawn, opening the f-file for attack.
notes.teaches: Recapturing away from the center (fxg3) opens a file for the rooks, which is often more important than central pawn structure.
notes.plans: Double rooks on the f-file and launch a kingside attack.

notes.explains: White takes on h5 with the queen. This is materialistic but effective; Black cannot recapture with the queen due to Rc8, and if ...Nxe5, then f6 cements the pawn.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, simple captures are often best. Do not overcomplicate; look for straightforward moves that maintain pressure.
notes.plans: After ...Qd8, continue with Ne5 or other consolidating moves.

notes.explains: White plays Rc6, threatening Rxe6 due to the pin on the e6 pawn. This is a strong move that exploits the pin along the c-file.
notes.teaches: When you have a pin, look for ways to increase the pressure. Here Rc6 creates an unstoppable threat against e6.
notes.plans: If ...Nxe5, then Rxc6; if ...Qxf6, then Nxd7. The pin decides.

notes.explains: After ...Qxf6, White plays Nxd7, a simple capture that wins material. The knight on d7 is under attack and the queen is loose.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, do not overlook simple captures. Checks, captures, and threats should include all captures, not just fancy ones.
notes.plans: After ...Kxd7, Rxc8 wins the queen; the rest is a matter of technique.

notes.explains: White wins the queen and reaches a winning endgame. The passed h-pawn decides.
notes.teaches: Convert a winning advantage by pushing passed pawns. Here h4-h5-h6 is the fastest route.
notes.plans: Push the h-pawn to promotion, using the queen to support it.

notes.explains: Black lifts the rook to g6 to prepare g4, threatening to open the g-file and attack white's king.
notes.teaches: A rook lift to g6 is an aggressive way to support the g4 pawn break, and the rook will be well-placed on the open file after ...gxf3.
notes.plans: After g4, black will open the g-file and bring heavy pieces to bear on white's king.

notes.explains: White plays Bf4, a creative but flawed move that hangs the bishop. Black can simply capture it.
notes.teaches: Always check if opponent's moves hang material, even if they seem aggressive. Simple tactics often decide games.
notes.plans: Black takes the bishop and remains up a piece, then simplifies to a winning endgame.

notes.explains: After taking the bishop, black captures on e5 and white recaptures with the queen. Now black has a winning tactic: Bg4 pins the queen to the rook, winning the exchange.
notes.teaches: Pins are powerful when the pinned piece is more valuable than the attacker. Look for pins after captures that open lines.
notes.plans: Black plays Bg4, winning the exchange, and then uses the open g-file to attack the king.

notes.explains: Black's Bg4 pins the queen to the rook. White cannot avoid losing the exchange, and black's attack continues.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify while maintaining pressure. Pins can force further concessions.
notes.plans: Black will win the exchange, then bring the queen to the kingside for a mating attack.

notes.explains: In the Scotch Gambit, white sacrifices a pawn for rapid development and attacking chances. Black's best responses are either to defend the pawn (e.g., Nf6) or counterattack (e.g., Bc5).
notes.teaches: The Scotch Gambit is a sharp opening where white gets a lead in development and central control in exchange for a pawn. It's playable even at grandmaster level.
notes.plans: White aims to develop quickly, castle, and launch an attack against black's king, often with moves like Bg5 or Nf3-g5.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Bc4, black's most common responses are …Nf6 (defending the pawn) and …Bc5 (counterattacking). Both lead to sharp play.
notes.teaches: In gambits, black can either accept the pawn and defend, or counterattack to disrupt white's development. Each choice leads to different types of positions.
notes.plans: Against …Nf6, white plays e5, and after …d5, the main line is Bb5 Ne4 Nxd4 Bd7, leading to complex play. Against …Bc5, white plays c3, and if …dxc3, then Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qd5+ recovers the pawn with a lasting attack.

notes.explains: Black's move …Bc5 is a natural developing move, but white can respond with c3, threatening to trap the bishop or win a pawn. Black should be careful not to fall into traps.
notes.teaches: In open positions, undefended pieces are vulnerable. Always check if your opponent's pieces are hanging before committing to a plan.
notes.plans: White can play c3, and if …dxc3, then Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qd5+ recovers the pawn with a strong attack. Black's best is to avoid this by playing 10...0-0 or …Qe7.

notes.explains: After …g5, white's bishop retreats to g3. Black then captures on g3 and later on e5, winning a pawn. However, white has compensation in the form of a lead in development and attacking chances.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, material is often not the only factor. White's active pieces and black's weakened kingside can offset a pawn deficit.
notes.plans: White should continue developing and look for tactical opportunities, such as Nf3-g5 or f2-f4 to open lines.

notes.explains: White plays f4, opening lines against black's king. Black's queen is forced to capture, and white gains a tempo.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development, opening the position often favors the attacker. Pawn breaks like f4 can create immediate threats.
notes.plans: White will continue to attack with pieces, aiming to exploit black's exposed king.

notes.explains: After exchanges, the game simplifies to a rook endgame where white's active king and passed pawns decide. Black's rook is passive.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, king activity and pawn structure are crucial. An active king can support passed pawns and create mating threats.
notes.plans: White will advance the a-pawn, using the king to support it, while black's rook is tied down.

notes.explains: Black promotes to a queen, but white's queen and king coordinate to deliver checkmate. The final position shows a classic ladder mate.
notes.teaches: Even when behind in material, if the opponent's king is exposed, a mating attack can succeed. Always look for checkmate patterns.
notes.plans: White uses checks to drive the black king to the edge and then delivers mate with queen and king.

notes.explains: After Bb5+, Black's most principled and challenging response is …Nbd7, aiming to eventually grab the bishop pair with a6. Other moves like …Nc6 or …Bd7 are playable but less ambitious.
notes.teaches: When facing an early bishop check, developing the knight to d7 prepares to force the bishop to commit while keeping flexible options.
notes.plans: Black will develop kingside, then play a6 to attack the bishop, often gaining the bishop pair.

notes.explains: Nc3 is not the most testing; White's main moves are d4 or 4.0-0. Black can now develop naturally without rushing a6.
notes.teaches: Don't hurry to force the bishop away; develop first and let White show their intentions. Sometimes White will retreat the bishop themselves, saving you a tempo.
notes.plans: Develop kingside with e6 and Be7, or g6 and Bg7, then castle.

notes.explains: e5 leads to a series of trades. After exchanges, Black's pawn on c5 gives better central control than White's d3 pawn, clamping d4.
notes.teaches: In symmetrical pawn structures, the side with the more advanced pawn (c5 vs d3) gains a long-term positional clamp on the center.
notes.plans: After trades, Black will have a slight but enduring advantage due to control of d4.

notes.explains: Black castles, threatening …Nxe5. White must deal with the threat, and Black can recapture with either bishop or knight. Taking with the knight (Nxd7 Nxd7) is a creative but slightly inferior option; it keeps the bishop on b5 as a potential target.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider long-term factors like bishop vs knight imbalances. Keeping the bishop can create a good bishop vs bad knight scenario later.
notes.plans: After Nxd7 Nxd7, Black's knight is centralized, and the bishop on b5 remains a target.

notes.explains: Ne4 is a mistake. Black's bishop on b5 is confined; playing a6 would force White to either take on d7 or retreat, allowing b5 and c4 to attack it. Black should first move the knight from d7 to remove White's escape route (Bxd7).
notes.teaches: When a piece is confined, create threats to trap it. Removing the opponent's defensive resources (like the knight covering d7) can make the trap decisive.
notes.plans: Play …Nb6 (or …Ne5) to prepare a6, threatening to win the bishop.

notes.explains: Qg4 is panicky but not an immediate blunder because …f5 can be met by Qg5. Black should instead play …c4!, opening the b4-square for a queen check that forks king and bishop.
notes.teaches: When a tactical idea almost works but fails to a specific defense, look to the other side of the board to create a distraction or open a line that makes the idea work.
notes.plans: Play …c4, threatening …Qb4+ forking king and bishop. If dxc4, then …Qb4+ wins the bishop.

notes.explains: After …Qxb2, Black forks the knight and rook. White's best is Kd2, but Black is up a pawn with a safer king and can continue pressuring the bishop on b5.
notes.teaches: Converting a material advantage requires patience and avoiding counterplay. Keep the king safe and simplify if possible.
notes.plans: Black should consolidate, target the bishop on b5, and advance the queenside pawns.

notes.explains: After Bb5+, the main line is d4 cxd4 Qxd4 (instead of Nxd4). White recaptures with the queen because Nxd4 allows …a6 with tempo, and White's bishop on b5 becomes misplaced.
notes.teaches: In the Moscow Variation, White often recaptures on d4 with the queen to avoid losing time to ...a6. Black should then play …a6 immediately to force the bishop to declare its intentions.
notes.plans: After …a6, White usually plays Bxd7+ Bxd7, leading to a unique structure where Black has the bishop pair and White has central control.

notes.explains: In the line d4 cxd4 Qxd4 a6 Bxd7+ Bxd7, the old main line is c4, aiming for a Maroczy bind. Black must act decisively with …Nf6, then fianchetto the bishop with g6 and Bg7, targeting the queen on d4.
notes.teaches: Against the Maroczy bind, Black should challenge White's center immediately with active piece play, not passive defense. The fianchettoed bishop puts pressure on d4.
notes.plans: Develop with Nf6, g6, Bg7, Rc8, and prepare ...b5 to break White's queenside clamp.

notes.explains: In the line with c4 Nf6 Nc3, Black can play …g6 9.0-0 Bg7. White often drops the queen back to d3. Black's plan includes Rc8, and a key tactical resource is ...Nxc4 if White plays b3, because after Qxc4 Nxc3 wins a pawn, or after Nxc4 Black wins the exchange.
notes.teaches: Always be alert for tactical shots when the opponent weakens the queenside. The move ...Nxc4 exploits the pin on the c3-knight.
notes.plans: Play Rc8, then if b3, consider ...Nxc4. Otherwise, prepare ...b5 to open lines.

notes.explains: If White plays Bg5 instead of Nc3, Black should not play …g6 because Bxf6 forces a weak pawn structure. Instead, play …e6, and if Bxf6 Qxf6, Black gets a Rauzer-style pawn structure (doubled f-pawns) which is solid and gives the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: Don't fear doubled pawns if they come with the bishop pair and a solid structure. In the endgame, the bishops can dominate knights if the position opens.
notes.plans: After Bxf6 Qxf6, Black has a solid position with two bishops. Plan ...Be7, ...0-0, and ...b5 to open the position.

notes.explains: If White avoids the Maroczy bind and plays Nc3, Black should play …e5, chasing the queen from d4. This is not anti-positional because White cannot easily control d5. After Qd3, Black must avoid …Nf6? due to Bg5, exchanging knights and planting a knight on d5 (the Smyslov-Radzhabov maneuver). Instead, play …Rc8 first.
notes.teaches: In positions with a central pawn on e5, the d5-square becomes a critical outpost. Keep a knight to contest it; don't allow White to trade it off.
notes.plans: Play …Rc8, then if Nd5, Black can play …Nf6 because now ...Bb5 is possible, controlling c4 and preventing White's knight from settling on d5.

notes.explains: In the line with Nc3 e5 Qd3, Black's correct plan is …Rc8, preparing ...Bb5 to control c4. If White plays Nd5, Black can play …Nf6, and if Bg5, then …Bb5! (not …Qa5+? immediately because b4! pushes the queen away). After Qd2 Qa5+ Kd1, Black has good play.
notes.teaches: Understanding the concrete purpose of each move is key. Rc8 is not just a developing move; it enables ...Bb5 without fear of c2-c4.
notes.plans: Play ...Bb5, then ...Qa5+ to create threats against White's uncastled king.

notes.explains: If White castles kingside early (4.0-0 instead of d4), Black should immediately play …a6, not …Nf6. The reason: after …Nf6 Re1, if Black plays …a6, White can retreat the bishop to f1 and then play c3 and d4, gaining a strong center. By playing …a6 first, Black prevents the bishop from going to f1.
notes.teaches: In opening preparation, small move orders matter. Playing a6 early can deny White a useful retreat square for the bishop.
notes.plans: After …a6, if Ba4, then …b5 Bb3 c4, winning a tempo. If Bxd7+, Black recaptures with the bishop and has the bishop pair.

notes.explains: After 4.0-0 a6, White's modern main line is Bd3, a slightly awkward move. Black should play …Ngf6, and if Re1, then …e6 Bf1 b5, preparing to fianchetto the bishop. Black beats White to the punch: if White tries c3, Black can play Bb7, hitting the e4 pawn.
notes.teaches: When White wastes a tempo with Bd3 and Bf1, Black can use that time to expand on the queenside and complete development.
notes.plans: Play ...b5, ...Bb7, and ...0-0, with a comfortable position.

notes.explains: In the Glek System (e4 c5 Nf3 d6 Bb5+), Black's passive setup with …Bd7 or …Nc6? is less challenging. The main lines are …Nc6 (the Rossolimo) or …Nbd7 (the Moscow). The Glek System is a flexible setup for White.
notes.teaches: The Glek System aims for a slow, positional game. White should avoid pushing d4 prematurely if it allows Black to pin with ...Bg4.
notes.plans: White develops with 0-0, Re1, and prepares d4 or d3 depending on Black's setup.

notes.explains: In the Glek, if Black plays ...Be6, White should not immediately push d4 because of ...Bg4, which attacks the d4 pawn. Instead, play h3 first to prevent ...Bg4, then d4 becomes strong.
notes.teaches: Prevent counterplay before committing to a central push. A simple prophylactic move like h3 can make d4 much more effective.
notes.plans: Play h3, then d4, forcing trades that leave White with a pleasant space advantage.

notes.explains: In a typical Glek position, Black's bishop on e6 can become a target. White can play f4, threatening f5 to trap the bishop. This gains space and creates a powerful threat.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's piece has no retreat squares, use pawn advances to trap it or force concessions.
notes.plans: Play f4, then f5, winning the bishop or forcing a favorable exchange.

notes.explains: After winning material, Black may try counterplay with ...Ng4+ checks. White should avoid unnecessary risks; simply capture the bishop and keep the king safe. The extra material will decide.
notes.teaches: In converting a material advantage, avoid complications. Simplify by trading pieces and keeping the king secure.
notes.plans: Trade queens, activate rooks, and penetrate the seventh rank.

notes.explains: White plays C4, and Black chooses the King's Indian setup. White's D3 instead of D4 is a downgrade because it cedes control of the d4 square.
notes.teaches: In the English Opening, if White plays D3 instead of D4, Black should consider playing C5 (Sicilian-style) rather than E5, fighting for the d4 square.
notes.plans: Black will aim to occupy d4 with a knight and develop naturally, while White struggles to find active play.

notes.explains: White plays the Steinitz Gambit (e4 e6 Nf3 d5 e5 c5 b4? is not played; instead, the gambit is e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bd3). White sacrifices a pawn for quick development and control of e5.
notes.teaches: In the Steinitz Gambit, the pawn on e5 is crucial; White must overprotect it and use the lead in development to create pressure.
notes.plans: White will play Re1, Nbd2, Nb3, and aim to recapture the pawn on d4 while maintaining the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Nxd4, and White recaptures with the knight. White has a strong knight on d4 and space advantage.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a centralized knight can be a monster. White should aim to keep the center closed and improve piece placement.
notes.plans: White will play c3 to support the knight, then h3 to prevent back-rank issues, and later expand on the queenside with b4.

notes.explains: White plays Bg5 to trade off Black's bad bishop, then a4 to open the queenside. Black's bishop is bad and White has a good knight.
notes.teaches: When you have a good knight vs. a bad bishop, you should aim to open lines on the side where your knight is strong and the bishop is weak.
notes.plans: White will play a4, then a5, and eventually break through on the queenside with b5.

notes.explains: White blunders with Re1, allowing ...Qc7 forking the e5 pawn and the rook. Black missed the fork, but White's position becomes messy.
notes.teaches: Always check for undefended pawns and tactical threats before making a move. One careless move can undo a whole game's worth of positional play.
notes.plans: White will try to survive the complications and use the time advantage to win.

notes.explains: Bf4 is a strong developing move that reinforces the e5 pawn and vacates the d1 square for the king. It avoids the awkward Kc2 which would allow Bf5+.
notes.teaches: Develop with a purpose: Bf4 checks multiple boxes (development, pawn defense, king safety). Avoid moving the king into check.
notes.plans: White will continue with Nbd2, aiming to complete development and keep the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Black's f6 helps white solidify the pawn advantage. Simple exf6 is fine; no need for fancy moves like Nbd2. White is up a pawn and should prioritize development.
notes.teaches: When ahead material, simplify and develop. Avoid unnecessary complications; simple chess is often best.
notes.plans: White will play Nbd2, connecting knights and preparing to develop the bishop. The king is safe on c1.

notes.explains: Nbd2 connects the knights and prepares to develop the bishop. Ng5 would allow Rd1+ and unnecessary calculation. Simple development is better.
notes.teaches: Prioritize development over tactical tricks. Connecting rooks and completing development is more important than speculative attacks.
notes.plans: White will develop the bishop to a good square, possibly Bb5 to pressure the knight on c6 and create pawn structure weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black offers a trade of bishops. White should accept; black has no attack and trading simplifies the position favorably. The pawn structure becomes more important as pieces are traded.
notes.teaches: In endgames, pawn structure becomes increasingly significant. Trade pieces when it simplifies to a favorable endgame, even if it helps opponent's development slightly.
notes.plans: White will develop the remaining bishop, likely to b5, and aim to create weaknesses in black's pawn structure.

notes.explains: Bb5 creates a positional threat of Bxc6, ruining black's pawn structure. H3 would be a mistake as it allows Bxf3 and Ne4.
notes.teaches: Use bishops to target weak pawn structures. Avoid unnecessary pawn moves that create weaknesses; develop first.
notes.plans: White will follow up with Nc4, targeting the d6 queen and preparing to double rooks on the d-file.

notes.explains: After Bxc6 bxc6, Nce5 forks the rook on e6 and threatens Nxf7. Black's rook has no safe square; if Rd6, Nxf7 wins. This sequence is crushing.
notes.teaches: When ahead, look for forcing sequences that win material. Calculate the most forcing continuation first (captures, checks, threats).
notes.plans: White will win the exchange and then simplify to a winning endgame.

notes.explains: White plays h5, winning the bishop. Black cannot save it because ...Bxh5 allows Rxh5, and ...f6 allows exf6. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: When you have a clear winning plan, execute it without hesitation. Don't look for fancy alternatives when a simple pawn push wins material.
notes.plans: After winning the bishop, White is up a piece and can simplify or continue the attack. The win is straightforward.

notes.explains: After Nxd6+, white is up the exchange. Now the priority is to connect rooks and activate them. Defending the f-pawn is less important than piece activity.
notes.teaches: In endgames, activate your rooks. Don't waste time defending weak pawns; counterattack instead.
notes.plans: White will play Kc2 to connect rooks, then bring rooks to active files, targeting black's weak pawns.

notes.explains: Kc2 connects the rooks. Black's rook on h8 is passive. White's rooks will dominate.
notes.teaches: Connecting rooks is a top priority in the endgame. It allows them to cooperate and control files.
notes.plans: White will bring rooks to active files (e1, g3) and target black's weak pawns on the queenside.

notes.explains: White activates both rooks: Rg3 defends the f-pawn while Re1 restricts the black knight and prepares to attack queenside pawns.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, active rooks are key. Defend pawns only when convenient; otherwise, counterattack.
notes.plans: White will target black's weak a-pawn and c-pawn, then push the passed pawn.

notes.explains: Ra4 attacks the a-pawn. Black's king is overextended and cannot defend all weaknesses. White wins a pawn.
notes.teaches: Identify and attack weak pawns. In rook endgames, the side with more active rooks can often win material.
notes.plans: White will win the a-pawn, then push the passed h-pawn or create another passer.

notes.explains: White wins the h7 pawn. The game is effectively over; white has a decisive material advantage.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, continue to improve your position and pick off weak pawns. Don't rush, but don't delay unnecessarily.
notes.plans: White will push the h-pawn and create a passed pawn, forcing black to give up more material.

notes.explains: Na4 attacks the bishop on c5. Black cannot avoid losing the dark-squared bishop, which is positionally devastating in the French. Black's king safety and dark squares become critical weaknesses.
notes.teaches: In the French, the dark-squared bishop is black's most important piece. Forcing its exchange leaves black with a 'bad' bishop and weak dark squares.
notes.plans: White will capture the bishop, then use the dark-square weaknesses to launch an attack, often with Qg4 and Bf4.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the queen for rook and bishop to avoid losing the bishop. White emerges with a decisive material and positional advantage. Black's knight on d8 is passive.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the opponent will sacrifice to avoid a worse fate. Accept the material and use your advantage to consolidate and attack.
notes.plans: White will develop with c3, then play Qg4 to pressure g7 and prevent black from castling. The plan is to open lines and attack the stranded black king.

notes.explains: Nd4 is a strong prophylactic move. It threatens Nxc6 and prepares Qg4. The threat is stronger than the execution; it forces black to deal with multiple ideas.
notes.teaches: Place pieces on active squares that create multiple threats. Let the opponent waste moves dealing with them.
notes.plans: White will follow up with Qg4, targeting g7 and preventing black from castling. Later, Bf4 or Be3 can create discovered attacks.

notes.explains: Qg4 attacks g7 and prevents black from castling. Black's king is stuck in the center. White should not rush to take on g7; instead, maintain pressure.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, keep the queens on and attack. Avoid premature captures that allow the opponent to trade queens.
notes.plans: White will continue with Bf4 or Be3, then play a4-b3-Ba3 to target the dark squares and open lines.

notes.explains: Bf4 develops with tempo and prevents black from castling. Black's queen on f8 is passive. White's pieces dominate.
notes.teaches: Develop with tempo whenever possible. Keep the opponent's king in the center and restrict their piece activity.
notes.plans: White will play a4, b3, and Ba3 to target the dark squares and open the a-file. The rook will join the attack via c1.

notes.explains: Ba3 is a classic plan in the French: it targets the dark squares and prevents black from castling. Black's king is stuck in the center and vulnerable.
notes.teaches: In positions with a space advantage, use pawn moves (a4, b3) to prepare a bishop on a3, controlling key diagonals and preventing castling.
notes.plans: White will double rooks on the c-file and infiltrate with queen and rooks, targeting the weak dark squares around black's king.

notes.explains: White's pieces dominate. Black is completely tied up. Bd6 is a nice prophylactic move, preventing any counterplay and preparing the final breakthrough.
notes.teaches: When you have a dominating position, don't rush. Improve your pieces to their maximum potential and wait for the opponent to run out of moves.
notes.plans: White will play h4 to create more weaknesses, then break through with Rxd7 or similar.

notes.explains: Rxd7 is a decisive breakthrough. Black's position collapses. White wins material or checkmates.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is completely tied up, a sacrifice to open lines can be decisive. Look for ways to break through.
notes.plans: White will win the queen or deliver checkmate after Rxc7.

notes.explains: Rxc7 wins material. Black's king is exposed and white has a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, choose the fastest way to win. Here, checkmate is imminent.
notes.plans: White will deliver checkmate or win the queen.

notes.explains: After cxd4, white should not recapture with the knight. Instead, castle kingside and overprotect the e5 pawn. White aims to cramp black's development.
notes.teaches: In the Nimzowitsch French, white often sacrifices the d4 pawn for a positional bind. The e5 pawn restricts black's pieces.
notes.plans: White will play Re1, Nbd2, and slowly build pressure, exploiting black's lack of space.

notes.explains: If black plays Nxe5 after Qg4, white's best response is Qg4 (not Qf3 or Qh5). Qg4 threatens g7 and prevents castling. After Bxa4, Qa3 is a beautiful move that traps the queen.
notes.teaches: In tactical sequences, look for queen moves that create multiple threats. Qa3 is a typical idea to trap the queen on a1.
notes.plans: White will win material or deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: White's Nf3 is unusual and aims for d4 followed by Qa4+ to pick up the c4 pawn, but it loses time.
notes.teaches: When the opponent wastes tempi with early queen sorties, punish by developing and attacking the queen.
notes.plans: Take the pawn on c4 and develop naturally, e.g., Nf6 attacking the queen.

notes.explains: After Qxc4, White may try Ne5, but Black can simply play Bd7, defending the pawn and developing.
notes.teaches: Don't fear tactical threats; simple developing moves often refute premature attacks.
notes.plans: Play Nf6 to attack the queen and continue development.

notes.explains: White's Bb5+ pins the knight, but Black can simply play Bd7, which is not passive here because it prepares a6 to gain time.
notes.teaches: A pin is not always dangerous; if you can break it with tempo, it becomes an opportunity.
notes.plans: Play a6, forcing the bishop to move; if Bxc6, Black recaptures with tempo.

notes.explains: After a6, White retreats to c6, and Black already has a lead in development and weak light squares on White's queenside.
notes.teaches: When the opponent plays poorly, look for ambitious moves to prevent them from stabilizing.
notes.plans: Consider Qd3 to prevent castling and freeze the d2 pawn.

notes.explains: Qd3 prevents White from castling and fixes the d2 pawn. White's only move is Qe2, offering a queen trade.
notes.teaches: Trading queens when you have an initiative is not always bad; minor pieces and rooks can maintain pressure in the endgame.
notes.plans: After Qe2, consider taking on e2 and then playing Bb5, but watch for Ne5. Alternatively, castle first to keep the king vulnerable.

notes.explains: Black takes the queen, forcing the white king to e2. Castling is better than immediate checks to keep flexibility.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, don't rush checks; develop and let the king's vulnerability be a long-term factor.
notes.plans: Castle, then develop with moves like Bb5+ or simply complete development.

notes.explains: White plays g5, attacking the knight, but Black can play Bxg2, winning a pawn. White's initiative is illusory.
notes.teaches: When the opponent attacks, calculate carefully; often their threats are not real and you can grab material.
notes.plans: Play Bxg2, then Rg1, Bd5, and the knight on h8 is trapped.

notes.explains: Black simplifies by taking on e5 with the bishop, then plays Rd8, attacking the queen and preventing White from castling kingside. The queen is tied to the defense of the e2 knight, and White's king is stuck in the center.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify by trading pieces. Opening files (here the d-file) and forcing the opponent's king to stay in the center accelerates the win.
notes.plans: Black will play Bc5 (prophylaxis against Re1), then after Qxc2, Re1, Black plays Qxf2+ winning the rook. The game ends with a decisive material advantage.

notes.explains: White's knight on e5 is his only active piece. Black should eliminate it with Nd7, then recapture with the king to bring it to a good square.
notes.teaches: Identify the opponent's best piece and trade it off. Also, consider king activity in the endgame.
notes.plans: Play Nd7, then after Nxd7, recapture with the king (Kxd7) aiming for c6, where it defends pawns and is safe.

notes.explains: The king on c6 is ideal: it defends c5 and is on a light square, safe from dark-squared bishop and knight.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, the king becomes a fighting piece. Place it on a safe, active square that supports pawns.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to f5, then play e5 to freeze the d3 pawn. Then stack rooks on the d-file to win the pawn.

notes.explains: Bf5 attacks the d3 pawn and prevents d4. It also prepares e5 to further restrict White.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, target the opponent's weak pawns and restrict their pieces.
notes.plans: Play e5, then double rooks on the d-file. If White defends, use pawn breaks like f5 to open lines.

notes.explains: White's Rg5 attacks the bishop. Black defends with g6, then can chase the rook with h6 or f6.
notes.teaches: When under attack, defend efficiently. Don't panic; simple pawn moves can repel pieces.
notes.plans: Play h6, forcing the rook to move, then continue with f5.

notes.explains: After h6, White's rook must move. Black should avoid weakening the g6 pawn with f5 prematurely.
notes.teaches: Always check for tactical weaknesses before advancing pawns. A single sloppy move can nullify an advantage.
notes.plans: First defend g6 with g5, then play f5. This creates a strong pawn phalanx.

notes.explains: g5 defends the pawn and prepares f5. The pawn chain on the kingside is solid.
notes.teaches: Build a robust pawn structure that supports your plans and denies counterplay.
notes.plans: Play f5, then target the d3 pawn by stacking rooks on the d-file.

notes.explains: f5 is played, but not f4, which would weaken e4. The plan is to squeeze White and then break through.
notes.teaches: Avoid unnecessary pawn advances that create permanent weaknesses. f4 can wait; f5 is more useful.
notes.plans: Play b5 to prevent the knight from rerouting, then f4, Bf5, and eventually e4 to open lines.

notes.explains: f4 is played now, preparing Bf5 and g4. Black builds pressure on all sides.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is cramped, open lines on multiple fronts to exploit their lack of space.
notes.plans: Play Bf5, then consider g4, h5, or e4 to break through.

notes.explains: Bf5 eyes the d3 pawn. White cannot take because of the rook. Black also has ideas like g4 and h5.
notes.teaches: Focus on the opponent's main weakness. Here, d3 is the target; all plans revolve around it.
notes.plans: Play g4 to open the h-file, then bring the rook to g8 to exploit the open file.

notes.explains: Rg8 prepares to take on g4 with the rook, opening the file. The rook on d-file is no longer needed.
notes.teaches: When a file opens, have a rook ready to occupy it. Transfer pieces to the active sector.
notes.plans: After gxh3, play Rxg8, then use the open file to infiltrate.

notes.explains: After the exchange, Black has a rook on the open g-file and threatens Bh4+ winning the exchange.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, tactical threats like discovered checks can win material.
notes.plans: Play Bh4+ to win the exchange, then convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: If White plays Bg3 instead of taking on f6, Black can immediately play …e5, forking the bishop and knight. This wins a piece because White cannot defend both.
notes.teaches: Always look for tactical shots like forks when the opponent's pieces are undefended or poorly coordinated.
notes.plans: Black captures the knight on d4, then decides where to put the queen. The best square is c6, pressuring c2 and the knight while staying safe.

notes.explains: Black plays Bf5, preparing Ne4 to challenge White's knight on c3. This is a standard maneuver to trade off the knight and enhance the dark-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: In Benoni structures, the maneuver Bf5 followed by Ne4 is a typical way to trade knights and activate the bishop on the long diagonal.
notes.plans: If White plays e4, Black retreats the bishop to d7 and continues with queenside expansion via a6 and b5.

notes.explains: Black plays Ng4, threatening to go to e5 and trade knights, further weakening White's control over the dark squares.
notes.teaches: When you have a powerful bishop on the long diagonal, trading off knights enhances its power. Ng4-e5 is a standard route to force such a trade.
notes.plans: After the knight trade, Black will continue with b5, opening the queenside and putting pressure on White's position.

notes.explains: White plays g4, attacking the knight. Black refrains from playing g5, which would weaken the kingside. Instead, Black continues with b5, ignoring the kingside.
notes.teaches: Avoid weakening pawn moves like g5 unless necessary. Here, g5 would create weaknesses; instead, focus on your own plan (b5) and let White's kingside expansion be harmless.
notes.plans: Black plays b5, starting a queenside pawn storm. White's g4 does not threaten anything serious, so Black can ignore it.

notes.explains: Black pushes b4, gaining space on the queenside and preparing to open lines. The pawn on b4 also indirectly defends the h6 pawn by threatening Bb5 if Qxh6.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is pushed, it can clear squares for pieces. Here, b4 clears b5 for the bishop, which can then defend h6 indirectly.
notes.plans: Black continues queenside expansion, aiming to open the c-file and put pressure on White's position.

notes.explains: Black plays Qa5, preparing c4 and also creating potential threats like b3. This move supports the queenside pawn push and adds pressure.
notes.teaches: In queenside pawn storms, bringing the queen to a5 is a common way to support the advance c4 and create tactical threats.
notes.plans: Black will play c4, opening lines and targeting White's weak pawns. The queen on a5 also eyes the b3 square.

notes.explains: Black plays bxc3, recapturing with the pawn. Black avoids Bxc3, which would give up the dark-squared bishop and weaken the kingside.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, the dark-squared bishop is crucial for defense. Trading it for a rook can leave the king vulnerable, even if material is won.
notes.plans: Black keeps the bishop on g7 to protect the king, while continuing queenside play. The pawn on c3 gives Black a strong pawn chain.

notes.explains: Black plays Qa4, offering a queen trade. This is a 'weaponized queen trade' – removing the queens allows Black's c-pawn to advance and trap White's rook on a1.
notes.teaches: The queen trade can be an attacking weapon. Here, it opens the c-file and leaves White's rook trapped, turning a positional advantage into a decisive one.
notes.plans: After the queen trade, Black pushes c2, winning the rook on a1. The rest is a matter of technique.

notes.explains: Black pushes c2, trapping White's rook on a1. The pawn cannot be stopped, and White loses material.
notes.teaches: After a weaponized queen trade, the resulting pawn push can trap enemy pieces. Always look for such tactical opportunities when simplifying.
notes.plans: Black wins the rook and then converts the material advantage with simple technique.

notes.explains: Black wins the exchange and now has a material advantage. The rest of the game is about converting with simple technique.
notes.teaches: Once you have a decisive material advantage, avoid complications. Use simple, direct moves to convert, like doubling rooks on the c-file.
notes.plans: Black will double rooks on the c-file, target White's weak pawns, and eventually promote a pawn or deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: After Be2 e5 Nb3 Be7 8.0-0 0-0 Be3 Be6 Qd3 Nbd7, black has clustered all four minor pieces around the center, making it hard for white to occupy d5. Black is ready for queenside operations.
notes.teaches: Clustering pieces around a weak square can neutralize the weakness. Black's setup with Nf6, Nd7, Be6, and Be7 overprotects d5.
notes.plans: Black will play Rc8, Qc7, b5, and aim for d5 break. The queen and rook on the c-file apply pressure on the knight.

notes.explains: Black plays Qc7 and Rc8, doubling on the c-file. This applies pressure on the knight on c3, even though it is defended. The knight cannot move without dropping the c2 pawn.
notes.teaches: Pressure is an abstract concept: a piece is 'under pressure' if moving it would lose material behind it. Doubling on a file can restrict the opponent's pieces even without immediate threats.
notes.plans: Black continues with b5, expanding on the queenside and creating an outpost on c4 for the knight or bishop. The queen may also go to b7 to pressure e4.

notes.explains: Black plays Qb7, preparing d5 while also pressuring e4. This is a flexible move: even if the d5 plan fails, Qb7 is a good move on its own.
notes.teaches: When executing a plan, choose the most flexible move—one that is useful even if the plan doesn't work. This avoids wasting tempos.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with Nc5, targeting c4, and then d5 break.

notes.explains: After Nc5, black wins a pawn on e4. With a material advantage, trading queens simplifies the game and reduces counterplay.
notes.teaches: When up material, trade pieces if it can be done without concessions. Simplification reduces the opponent's attacking chances and makes the win easier.
notes.plans: Black takes on e4 with the queen, forcing a queen trade, and then wins a second piece.

notes.explains: In the Scheveningen (…e6), black's pawn on e6 obstructs the c8-bishop and creates a target for white's f4-f5 break. Black is cramped and vulnerable to kingside attacks.
notes.teaches: The Scheveningen is a 'come to papa' system—black invites white to attack. It requires precise defense and can be dangerous if black is not familiar with the typical plans.
notes.plans: White will aim for f4-f5, opening lines against the black king. Black must counter on the queenside with b5 and d5.

notes.explains: After Be2 e5 Nb3 Be7 8.0-0 0-0 Be3 Be6 Qd3 Nbd7, white plays Bg5. Black responds with Nbd7, maintaining the cluster of pieces around d5. If white takes on f6, black recaptures with the knight, keeping control.
notes.teaches: In the Najdorf, the move Nbd7 is a standard response to Bg5, reinforcing the f6-knight and keeping the center solid.
notes.plans: Black will continue with Rc8, Qc7, b5, and prepare d5.

notes.explains: White plays f4 in the Najdorf. Black can take on f4 with the bishop, then play g5 and Nc6-e5, establishing a strong knight on e5. This is a classic idea.
notes.teaches: When white plays f4 in the Najdorf, black's typical response is Bxf4, followed by g5 and Ne5. The knight on e5 is a powerful outpost, supported by the pawn on d6.
notes.plans: Black plays Bxf4, g5, and Nc6-e5, then continues with queenside play.

notes.explains: In the Italian Game, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Nf6 d3 Be7 5.0-0 0-0 h3 h6 d6 d4, white's d4 is premature because the queenside is undeveloped. The pawns become weak.
notes.teaches: Don't push central pawns without completing development. White's d4 weakens the center and allows black to win a pawn.
notes.plans: Black should develop with Bb6, then play d5 to close the center, and later exploit the weak pawns.

notes.explains: After white plays h3, the g3 square becomes weak. Black can exploit this with a knight fork on g3, attacking the queen and rook.
notes.teaches: When the opponent plays h3, always check if the g3 square is weak. A knight on g3 can fork the queen and rook, especially if the f2-pawn is pinned.
notes.plans: Black plays Ng3, forking queen and rook, winning the exchange.

notes.explains: In the Italian Game, white's rook on e1 and knight on d2 can maneuver to f1 and g3, aiming for f5. This is a typical plan to pressure the black king.
notes.teaches: In closed Italian positions, white often reroutes the knight via f1 to g3, targeting f5. Black must be aware of this plan and counter it.
notes.plans: White plays Re1, Nbd2-f1-g3, and then f4-f5. Black should prepare ...d5 or ...f5 to counter.

notes.explains: In a French Defense structure, the g3 square is weak due to a pin on the diagonal. Black can exploit it by playing ...Qg3, but must check move order: first ...hxg3 might be necessary to avoid interception.
notes.teaches: When exploiting a weak square, always check the move order. Sometimes a preparatory capture is needed to prevent the opponent from blocking the attack.
notes.plans: Black plays ...hxg3 first, then ...Qg3+ with a devastating attack.

notes.explains: After trades, Black is up two pawns. White plays Bc3 attacking the queen. Black should not waste time on unimportant decisions like where to put the knight; simple development is fine.
notes.teaches: Not all decisions are equally important. When you have a large material advantage, spend time only on critical choices; otherwise, play natural moves quickly to avoid time pressure.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Nc6, ...d5, ...Be6, developing pieces and consolidating.

notes.explains: Black has played ...d5 and ...Be6. The bishop on e6 is well-placed, defending d5 and f7, and is less vulnerable than on f5.
notes.teaches: Place bishops on squares where they serve multiple purposes (defense, control, flexibility) and are not easily attacked. A bishop on e6 is often more solid than on f5.
notes.plans: Black continues with ...Qf6, activating the queen, and later brings rooks to the center.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Qf6, activating the queen and preparing to bring rooks to the center. White plays Rb1, attacking the b7 pawn. Black can defend with ...b6, which blunts the rook but weakens the knight. The knight can later go to a5 and c4.
notes.teaches: When defending a pawn, consider both the immediate defense and long-term consequences. ...b6 is often good against Rb1 because it blocks the rook, but be aware of the weakening of the knight's defense.
notes.plans: Black plays ...b6, then ...Na5, ...c5, and ...d4 to create a passed pawn.

notes.explains: White plays Qb3, threatening the knight on c6. Many would play ...d4, but that allows Qa4 or Qb5 hitting the knight, potentially losing the d4 pawn. Instead, ...Na5 is better, hitting the queen and moving the knight to a safe square.
notes.teaches: When your opponent attacks a piece, don't automatically push a pawn. Consider moving the piece to a safe square that also creates threats. A knight on the rim can be fine if it is anchored by a pawn and has good squares to go to.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Na5, then ...c5, ...d4, creating a passed pawn and activating the rooks.

notes.explains: Black plays ...c6, kicking the queen away and creating a pawn chain that relieves the bishop on e6. This also prepares ...Bf5, which is now possible because White cannot take on d5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is annoying, kick it away with a pawn move that also improves your pawn structure. ...c6 kills two birds with one stone: it chases the queen and supports the center.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Bf5, then ...Re8, controlling the e-file and preparing to double rooks.

notes.explains: Black has won the exchange and is up material. The position is simplified. Black should prioritize controlling the e-file with the rook, not the other rook, because the rook on f8 would be passive.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify by trading pieces and controlling open files. Choose which rook to activate based on which one will be more useful.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Re8, then ...Rd8 to support the d5 pawn, and later creates luft with ...g6.

notes.explains: Bb5+ is the Rossolimo, analogous to the Ruy Lopez against the Sicilian. Black's accelerated dragon setup with g6 is consistent here.
notes.teaches: In the Rossolimo, black often fianchettoes the king's bishop to maintain typical Sicilian structures.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, aiming for a solid pawn structure and piece activity.

notes.explains: Taking on d7 with the bishop is better than taking with the knight because it opens the d-file for the queen and keeps the pawn structure flexible. White's c3 is not a threat to play d4 immediately because black can simply capture.
notes.teaches: When choosing between captures, consider which one improves your piece activity and pawn structure. Opening lines for your pieces is often more important than capturing toward the center.
notes.plans: Black will play e5 to clamp the center and develop the knight to e7.

notes.explains: e5 is a strong move that clamps down on the center, especially the d4 square. It may temporarily block the bishop, but the pawn on e5 becomes a powerful asset.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must make a piece temporarily bad to achieve a strategic goal. The pawn and the bishop can function as a unit: the bishop defends the pawn, and the pawn controls key squares.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to e7 (not f6) to avoid blundering the pawn and to keep control of d4.

notes.explains: White's d3 is a weakness because it is isolated and can be attacked. Black has two main ways to pressure it: doubling rooks on the d-file or bringing the bishop to a6.
notes.teaches: Identify weak pawns and attack them with multiple pieces. The two common methods are direct pressure (doubling rooks) and diagonal attacks (bishop to a6).
notes.plans: Play f6 to defend e5 (temporarily safe as white has no pieces to exploit it), then Qd7 and Rfd8 to double on the d-file.

notes.explains: Nf6 would blunder the e5 pawn because it no longer defends it. The knight belongs on e7, where it also supports the center.
notes.teaches: Always ensure your moves do not leave important pawns undefended. Knight to e7 is natural here because it defends e5 and does not block the bishop.
notes.plans: Continue with f6, Qd7, and Rfd8 to pressure d3.

notes.explains: f6 is played to defend e5, but it has two drawbacks: it weakens the dark-squared diagonal (making d4 easier for white) and it weakens the kingside. However, it is acceptable if white cannot exploit it immediately.
notes.teaches: Every pawn move has both benefits and costs. f6 defends e5 but creates long-term weaknesses. Be aware of the trade-offs.
notes.plans: Continue with Qd7 and Rfd8 to pressure d3.

notes.explains: White's a4 aims to push a5, which would block black's bishop on a6 and weaken the c5 pawn. Black must respond carefully.
notes.teaches: When the opponent attacks your bishop with a pawn push, consider whether you can maintain the pressure on the weak pawn. Here, b5 is necessary to keep the bishop active.
notes.plans: Play b5 to keep the bishop on a6, then continue pressuring d3.

notes.explains: b5 keeps the bishop on a6, but white can now play Nc4 to block the bishop. Black must find a way to continue the attack on d3.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is blocked, consider rerouting or using other pieces to maintain pressure. Here, black can play Qe6 to prepare b4 and prevent white's queen from checking on b3.
notes.plans: Play Qe6 to cover the b3 diagonal, then b4 to undermine white's knight on c4.

notes.explains: Qe6 defends against Qb3+ and prepares b4. This is a prophylactic move that prevents white from exploiting the b3 diagonal.
notes.teaches: Prophylaxis means anticipating your opponent's threats and neutralizing them before they become dangerous. Here, covering the b3 square is essential before playing b4.
notes.plans: Play b4 to chase the knight from c4, then double rooks on the d-file.

notes.explains: b4 attacks the knight on c4. If white captures, black recaptures with the pawn, opening lines. The battle now revolves around the d4 pawn.
notes.teaches: When you have a weak pawn to attack, use pawn breaks to undermine the opponent's defenders. Here, b4 targets the knight that defends d4.
notes.plans: Double rooks on the d-file to increase pressure on d4.

notes.explains: After b4, white captures and black recaptures. Now black's queen is active, and the d4 pawn is under pressure. White plays Be3 to defend d4.
notes.teaches: In such positions, the side with the weak pawn must defend it while the attacker piles on pressure. The queen can be a powerful attacker when placed on an open file.
notes.plans: Continue doubling rooks on the d-file, and consider playing c4 to bury white's knight on a3.

notes.explains: Be3 defends d4 and threatens to capture on c5. Black must decide how to maintain the pressure. Playing c4 would bury white's knight on a3, but it also closes the position and limits black's bishop.
notes.teaches: When you have a structural advantage (weak pawn), you can sometimes close the position to restrict the opponent's pieces. However, be careful not to limit your own pieces too much.
notes.plans: Play c4 to trap the knight on a3, then double rooks on the d-file.

notes.explains: c4 buries the knight on a3, but it also blocks black's bishop on a6. The position becomes closed, and both sides need to improve their pieces before the next phase.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, maneuvering becomes key. Improve your worst pieces and find outposts for your knights. The battle may shift from a direct attack to a slow improvement of piece placement.
notes.plans: Reroute the knight to d6, improve the bishop to a safe square, and prepare to open the position later.

notes.explains: White tries to free the knight from a3. Black should continue improving pieces: knight to d6, bishop to a safe square, and rook to d8.
notes.teaches: In maneuvering phases, every move should improve your position. Look for squares where your pieces are active and safe.
notes.plans: Play Nd6 to centralize the knight, then a6 to defend the bishop, and eventually reroute the knight to f7 to open the rook's line.

notes.explains: Nd6 centralizes the knight and eyes the e4 square. Black is improving piece by piece.
notes.teaches: Centralized knights are powerful. Look for squares like d6 that control key central points.
notes.plans: Play a6 to defend the bishop, then Nf7 to open the rook's line and prepare pressure on d4.

notes.explains: a6 defends the bishop on a6 and prevents white from capturing it. This is a useful prophylactic move.
notes.teaches: Defend your pieces to avoid tactics. A simple move like a6 can prevent future threats and solidify your position.
notes.plans: Play Nf7 to open the rook's line, then double rooks on the d-file.

notes.explains: Nf7 opens the rook's line to the d-file and also covers g5. This is a flexible move that improves coordination.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a knight retreat can be an improvement if it opens lines for other pieces. Always consider how your pieces work together.
notes.plans: Double rooks on the d-file to pressure d4.

notes.explains: Doubling rooks on the d-file increases pressure on the d4 pawn. This is a standard method to attack a weak pawn.
notes.teaches: When you have a target, concentrate your forces against it. Doubling rooks is a classic way to maximize pressure on a file.
notes.plans: After doubling, consider playing c5 to lock out white's bishop and further restrict his pieces.

notes.explains: c5 locks out white's bishop on b6, trapping it. This is a strong positional move that restricts the opponent's pieces.
notes.teaches: When you have a positional advantage, look for moves that permanently restrict the opponent's pieces. Locking out a bishop can turn it into a 'bad bishop'.
notes.plans: Continue pressuring the d4 pawn, and prepare to activate the knight via g5 or other squares.

notes.explains: Qd6 was a mistake because it allowed white to play Nf2, threatening to trade rooks. Black should have played Ng5 to prevent Nf2, as Ng5 would fork the rook and queen if white captures.
notes.teaches: Always consider your opponent's threats. Prophylactic moves like Ng5 can prevent dangerous ideas. Ask yourself what your opponent wants and stop it.
notes.plans: After the mistake, black must deal with the loss of the exchange. The resulting position is still complex with a strong pawn.

notes.explains: Nf2 threatens to trade rooks on d3. Black's rook on d3 is powerful, so black must avoid the trade. Black can sacrifice the exchange with Nxh3, leading to a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong outpost rook, you may need to sacrifice the exchange to maintain the initiative. The resulting pawn can be a powerful asset.
notes.plans: Play Nxh3, sacrificing the exchange, to create a passed pawn and attack the king.

notes.explains: Nxh3 sacrifices the exchange. If white takes the knight, black plays Qxh3, threatening checkmate on h2. This forces white to give up material or get mated.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices can be justified by a direct attack on the king. Always calculate forcing lines when you see a potential checkmate.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, black will have a strong passed pawn on the h-file and attacking chances.

notes.explains: After Qxh3, black threatens Bh2+ followed by Qg2#. White must defend carefully. Black's passed pawn on h3 becomes a key asset.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, a passed pawn can be as valuable as a piece. Use it to restrict the opponent's king and create threats.
notes.plans: Push the h-pawn to create a passer, and use the knight to support it. The queen and bishop will continue the attack.

notes.explains: Qf6 ties white's queen to the defense of the f2 pawn, preventing it from moving. Black's knight on d4 is well-placed, and the passed h-pawn is a threat.
notes.teaches: Tying down the opponent's queen to a defensive task can limit their options. Use such tactical motifs to maintain pressure.
notes.plans: Continue advancing the h-pawn and look for ways to open the position further.

notes.explains: Nd4 centralizes the knight and blocks the queen's access to a7. It also supports the h-pawn and creates threats.
notes.teaches: In complex positions, centralize your pieces to maximize their influence. A knight on d4 is powerful and can support both attack and defense.
notes.plans: Trade queens to enter an endgame where the passed h-pawn is a decisive advantage.

notes.explains: After queen trade, black is down the exchange but has a powerful passed pawn on h3. White's knight is tied down to defending the d3 pawn, making it difficult for white to make progress.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a passed pawn can compensate for a material deficit if the opponent's pieces are passive. The d3 pawn ties down white's knight, giving black time to advance the h-pawn.
notes.plans: Advance the h-pawn, bring the king to support it, and use the knight to create threats. White's time pressure may lead to mistakes.

notes.explains: White plays Nc3, a blunder. Black can now play …Nxe3 Qxe3 Nxd4, winning a pawn because the knight on d4 is undefended. White's queen on e2 is misplaced, unable to defend both e3 and d4 effectively.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a small inaccuracy, be alert for larger mistakes. Mistakes often come in pairs. Exploit misplaced pieces by targeting undefended points.
notes.plans: Capture on e3 and d4 to win material, then consolidate.

notes.explains: After …Nxd4, Black has won a pawn. White tries Qd2, but Black can play …Nxc2+ Kd1 Nxa1, winning the exchange. The knight on c2 forks the king and rook, and White cannot capture both knights.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for forcing sequences that win more material. Knight forks are a common way to convert an advantage.
notes.plans: Win the exchange with ...Nxc2+, then simplify while keeping pressure.

notes.explains: Black is up the exchange and a pawn. The game is not over; White still has active minor pieces. Black should continue accurately, avoiding complacency.
notes.teaches: Even when winning, stay precise. Do not assume the game is over; your opponent may have counterplay. Focus on the most efficient winning plan.
notes.plans: Consolidate, open files with ...d6, and activate the rook. Aim to trade pieces and simplify into a winning endgame.

notes.explains: Black plays …d6, opening the d-file and forcing a trade on e5. This is a professional move when up material: open lines to activate the rook and create threats.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, open files to increase the activity of your rooks. This often leads to a decisive attack or simplifies into a winning endgame.
notes.plans: Play ...dxe5, then ...Rae8, and eventually ...Qf6-d4 to target weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black plays …Rae8, offering a rook trade. White's rook on e5 looks active but is not threatening anything because Black's queen defends the kingside. Black can safely trade rooks or force White's rook away.
notes.teaches: Don't fear an active rook if it has no targets. Offer rook trades to simplify when you have a material advantage; the opponent's rook may be a phantom threat.
notes.plans: Trade rooks on e5, then reposition the queen to d4 and play ...h6 to chase the rook away.

notes.explains: After trading rooks, Black's queen goes to f6, heading to d4. The queen on d4 will be active and also defends g7. Black then plays ...h6 to chase White's rook from g5, gaining more space.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, activate the queen to a central square where it controls key diagonals and defends weaknesses. Use pawn moves like ...h6 to improve your position.
notes.plans: Play ...Qd4, ...h6, then ...Rg8 or ...Be4 to create mating threats or win more material.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Rg8, preparing to infiltrate. White's rook on g5 is poorly placed. Black can now play ...Be4 or ...Qd4+ with decisive threats.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for the most forcing continuation. Do not be afraid of scary-looking moves like ...Qxd3 if you have calculated that the resulting position is winning.
notes.plans: Play ...Qd4+ and then ...Rg8-g2 or ...Be4 to force mate or win the queen.

notes.explains: White is down a piece after a blunder on move 5, but has two pawns for the knight and a central pawn mass. Black's queen f6 is premature, allowing White to gain time with Nd5 and later f4.
notes.teaches: When down material, prioritize completing development and creating counterplay. Moves that improve your position while setting traps are ideal.
notes.plans: White aims to open the f-file with f4, then push the center with c3 and d4, leveraging the pawn mass.

notes.explains: The Four Pawns Attack (f4) aims for central domination at the cost of development. Black's c5 gives up the d5 outpost, so White avoids Nf3 early due to Bg4, instead playing Be3 and Nc3. Later, after developing, Nf3 is safe, and White sacrifices a pawn on c4 for a lead in development and the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings like the Four Pawns Attack, prioritize central control but compensate for lagging development by avoiding early piece exchanges that create weaknesses. Sacrificing a pawn for rapid development and two bishops can provide lasting compensation.
notes.plans: White aims to complete development, then launch a queenside attack with b4-b5, targeting Black's knight on c6 and opening lines against Black's castled king.

notes.explains: After Qe4, White missed the winning move Ng5. Black's queen is overloaded defending the bishop on f5 and the pawn on e5. Ng5 threatens Nxf7 and Qxe5, and after g3, Black's queen has no safe square, leading to material gain.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is active but short on squares, look for tactical blows like knight forks or discovered attacks that exploit the queen's lack of retreats. Calculate forcing sequences fully before dismissing them.
notes.plans: White should have played Ng5, forcing Black's queen to move, then captured on e5 or f7 with a winning attack.

notes.explains: In the rook endgame, White's active rook on the seventh rank and passed b-pawn create winning chances. Black's blunder (g4 allowing Nxg4) resulted from White's consistent pressure, not just luck.
notes.teaches: In endgames, maintain pressure by improving piece activity and targeting weaknesses. Opponents often blunder when they misinterpret your intentions or feel the cumulative weight of your threats.
notes.plans: White should activate the king, double rooks on the seventh, and push the passed pawn. Avoid unnecessary pawn weaknesses and keep the king safe from counterplay.

notes.explains: After the sequence e5 h6 Bxf6 hxg5 fxg7 Rg8, White plays Qh5. This threatens Qh8+ forking the rook and king if Black captures on g7. Black can defend with Qf6, but White has opened lines and created weaknesses on the kingside.
notes.teaches: When down material, look for forcing sequences that create threats. A single queen can be dangerous if the opponent's king is exposed, but you need to bring more pieces into the attack.
notes.plans: After Qh5, if Black plays Qf6, White should continue with h4 to open the h-file and activate the rook. The goal is to build up pressure before Black consolidates.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the h-pawn to open the h-file. After Rxh4, the rook is active and can later lift to f4 or g4. Black's queen on f6 is well-placed, but White's rook and queen create potential threats.
notes.teaches: When you are behind in material, every tempo must count. Opening lines to involve your rooks is often more important than preserving pawns. Force your opponent to make decisions under pressure.
notes.plans: White plans to bring the rook to g4 or f4, and eventually develop the knight to f3. The immediate threat is to increase pressure on the kingside, possibly with ideas like Qg5 or Rg4.

notes.explains: White castles queenside after Black captures on g2. Now the rook on d1 is active, and White threatens ideas like Rg1 skewering the queen. Black's queen is exposed on g2, and White's pieces are coordinated.
notes.teaches: Castling into an attack can be a powerful way to activate your rook and create counterplay. Even when down material, if your opponent's queen is far from home, you can generate threats.
notes.plans: White plans to play Rg1, attacking the queen, and then follow up with moves like d5 or Ne5 to open the center. The king on c1 is relatively safe, and White's rooks can double on the g-file.

notes.explains: Black trades queens with Qg5+, leading to an endgame where White is still a pawn down but has an active knight on e5 and an open h-file. The material deficit is reduced, and White has compensation in piece activity.
notes.teaches: When you are down material, trading queens can sometimes be beneficial if your remaining pieces become more active. In the endgame, activity and king safety can outweigh a pawn deficit.
notes.plans: White plans to use the knight on e5 to target weak squares like d6 or f7, and the rook on h4 to create threats on the h-file. The king on b1 is safe, and White can try to generate tactical ideas.

notes.explains: White plays Rd3, defending the pawn on c3 while preparing to lift the rook to g3. This is a multi-purpose move: it defends, activates the rook, and sets up potential threats on the g-file.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, every move should have multiple purposes. Defending a pawn while simultaneously improving your piece's activity is a hallmark of good endgame play.
notes.plans: White plans to play Rg3, doubling rooks on the g-file, and then use the knight to target f7 or d6. Black's king is still in the center, and White aims to create mating threats.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the exchange with Rxd7, winning back material and creating a passed pawn on g5. The knight on f7 is powerful, and Black's king is exposed. White's rooks are active, and the passed pawn becomes a decisive factor.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, a passed pawn is a powerful asset. Even if you are down material, creating a passed pawn can turn the tables. Rooks are excellent at supporting passed pawns.
notes.plans: White plans to push the g-pawn to g6 and g7, supported by the rooks. Black's king is cut off, and White aims to promote the pawn or create a mating attack.

notes.explains: White plays f4, breaking open the position and creating a passed pawn on g6. Black's pieces are passive, and White's rooks dominate. The passed pawn is a decisive threat.
notes.teaches: When you have a passed pawn, use your pawns to create further weaknesses and open lines. The advance f4 forces Black to make difficult decisions and can lead to a decisive breakthrough.
notes.plans: White plans to push the g-pawn to g7 and then promote, or use the threat to force Black into a losing endgame. The rook on g7 cuts off the black king, and White's king can join the attack.

notes.explains: Black blunders with Nf6, allowing White to win the knight with Rxf6. The passed pawn on g6 is now unstoppable, and White's rooks are active. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is under pressure, they are likely to make mistakes. Keep the tension and force them to find accurate moves. Patience and maintaining threats often lead to blunders.
notes.plans: White will capture the knight and then push the g-pawn to promotion. The rooks can also create mating threats if Black's king becomes exposed.

notes.explains: White promotes the pawn and wins easily. The rook endgame is trivial; White's king is safe, and Black's pawns are weak.
notes.teaches: Once you have a decisive advantage, simplify to a winning endgame. Converting a material advantage requires technique, but the hardest part is creating the advantage.
notes.plans: White will capture all of Black's queenside pawns and then promote another pawn or force resignation.

notes.explains: White plays Ne2 instead of Nf3 to avoid blocking the bishop on g2.
notes.teaches: When you fianchetto a bishop, avoid placing your own pieces on its diagonal unless necessary.
notes.plans: White will continue with d3, castle, and then push b4-b5.

notes.explains: Black pins the knight with Bg4. White can play h3 to create the possibility of g4 later, unpinning the knight.
notes.teaches: Playing h3 early in such positions is a useful prophylactic move that gives you the option to kick the bishop with g4 if needed.
notes.plans: White will continue with d3, castle, and then prepare b4-b5.

notes.explains: White plays d3, a modest center control that fits the setup. The bishop on g2 now has a clear diagonal.
notes.teaches: In this system, d3 is preferable to d4 because it keeps the center flexible and supports the queenside expansion.
notes.plans: White will castle kingside and then push b4-b5.

notes.explains: White castles kingside. Black's king is still in the center, making queenside expansion even more dangerous.
notes.teaches: Castling into a pawn storm is risky. Here Black's king on e8 is exposed to White's coming b4-b5 attack.
notes.plans: White will now play b4 immediately or prepare it with a3.

notes.explains: Black pins the knight with Bb4. White can now play b4 immediately, sacrificing a pawn to open lines.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a pawn for an attack is often worth it in the middlegame, especially when the opponent's king is exposed. Don't overcalculate; trust the dynamic potential.
notes.plans: White plays b4, and if Black takes, White recaptures with the rook, opening the b-file.

notes.explains: Black takes the pawn, but White recaptures with the rook, opening the b-file and gaining a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When sacrificing a pawn, ensure you get concrete compensation like open files or attacking chances.
notes.plans: White will continue with b5, pushing the pawn further to create weaknesses in Black's queenside.

notes.explains: White pushes b5, and Black blocks with c5. White now has a passed pawn and can continue pushing with a4-a5.
notes.teaches: In a pawn storm, pushing pawns to create weaknesses and open lines is more important than material.
notes.plans: White will play a4, a5, and then consider taking on b6 or developing the bishop to f4.

notes.explains: White pushes a5, creating a hook on b6 and further weakening Black's queenside pawns.
notes.teaches: When attacking, create as many weaknesses as possible in the opponent's pawn structure to make it easier for your pieces to penetrate.
notes.plans: White will develop the bishop to f4, then consider taking on b6 or d6.

notes.explains: White develops the bishop to f4, connecting the rooks and preparing to take on b6 or d6.
notes.teaches: Before capturing, develop your pieces to maximize their activity. Connecting rooks is often a key preparatory step.
notes.plans: White will capture on b6 or d6, depending on Black's response.

notes.explains: Black plays Bd6, offering a trade of bishops. White must choose the correct order of captures.
notes.teaches: When multiple captures are possible, consider the order carefully. Taking on d6 first is better because if White takes on b6 first, Black can recapture with the knight and keep the a7 pawn defended.
notes.plans: White will take on d6 first, then on b6.

notes.explains: White captures on d6 and then on b6, leaving Black with a weak a7 pawn and an exposed king.
notes.teaches: Correct move order can leave the opponent with structural weaknesses and no good way to defend.
notes.plans: White will play Ra6, pinning the knight and threatening to win material or deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: White plays Ra6, pinning the knight on b6 and threatening Nc3-a4, winning material. This is stronger than immediately playing Qa1.
notes.teaches: In attacks, use your rooks as the main attackers and keep the queen as a supporting piece. The queen should enter later, when the attack is ready to deliver the final blow.
notes.plans: White will follow up with Qa1, doubling on the a-file and increasing pressure.

notes.explains: White plays Qa1, doubling on the a-file and threatening to take on a7. The queen supports the rook from behind.
notes.teaches: The queen should be the last piece to join the attack, used to deliver the final blow rather than leading the charge.
notes.plans: White will continue with Nc3, threatening Nxd5, and eventually break through on the queenside.

notes.explains: White plays Nc3, threatening Nxd5 and exploiting the pin on the knight on b6. Black cannot defend all threats.
notes.teaches: When attacking, look for ways to bring all your pieces into the attack. The knight on c3 adds pressure and creates new threats.
notes.plans: White will capture on d5, winning material, and then continue the attack.

notes.explains: White captures on d5, winning a pawn and maintaining the attack. The pawn on g7 is less important than the central pawn.
notes.teaches: When attacking, prioritize capturing central pawns over flank pawns if they are equally available. Central pawns are more valuable and often lead to further gains.
notes.plans: White will continue to press the attack, eventually forcing checkmate or winning more material.
