notes.explains: White captures on b6, opening the a-file and allowing the rook to deliver check on a8.
notes.teaches: When the attack is overwhelming, the simplest continuation is often the best. Don't look for heroics; just take material and force checkmate.
notes.plans: White will play Ra8+ and then Qa7, winning the rook and the game.

notes.explains: White delivers check on a8 and then Qa7+, winning the rook. The queen finally enters the attack to deliver the final blow.
notes.teaches: The queen should be used as the 'supporting actress' until the decisive moment, then it can take over to finish the game.
notes.plans: White will capture the rook and win easily.

notes.explains: Black's knight maneuvers to g6 via d7 and f8, reminiscent of the Lopez style, preparing a kingside pawn storm with h5-h4.
notes.teaches: When attacking on the kingside, reroute the knight to g6 to support the pawn storm and potential sacrifices.
notes.plans: Push h5 and h4 to open lines against White's king.

notes.explains: Black closes the center with e4 in response to d4, ensuring the kingside attack is not disturbed.
notes.teaches: When attacking on one wing, close the center to prevent counterplay and keep the attack focused.
notes.plans: Continue with h5, h4, and prepare to open the h-file.

notes.explains: Black pushes h5 immediately, ignoring development of the c8 bishop. The bishop is fine on c8 for now.
notes.teaches: In a direct attack, don't develop pieces just for the sake of it; prioritize the attack over routine development.
notes.plans: Follow with h4 to threaten checkmate.

notes.explains: Black recaptures on d5 and continues the pawn storm. White's c4 does nothing as d5 is well defended.
notes.teaches: Don't be distracted by irrelevant pawn moves; keep pushing the attack when the opponent's moves lack effect.
notes.plans: Prepare to open the h-file with hxg3 or sacrifice on g4.

notes.explains: Black considers hxg3 but notes that fxg3 opens the f-file for White's rook. Black decides to delay the capture and first play a prophylactic move.
notes.teaches: When opening a file, consider if it benefits the opponent. Sometimes it's better to prepare first with a defensive move.
notes.plans: Play Bb6 to defend d5, then later hxg3 followed by Ng4.

notes.explains: Black plays Bb6 to defend the d5 pawn, enabling Ng4 later without losing the center.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves that defend key pawns can make the attack smoother and prevent counterplay.
notes.plans: After Bb6, play hxg3 and Ng4, exploiting the overloaded bishop on c1.

notes.explains: Black plays hxg3 and Ng4, attacking f2 and threatening Nxh2. The bishop on c1 is overloaded, defending both d5 and the knight on g4.
notes.teaches: Look for overloaded pieces; moving a piece with tempo can create multiple threats.
notes.plans: If Nxh2, the rook moves and Black wins the knight. If White defends, Black continues the attack.

notes.explains: Black wins the exchange with Nxh2 and Nxf1, converting the attack into material advantage.
notes.teaches: When the attack yields material, convert by simplifying while maintaining pressure.
notes.plans: Consolidate and use the extra exchange to win the endgame.

notes.explains: Black plays f5 to defend the e4 pawn, then retreats the bishop to f7 after d5, giving up a pawn to keep the e4 pawn strong.
notes.teaches: In a material advantage, prioritize keeping strong central pawns; sometimes giving back a pawn is acceptable to maintain structure.
notes.plans: Defend e4 and use the bishop pair to attack the weakened king.

notes.explains: White blunders with Bh6, allowing Qb6+ forcing the king to h1, then Rh8 pins and wins the bishop.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed on g1, look for checks on the long diagonal and pins on the h-file.
notes.plans: After winning the bishop, convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: Black is up an exchange and a pawn. The plan is to double rooks on the h-file and target the vulnerable knight on h2.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, activate the king and double rooks on the open file to maximize pressure.
notes.plans: Move the king to e7, then bring the rook to h8, threatening mate or further material gain.

notes.explains: Black centralizes the king to e7 and brings the rook to h8, preparing to double and threaten mate.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, centralizing the king is often safer and more active than hiding it.
notes.plans: Double rooks on the h-file and target the knight on h2.

notes.explains: Black delivers checkmate by sacrificing the rook on h2, then bringing the other rook to h8, and after Bh3 blocks, Qf2#.
notes.teaches: Pattern recognition: when the g2 bishop is gone, the f2 square becomes weak; look for sacrifices to expose the king.
notes.plans: Execute the forced mate sequence.

notes.explains: f4 is an aggressive move that weakens the kingside but exploits the pin on the knight. If Black takes, e5 wins the knight; if Black plays g5, White takes the knight attacking the queen.
notes.teaches: When you have a pin, look for pawn breaks to exploit it, even if they weaken your own position. The threat of winning material can outweigh the weakness.
notes.plans: After f4, if exf4, play e5 winning the knight. If g5, take the knight and follow up with Bf2 to meet Qc5+.

notes.explains: After Qc5+, Bf2 interposes with an attack on the queen, winning the e5 pawn. This is a key defensive resource that also creates a threat.
notes.teaches: Against a check, remember the three defenses: capture, move the king, or interpose. Interposing can be especially powerful if it also attacks the checking piece.
notes.plans: After Bf2, Black must move the queen, allowing White to capture the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: White recaptures with the knight rather than the pawn because taking with the pawn would open the rook and leave the e5 pawn weak. The knight recapture keeps the extra pawn and maintains a strong center.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which piece gives better control and long-term stability. A move that creates a threat is not always best if it leaves weaknesses.
notes.plans: Defend the knight with Qe2 to avoid a pin from Rd8, then continue developing and pressuring Black's position.

notes.explains: White plays Bg5 to force Black to capture, opening the f-file and weakening Black's kingside. After the exchange, White has an open file and an extra pawn.
notes.teaches: Exchanging pieces to open files and weaken the opponent's king position is a common middlegame strategy. Even simple trades can create lasting advantages.
notes.plans: Continue with Rf1, bringing the rook to the open file, and then consider Rf5 or other active moves.

notes.explains: Rf5 is a strong stabilizing move that protects the bishop and prepares to bring more pieces into the attack. It also threatens to double rooks on the f-file.
notes.teaches: In positions with an open file and weak king, centralize your pieces and prepare a slow, methodical attack. Overprotection of key points allows you to build up pressure safely.
notes.plans: Play Rd1 to overprotect the d-pawn and prepare a future advance. Then consider bringing the queen into the attack.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the exchange with Nxf7, exploiting the weak king. After Rxf7, the rook and king are on the same diagonal, allowing Bc4 to pin the rook and win material.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, look for sacrifices that open lines and create pins. A temporary material loss can lead to a decisive attack.
notes.plans: After Nxf7, follow up with Bc4, threatening to win the rook. If Black defends, continue with queen checks and bring more pieces into the attack.

notes.explains: White plays Qe2 to defend the pawn and avoid a pin from Rd8. This is a prophylactic move that also keeps the queen active.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must violate the principle of using the least valuable piece to defend, in order to prevent a tactical problem like a pin.
notes.plans: After Qe2, continue to press with Rf7 and consider advancing the kingside pawns.

notes.explains: White centralizes the queen to e5, threatening to invade and also defending the rook. This puts pressure on Black's weakened pawns.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, centralize your queen to maximize its power. It can both attack and defend effectively from the center.
notes.plans: Consider advancing the kingside pawns (h4) to create more weaknesses and open lines for the rook.

notes.explains: h4 threatens to open the h-file and create a passed pawn. If Black takes, Qg4+ picks off the rook on d7. This is a double attack exploiting the weak king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is weak, pawn advances can create threats of double attacks or checkmate. Always look for undefended pieces to combine with checks.
notes.plans: After h4, if gxh4, play Qg4+ winning the rook. Then continue to push the h-pawn and bring the rook into the attack.

notes.explains: White wins a pawn with Qg5+ and then captures the rook, leaving Black's kingside shattered.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, a material advantage combined with a weak king is often decisive. Simplify when you are clearly winning, but keep attacking if the opponent has counterplay.
notes.plans: Consolidate by defending the pawns and bringing the rook to the seventh rank.

notes.explains: White exchanges queens and wins the exchange, leaving a winning endgame with an extra pawn and a strong bishop.
notes.teaches: When up material, exchanging pieces simplifies the position and reduces the opponent's counterplay. A bishop is often better than a rook in open positions with pawns on both sides.
notes.plans: Push the passed pawns and use the bishop to support them. The king should also become active.

notes.explains: White lifts the rook to g3, preparing to deliver checkmate or win more material. The king is exposed and White's pieces coordinate well.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, activate your rook by lifting it to an open file or rank. Rook and bishop can create mating threats against a weak king.
notes.plans: Play Rg3, then Qg6+ and Rg7 to force checkmate or win the queen.

notes.explains: White wins another pawn with Rxc6, now three pawns up. The endgame is completely winning.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, continue to pick off weak pawns while keeping your pieces active. Avoid unnecessary risks.
notes.plans: Push the passed pawns and use the rook to support them. The king can also join the attack.

notes.explains: White plays Rh6 to stop Black's pawn from promoting and to prepare a mating attack. The rook is well placed to switch between defense and attack.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, a rook on the sixth rank can be very powerful, both for stopping passed pawns and for creating mating threats.
notes.plans: Bring the king up and push the f-pawn to create a passed pawn. The rook can also deliver checkmate if Black's king is exposed.

notes.explains: White exchanges rooks, leaving a winning king and pawn endgame. The extra pawns and active king decide.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, simplifying to a king and pawn endgame is often the most efficient way to win, provided you have a clear advantage.
notes.plans: Use the king to support the passed pawns and promote.

notes.explains: After ...Qb4, White plays b3 instead of Bb3. If Bb3, Black could play ...Na5 attacking the bishop, and after the bishop moves, ...Qxb2 would be annoying. b3 defends the bishop and prevents ...Qxb2.
notes.teaches: Sometimes defending a piece with a pawn is better than moving it, especially when the opponent's queen is misplaced. This kills two birds with one stone.
notes.plans: White will continue with Bxe7, Re3, and Ng3 to improve piece coordination.

notes.explains: White retreats the knight from c5 to d3, seemingly a retreat, but the goal is to reroute it to e5, a powerful central outpost. The knight on c5 had no future, so improving it is more important than keeping it forward.
notes.teaches: Retreating moves are not necessarily bad. Always look for better squares for your pieces, even if it means moving backward first. The knight on d3 threatens to go to e5.
notes.plans: White will play Ne5, then possibly Bf3 or Bd3, targeting the black king.

notes.explains: White plays Bd3, aiming the bishop at the black king. The knight on d5 is well placed, and the bishop on d3 supports a future kingside attack.
notes.teaches: In positions with a space advantage, point your pieces toward the opponent's king. The bishop on d3 is more active than on c4 because it eyes the kingside.
notes.plans: White will continue with Ne5, possibly followed by f4 or g4 to open lines.

notes.explains: Black plays ...f6, trying to kick the knight from e5, but this weakens the e6-pawn. The bishop on d8 is overloaded: it defends both e6 and c7. White can exploit this with Nxc6, winning a pawn.
notes.teaches: Be careful when pushing pawns in front of your king, especially if they weaken central pawns. An overloaded piece can be exploited by a simple capture that forces it to abandon one of its duties.
notes.plans: White will play Nxc6, winning a pawn and leaving Black's position crumbling.

notes.explains: After Nxc6 and Rxe6, the black queen is trapped. White plays g3, attacking the queen, which has no escape squares because the rook on e6 guards d6 and the knight on d5 covers other squares.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is surrounded by pieces, look for a way to trap it. Even a seemingly safe queen can run out of air if you control all its escape squares.
notes.plans: White will win the queen for two pieces, leaving a winning material advantage.

notes.explains: White is up material and now plays Ng5, threatening Ne6 and Nxg7. The king is exposed, and White's pieces are active. The endgame is winning because White's pieces coordinate well against the black king.
notes.teaches: Even in endgames, keep attacking if the opponent's king is exposed. Don't relax just because queens are off; piece activity still matters.
notes.plans: White will play Ne6, then Nxg7, winning more material, or force checkmate.

notes.explains: White plays Nge5, not capturing either hanging knight. If White captures, Black recaptures and attacks the other knight. By moving the knight to e5, White threatens to win a knight because Black cannot save both.
notes.teaches: When two enemy pieces are hanging, don't capture immediately if your opponent can save one. Instead, move your own piece to a better square, forcing your opponent to lose material.
notes.plans: White will win a knight next move, leaving a decisive material advantage.

notes.explains: White plays Bc4, pinning the knight on d5 to the king. This is a simple tactic that wins material because the knight cannot move without exposing the king.
notes.teaches: Pins are powerful in endgames. Always look for ways to restrict the opponent's pieces with simple threats.
notes.plans: White will capture the knight or force Black to give up more material.

notes.explains: White plays Rd7, threatening to capture on d5. If Black takes on d7, White recaptures with the bishop and attacks the rook on a8. This is a simple tactical sequence that wins material.
notes.teaches: In endgames, look for tactics that involve multiple threats. A rook on the seventh rank can be very powerful.
notes.plans: White will win the knight on d5 and then pick up more pawns.

notes.explains: White captures on d5 with the bishop, not the rook, because the rook on a8 is hanging. After Bxd5, Black's rook on a8 is attacked, and White wins a second piece.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which piece to use. Sometimes capturing with a less valuable piece can create additional threats.
notes.plans: White will win the rook on a8 and then convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: White plays Bxf7+ as an intermediate move, giving Black the f-file and two bishops but weakening Black's kingside. Black responds with h6 to prevent Ng5, which would threaten e6 and cause problems.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a knight that can jump to a dangerous square (like g5), a prophylactic pawn move like h6 can be worth the slight weakening of your kingside.
notes.plans: Black will develop with ...d5, ...Nc6, and ...Qd6, controlling the center and preparing ...e5.

notes.explains: Black plays Qd6, controlling e5 and preventing Bf4. If White plays Bf4, Black can capture with ...Qxf4, winning two pieces for a rook (since the knight on c3 is also attacked). This is a concrete tactical idea.
notes.teaches: In hypermodern openings, concrete tactics matter. Queen to d6 serves two purposes: it controls key squares and stops a dangerous bishop move.
notes.plans: Black will continue with ...b6, ...Bb7, and possibly ...e5 to liquidate the center weakness.

notes.explains: Black wins two pieces for a rook after Bf4, but the resulting position is good for Black because the two pieces are active and the rook is not yet coordinated. However, in the endgame, a rook can be superior to two pieces if there are many pawns.
notes.teaches: Two pieces are usually better than a rook in the middlegame, but in the endgame, a rook can be stronger because it can pick off pawns more easily. Always consider the phase of the game.
notes.plans: Black will continue developing and use the two bishops to attack White's king.

notes.explains: Black plays c5, preparing a4 to attack the knight on b3. Before playing a4, Black first plays c5 to prevent the knight from retreating to d4. This is a prophylactic move that ensures the knight has no good squares.
notes.teaches: When planning to chase an enemy piece, first take away its retreat squares. This makes the threat more effective and forces the opponent to lose material or time.
notes.plans: Black will play a4, then a3, shattering White's queenside pawns.

notes.explains: Black plays a4, then a3, forcing the knight to retreat to a1 or be captured. This opens up the queenside and creates weaknesses in White's pawn structure.
notes.teaches: Pawn advances can be used to drive away enemy pieces and create structural weaknesses. Even if the pawn is captured, the resulting open files can be used by your rooks.
notes.plans: Black will use the open a-file to invade with the rook and pick up pawns.

notes.explains: Black plays Rc8, forcing White's rook to a passive square. This simplifies the position and leaves Black up a piece.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, simplify by forcing trades that leave you with a material advantage. Don't give your opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: Black will pick up the hanging pawns on c3 and f2, then create a passed pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays g5, isolating the f5-pawn. This creates a target that Black can attack with the rook and knight.
notes.teaches: In endgames, create weaknesses in the opponent's pawn structure and then target them. Isolated pawns are easy to attack.
notes.plans: Black will win the f5-pawn and then the h-pawn, creating a passed h-pawn.

notes.explains: Black wins the h5-pawn, creating a passed h-pawn. The rook and knight coordinate to push the pawn forward.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a passed pawn is a huge asset. Use your pieces to support its advance while the opponent's pieces are tied down.
notes.plans: Black will push the h-pawn to promotion, using the rook to shield the king from checks.

notes.explains: Black promotes the h-pawn to a queen. The key was to use the rook to force the white king onto a square where a check would allow promotion. By capturing on c3 and then checking, Black forces the king to c3, then promotes with check.
notes.teaches: When promoting a pawn, look for ways to give check during the promotion to prevent the opponent from capturing the new queen. Ladder mates are a simple way to finish.
notes.plans: Black will checkmate with the queen and rook.

notes.explains: White has won a pawn and is up material, but the king is still on c1 and the kingside undeveloped. Black threatens Rfd8 and Bg5+ to create a pin. White must consolidate carefully.
notes.teaches: After winning material, don't relax; identify the opponent's threats and neutralize them before developing. Keep the queen near the king for defense.
notes.plans: Play Qd2 to defend the rook and prevent Bg5+. If Black plays Rfd8, retreat the queen to c2 or e1, maintaining defense of the rook.

notes.explains: After Qc2, Black plays Nd4, but White simply captures. Now Black's bishop is blocked by the d4 pawn, and White can develop safely with Bd3.
notes.teaches: Don't fear moves that attack your queen if you have safe retreat squares. Calculate concretely; here the pawn on d4 is harmless.
notes.plans: Play Bd3 to complete development and prevent Black from sacrificing on d3. Then bring the knight out and consolidate the extra piece.

notes.explains: White plays Bd3, completing development and securing the king. Black has no real threats. White is up a piece and can now convert.
notes.teaches: Once material up and developed, look for prophylactic moves like Ka1 to prevent back-rank issues and prepare to activate the rook.
notes.plans: Play Ka1, then bring the rook to b1 if needed. Meanwhile, start a kingside attack with h4-h5, exploiting Black's weakened king.

notes.explains: White launches a kingside attack with h4, ignoring Black's queenside play. Black's rook sacrifice on b2 is unsound; White's king is safe on a2. White now plans e5 and f5 to open lines.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage and the opponent's counterplay is insufficient, continue with your own attacking plans. Don't be distracted by threats that don't work concretely.
notes.plans: Play e5, then f5 to break open the kingside. If Black defends, reroute the bishop to d5 and sacrifice on h7 or g6 to deliver mate.

notes.explains: White opens the kingside with f5, then captures on g6. The bishop retreats to e4, aiming for d5 to open the diagonal for the queen. Black's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: When hunting the king, don't rush to give the first check you see. Map out the king's escape routes and tailor your checks to prevent them.
notes.plans: Play Be4-d5, then give check on h8 to force the king to e7, followed by a decisive check on the e-file or h-file for mate.

notes.explains: Black plays c5, attacking the queen. This is a positional mistake because it weakens d6 and the d5 square without gaining anything substantial.
notes.teaches: Never make a move solely to attack a piece unless it's part of a larger plan or sets an unstoppable threat. Weakening your structure for a temporary attack is often bad.
notes.plans: White should not move the queen automatically; instead consider Bb5+ to trade light-squared bishops and further weaken d5.

notes.explains: Bb5+ is strong because after Black blocks with Bd7, White trades bishops, removing the defender of d5. This makes d5 a permanent outpost for a white knight.
notes.teaches: When you have a positional advantage (like a weak square), trade off pieces that defend that weakness. Long-term structural gains outweigh short-term tempo concerns.
notes.plans: After Bxd7+ Nxd7, White should find a good square for the queen (e.g., c4) and then play e5 to force the knight back.

notes.explains: White's queen needs a good square. e3 is bad (blocks pieces, allows Ng4), d3 blocks the rook's x-ray. c4 is ideal: active, safe, and prepares e5.
notes.teaches: Place your queen on a square where it is active but not in the way of your other pieces. Consider long-range potential and vulnerability to attacks.
notes.plans: Play e5, forcing the knight back and exploiting Black's weakened center.

notes.explains: Black plays Ng4, which loses a piece to Bxc7 because the queen on c4 defends the bishop. This is a direct tactical win.
notes.teaches: Always check if your opponent's 'threat' is real. Here, Ng4 attacks nothing important and leaves a piece hanging.
notes.plans: Take the knight on c7 and win a piece.

notes.explains: If Black plays h6, White can still take the knight with the pawn because the x-ray against d6 prevents Black from recapturing with the queen. d5 also fails for the same reason.
notes.teaches: An x-ray (or pin) along a file can make a pawn recapture impossible, turning a simple capture into a winning tactic.
notes.plans: Take the knight with the pawn, and if Black takes the queen, recapture with the rook, winning a piece.

notes.explains: g6 is a blunder because Nf6+ forks the king and rook. Black's position collapses under pressure.
notes.teaches: When under sustained pressure, players often make irrational moves. Stay alert for tactical shots like knight forks.
notes.plans: Play Nf6+ winning the exchange.

notes.explains: Black's b6 and Bb7 are playable but risky; if Black doesn't know the theory, White can get a quick attack.
notes.teaches: Against offbeat openings, develop naturally and don't try to refute them immediately.
notes.plans: Play d4, Nc3, then develop the bishop to d3 to protect e4 and prepare e5.

notes.explains: Bishop to d3 is best because it defends e4 and has latent potential after e5, setting up a possible Greek Gift sacrifice.
notes.teaches: Place pieces on squares that serve both defensive and offensive purposes.
notes.plans: After e5, the bishop's diagonal opens; if Black castles kingside, consider Bxh7+.

notes.explains: Black plays Bb4 pinning the knight. White doesn't need to break the pin with Bd2 because taking on c3 is fine—it strengthens d4.
notes.teaches: Don't fear doubled pawns if they improve your center or eliminate an important defender.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to f3, then defend e4 again (e.g., Qe2 or d5).

notes.explains: Bg5 to pin the knight is inaccurate because Black can play h6, g5, and win the e4 pawn. The weakening of Black's kingside doesn't compensate for losing the center.
notes.teaches: Don't pin a piece if the pin can be broken with a gain of tempo and loss of a central pawn.
notes.plans: Instead play d5 to close the center and prevent ...Ne4.

notes.explains: After d5, Black played Nd7 (inaccurate; Ne4 was better). White can now play a3 to ask the bishop to declare its intentions, or simply castle.
notes.teaches: Ask your opponent questions; force them to make decisions that may weaken their position.
notes.plans: If Black takes on c3, White's light-squared bishop becomes very strong. If Black retreats, White avoids the pin.

notes.explains: Black plays c5 threatening c4 trapping the bishop. White can prevent this by moving the queen (e.g., Qe3) to allow the bishop to retreat to e2.
notes.teaches: When a piece is threatened with entrapment, create a retreat square or move the piece before it's too late.
notes.plans: Qe3 supports d4 and prepares to transfer the queen to the kingside via f4-g4.

notes.explains: White plays Qf4 then Qg4, aiming at g7. Black trades bishops with Ba6, which is fine for White.
notes.teaches: Transfer the queen to an aggressive post where it attacks weaknesses (g7) while still defending key pawns (d4).
notes.plans: Prepare f4-f5 to open the f-file and launch a kingside attack.

notes.explains: Black plays g6 to prevent Qxg7. White develops the bishop to e3 and prepares the f4-f5 break.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their kingside pawn structure, target the weaknesses with piece play and pawn breaks.
notes.plans: Play f4-f5, possibly sacrificing on f5 to open lines against the king.

notes.explains: Black plays Ne7 and g5 to control f5. White responds with Rc1, a patient improving move, and later Qh3 to prepare g4.
notes.teaches: When your attack is temporarily blocked, make useful moves on other parts of the board (e.g., occupying open files) and reposition pieces.
notes.plans: Play g4 to chase the knight away from f5, then use the open f-file for the rooks.

notes.explains: Black takes on g4, opening the f-file. White now has a tactic: Nxg5! because if hxg5, Qxe6+ wins; if Qxg5, Qxe6+ picks up the pawn on f7.
notes.teaches: When a pin exists on the f-file, look for sacrifices that exploit the pinned pawn and open lines to the king.
notes.plans: Play Nxg5, and after ...hxg5, Qxe6+ wins material; if ...Qxg5, Qxe6+ and then take on f7.

notes.explains: After Nxg5, Black's best is ...Qe7. White can simply take on d5, consolidating material and keeping the attack.
notes.teaches: When attacking, it's often better to convert the attack into a material advantage than to force a speculative checkmate. 'Attack slowly' sometimes means taking a pawn and reorganizing.
notes.plans: Take on d5, then double rooks on the f-file or invade with the queen.

notes.explains: A pinned piece can still defend another piece. In the game, Black's rook on f8 is pinned but still defends the queen on f7, so White cannot simply take the queen.
notes.teaches: Remember: a pinned piece cannot move, but it can still protect other pieces. This is a common tactical pitfall.

notes.explains: In the theoretical line, after Qe2 d5 e5, Black's best is ...Ne4. White can sacrifice a pawn with O-O, and after ...Bxc3, bxc3 Nxe4, White gets strong compensation with Bg5 trapping the queen or Nh4 with attacking ideas.
notes.teaches: Pawn sacrifices for development and initiative can be very practical, even if engines evaluate them as equal.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, play Nh4, Qh5, and double rooks on the e-file.

notes.explains: In a similar French-like structure, if Black plays g5 to prevent f5, White can play f4 anyway, sacrificing the pawn. After ...gxf4, Rxf4, White's attack is overwhelming because the f-file is open and Black's knights are poor defenders.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you can ignore your opponent's threat and execute your plan anyway if the resulting position is strong enough. Ask yourself: 'What if I do it anyway?'
notes.plans: Play f4, recapture with the rook, double rooks, and attack f7.

notes.explains: After Black plays Ne7 and g5, White plays Rc1 (a waiting move) and then Qh3 to prepare g4. This shows patience and flexibility.
notes.teaches: Don't force the attack when the opponent has good defensive resources. Make useful improvements elsewhere and wait for the right moment.
notes.plans: Play g4 to chase the knight, then use the open f-file.

notes.explains: After Nxg5, Black played ...Qe3? (a blunder). White can simply take on d5, remaining up a pawn with a continuing attack. The immediate rook sacrifice Rf7 is unnecessary and less clear.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, don't feel obliged to find a spectacular finish. Simple consolidation is often best.
notes.plans: Take on d5, then bring the rook to c7 and pick off more pawns.

notes.explains: In a Sicilian position, White launched a kingside attack but Black defended accurately with c4 and queen maneuvers. White then switched to a material-grabbing strategy, taking pawns and converting to a technical win.
notes.teaches: When an attack is repulsed, be ready to switch gears and convert the initiative into a material advantage. Use tactical ideas (like forks) to defend while gaining material.
notes.plans: Take on h5, then a6, and use queen checks to force favorable trades.

notes.explains: Against the Philidor (e4 e5 Nf3 d6), the correct response is d4, opening the center. Black has not developed a piece and has blocked his bishop, so white should exploit this by opening lines.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a passive move like d6, open the center to exploit their lack of development and cramped position.
notes.plans: Play d4, then develop naturally: Nc3, Bc4, O-O, Re1.

notes.explains: Black's move ...c5 is a common mistake because it weakens the d5 square. White should not fear moving the queen; instead, retreat to d1 if necessary (e.g., after ...Nc6 attacking the queen). Queen d1 is safe and keeps the position solid.
notes.teaches: Retreating is not a concession; it's okay to move the queen back to a safe square. Avoid placing the queen in the center where it can be harassed (e.g., Qd5 allows ...Be6; Qd3 allows ...Ne5).
notes.plans: Retreat the queen to d1, then continue development: Bc4, O-O, and prepare to occupy the d5 outpost with a knight.

notes.explains: The knight on d5 is a strong outpost, but black may try to challenge it with ...Ne7 or ...c6. The key is to think transformationally: if the knight is traded, the bishop can take its place on d5, or the time black spends to remove the knight can be used to launch an attack elsewhere.
notes.teaches: Chess advantages are not permanent; think about what you gain if the opponent removes your outpost. Time is a valuable resource—if it takes the opponent several moves to eliminate your outpost, you can use those moves to improve your position.
notes.plans: If black plays ...Ne7, consider trading knights to give black doubled pawns, or retreat the knight to f4 and continue attacking.

notes.explains: Maneuvering the bishop to the long diagonal (e.g., via Bc1-b2) is a powerful idea. It may look awkward initially, but the bishop becomes very strong on b2, cooperating with the other bishop and the queen.
notes.teaches: Don't settle for a passive square; maneuver pieces to their best squares even if it takes a couple of moves. The long diagonal is often a great destination for the bishop.
notes.plans: Play Bc1-b2, then consider Qd2 or Qe3 to create a battery on the long diagonal, threatening ...Qxg7.

notes.explains: When the opponent's knight is undefended, look for tactics. Here, Qd4 attacks the pawn on g7 and threatens ...Qxg7#. If black defends with ...Bf6, white can trade everything and win.
notes.teaches: Always scan for undefended pieces and potential checkmate threats. A queen and bishop battery on the long diagonal can be deadly.
notes.plans: Play Qd4, threatening Qxg7#. If ...Bf6, then Bxf6 Qxf6 Qxf6, winning a pawn and maintaining pressure.

notes.explains: In the French Advance (e4 e6 d4 d5 e5), black's move ...f6 attacks the tip of the pawn chain (e5) instead of the base (d4). This is a mistake because it weakens the e5 square, which becomes an outpost for white's knight.
notes.teaches: When attacking a pawn chain, target the base (d4) not the tip (e5). Attacking the tip often creates weaknesses that the opponent can exploit.
notes.plans: After ...f6, white can simply develop (e.g., Nf3, Be2, O-O) and later occupy e5 with a knight. There's no rush to take on f6 immediately.

notes.explains: To occupy the e5 outpost, white needs to remove the bishop on d6 that defends it. The maneuver Bg5-h4-g3 invites a trade of bishops, clearing the way for the knight to reach e5.
notes.teaches: Use piece maneuvers to eliminate defenders of key squares. A bishop can be repositioned to force a favorable trade.
notes.plans: Play Bg5, then Bh4, then Bg3. If black trades on g3, the knight goes to e5. If black doesn't trade, the bishop stays active on g3.

notes.explains: When the knight reaches e5, white should consider trading it for the bishop on g6 to open the f-file and expose the black king. The queen and knight are a powerful attacking duo.
notes.teaches: The queen and knight are the strongest attacking pair because they control complementary squares and can deliver checkmate. Look for ways to combine them.
notes.plans: Play Nxg6 hxg6, then Qg4 or Qh4, threatening Qxg7#. If ...Rg8, then Bxg6+ etc.

notes.explains: If black defends with ...Rh6, white can change plans: instead of forcing the bishop trade, play Bg5, attacking the rook and threatening to win material. Flexibility is key.
notes.teaches: Don't be stubborn; adapt your plan based on the opponent's moves. If one idea fails, look for another tactical opportunity.
notes.plans: After ...Rh6, play Bg5, threatening Bxh6. If ...Rxh6, then Qxh6+ and white wins. If ...Rg6, then Bf4 etc.

notes.explains: Black plays Bd6, offering a trade on e5. This is 'trading on our own terms' – black forces white to recapture on e5, avoiding the intermediate check on f7.
notes.teaches: When ahead material, trade pieces to simplify. Here, Bd6 forces a favorable exchange and maintains the extra pawn.
notes.plans: After the trade on e5, continue development with Bd7 and connect rooks.

notes.explains: White plays Ne4, threatening Nxf2+ and a fork. Black must not panic; the threat is only one move deep, and black can simply continue development with Bd7.
notes.teaches: When facing a tactical threat, first identify the actual threat. Often the best response is to ignore it and proceed with your plan if the threat is not immediate.
notes.plans: Play Bd7, completing development. If white plays Bf4, black can trade on f4 and then push f5 to defend the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: Black recaptures with gxf6, accepting a damaged pawn structure. This opens the g-file for attack and creates a solid pawn chain (f5, e6, d6) where pawns defend each other.
notes.teaches: Pawn structure should not be judged in isolation. Here, the 'ugly' pawns are well-defended and give black attacking chances on the g-file.
notes.plans: Use the g-file to pressure g2. Play Bc6, then f5 to solidify the pawn chain, and activate rooks.

notes.explains: Black refrains from the obvious Rg8-g2 because of the defensive resource Rh4. Instead, black targets the b2 pawn with Rc4, winning material without allowing counterplay.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, avoid giving the opponent unnecessary counterplay. Choose the most direct and safe way to convert a material advantage.
notes.plans: Play Rc4, then after white's response, trade rooks and use the open file to attack weak pawns.

notes.explains: Black uses a lateral pin (Rb3) to win the b4 pawn. This is a classic endgame technique: pin a pawn laterally and advance your own pawn to capture it.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, lateral pins are a powerful tool to win pawns. Always look for ways to immobilize and capture weak pawns.
notes.plans: After winning the b4 pawn, use the pawn majority on the kingside to create a passed pawn and promote.

notes.explains: Black plays b6, a pawn breakthrough sacrifice. White's king cannot stop the a-pawn from queening after axb6 axb6.
notes.teaches: A pawn breakthrough can break a 'deep freeze' where one pawn holds two. Sacrificing a pawn to create a passed pawn is a common endgame technique.
notes.plans: After b6, white's best is to take, then black promotes the a-pawn. In the resulting queen endgame, black wins by zugzwang or checkmate.

notes.explains: Black plays Kb7, forcing white into zugzwang. White must move the king away from the pawn, allowing Qf8#.
notes.teaches: In queen vs. pawn endgames, zugzwang is a key winning method. The king can often force the opponent into a losing move.
notes.plans: After Kb7, white's only move is to push the h-pawn, then black checkmates.

notes.explains: Black plays Nd4, occupying the outpost. White's knight on b1 is misplaced, and black threatens Nxc2 or further queenside pressure.
notes.teaches: Once the knight on c3 is driven away, the d4 square becomes a powerful outpost for black's knight.
notes.plans: Use the knight on d4 to create threats, possibly targeting c2 or supporting a pawn push.

notes.explains: Black retreats the bishop to g7 instead of capturing on a3. This keeps the bishop on the long diagonal, maintaining dark-square control and avoiding a weakening of the kingside.
notes.teaches: When ahead, don't grab material if it weakens your position. The fianchettoed bishop is a key defensive piece; leaving its diagonal can expose your king.
notes.plans: After Bg7, continue to press on the queenside with b3, threatening to open lines.

notes.explains: White plays f5, creating an outpost on e5. Black immediately occupies it with Ne5, a typical response to f5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent pushes f5, look to occupy the e5 outpost. This is a common idea in many Sicilian structures.
notes.plans: Use the knight on e5 to pressure white's position, while continuing queenside operations.

notes.explains: Black plays b3, a pawn sacrifice that opens lines. White cannot take the queen because after Bxa5, Rxa5, the pawn promotes.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a move that seems impossible (like b3, exposing the queen) is actually winning. Creativity means allowing yourself to consider such moves.
notes.plans: After b3, white's best is to avoid immediate loss, but black will win material and promote the b-pawn.

notes.explains: Black refuses the gambit pawn and transposes into the Alapin Sicilian with Nf6, which is a solid way to avoid the gambit's complications.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, declining the pawn can lead to familiar territory and frustrate the gambit player.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, aiming for e6 and f5 to challenge the queen, then b5 and a5 for queenside counterplay.

notes.explains: After Qxd4, Black plays e6 to defend the knight, then f5 chasing the queen away. The key idea is to sacrifice a pawn with b5 for queenside counterplay.
notes.teaches: In sharp lines, remember that pawn sacrifices can open lines and create long-term pressure.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to a6 to skewer the queen, then a5 to expand, aiming for ...Nbd7 and ...Qc7.

notes.explains: Black plays d6 instead of d5, avoiding the main Caro-Kann. White develops simply with Nf3, Bf4, and castles, ignoring Black's pawn pushes.
notes.teaches: When your opponent pushes pawns without developing, just develop naturally and prepare to open the center.
notes.plans: Open the center with d5 to exploit Black's lack of development.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, Black needs to develop actively. Bf5 is a key move: it prevents White's knight from jumping to e4 (which would threaten f6) and also attacks the c2 pawn. Developing with a threat is ideal.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, development still matters. Look for moves that both improve your pieces and restrict your opponent's best squares.
notes.plans: Black plays Bf5, then doubles rooks on the e-file to control the open file and pressure White's position.

notes.explains: Black has a choice: trade all rooks into a bishop endgame, or keep rooks and improve the king. The best approach is to improve the king (Kg7) while White trades rooks, as bishop endgames up a pawn are not always winning, but a centralized king is a major asset.
notes.teaches: In endgames, improving your king is often the top priority. Do not rush to simplify if you can first strengthen your position.
notes.plans: Black plays Kg7, bringing the king toward the center, and only trades rooks when convenient. The king will support the creation of a passed pawn.

notes.explains: Black's bishop is currently on c5, but White threatens c3 to trap it. To avoid being confined, Black should immediately play Bd4, with the idea that if c3, the bishop can go to e5. This keeps the bishop active and centralized.
notes.teaches: In endgames, bishop mobility is crucial. Anticipate your opponent's plans to restrict your pieces and find a way to keep them active.
notes.plans: Black plays Bd4, and if c3, then Be5, maintaining a strong diagonal. The bishop will support the king's advance and the creation of a passed pawn.

notes.explains: White's f4 is a mistake because it pushes the pawn to a dark square, creating weaknesses. Black can now trade bishops and enter a pawn endgame that is winning due to the plan of pushing c5, d5, and d4 to create a passed pawn.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, a pawn on a dark square can be a weakness. Look for plans to create a passed pawn by advancing your central pawns.
notes.plans: Black trades bishops, then advances c5, d5, and d4 to create a passed pawn on the queenside. The black king will support the pawn's promotion.

notes.explains: Black's plan of c5, d5, and d4 creates a passed pawn on d4. White's king cannot stop both the d-pawn and the potential queenside passer. The pawn race is easily won by Black.
notes.teaches: When you have a pawn majority and a centralized king, creating a passed pawn is a clear winning plan. Do not assume your opponent can stop it without concrete calculation.
notes.plans: Black pushes the d-pawn to promotion, using the king to support it. If White tries to counter on the kingside, Black's queenside passer is faster.

notes.explains: In the resulting pawn endgame, Black's king is more active and can win White's kingside pawns. The technique of shepherding the king away from the pawn with the queen is not needed here; Black can simply promote the d-pawn.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, king activity is decisive. A centralized king can both support its own pawns and attack the opponent's weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black's king captures White's pawns on the kingside while the d-pawn is unstoppable. The win is straightforward.

notes.explains: After …Nxe4, Black has a material advantage and White's queen is developed early. Black should not move the knight again but instead play d5 to open the bishop and occupy the center.
notes.teaches: When a bishop is on c4 and the center opens, look for ways to develop with counterattack rather than moving the same piece multiple times.
notes.plans: Play d5, opening the bishop and attacking the queen, then recapture with the knight after White takes on d5.

notes.explains: White's check with Bxf7+ looks intimidating but Black can block with Be6. Black is better because he has more development and White's queen is exposed.
notes.teaches: Don't be intimidated by checks; if you can block with a developing move, it's often good. Principles of development outweigh flashy checks.
notes.plans: Block the check with Be6, then continue developing with Nc6 and Qe7, attacking the queen.

notes.explains: Black should castle long rather than short because the g7 pawn is missing, making the kingside vulnerable to threats like Ng5 and Qh4.
notes.teaches: When a pawn in front of your king is gone, castling to that side is risky. Consider the safety of the pawn cover before castling.
notes.plans: Castle long to keep the king safe, then prepare an attack on the g-file using the semi-open file.

notes.explains: After castling long, Black has a semi-open g-file because the g7 pawn is gone. This is a good attacking file. Black should not trade pieces but instead increase pressure on g2.
notes.teaches: A semi-open file can be a powerful attacking asset. Avoid unnecessary trades when you are close to launching an attack.
notes.plans: Put a rook on g8, move the bishop away from d5 to open the file, and chase away the knight on g5 to crash through on g2.

notes.explains: Black plays a5 to prevent a6, which would attack the bishop. This is prophylaxis. Then Black finds a queen trap: Bf8 attacks the queen and opens up an attack on the g2 pawn.
notes.teaches: Prophylaxis means preventing your opponent's threats before they happen. Also, when you see a good move (like taking the queen), look for a better one (like Bf8 which also attacks the pawn).
notes.plans: Play a5 to stop a6, then Bf8 trapping the queen and threatening g2. If White avoids the trap, continue with the attack on the g-file.

notes.explains: Instead of taking the queen, Black has a checkmate in two: Qh3+ (double check) and Qg4#. The double check forces the king to move, and the bishop and rook cover escape squares.
notes.teaches: In a double check, the only defense is to move the king. Always consider forcing sequences like double checks when the king is trapped.
notes.plans: Play Qh3+ (double check), then Qg4#. If White blocks with Rg1, the double check still works.

notes.explains: After …Nxe4, if White moves the knight away (e.g., Nbd2), Black can take on d4 and attack the knight. The correct move is d5, opening the bishop and occupying the center.
notes.teaches: Don't move the same piece multiple times in the opening if you can develop with a counterattack. d5 simultaneously attacks the queen and opens lines.
notes.plans: Play d5, then after exd5, recapture with the knight, developing with tempo.

notes.explains: After d5, White could try Bb5+ to win a piece, but Black can defend with c6 or Nd7. The key is that the queen on d4 is undefended and can be attacked with tempo.
notes.teaches: When you have two pieces hanging, look for a check that forces your opponent to deal with it, allowing you to save the other piece. Also, an undefended queen is a major tactical weakness.
notes.plans: If Bb5+, play c6 or Nd7. If White retreats the bishop, play Ne4 attacking the queen, then develop with tempo.

notes.explains: White could play en passant on d5, but then Bxd6 reveals a discovered check on the queen, winning the queen. If White plays c3, Qxd1+ and the rook is pinned, so Black can't recapture.
notes.teaches: Discovered checks are powerful. Also, be aware of pins that prevent recaptures, especially when undefended pieces are involved.
notes.plans: After en passant, play Bxd6 with discovered check. If c3, Qxd1+ and the rook is pinned, so Black wins the rook.

notes.explains: If White plays f3 to block the check, Black can play Qh4+ and then take on g3, exploiting the undefended rook. This is a typical tactical idea when pawns in front of the king are moved.
notes.teaches: Moving pawns in front of your king can open dangerous diagonals. Always check for undefended pieces when considering such moves.
notes.plans: Play Qh4+, then after g3, take on g3 with the queen, winning the rook because it is undefended.

notes.explains: Black chose Qd7 over Qe7 to avoid potential pins and to keep the bishop on d5 active. This is about taking care of future self and minimizing risk.
notes.teaches: When choosing between moves, consider not only immediate threats but also potential future problems. Prophylaxis applies to your own pieces too.
notes.plans: Play Qd7 to avoid pins and keep the bishop active. Then continue with the plan to attack on the g-file.

notes.explains: White played a4, but it's not scary because he has no pieces on the queenside. Black continues with Rg8 and then Nxf7 blunders the knight. Black returns to d5 to keep pressure on g2.
notes.teaches: Don't fear pawn advances if your opponent has no pieces to support them. Focus on your own attack and punish opponent's mistakes.
notes.plans: Play Rg8, then after Nxf7, recapture and continue pressuring g2 with the bishop on d5.

notes.explains: If White had played Qa4, Black could sacrifice the queen with Qh3 to remove the g2 pawn, then checkmate with the bishop. The key is to not sacrifice the piece that controls the mating square.
notes.teaches: When removing a defender, ensure you don't sacrifice the piece that is crucial for the mating pattern. Look for decoy sacrifices that remove the key defender.
notes.plans: Play Qh3, forcing gxh3, then move the bishop away and deliver checkmate with the rook or bishop.

notes.explains: White played Qc5 to prevent Qh3, but Black can still play Bf8 trapping the queen. The queen syndrome: people assume a hanging queen must be captured, but here Black takes the bishop instead.
notes.teaches: Don't automatically capture a hanging queen; consider if there is a better move. The queen syndrome is the tendency to fixate on the queen.
notes.plans: Play Bf8, attacking the queen and the g2 pawn. If White moves the queen, continue the attack.

notes.explains: After Bf8, White played Rxf8, and Black found Rg1+ leading to a windmill. The rook check forces the king to move, and Black can repeat checks to win material.
notes.teaches: A windmill is a series of checks using a discovered check to win material. Look for patterns where a piece can check and then move away with a discovered check.
notes.plans: Play Rg1+ (discovered check), then when the king moves, move the rook back to g1 with check, repeating to win pieces.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nc3 d6 Bb5+, Black should not rush a6 because the bishop isn't threatening anything. Playing Nbd7 is a solid, flexible response that prepares to challenge the center later.
notes.teaches: When your opponent plays a non-threatening check, don't automatically push the attacking pawn. Develop a piece instead, keeping your options open.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with Nf6, e6, and later a6 to force the bishop to declare its intentions, then expand on the queenside with b5.

notes.explains: Black plays Qc7 to prevent White's b4 expansion. The queen eyes the c4 pawn and the knight on c3, making b4 met by cxb4, attacking the knight. This is type 2 prophylaxis: allowing the move but preparing a response.
notes.teaches: Prophylaxis can be physical (blocking a move) or strategic (making the move harmless). Here, Qc7 takes the sting out of b4 by creating a tactical threat.
notes.plans: After a6 and Bxd7+ (or Ba4), Black will play b5, gaining space on the queenside, then develop the light-squared bishop to b7.

notes.explains: White played Bf4, a natural-looking move that attacks the queen, but it overlooks Black's tactical resource e5. This pawn push hits the bishop and threatens the e4 pawn, winning material.
notes.teaches: Avoid automatic thinking. When a pawn is hanging (here e4), always check if you can create a double attack or win material. Patience and a quick tactical scan can turn a quiet position into a winning one.
notes.plans: Black plays e5, forcing the bishop to move, then follows up with c4 to shut out the bishop and later capture on e4 with the knight.

notes.explains: After e5 and Bg3, Black plays c4 instead of dxc4. The reason: dxc4 allows Ng5, threatening f7 and making it hard to defend the c4 pawn. By playing c4, Black closes the diagonal and keeps the bishop passive.
notes.teaches: When a pawn capture opens lines for the opponent's pieces, consider a different move that restricts their activity. Here, c4 is a prophylactic move that also prepares to win the e4 pawn safely.
notes.plans: Black will eventually capture on e4 with the knight, establishing a strong outpost on c5 and preparing to open the d-file.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 c3 g6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 e6, Black has mixed e6 and g6, creating dark-square weaknesses. White should not rush d5 but instead develop patiently, keeping the center flexible.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a shaky pawn structure, don't commit to a pawn push immediately. Develop pieces and wait for the right moment to strike. Patience is key.
notes.plans: White plays Nf3, Bc4, O-O, and then looks to play e5 or d5 at the right moment, exploiting the dark-square weaknesses.

notes.explains: White plays e5, putting the bishop on e4 and later pushing d5. The idea is to use the light-squared bishop on the long diagonal and open the center, exploiting Black's uncastled king and weak dark squares.
notes.teaches: When your opponent delays castling and has a weak pawn center, a central pawn break (e5, d5) can create a devastating attack. The bishop on e4 is a powerful piece that controls key diagonals.
notes.plans: White pushes c4 to chase the knight from d5, then plays d5, opening lines. The queen joins via d2, and the attack on the kingside becomes irresistible.

notes.explains: White avoids taking on d4 immediately because it allows the black knight to re-enter via c5. Instead, White plays Nc3, keeping the knight on d4 out of the game and preparing to use the f6 and d6 squares.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's better to leave a pawn on the board to restrict the opponent's pieces. Here, keeping the pawn on d4 limits Black's knight and maintains pressure.
notes.plans: White will eventually take on d4 when the queen can join the attack via d2, then deliver checkmate or win decisive material.

notes.explains: Black plays Nbd7, preparing e5. This is a traditional King's Indian setup. White's d5 is premature because it allows Black to target the d5 pawn with c6 and Nb6, gaining counterplay.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, don't automatically push e5. If White plays d5 early, Black can undermine it with c6 and Nb6, often winning the pawn or gaining activity.
notes.plans: Black will play Bd7, a5, c6, and eventually e5, creating a typical King's Indian pawn structure with counterplay on the queenside and center.

notes.explains: Black plays a5 to prevent b4, then a4 to provoke weaknesses in White's queenside pawn chain. White's b4 is a mistake because it allows Black to create a passed pawn on a3 and open lines for the knight.
notes.teaches: Use pawns to probe and provoke weaknesses. When your opponent's pawns become overextended, you can create passed pawns and open files for your pieces.
notes.plans: Black plays a3, then Na4 with tempo, followed by cxd5, opening the c-file. The knight on g4 and queen on b6 create threats against f2, winning material.

notes.explains: Black plays Ng4, threatening Nxf2 and Qb6+. White cannot defend f2 without losing material. The knight sacrifice on f2 is a typical King's Indian tactic, exploiting the weak f2 pawn.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, the f2/f7 pawn is often a target. A knight sacrifice on f2 can open the king and lead to a winning attack, especially when the opponent's king is still in the center.
notes.plans: Black will play Qb6, forcing White to give up material to defend f2. After the sacrifice, Black's pieces become very active, and the attack is decisive.

notes.explains: Black simplifies by trading queens and infiltrating with the rook on c2. The bishop on h6 is a typical King's Indian idea, trading off the dark-squared bishops to create weaknesses on the kingside.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, activate your rooks and use them to infiltrate the opponent's position. Trading off the opponent's good bishop (here the dark-squared one) can leave lasting weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black will play Rc2, then Bh6, and eventually collect material. The extra piece and active rooks make the win straightforward.

notes.explains: Black plays Bh6, a typical King's Indian move to trade off the dark-squared bishops. This weakens White's kingside dark squares and allows Black's rook to infiltrate.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, trading your dark-squared bishop for White's can be a key strategic goal. It exposes weaknesses on the dark squares around the king and gives your pieces more scope.
notes.plans: After Bh6, Black will play Rc2, then use the queen and rook to create threats. The bishop trade is often the prelude to a decisive attack.

notes.explains: After e4 c6 d4 d5 e5 Bf5 Nf3 e6, Black's e5 variation is a principled response. White's main move is Be2, but here the teacher considers Bc4, which threatens Bxf7+ and Nxe5. Black's typical reply is …Nd7 to cover e5, then 6.0-0 Ngf6, and White's best is c3 to support d4.
notes.teaches: In the Fantasy Variation, White's light-squared bishop is powerful on c4, pressuring f7. Black must be careful not to allow Bxf7+ tactics.
notes.plans: White aims to complete development and launch a kingside attack after Black castles short. Black should consider ...Qb6 to pressure d4 and b2.

notes.explains: White checks on b5, but Black covers with the knight, not the pawn, to avoid losing the e5 knight. This is a precise defensive move.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, every move must be precise. Consider all checks and captures carefully.
notes.plans: Black's knight on d7 is awkward but White's queen is also misplaced. Black will target the queen with Rb8 and Bb4.

notes.explains: Black plays Rb8, attacking the queen and threatening to win the b2 pawn. White's bishop on f4 is undefended, creating additional tactical opportunities.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are undefended, look for ways to exploit that with tempo-gaining moves.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with Bb4 or Rxb2, depending on White's response.

notes.explains: Black plays Bb4, pinning the knight and threatening to win the bishop on f4. White's queen is far from the action.
notes.teaches: Pins are powerful in open positions. Combine them with threats to win material.
notes.plans: Black will capture the bishop on f4, gaining a decisive material advantage.

notes.explains: Black captures on c3, winning a piece. White's queen is still out of play, and Black has a huge lead in development.
notes.teaches: Once you have a material advantage, simplify if it maintains your initiative. Keep the pressure on.
notes.plans: Black will continue developing and eventually convert the extra piece.

notes.explains: Black takes the rook on b1, winning more material. White's position is collapsing due to lack of development.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has no developed pieces, every capture and threat becomes devastating.
notes.plans: Black will consolidate and finish the game with the extra material.

notes.explains: Black's queen goes to a5, threatening both the knight on c3 and the pawn on a2. This double threat is decisive.
notes.teaches: Always look for multiple threats. A single move can attack several weaknesses simultaneously.
notes.plans: Black will capture on a2 and then b2, winning more material.

notes.explains: Black wins the b2 pawn, and White's king is exposed. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: Initiative and development can lead to a quick knockout. Don't let the opponent consolidate.
notes.plans: Black will continue the attack, targeting White's king.

notes.explains: Black captures the bishop on c3, winning another piece. White's position is hopeless.
notes.teaches: Once you have a decisive advantage, look for the most efficient way to convert.
notes.plans: Black will simplify further and win the endgame.

notes.explains: After c3, Qb6 is flexible: it attacks d4 and prepares to recapture on c5 with the queen if White takes. White's b3 is a mistake that loses a pawn, as Black can simply take on d4.
notes.teaches: When the opponent defends a pawn you're attacking, consider whether you can win it by capturing first and then renewing the threat. Flexibility in move order can exploit weaknesses.
notes.plans: Take on d4 with the knight, then develop with Bc5 and castle, exploiting the broken pawn chain and the protected passed pawn on d5.

notes.explains: White's Kh1 avoids a discovered check, but Black can now play h5, threatening to open the h-file. The key is not to rush: Black should consider whether immediate captures are necessary.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, don't force tactics. Prioritize safety and gradual improvement. A safe knight is better than an active one that can be trapped.
notes.plans: Play h5 to open lines, then consider g3 or other moves to maintain pressure. Avoid automatic captures like Bxa1 if they allow counterplay.

notes.explains: After g4, Black's knight is attacked. The correct move is to retreat the knight to a safe square, not to seek an active post. The priority is preserving the piece and winning the rook on a1.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, safety trumps activity. Retreating a piece to preserve it and maintain the material advantage is often the best plan.
notes.plans: Retreat the knight (e.g., Ng6 or Nf5) to safety, then win the rook on a1. After that, consolidate and exploit the extra material.

notes.explains: White plays Nc3 to block the rook's defense. Black can now win the rook by simply retreating the knight (e.g., Ng6) and then taking on a1. The immediate capture Nxg4? would lose the knight.
notes.teaches: Always consider the opponent's resources. A simple retreat can be more effective than a flashy capture. Calculate captures carefully.
notes.plans: Retreat the knight (Ng6 or Nf5), then take the rook on a1. After that, activate the queen and rook, and consider exploiting White's weak king.

notes.explains: Black retreats the knight to g6, winning the rook on a1. White's king is weak due to g4, and Black can continue with d4 to secure the bishop and prepare Qc6 with threats.
notes.teaches: After winning material, consolidate by improving your pieces and restricting the opponent's counterplay. A weak king is a long-term target.
notes.plans: Play d4 to secure the bishop and advance the passed pawn. Then Qc6 to threaten discovered checks and activate the rook. Castle only when necessary.

notes.explains: Black wins the exchange and has a decisive material advantage. The game is effectively over; Black just needs to make reasonable moves to convert.
notes.teaches: When you have a large material advantage, avoid unnecessary risks. Simple, solid moves are sufficient to win.
notes.plans: Continue with Qc6, then castle or bring the rook into play. Avoid blundering the advantage back.

notes.explains: The Caro-Kann and French Defenses are structurally similar: both allow White to build a pawn center (d4, e5) while Black attacks it with c5 and f6. The key difference is that in the Caro-Kann, Black develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain (Bf5), but spends two tempi on c5 later.
notes.teaches: Understanding pawn structures is crucial. In closed positions, the side with more pawn breaks (levers) often has the initiative. The Caro-Kann trades a tempo for a better bishop.

notes.explains: A common tactical pattern in the Caro-Kann: when White's king is boxed in on h1 and the h-file is open, a rook lift to h8 can deliver checkmate. This pattern also appears in other openings.
notes.teaches: Keep a mental notebook of tactical patterns. Recognizing patterns like the h-file mate can help you spot winning combinations in similar positions.

notes.explains: In the Caro-Kann, Black often faces development challenges with the kingside pieces. The knight on h6 (aiming for f5) and the dark-squared bishop on e7 or c5 are typical solutions.
notes.teaches: When natural squares are unavailable, consider rim moves or trades to activate pieces. The knight on h6 is not necessarily bad if it can reach f5.

notes.explains: The 'best case scenario test' helps evaluate a plan: imagine the opponent does nothing to stop you. If the plan still doesn't achieve a clear advantage, it's probably not good. For example, playing c4 in the Caro-Kann closes the center and makes it hard to break through, even with b5-b4.
notes.teaches: Evaluate plans by considering the best-case outcome. If the plan is not convincing even then, look for alternatives.

notes.explains: White's Bf4 is a slightly weird move that locks in the bishop on f1. Black should continue developing and prepare to challenge the center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is poorly placed, don't rush to trade; instead, exploit the tempo by improving your own position.
notes.plans: Play c6 to attack the d5 pawn, opening lines for the queen and potentially recapturing with a piece if dxc6.

notes.explains: White blunders a pawn with Qc2. Black simply captures on d5, winning a pawn.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to simple tactical blunders; don't overcomplicate when you can just take free material.
notes.plans: Capture the pawn on d5 and continue developing.

notes.explains: White offers a knight trade with Nc6? Actually Black plays Nc6, then White plays e3. Black should keep the tension and not trade knights automatically.
notes.teaches: Default to keeping the tension in the opening; only trade if there is a concrete reason. Trading here would allow White's bad bishop to improve.
notes.plans: Continue development with d6, preparing to expand with e5.

notes.explains: Black has a massive pawn center and should set it in motion. The immediate e5 is good, but first take on d4 to prevent White from gaining a tempo with Nxc6.
notes.teaches: When you have a pawn center, advance it with careful move order to deny the opponent counterplay. Capture first if it removes a defender.
notes.plans: Play exd4 first, then e5, chasing the bishop, then d4 to drive a wedge.

notes.explains: Before playing d4, throw in Bf5 with tempo, attacking the queen. This has no downside and forces White to respond, gaining time.
notes.teaches: Always look for 'free' tempo moves that improve your position before committing to a pawn push. Low-hanging fruit can be decisive.
notes.plans: After Bf5, play d4 to wedge the pawns, then consider dxc5 if possible.

notes.explains: Instead of d4, dxc5 wins another pawn and suffocates White's kingside. White cannot play without developing the kingside pieces.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are undeveloped, winning material is often more important than maintaining a pawn center. Suffocation is a winning strategy.
notes.plans: Capture on c5, then continue to exploit White's lack of development.

notes.explains: Nd5 attacks the queen and threatens to take the bishop. If the queen drops back to d2, then Nxe3 wins the bishop because White cannot recapture with the queen (the pawn would have to take, ruining the structure).
notes.teaches: Sometimes the threat of winning material is not the only point; inducing structural damage can be even more valuable. Always consider the consequences of recaptures.
notes.plans: After Nd5, if Qd2 then Nxe3, forcing fxe3 and leaving White with a shattered pawn structure.

notes.explains: After Nxe3, White cannot recapture with the queen because of the pin, so must play fxe3, destroying the pawn structure. Black is completely winning.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, simplifying by trading pieces is often good, but do it with a purpose. Here, the trade also ruins White's structure.
notes.plans: Continue to exploit the weak pawns and the exposed king.

notes.explains: White plays Nxb7, but Black has Nc2+ forcing trades and remaining up a piece. The desperado sequence works in Black's favor.
notes.teaches: In tactical sequences, calculate all checks and captures. A desperado can sometimes save the opponent, but here it simplifies to a winning endgame.
notes.plans: After Nc2+, trade pieces and convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: Black is up a piece and should convert. The principle is to trade when up material, but not indiscriminately. Here, trading queens and rooks simplifies the win.
notes.teaches: When up material, trading pieces usually simplifies the win, but always consider if the opponent has counterplay. In this case, it's safe.
notes.plans: Trade pieces, control the c-file, and promote a pawn or deliver mate.

notes.explains: Black sets up a mating net with bishops on d3 and c3, threatening Rb1#. The pawn move e4 opens a diagonal for the bishop to h6 if needed.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, look for the quickest mate. Pawn moves can open diagonals and create mating threats. Always be aware of how pawn moves change the board.
notes.plans: Play e4, then Bc3 and Rb1, threatening mate. If White plays e4 themselves, then Bh6 is unstoppable.

notes.explains: After Bh6, White trades bishops, but Black plays f6, winning the knight on h6. Black is up a piece.
notes.teaches: When you have a tactical threat, follow through with it. The hyper-fianchetto can directly win material.
notes.plans: Capture the knight and convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: Black is up a piece and should convert. The simplest method is to trade pieces and promote a pawn.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, trade pieces to reduce counterplay, but keep at least one rook to support the pawns.
notes.plans: Trade rooks and queen if possible, then advance the queenside pawns.

notes.explains: Black is up a rook and should win easily. The key is to avoid blunders and use the rook to support pawn promotion.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, stay alert for counterplay. Use your rook actively to cut off the opponent's king.
notes.plans: Advance the queenside pawns, using the rook to protect them.

notes.explains: In a King's Indian Attack setup, White often plays f4 to start a kingside attack. But if Black hasn't castled kingside, this can backfire.
notes.teaches: Don't assume your opponent will castle into your attack. If they can castle queenside, your pawn pushes become targets.
notes.plans: Instead of automatic f5, consider a positional move like Bh3 to trade off Black's good bishop and weaken the light squares.

notes.explains: Bh3 is a 'positional tactic' – it trades White's bad bishop for Black's good one, weakening the light squares and allowing queen infiltration.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a trade that seems equal is actually a strategic victory. Exchanging a bad piece for a good one can transform the position.
notes.plans: After Bh3, if Black takes, recapture with the queen and use the light squares to infiltrate.

notes.explains: In a typical King's Indian position, Bh6 is a powerful move that can lead to immediate checkmate by opening the dark-squared diagonal to e3.
notes.teaches: The hyper-fianchetto (Bh6) is not just a defensive idea; it can be a devastating attacking weapon, especially when the opponent's dark squares are weak.
notes.plans: After Bh6, the bishop goes to e3, threatening mate on g7 or h6.

notes.explains: After h3, Black sacrifices the knight with Nxh3+ to open the h-file. White's king is exposed, and Black's attack is overwhelming.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices to open lines against the enemy king are often justified when the king is exposed and the attacker has many pieces ready.
notes.plans: Follow up with Qg5 or Qh4, threatening mate on h2 or g3, and bring the rook to h8.

notes.explains: The attack culminates in a forced checkmate. Black's queen and bishop coordinate to exploit the light squares around White's king.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, look for ways to combine material gain with mating threats; precision is key to avoid unnecessary complications.
notes.plans: Execute the mate with queen checks and bishop support, using the light squares.

notes.explains: The game demonstrates a classic kingside attack against the Hippopotamus setup, using the g3 hook and a knight sacrifice to open lines.
notes.teaches: The Hippopotamus is playable at high levels but dangerous for beginners; it's better to learn classical openings first to build fundamentals.

notes.explains: The Elephant Gambit (…d5) is a risky sideline. Black's main problem is lack of development.
notes.teaches: Against gambits, prioritize development over material. Don't laugh at tricky lines; they can be dangerous if mishandled.
notes.plans: White should aim to exploit Black's lagging development and exposed king.

notes.explains: Nxe5 is a strong response, taking the pawn and challenging Black to prove compensation.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, capturing the pawn is often best if you can handle the resulting activity.
notes.plans: After …Qe7? d4 f6 Nd3! is key; the knight goes to d3, not f3, to avoid harassment and keep the bishop's diagonal open.

notes.explains: Nd3 is the secret sauce. If Black captures on c4, the knight goes to f4, dominating light squares and not blocking the dark-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: When retreating a knight, choose a square that maximizes future activity and doesn't hinder your other pieces.
notes.plans: Follow up with Bc4, Nc3, and target Black's weaknesses, especially the f7 pawn and the exposed queen.

notes.explains: Nf4 is fantastic: it eyes h5 and e6, and doesn't block the c1-bishop. Black's f6 weakens e6 and g6.
notes.teaches: A knight on f4 in such positions can be a decisive attacking piece, especially with the queen on h5 and bishop on c4.
notes.plans: Play Bc4, then Qh5+ or Nc3, exploiting Black's vulnerable king and lack of coordination.

notes.explains: Bc4 threatens Qh5+ and prevents ...Qf7 after Nxg6. Black's position is already critical.
notes.teaches: Develop with threats; Bc4 here is both developing and attacking, creating immediate tactical problems.
notes.plans: After …Bg4? Qxg4 Nxg4 Bxf7+ Ke7 Ng6+ wins the rook. Simpler is Qh5+ g6 Nxg6 hxg6 Qxh8.

notes.explains: After …Bd6, d4 is natural. Black's main try is …dxe4, but Bc4! is strong, threatening Bxf7+.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, look for moves that attack f7 and disrupt Black's coordination.
notes.plans: After …Nf6 Qe2 or Nc3, White has a clear advantage. If …Qe7, Qe2!? is a good practical move.

notes.explains: Black plays Qf6, threatening Rf4 and Qd4. This is a patient, strong move that sets up unstoppable threats.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move is a quiet one that improves your position and creates multiple threats. Patience is rewarded.
notes.plans: Black threatens Rf4, and if White plays Rc1, Black plays Rf8, defending against back rank and threatening Rf4 again.

notes.explains: White wins a pawn and Black's king is exposed. The endgame is very favorable for White.
notes.teaches: Converting a material advantage often involves simplifying to a winning endgame, but keep the initiative if possible.
notes.plans: Develop quickly, trade pieces, and use the extra pawn to create a passed pawn or attack the king.

notes.explains: Against the Bowdler Attack (Bc4), Black should play …e6 to prepare d5 or transpose to the Open Sicilian.
notes.teaches: In anti-Sicilians, choose a setup that allows you to revert to main lines if White plays d4.
notes.plans: After d4 cxd4 Nxd4 a6, we reach a Scheveningen-type position. If White avoids d4, play ...d5 or ...b5 and ...Bb7.

notes.explains: White's knight on e5 looks active but is actually poorly supported. Black's central control (c5 pawn) and development give a clear advantage.
notes.teaches: A centralized knight without pawn support can be a target. Control of the d4 square is crucial in the Sicilian.
notes.plans: Play ...Qc7, then ...Rfd8, and eventually ...d5 or ...Nd4 to exploit White's weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black's knight on e5 is well placed. White's knight on h4 is misplaced. Black can now play ...Ng4 or ...Nc4 with advantage.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pieces are poorly coordinated, look for ways to increase pressure and force weaknesses.
notes.plans: Play ...Ng4, threatening ...Nxf2, or ...Nc4 attacking b2. Black's position is already winning.

notes.explains: Black wins a pawn with ...Nxf2, exploiting the loose knight on h4 and the weak f2 square.
notes.teaches: Pattern recognition: a knight on h4 often allows ...Ng4 and ...Nxf2 tactics. Always be alert for such motifs.
notes.plans: After Kxf2 Nxe4+ Kg1 Nxd2, Black is up a pawn with a great position. Simplify and convert.

notes.explains: The Latvian Gambit (…f5) is a sharp but dubious line. White should play d4! immediately.
notes.teaches: Against gambits, central counterplay is often the best response. Don't be tempted to grab material immediately.
notes.plans: After …exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3, White has a comfortable advantage. If …fxe4 Nxe5 Nf6 Bc4, White is better.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6, Black plays Bb5 Nxd4? which is a mistake. White recaptures Nxd4 exd4 e5 Ne4 Qe2 Qe7 Bg5 h6 Bc4 Qg4 O-O Qxf4 Qh4 Nxe5 Ng4 Nd5 O-O Nxc7 Bxf2+ Rxf2 Qxf2+ Rxf2, White wins the queen and the game.
notes.teaches: In the Four Knights Scotch, Black's early ...Nxd4 is a mistake because it allows White to push e5 with tempo, gaining space and attacking the knight. White should develop naturally and exploit Black's lack of development.
notes.plans: White castles kingside to complete development, then targets the c7 pawn with Nd5, eventually winning material.

notes.explains: White wins the exchange and a pawn. Black's compensation is insufficient.
notes.teaches: In sharp lines, calculate carefully but trust your development advantage. Don't be afraid to take material if you can survive the attack.
notes.plans: Consolidate by developing and trading pieces. Black's king is exposed, but White's material advantage should decide.

notes.explains: Black's early queen sortie and retreat gifted White a tempo; now Black's f6 and Nh6 weaken the kingside dark squares and leave the king vulnerable.
notes.teaches: Don't chase the queen with reactive moves like g3; instead, develop naturally and let the opponent's misplaced queen become a target.
notes.plans: White should continue developing with Re1, preparing ideas like Ne5 or Qh5, and exploit the weakened dark squares around Black's king.

notes.explains: After Bxh6, Black's pawn structure is ruined. White has a huge development lead and Black's king is exposed.
