notes.teaches: When attacking, prefer simple, risk-free moves over flashy sacrifices. Re1 is a classy setup move that prepares multiple threats without burning bridges.
notes.plans: Play Re1, x-raying the king and setting up ideas like Ne5 or Qh5. If Black plays Bd7, Ne5 wins immediately because the king's escape square is gone.

notes.explains: With Bd7 blocking the king's escape, Ne5 forces a decisive attack. Black's lack of development means there is no defense.
notes.teaches: Just because an idea didn't work earlier doesn't mean you should abandon it; re-evaluate when the position changes.
notes.plans: After Ne5, Black is mated or loses material. For example, Bb5 allows Bxf7+ and Qh5#.

notes.explains: After Nxe5, Black's main move is Bd6, not Qe7 or f6. If Qe7, White plays d4 cementing the knight; if f6, retreating the knight is fine—don't be afraid to lose tempo.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, don't rush to refute every threat; sometimes retreating is best. Black's queen on h4 can be ignored if it's not supported—it may become a target.
notes.plans: After Nxe5, play d4 and develop naturally. If Black plays Bd6, respond with Bc4, forcing Bxe5, then play Qh5 as an intermediate move, trading queens on favorable terms.

notes.explains: If Black plays dxe4, White should play Bc4, not d4. Bc4 threatens f7 and leads to a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When a sacrifice is both the best and the coolest move, play it. Bxf7+ forces the king out and ruins Black's castling rights.
notes.plans: After Bc4, if Black plays Qh4, ignore it and continue development. The queen on h4 is not dangerous; instead, look for tactics like Bg5 trapping the queen.

notes.explains: Bg5 traps the queen because if Qxg5, Nxf7 forks queen and rook. This works because the f7 square is vacated.
notes.teaches: Look for deflection and fork combinations. The queen on h4 is unsupported and vulnerable.
notes.plans: Play Bg5, winning the queen or decisive material. If black avoids the trap, White still has a huge development advantage.

notes.explains: After Bc4, Black must take on e5 to defend f7. Then Qh5 is an intermediate move that forces a favorable queen trade or wins material.
notes.teaches: Intermediate checks can disrupt the opponent's coordination and force a favorable endgame.
notes.plans: If Qxh5, Bxh5+ and then take the knight on e5. Black's king is exposed and White has a clear advantage.

notes.explains: After Bxe5, Black should not rush to recapture. Playing Nc6 first avoids leaving the fianchettoed square, which would allow White Bh6. The pawn is not going anywhere.
notes.teaches: Don't automatically recapture; consider intermediate moves that improve piece placement. Leaving the fianchettoed bishop can be exploited.
notes.plans: Play Nc6, threatening the bishop. If White moves it, capture the pawn with the knight, keeping the bishop on g7.

notes.explains: Black has an extra pawn and the bishop pair. White's knight is passive, and the c4 pawn is weak. Black should prioritize controlling the only open d-file before completing development.
notes.teaches: When there is only one open file, fight for it immediately. Infiltrating the second rank can win material before the opponent can defend.
notes.plans: Play Rd8, threatening to double rooks and invade on d2. After White defends, capture the b2 pawn if possible.

notes.explains: White's bishop on f3 looks clumsy. Black plays c6 to solidify the center and prepare to invade on d2. The bishop on f3 is now poorly placed.
notes.teaches: Use pawn moves like c6 to restrict the opponent's pieces and create a solid pawn chain. This also prepares further infiltration.
notes.plans: Continue with Rd2 or capture the b2 pawn. The bishop on f3 is a target; Black can later challenge it with ...b5 or ...Bf5.

notes.explains: Black infiltrates with Rd2, attacking b2. White offers the pawn, so Black takes it, gaining a second extra pawn. The d-file is now controlled.
notes.teaches: When the opponent offers material, take it unless there is a concrete tactical reason not to. Simplify when ahead.
notes.plans: Capture on b2, then consolidate. Avoid unnecessary complications; simplify by trading rooks if possible.

notes.explains: After taking on b2, Black is up two pawns. White tries to complicate with Rfd1. Black should avoid unnecessary risks and find a safe way to consolidate.
notes.teaches: When up material, avoid complications. Look for moves that maintain the advantage without creating counterplay. Self-pinning moves can be safe if you have a release valve.
notes.plans: Play Bd4, a self-pin that is safe because e5 can always push. Then develop the bishop to e6 and prepare to trade rooks.

notes.explains: Bd4 pins the bishop to the king, but Black can always push e5 to break the pin. The bishop is safe and well-placed. White's knight on g4 is misplaced.
notes.teaches: A pin is only dangerous if the pinned piece cannot be defended or moved. Here, e5 is a ready resource, so the pin is harmless.
notes.plans: Develop Be6, then drop the bishop back to safety. Prepare to trade rooks and push the a-pawn.

notes.explains: Black completes development with Be6. The bishop on d4 is no longer pinned, and Black is ready to trade rooks. White's knight on g4 is poorly placed.
notes.teaches: Complete development even when ahead. A well-placed piece is more valuable than a rushed attack.
notes.plans: Trade rooks on the d-file, then target the c4 pawn. After winning more material, push the a-pawn to promote.

notes.explains: Black drops the bishop back to d4, opening the d-file for rook trades. White's rook on d1 blunders the c4 pawn after the trade.
notes.teaches: In endgames, trade pieces to reduce counterplay. Use the open file to infiltrate and win more pawns.
notes.plans: Trade rooks on d1, then capture the c4 pawn. After that, push the a-pawn while keeping the king safe.

notes.explains: Black wins the c4 pawn after trading rooks. Now up three pawns, the conversion is straightforward: push the a-pawn.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, focus on the most direct plan: advance your passed pawn. Avoid unnecessary risks.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn. If the opponent's knight tries to block, use the bishop to support the pawn or create threats.

notes.explains: Black pushes the a-pawn. White's knight cannot stop it. The bishop supports the pawn, and the king is safe from checks.
notes.teaches: A passed pawn must be pushed. Use your pieces to support it, and don't be distracted by side threats.
notes.plans: Continue pushing the a-pawn. If White tries to block, trade pieces or use the bishop to clear the path.

notes.explains: Black's setup with ...e6, ...d6, ...Bb7, ...c6, ...h6, ...g5 is extremely passive and neglects development. White has built a strong center with d4, e4, and c4, and now must decide how to break through.
notes.teaches: Against passive play, complete your development first before striking in the center. Patience is key; premature pawn breaks can allow the opponent to close the position.
notes.plans: Prepare e5 with Rfe1 to support the break. After e5 d5, recapture with the knight on e5 to keep the center fluid and exploit light-square weaknesses.

notes.explains: After e5 d5 cxd5 cxd5, the position resembles a favorable French Defense structure for White. Black's bishop on b7 is bad, and the knight on g8 cannot develop to f6. White has a clear space advantage.
notes.teaches: When the opponent allows a central pawn break that leaves them with a bad bishop and no counterplay, you should aim to keep the position closed and slowly improve your pieces.
notes.plans: Play Be3 to prepare Rc1, then Nd2 to reroute the knight to c5 or f3, and eventually switch to the kingside with Qh5.

notes.explains: White has completed development and now switches the attack to the kingside with Qh5. The queen pins the g5-pawn and threatens tactical ideas like Nxd5 exd5 e6, or Bxg5. Black is paralyzed.
notes.teaches: When one side has no counterplay, you can often switch the attack from one flank to the other. The principle of two weaknesses: overloading the opponent's defenses by creating threats on both sides.
notes.plans: Threaten Nxg5, forcing the queen back to d8. Then play h4 to open the h-file, or reroute the knight to f3 to renew threats. If Black defends, continue accumulating pressure.

notes.explains: Black blunders the exchange with Rg7, allowing Nxg5. After taking, White must strike while the iron is hot: the kingside is weakened, and the queen is far away.
notes.teaches: After winning material, immediately look for ways to exploit the new weaknesses. Don't relax; the opponent's blunder often creates tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: Play h4 to open the kingside. After g6, break through with g6 fxg6 Nxg6, threatening Nxe7+ and Qxe6+.

notes.explains: The final sequence: after g6, Black's kingside collapses. White sacrifices the knight on g6 to remove the defender of f7, then wins with Qxe6+ and Bf4#.
notes.teaches: In a winning attack, don't hesitate to sacrifice material to remove key defenders. The queen and bishop coordinate for a mating net.
notes.plans: After Nxg6 Rf7, take on e7 with the knight, then Qxe6+ forces the king to d8, where Bf4 delivers checkmate.

notes.explains: Black's bishop will go to b7, so White plays f3 to reinforce the e4-pawn and neutralize that pressure.
notes.teaches: When the opponent fianchettoes, reinforce the central pawn that the bishop will target.
notes.plans: Prepare h4 and g3 to fianchetto the kingside bishop, then develop with flexibility.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf8 to defend e6, so White castles patiently and then plays Kb1 as a waiting move, improving the king's safety while keeping all options open.
notes.teaches: When the opponent defends a threat, don't rush; improve your position with useful waiting moves.
notes.plans: After Kb1, look to open the position with c3 or f4 to exploit Black's weakened dark squares.

notes.explains: Black trades his dark-squared bishop, leaving his dark squares weak. White opens the position with cxd3, opening the c-file and preparing f5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent gives up a key defender, open the position to exploit the weakened squares.
notes.plans: Play f5, then recapture with the rook to preserve the bishop for the attack. Follow up with Bf4, Qg5, and Rc6 to target the knight and deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the d4-pawn for a lead in development. Black has three pieces developed to White's zero, but Black is up a pawn.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, development lead can compensate for a pawn deficit. Don't overthink; just keep developing.
notes.plans: Castle, then put pressure on Black's position with moves like Qb3, Rc1, and later double rooks on the c-file.

notes.explains: Black's knight on c6 is undefended by pawns and overloaded defending the rook on c7. White doubles rooks on the c-file to pressure the knight.
notes.teaches: Identify undefended pieces and overloaded defenders. Pile up pressure on such targets.
notes.plans: Play Qa4 to force the knight to move, then consider Nc4 or Nxe5 to win material or maintain the initiative.

notes.explains: White has a winning position but blunders with Rc7, allowing Black to trade rooks and win an exchange. The correct move was Nd8, forking king and rook.
notes.teaches: Always check for tactical motifs like forks before committing to a move. One mistake can turn a winning position into a losing one.
notes.plans: In the winning line, play Nd8 to fork king and rook, then take on e6 and win Black's pawns.

notes.explains: After trading rooks on c8, White plays Qd2, connecting the rooks and preparing to bring the other rook to d1. Black's bishop on c8 is passive, and White's center is solid.
notes.teaches: Trading rooks can be beneficial when it leaves the opponent with a passive piece and you have a space advantage. The queen is well-placed on d2, supporting the center and eyeing the kingside.
notes.plans: White will continue with Rd1, f3, and then consider h4 to create weaknesses on the kingside. The long-term plan is to prepare d5 under favorable conditions.

notes.explains: White plays f3 to reinforce e4 and prepare a future d5. Black's bishop on b7 is passive, and White's pieces are optimally placed. The position is slightly better for White.
notes.teaches: f3 is a useful consolidating move that strengthens the center and prevents Black from occupying e4. It also prepares a later d5 push.
notes.plans: After f3, White can consider h4 to create kingside weaknesses. The idea is to probe Black's position without committing to a central break too early.

notes.explains: With all pieces optimally placed, White plays h4 to create weaknesses on the kingside. This move is not a pawn storm but a probe: it forces Black to decide between h5 (weakening dark squares) or allowing h5-h6 (creating a hook for later attacks).
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and your pieces are well-placed, use pawn moves like h4 to create long-term weaknesses in the opponent's camp. Even on the same side as your own king, such moves are safe if the opponent has no counterplay.
notes.plans: If Black plays h5, White can follow up with Bh6 to trade the dark-squared bishops, exploiting the weakened dark squares. If Black ignores, White pushes h5-h6 to deprive the black king of luft and create tactical opportunities.

notes.explains: Black plays h5, weakening the dark squares. White immediately exploits this by playing Bh6, threatening to trade off Black's powerful fianchettoed bishop. Black cannot save it with Bh8 because the rook is still on f8.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their kingside dark squares, trading off their fianchettoed bishop is often a strategic victory. The timing is crucial: do it before Black can move the rook and save the bishop with Bh8.
notes.plans: After Bh6, White intends to trade on g7, then bring the queen to g5 and the knight to g3 or f4, creating a powerful attack against the weakened black king.

notes.explains: White plays Ng3, preparing to trade on g7 and then bring the queen to g5. The knight on g3 supports the kingside attack and does not block the queen's path to g5 (unlike Nf4).
notes.teaches: When attacking, choose the knight's square to maximize coordination. Ng3 keeps the queen's route to g5 open and allows the knight to later jump to f5 or h5.
notes.plans: White will play Bxg7 Kxg7, then Qg5, threatening Nxh5. Black must defend, but White can then open the center with d5, creating multiple threats.

notes.explains: After the bishop trade and Qg5, Black's king is on h8. White plays d5, opening the center and creating a passed pawn. The knight on g3 and bishop on b3 now have clear paths to join the attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, opening the center with a pawn break like d5 can be devastating. The passed pawn also adds pressure and can be pushed further.
notes.plans: After exd5, White recaptures with the rook (or bishop), threatening to push d6. The knight can go to e4 or f5, and the bishop can drop back to c2, pinning the g6 pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays f5 to block the knight and bishop, but White pushes d6, reopening the bishop's diagonal and threatening the rook on d8. The pawn on d6 is a powerful passed pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to block your pieces, push the passed pawn further. It creates new threats and forces the opponent to defend passively.
notes.plans: After d6, White threatens Bxf7 (if the knight moves) or simply pushes d7. The immediate threat is Bxf7, winning the queen or checkmating.

notes.explains: Black plays Ng8, hoping to defend, but White plays Bxf7, a deflection sacrifice. Black must take with the queen (Qxf7), after which White captures the rook on d8 with the queen, winning material.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is the only defender of a key piece, a sacrifice on a square defended by the queen can deflect it and win material. Always look for such tactical opportunities when the opponent's pieces are overloaded.
notes.plans: After Qxf7 Qxd8, White has a winning material advantage. The simplest continuation is to push the d-pawn to promotion.

notes.explains: After the deflection, White simplifies to a winning endgame. The d-pawn promotes, and Black's king is vulnerable. The final checkmate is Qh8#.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive material advantage, simplify by trading pieces while avoiding counterplay. Promoting the passed pawn is often the most straightforward path to victory.
notes.plans: Push the d-pawn to promotion, using checks to avoid stalemate or perpetual check. In this game, the queen delivers checkmate on h8.

notes.explains: This is the prettier mate line, demonstrating how a queen and pawn can deliver mate with the king trapped on the h-file.
notes.teaches: Aesthetic mating patterns often arise from precise king-hunt technique; knowing these patterns helps in practical play.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...Bg4, White has the classic Bxf7+ and Ng5+ tactic, winning the bishop on g4. This is a common amateur trap.
notes.teaches: Always be alert for tactical motifs like the Greek Gift sacrifice when the opponent pins a knight to the queen.
notes.plans: Play Bxf7+ Kxf7 Ng5+ Kg8 Qxg4, winning a piece.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...e6 instead of ...a5, White can push d4, opening the center and activating the pieces. Black's position becomes cramped and vulnerable.
notes.teaches: When the opponent delays development, strike in the center to open lines and increase the initiative.
notes.plans: After d4, if Black captures, recapture with the knight and continue developing with Re1, etc.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...Bc5, White can play Be3 or simply develop, maintaining pressure. The position is dynamically balanced but White has a slight edge due to better development.
notes.teaches: In open positions, piece activity and king safety are more important than material equality.
notes.plans: Continue developing with Be3, Rad1, etc., aiming to exploit Black's exposed king or weak pawns.

notes.explains: Black castles, walking into a classic Greek Gift sacrifice. White can play Bxh7+ followed by Ng5+, Qh5, etc., leading to a winning attack.
notes.teaches: The Greek Gift sacrifice is a standard attacking motif when the bishop is on d3 and the knight can reach g5. It exploits the weakened kingside after castling.
notes.plans: Execute Bxh7+ Kxh7, Ng5+ Kg6 (or Kg8), Qg4, etc., with a mating attack.

notes.explains: White recaptures on d4, and Black's bishop on c8 remains hemmed in. White has a small but lasting advantage due to superior piece activity and Black's bad bishop.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a bad bishop can be a decisive weakness. White should aim to keep the position closed and exploit Black's lack of space.
notes.plans: Play c3 to support the bishop, then develop the queenside with b3 and Bb2, gradually increasing pressure.

notes.explains: Black plays Qb6, attacking the b2 pawn and preparing to support the queenside pawns. White should respond with a4 to break up Black's pawn chain.
notes.teaches: When Black builds a queenside pawn chain (b5, c4), White can undermine it with b3 and a4. The timing is critical: a4 is strong when the rook on a8 is undefended.
notes.plans: Play a4 immediately, exploiting the undefended rook on a8. If Black plays ...a6, then axb5 axb5? loses the rook. This forces Black to defend passively.

notes.explains: White plays a4, threatening to break the queenside pawn chain. Black cannot play ...a6 because axb5 axb5? loses the rook. This forces Black to defend with a piece.
notes.teaches: A pawn break like a4 can be devastating when the opponent's rook is undefended. The threat of winning a pawn or exposing weaknesses forces concessions.
notes.plans: After a4, if Black plays ...Ba6, White can capture on b5 and c4, leaving Black with a weak pawn on c4. Then White will target that pawn with Rb1, Qe2, etc.

notes.explains: White clears the queenside pawns, leaving Black with a weak isolated pawn on c4. White now has a clear target and better piece activity.
notes.teaches: Exchanging pawns to create a permanent weakness (isolated pawn) is a key strategic idea. The c4 pawn is a long-term liability for Black.
notes.plans: White will complete development (c3, Nbd2, Rc1, etc.) and then surround and win the c4 pawn. Black cannot easily defend it.

notes.explains: White plays c3 to solidify the center and prepares Nbd2 to target the c4 pawn. Black's rook on d8 does not threaten d4 because the knight on f3 guards it.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, solidifying the center with c3 is often necessary before pursuing a queenside plan. The knight on f3 is a key defender.
notes.plans: White will play Nbd2, then perhaps Ne4 or Nf1-e3 to pressure c4. The c4 pawn is a fixed target that cannot be easily defended.

notes.explains: Black plays f6, challenging the e5 pawn and opening the center. White must reassess: the plan to target c4 is now secondary to exploiting the new weakness on e6.
notes.teaches: Flexibility is crucial. When the opponent changes the structure, be ready to switch plans. Here, the opening of the center favors the better-developed side (White).
notes.plans: White should capture on f6 (exf6), opening the e-file and targeting the weak e6 pawn. Then Qe2 or Rfe1 puts pressure on e6.

notes.explains: White captures on f6 and plays Rfe1, putting pressure on e6. Black's king is still in the center, and the e6 pawn is a major weakness.
notes.teaches: After opening the center, the side with better development should target the opponent's weak pawns. The rook on e1 adds pressure and prepares to double on the e-file.
notes.plans: White will play Qe2 or Qd3, attacking e6. Black cannot easily defend it because the king is exposed and pieces are undeveloped.

notes.explains: Black plays Kf7 to defend e6, but this is a decisive mistake. White can now play Ng5+, forcing the king back or to a worse square.
notes.teaches: The king is a poor defender in open positions. Moving it forward often creates new tactical opportunities for the opponent.
notes.plans: Play Ng5+ Ke7 (or Kg8), then capture on e6 with the rook or knight, winning a pawn and exposing the king further.

notes.explains: White plays d5, winning the knight on c6 because the queen on b6 is pinned to the king. Black's position collapses immediately.
notes.teaches: A pin can be decisive. Here, the queen's pin on the knight allows a simple pawn advance to win material and launch a mating attack.
notes.plans: After d5, Black cannot avoid losing the knight. White will then deliver checkmate with Qd4+ and Bf4, or similar.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with Qxd6#. The game is a clear example of converting a positional advantage into a direct attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and pieces are undeveloped, a coordinated attack can end the game quickly. Accurate calculation of forcing moves is essential.
notes.plans: The mating sequence is forced: d5 wins the knight, then Qxd5+ forces the king to c7, and Bf4+ Bd6 Qxd6#.

notes.explains: This game illustrates key ideas of the Nimzowitsch French: rapid development, undermining the queenside pawn chain, flexibility in switching plans, and exploiting the opponent's king exposure.
notes.teaches: The Nimzowitsch French is a practical weapon that teaches closed position strategy, pawn breaks, and attacking chess. It is effective up to a high level.

notes.explains: After Qxd8+ Kxd8, White has a slight advantage due to the d5 square being a permanent weakness, while d4 is protected by the c3 pawn.
notes.teaches: In queenless middlegames, a central outpost like d5 can provide a lasting advantage.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to d5 via Na3-c4-e3, using Bg5 to eliminate the f6 knight if needed.

notes.explains: If Black plays Be6, White can trade bishops to weaken Black's pawn structure and maintain the d5 outpost.
notes.teaches: Trading pieces to create a lasting structural weakness is a common strategic theme.
notes.plans: Play Bxe6, then continue with Na3-c4-e3 aiming for d5.

notes.explains: Black's doubled e-pawns and the d5 hole give White a stable advantage. The knight aims for d5.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns can be a long-term weakness, especially when they leave an outpost.
notes.plans: Play Na3, then Nc4, and eventually Ne3-d5. Use Bg5 to trade off the f6 knight if needed.

notes.explains: Na3 begins the knight's journey to d5. Black may try to prevent it with b5 or other moves.
notes.teaches: A multi-move knight maneuver is a plan, not a forced sequence; adapt to the opponent's responses.
notes.plans: Continue with Nc4, and if Black plays b5, consider Bg5 to exchange the f6 knight or play a4 to undermine b5.

notes.explains: If Black plays b5 to prevent Nc4, White can play Bg5 to exchange the f6 knight, then Nc4 is possible because b5 no longer attacks c4.
notes.teaches: When a pawn move threatens your knight, consider removing the defender of the square.
notes.plans: Play Bg5, then after ...h6 Bxf6, play Nc4, and continue towards d5.

notes.explains: Black develops the bishop to b7. White can now play Ne3, but must be careful because the d3 bishop is undefended.
notes.teaches: Always check for tactical vulnerabilities before executing a knight maneuver.

notes.explains: In the Steinitz Defense, Black plays d6, creating a pin on the e5 pawn. White can exploit this by opening the center with d4.
notes.teaches: When the opponent creates a pin, consider opening the center to exploit the pinned piece.
notes.plans: Play d4, and after exd4, Nxd4, then Bxc6 to soften the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: White develops with Bg5, pinning the knight and increasing pressure. Black's doubled c-pawns are a long-term weakness.
notes.teaches: In positions with a structural advantage, develop actively and maintain pressure.
notes.plans: Continue with Nc3, Qe2, and eventually target the e5 pawn or the c5 pawn.

notes.explains: White centralizes the queen and prepares to take on e5. Black must be careful not to allow Qxe5 due to tactics.
notes.teaches: Centralize the queen to increase pressure and threaten captures.
notes.plans: Play Qxe5 after ensuring safety, or play c3 to control b4 and d4, then take on e5.

notes.explains: Black weakens the kingside with ...g5. White retreats the bishop to g3, maintaining pressure.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their kingside, keep pieces aimed at that area.
notes.plans: Consider playing h4 to exploit the weakened kingside, or continue with central play.

notes.explains: Black has won two pawns and the queen is active. White's king is exposed, but Black is winning easily.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplify by trading queens if possible, but avoid unnecessary risks. Keep pieces active to prevent counterplay.
notes.plans: Black can develop the rook to d8, play b6, and eventually push the queenside pawns.

notes.explains: White plays c3 to control d4 and b4, preparing to develop the bishop and consolidate the extra material.
notes.teaches: Consolidate by controlling key squares and preventing counterplay.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to e3 or f4, then bring the rook to d1.

notes.explains: Black trades queens, entering an endgame where White is up a pawn but has a passive bishop on c1. White must untangle.
notes.teaches: In endgames with a passive piece, prioritize activating that piece even if it requires awkward moves.
notes.plans: Play Kf1 to prepare Re1, then find a way to develop the bishop, possibly via a4 and Ra2.

notes.explains: White plays a4, preparing Ra2 to defend b2 and free the bishop. This is a creative way to activate the bishop.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must make a temporary passive move (Ra2) to achieve a greater goal (bishop activation).
notes.plans: Play Ra2, then Bf4 or Be3, and eventually bring the rook back into play.

notes.explains: Ra2 defends b2, allowing the bishop to move. The rook is temporarily passive but will be freed later.
notes.teaches: Static vs dynamic: a piece can be temporarily passive if it enables a more important plan.
notes.plans: Play Bf4, then bring the king to c2 or e2, and eventually activate the rook.

notes.explains: White finally activates the bishop and rook, and the king centralizes. White is up a pawn with active pieces.
notes.teaches: In endgames, centralize the king and activate all pieces before pushing pawns.
notes.plans: Play a5 to fix the a6 pawn, then create a passed pawn on the queenside.

notes.explains: White converts the extra pawn into a passed pawn and wins the rook endgame. The king is active.
notes.teaches: In pawn endgames, active king and passed pawns are decisive. Make all improvements before pushing.
notes.plans: Push the c-pawn, using the king to support it.

notes.explains: After f5, if White prevents f4, Black can still play f4 anyway. If White captures, Black recaptures and White drops a knight on f4. Black then centralizes the bishop on e5 and eyes a sacrifice on g3.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you can force a break even if the opponent tries to stop it. The knight on g3 check is a typical sacrifice to open the king.
notes.plans: Play f4, then after exchanges, play Ng3+ to open lines. If White avoids the sacrifice, take the exchange and continue the attack.

notes.explains: Black wins the exchange but must continue developing. The key is to not forget basic principles after gaining material. Black plays Nd7, defending the pawn and preparing to bring the rook to d8.
notes.teaches: After winning material, continue developing and consolidating. Don't become complacent.
notes.plans: Play Nd7, then Qe7 to smoke out the queen, and bring the rook to d8.

notes.explains: In the endgame, Black still applies middlegame ideas. The pawn push g4 breaks through, and the bishop maneuver Bh3 forces White's pawn to g3, weakening the king.
notes.teaches: Endgames can still feature attacking ideas. Look for pawn breaks and piece maneuvers to create weaknesses.
notes.plans: Push g4, then play Bh3 to force g3, then take on g2 and promote the pawn or force White to give up the bishop.

notes.explains: White plays Bb2, a prophylactic move to discourage Black from using the long diagonal. It also connects rooks and prepares for potential pawn breaks.
notes.teaches: Not every piece needs to be aggressively placed; prophylactic moves can prevent opponent's ideas and improve coordination.
notes.plans: After Bb2, continue development and wait for Black to commit. If Black takes on b4, the bishop becomes strong on the long diagonal.

notes.explains: White is up a piece and must avoid passive play. The knight goes to c4, a central square, threatening d7. Black prevents Nd7 with Rxd7, but White's queen is undefended, so White moves the queen to g3, x-raying g7.
notes.teaches: When up material, play actively but watch for tactical details like undefended pieces and standoffs.
notes.plans: Play Qg3 to pressure g7, then after Black retreats the bishop, play Rfd1 and prepare Nd7.

notes.explains: White notices the black king has no escape squares. By sacrificing the rook on f6, White opens the diagonal for the bishop to deliver checkmate. The key is to ensure the sacrifice is forced.
notes.teaches: When the king is trapped, look for sacrifices to open lines. Check move orders to ensure the opponent cannot escape.
notes.plans: Play Rxf6, forcing gxf6, then Bxf6+ and Qg7#. If Black doesn't recapture, use other threats to win.

notes.explains: Recapturing with the pawn (axb3) opens the a-file and secures the bishop on c4, creating imbalance. The doubled b-pawns are not a concern; piece activity matters more.
notes.teaches: In endgames, prioritize active pieces and open files over pawn structure. Doubled pawns are often less important than dynamic factors.
notes.plans: Use the open a-file and active bishop to pressure Black. Aim to infiltrate with the rook on the seventh rank.

notes.explains: White has a rook and two pieces for the queen, but the key is the active rook on e7 and the knight on d5. Black's bishop is hanging, and White threatens Nxc7+.
notes.teaches: In piece imbalances, coordination and threats matter more than material count. Avoid assumptions—keep looking for tactical resources even when ahead.
notes.plans: Play Nd5, threatening Nxc7+ and Bxe5. If Black defends, continue with active rook play and centralize the king.

notes.explains: After Nd5, Black's best defense was Kg7 to protect the bishop, but instead Black blundered with ...Nc6, allowing Ne8+ winning the exchange.
notes.teaches: After a blunder, stay calm and assess the actual threats. The only move to defend the bishop was Kg7; panic leads to collapse.
notes.plans: If Black plays Kg7, White has the bishop pair and initiative, but the game continues. Avoid rushing; untangle pieces methodically.

notes.explains: In the King's Indian, White often plays f3 (Sämisch variation) to support e4. Black's plan is to fianchetto the bishop and later attack White's center with pawn breaks like e5 or c5. The key is not to allow White to close the center with d5.
notes.teaches: In hypermodern openings, let White occupy the center, then undermine it with pawn breaks.
notes.plans: Fianchetto the bishop, play d6, castle, then prepare e5 or c5.

notes.explains: White's f3 pawn move weakens the e3 bishop, which becomes undefended (type 2). Black exploits this by playing ...Nh5, attacking the defender of the e2 bishop, winning a piece.
notes.teaches: Categorize pieces as type 1 (undefended), type 2 (defended by one piece), or defended (by pawn or multiple pieces). Target type 2 pieces by removing their defender.
notes.plans: After winning the bishop, consolidate by developing and connecting rooks. Use the extra material to simplify into a winning endgame.

notes.explains: The queen is always 'undefended' because it must move when attacked by a lesser piece, regardless of how many pieces 'defend' it.
notes.teaches: Treat the queen as a type 1 undefended piece in tactical calculations, since it can't be defended in the usual sense.

notes.explains: A piece defended by a pawn is much harder to undermine than one defended by a piece, because pawns cannot be easily removed or deflected.
notes.teaches: Prefer to defend your pieces with pawns when possible; it makes them 'defended' in the safest sense. To attack such a piece, you must first remove the pawn.

notes.explains: Black fianchettoes the bishop and allows White a big center, then attacks it with ...e5. White's f4 (Austrian Attack) is met by ...e5, opening the center.
notes.teaches: In the Modern, Black's strategy is to let White build a center and then undermine it with pawn breaks like ...e5 or ...c5, using the fianchettoed bishop for pressure.
notes.plans: Develop pieces (Nf6, O-O), then play ...e5 to challenge the center. After exchanges, aim to win White's central pawns or create a passed pawn.

notes.explains: Black avoids taking on c3 because it would give White a pawn chain supporting d4. Instead, Black plays ...Be6 to defend the knight and maintain the blockade on d5.
notes.teaches: Don't automatically take on c3 to create doubled pawns; consider whether the doubled pawns actually help the opponent by supporting the center or opening files for their rooks.
notes.plans: Keep the knight on d5 as a blockader. After White's mistake (Bc4?), exploit the undefended bishop with ...Nxe5, winning two central pawns.

notes.explains: After winning two pawns, Black simplifies by trading queens and knights, then activates the rooks. The knight on g7 covers key squares, making Black's king safe.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplify by trading pieces, especially queens, and activate your rooks. Don't panic if your king is exposed; use your pieces to defend.
notes.plans: Develop quickly (Nc6, connect rooks), then infiltrate the second rank with the rook. Use the extra pawns to create a passed pawn and win the endgame.

notes.explains: After Qh4, White deliberately gives up the e5 pawn to create a powerful attack. Black takes on e5, but White has a follow-up that wins on the spot (though the opponent avoids it by playing Ng4).
notes.teaches: Sometimes sacrificing a pawn for the initiative is stronger than a safe retreat. Qh4 is a master-level idea that sets up threats against f6 and h7, exploiting Black's lack of coordination.
notes.plans: White intends to follow Qxe5 with a rook lift to e1, but since the bishop isn't developed, the immediate threat is less clear; however, the queen on h4 creates pressure that Black cannot easily handle.

notes.explains: After Nxc7, White wins a pawn and threatens the rook. Black is undeveloped and cannot defend properly.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is behind in development, every tactical blow is more effective. The knight fork on c7 exploits the loose pieces and the king's vulnerability.
notes.plans: White will capture the rook on a8 or continue attacking the queen and king, maintaining the initiative.

notes.explains: Black plays …Bxf2+? hoping to create counterplay, but White replies Rxf2! Qxf2+ Rxf2, winning the queen. The f2 pawn's absence allows the rook to capture with check, and Black's queen is overloaded.
notes.teaches: When the opponent sacrifices material to open lines, you must calculate carefully. Here, capturing with the rook is winning because it comes with check and wins the queen. The f2 pawn's removal creates a discovered attack.
notes.plans: After Rxf2, White is up a piece and Black's king is exposed. White will consolidate and win.

notes.explains: The move Rxf2 is more elegant than Rd1 because it prevents Black from playing Qxc1+ with check. The rook on f2 also attacks the queen, forcing a win.
notes.teaches: In tactical positions, prefer the move that gives the opponent the fewest counter-chances. Rxf2 is 'cultured' because it avoids unnecessary checks and keeps the attack flowing.
notes.plans: White will capture the queen and remain with a decisive material advantage.

notes.explains: After Rxf2, White is up a piece and Black's king is exposed. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: Once you have a decisive material advantage, simplify and avoid unnecessary risks. The endgame is a matter of technique.
notes.plans: White will activate the king and push pawns, while Black has no counterplay.

notes.explains: White places the bishop on d3 and will follow with c3 and Bf4, resembling a London system. Black's main challenge is finding a good square for the light-squared bishop on c8.
notes.teaches: In the Caro-Kann Exchange, black often struggles to develop the c8-bishop; delaying ...Nc6 in favor of ...Nf6 can allow an early ...Bg4.
notes.plans: Black aims to develop the knight to f6 and then the bishop to g4 before white can play h3.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6 instead of the automatic Nc6, intending to develop the c8-bishop to g4 before white can play h3.
notes.teaches: Sometimes delaying natural moves like ...Nc6 can solve development problems; here ...Nf6 prepares ...Bg4, which is more active than ...Bf5.
notes.plans: After ...Nf6, if white plays c3, black can play ...Bg4; if white plays h3, black can revert to ...Nc6 and aim for ...e5.

notes.explains: White plays h3 to prevent ...Bg4, so black develops the knight to c6. Now white has played c3, and black can play ...e5 to challenge the center and create an IQP.
notes.teaches: When white delays knight development (e.g., playing c3 and h3 instead of Nf3), black can strike in the center with ...e5, often leading to an isolated queen pawn (IQP) for white.
notes.plans: Black plays ...e5, aiming to open the position and give white an isolated pawn on d5.

notes.explains: White plays Nf3, the best line. Black must decide which piece to capture on d3. Taking with the knight eliminates the light-squared bishop, which is more valuable than the knight.
notes.teaches: When given a choice of captures, consider which piece is more important to remove. Here, the light-squared bishop is a key attacking piece, so capturing it with the knight is preferable.
notes.plans: Black plays Nxd3+, forcing Qxd3, then develops the dark-squared bishop to d6.

notes.explains: Black develops the dark-squared bishop to d6, a safe and active square. It eyes the kingside and avoids the problems of ...Bc5 (which allows Bb5+ forcing ...Nd7) or ...Be7 (too passive).
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, the dark-squared bishop is often best placed on d6, where it is safe and contributes to the attack.
notes.plans: Black will castle, and if white plays Bg5, black will sacrifice the d5-pawn with ...h6 to activate the bishops.

notes.explains: White captures the pawn on d5, giving black the bishop pair. Black now has two bishops against two knights in an open position, which is a favorable imbalance.
notes.teaches: The bishop pair is a powerful asset in open positions. Sacrificing a pawn to obtain it is often worth it, especially when the opponent's knights are not well-coordinated.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Rd8, attacking the queen and threatening ...Bh2+ to force the queen away from the center.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Rd8, attacking the queen and threatening ...Bh2+ (which would win the queen if it captures on d5). White moves the queen to e3, the best square.
notes.teaches: When you have the bishop pair and an open position, look for tactical threats like ...Bh2+ that exploit the opponent's undeveloped pieces. X-ray attacks on the queen are common.
notes.plans: Black now plays ...Bf5, developing with tempo and threatening to capture on b7. The idea is to keep the initiative and prevent white from completing development.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Bf5, developing the bishop and threatening ...Qxb7. White cannot take on b7 because ...Rab8 would trap the queen. This move keeps the pressure on white's position.
notes.teaches: When you have the initiative, develop with tempo. Moves like ...Bf5 force the opponent to react and prevent them from consolidating.
notes.plans: Black will continue to harass the queen and look for ways to exploit white's lack of development, possibly with ...Bd3 or ...Bc7 ideas.

notes.explains: White plays Rd1, a natural move to contest the d-file. Black now has a choice between the direct ...Bd3 and the more subtle ...Bc7. Both are good, but ...Bd3 is more forcing.
notes.teaches: When you have multiple good options, trust your intuition and pick the most aggressive one. Spending too much time on equal alternatives is wasteful.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Bd3, attacking the rook and preparing ...Bf4 to harass the queen. The bishop on d3 is untouchable and sets up further threats.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Bd3, attacking the rook and threatening ...Bf4. The bishop is immune because ...Bf4 would attack the queen and create mating threats. White's queen is running out of squares.
notes.teaches: Initiative can be maintained by placing pieces on active squares that create multiple threats. The bishop on d3 is a classic example: it attacks the rook and prepares a battery with the other bishop.
notes.plans: After white moves the rook, black will play ...Bf4, forcing the queen to a worse square. The goal is to trap the queen or win material.

notes.explains: White plays Rd2, avoiding the immediate threat. Black now plays ...Bf4, attacking the queen. The queen's only safe squares are e1 and c5; e1 loses to ...Re8 trapping the queen, so c5 is forced.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is short of squares, look for ways to restrict it further. Here, ...Bf4 forces the queen to c5, where it is exposed.
notes.plans: Black will continue to harass the queen, possibly with ...b6 and ...a5, driving it to a3. The ultimate idea is to trap the queen with ...Bd6.

notes.explains: Black chases the queen to a3 with ...b6 and ...a5. The queen is now on the edge of the board, severely restricted. Black's bishops dominate the center and kingside.
notes.teaches: Pushing the opponent's queen to the edge of the board is a strategic success. It reduces the queen's influence and makes it a target.
notes.plans: Black now looks for a way to trap the queen or win material. The key idea is ...Bd6, threatening ...b4 and ...axb4, opening lines against the queen.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Bd6, threatening ...b4 and ...axb4, opening the a-file against the queen. White must respond with b4, but then ...axb4 opens the a-file and the queen is trapped.
notes.teaches: A retreating move like ...Bd6 can be powerful when it sets up a tactical threat. Here, the bishop returns to d6 to force b4, after which the queen is trapped.
notes.plans: After ...b4, black plays ...axb4, opening the a-file. The queen on a3 is then attacked by the rook on a8, and white must give up material to save it.

notes.explains: White plays b4 and Qb2, trying to save the queen. Black now has a choice: capture on b1 or keep the bishops. Keeping the bishops with ...Bg6 is stronger, as it maintains pressure.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage (here, the bishop pair), avoid unnecessary piece exchanges. Keeping the bishops increases your winning chances.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Bg6, maintaining the bishop pair and keeping the knight on b1 under pressure. White's position is paralyzed.

notes.explains: White plays cxb4, opening the c-file. Black now has a choice between ...Bc7 and ...Bf8. ...Bf8 is better because it keeps the bishop on the long diagonal and maintains pressure on d4.
notes.teaches: In complex positions, keep your bishops on active diagonals. ...Bf8 keeps the bishop on the a3-f8 diagonal, where it can later go to b6 or c7.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Bf8, preparing to put the bishop on b6 or c7. The idea is to keep the initiative and eventually win the knight on c3.

notes.explains: White plays Rxd8+ and Nc3, trying to simplify. Black now has a winning tactic: ...Rd3 attacks the knight, and if it moves, ...Bxb4 wins the queen. White's best is ...Rc1, but then ...Bf4 and ...Rc2 follow.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's knight is undefended, look for ways to attack it with your rook. Here, ...Rd3 is a simple move that creates multiple threats.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Rd3, attacking the knight. If the knight moves, ...Bxb4 wins the queen. White's best defense is ...Rc1, but then ...Bf4 and ...Rc2 maintain the pressure.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Bf5, a subtle move that prepares ...Rxf3 gxf3 Qg6+ forking the king and rook on c2. This wins material.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a quiet move like ...Bf5 can set up a tactical shot. Here, it clears the g6 square for the queen, creating a fork.
notes.plans: After ...Bf5, if white plays ...Ne1, black plays ...Rd8, attacking the rook on c2. The rook must move to e2, then ...Be5 pins the knight, and ...Rc8 wins the knight on c3.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Rc8, attacking the pinned knight on c3. The knight is lost because it is attacked twice and defended only once. White cannot save it without losing more material.
notes.teaches: When a piece is pinned, attack it with another piece. Here, the knight on c3 is pinned by the bishop on e5, and ...Rc8 adds a second attacker, winning the knight.
notes.plans: After winning the knight, black will simplify to a winning endgame with an extra piece.

notes.explains: Black wins the knight and simplifies to a winning endgame with an extra piece. The rest is technique: trade queens, freeze white's pawns with ...b5, and pick them off with the bishop.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, simplify by trading pieces while keeping a material advantage. Use the 'deep freeze' technique (playing ...b5) to immobilize enemy pawns and then capture them.
notes.plans: Black will trade queens, play ...b5 to freeze white's queenside pawns, and then use the bishops to capture them. The extra piece will decide the game.

notes.explains: Against Bc4 in the Sicilian, Black can play e6 at any moment to blunt the bishop. Developing Nf6 first is better than Nc6 because Nc6 might allow e5. After e6, d5 opens the center, which is especially good when White has played f3.
notes.teaches: When White plays Bc4 in the Sicilian, Black can neutralize it with e6 and later d5, exploiting White's f3 weakness.
notes.plans: Develop Nf6, then e6, then d5 to open the center.

notes.explains: After d5 and cxd5, Black recaptures with the bishop (Bxd7) to avoid ruining the pawn structure with Nxd7. Then Bd7 is a solid developing move, not the most active but effective.
notes.teaches: Not every development move needs to be the most active; solid, normal moves are often sufficient.
notes.plans: Play Bd7, then consider Qb6 to pressure b2 and eye the weakened diagonal a7-g1 caused by f3.

notes.explains: Qb6 attacks b2 and eyes the a7-g1 diagonal, weakened by White's f3. Then c4 opens the diagonal and attacks the knight on d5, which lacks defenders. After cxd5, Black can win material by reinforcing pressure on the knight with d4 or simply recapturing.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens a diagonal (e.g., with f3), look for ways to exploit it with queen moves and pawn breaks.
notes.plans: Play c4, then after cxd5 recapture with the pawn, then long castle and open files to attack the exposed king on e2.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6, White's d3 is passive; it blunts his bishop and often leads to a King's Indian Attack setup. Black develops harmoniously with Bg7 and later Nf6.
notes.teaches: Against passive setups, develop naturally and look for pawn breaks like f5 to create kingside pressure.
notes.plans: Play Bg7, Nf6, O-O, then f5 to expand on the kingside.

notes.explains: When White plays Nd5, Black should take with the pawn to ruin White's pawn structure. Then the knight goes to f4, attacking d5 and creating a double attack. The bishop retreats to g7, and the knight can go to a2, threatening c3 and trapping the rook if White blunders.
notes.teaches: Exchanging to damage the opponent's pawn structure is often worth it. Look for knight outposts like a2 that attack weak squares and can't be easily trapped.
notes.plans: Play exd5, then Nf4, then Na2, aiming for Nc3.

notes.explains: In the Bird Variation (e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 b5 Bb3), Black's natural move is d6, but if White forgets it, Black can play e5 to shatter White's pawns. After Nxd5, Black recaptures with the pawn, leaving White with tripled pawns.
notes.teaches: Punish the opponent's neglect of central pawn moves by breaking their pawn structure.
notes.plans: Play e5, then develop quickly, fianchetto the dark-squared bishop to attack the d4 pawn, and use the bishop to win the pawn.

notes.explains: After winning the d4 pawn, Black has a strong attack. The bishop on f6 is immobilized because it cannot leave the diagonal without allowing checkmate. Rook to e7 exploits this, threatening mate and forcing concessions.
notes.teaches: When a piece is tied to a defensive task, use that to create threats. Look for moves that exploit the opponent's immobility.
notes.plans: Play Re7, then if Bxd4, Qxd4 threatening mate; after Rf7, bring the knight to e5 forking king and rook.

notes.explains: When Black plays b6 and g6, the combination weakens the dark squares. White can play h4 to attack the g6 pawn, pushing it to h6. The pawn on h6 becomes a long-term weakness that can later be used to create a passed pawn or deliver checkmate.
notes.teaches: Punish the combination of b6 and g6 by advancing the h-pawn to create a permanent weakness.
notes.plans: Play h4, then h5, then h6, then develop normally while keeping pressure on h6.

notes.explains: After h6, White should not rush with g4 but instead develop pieces. The pawn on h6 is well-defended and Black cannot easily reinforce it. White can expand in the center with e5 and d5, creating more weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When you have a fixed weakness, don't overcommit to attacking it immediately; improve your position and create additional threats.
notes.plans: Play e5, then d5, then develop the knight to d2 to pressure d6, and eventually use the h6 pawn to win by promoting or creating a passed pawn.

notes.explains: In the endgame, piece activity is crucial. The rook on h1 can be activated via a rook lift to c7. The h6 pawn is far advanced and can become a passed pawn. Taking on g6 dislodges the h7 pawn, allowing the h6 pawn to promote.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, activate all pieces, especially rooks. Far-advanced pawns are powerful because they are closer to promotion.
notes.plans: Play Rc7, then Rxg6, then push the h-pawn to promotion.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6, Black can recapture on c6 with the pawn (dxc6) instead of the usual capture toward the center. This opens the bishop on c8 and gives Black a solid setup with pawns on e5 and f5.
notes.teaches: Sometimes capturing away from the center is better if it activates a piece or creates a favorable pawn structure.
notes.plans: Play dxc6, then Bg7, Nf6, O-O, and prepare f5 to attack on the kingside.

notes.explains: When White plays f3, it weakens the a7-g1 diagonal. Black can exploit this with c4, opening the diagonal for the queen and bishop. After Qc5, Black threatens to win the exchange. Trading queens on Black's terms (e.g., Bf8) improves Black's position.
notes.teaches: Exploit weakened diagonals with pawn breaks. When trading, look for ways to improve your position simultaneously (trading on your own terms).
notes.plans: Play c4, then Qc5, then after Qxc5, recapture with the bishop to attack the rook and pin it.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, Black activates the rook to d2 to collect pawns. The bishop on c8 is locked out, so Black repositions it via f4? (actually e6) to keep pressure. The knight on g3 is undefended, and Black can win it by exploiting the hanging rooks.
notes.teaches: In the middlegame, keep pieces active and look for hanging pieces. When both rooks are hanging, if the opponent takes one, you take the other.
notes.plans: Play Rd2, then reposition the bishop to e6, then take on a2, and eventually win the knight on g3.

notes.explains: In a similar position, if White plays Rad1, Black can lock the center with f4, making it easier to attack on the kingside. The pawn on c5 stops d4 and controls b4, preventing White's counterplay. Black then slowly pushes pawns on the kingside.
notes.teaches: Locking the center can simplify the attack on the flank. Use pawns to control key squares and limit the opponent's counterplay.
notes.plans: Play f4, then slowly push kingside pawns, using the c5 pawn to control the center.

notes.explains: Another example of trading on own terms: e3 pushes the passed pawn and prepares to recapture with the rook, improving its activity. This forces Black to deal with the pawn while White gains piece activity.
notes.teaches: When trading, look for moves that simultaneously improve your position, such as pushing a passed pawn or activating a piece.
notes.plans: Play e3, then after dxe3, recapture with the rook, then continue to attack the knight on g3.

notes.explains: Black plays Bg4, pinning the knight. White cannot take on f6 because Black recaptures with the h-pawn, developing the rook.
notes.teaches: In bishop standoffs, neither side wants to capture if it opens lines for the opponent. Let the tension remain.
notes.plans: Black continues development with e6 and Bd6, mirroring White's setup.

notes.explains: After the bishop trade, Black's knight goes to d7. White's kingside is overextended. Black should consider the advanced idea Bh5, using the knight on f6 as a temporary defender.
notes.teaches: When a pawn moves to the fifth rank, it can allow a bishop to slide in (Bh5) to create threats. This is a recurring tactical motif.
notes.plans: Bh5 hits the queen and forces White to decide between f3 (weakening the king) or moving the queen.

notes.explains: Black plays Bh5, attacking the queen. White's best is Be2 or Bb2, but White plays f3, a mistake. Black then wins two pawns.
notes.teaches: Give your opponent a dilemma; unexpected moves often induce blunders. Here, White's planned f4 was disrupted.
notes.plans: After f3, Black plays Nxd5, winning a pawn, then Qxe5, keeping the initiative.

notes.explains: Black has two extra pawns. White's king is exposed. Black castles queenside to safety, then consolidates. The plan is to trade pieces and simplify.
notes.teaches: When up material, choose a safe king position and trade down. Let the opponent come to you.
notes.plans: Black plays Kc8, Qc5 or Qb6, and slowly improves piece placement, avoiding counterplay.

notes.explains: Black wins a pawn and has a dominating position. The knight on g4 is active, and White's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: Once you have an initiative, keep the pressure. Simple moves like Rxd8 and Nxg4 are good enough; no need for flashy tactics.
notes.plans: Black plays Rd8, bringing the rook to the open file. Then Qc5 forks the knight and bishop, winning material.

notes.explains: Black played Nc6 early, blocking the bishop and the queen's defense of the e5 pawn, which is a mistake in the French. White can simply capture the e5 pawn for free.
notes.teaches: In the French Defense, avoid blocking the queen's defense of the e5 pawn with the knight on c6. Always be alert to early pawn captures.
notes.plans: After taking the pawn, simplify by exchanging knights on f6 and developing with Nf3, staying a pawn up.

notes.explains: The bishop on f1 should go to d3, not b5. Bb5 is often overestimated because Black can play c6, gaining a tempo and controlling central squares.
notes.teaches: Don't overestimate pins; they can be broken with tempo-gaining moves like c6. Place bishops on active central squares like d3 rather than pinning pieces that can easily be chased away.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to d3, then consider castling or Bg5. Avoid passive moves like Bb2.

notes.explains: The bishop on c1 is fine staying put for now; it already supports the center. The typical plan is to build a battery with Bc2 and Qd3, threatening checkmate on h7.
notes.teaches: In positions with a pawn on d4 and a bishop on d3, the battery Bc2 + Qd3 is a powerful attacking setup. Play c3 first to support d4, then Bc2, then Qd3.
notes.plans: Play c3, then Bc2, then Qd3, threatening Qh7#. If Black prevents Qd3 with c4, undermine the c4 pawn with b3.

notes.explains: After Black plays c4 to block Qd3, the c4 pawn becomes weak. The correct plan is to play b3 to undermine it, not a4 which would distract the bishop from c2.
notes.teaches: When an opponent's pawn sticks out, undermine it with a pawn break rather than attacking it directly with pieces. Keep your bishop on its active diagonal.
notes.plans: Play b3, and if Black takes, recapture with the pawn. If Black pushes b5, then take on c4 first to soften the pawn, then play Nd2 to attack it again.

notes.explains: After the battery is set up, Black is in a lose-lose situation: if Bf5, White can take with the queen due to x-ray defense; if g6, the kingside is weakened; if Qg6, White can play a desperado sacrifice.
notes.teaches: A battery threatening checkmate forces concessions. When the opponent defends with a queen, consider a desperado sacrifice: trade your queen for multiple pieces, exploiting x-ray attacks.
notes.plans: If Qg6, play Qxa8! (desperado), exposing the bishop's attack on the rook. Then the queen can continue capturing pawns or escape.

notes.explains: After the desperado, White is up material but must be careful. The move Qxb6 was slightly greedy; Qc6 would have been more accurate. However, White still has winning tactics: Bd2 attacks the queen and knight simultaneously, and after Qb2, Rfb1 skewers the queen to the knight.
notes.teaches: Loose pieces drop off. When you have multiple threats, look for moves that attack two pieces at once. A skewer can win material when the opponent's queen is overloaded.
notes.plans: Play Bd2, forcing the queen to protect the knight, then Rfb1 skewering. Alternatively, take on b6 and then capture the rook.

notes.explains: When up a rook, the two methods to convert are trades and attack. Here, trading off the last minor pieces is worth giving up a pawn. The pawn on d4 is irrelevant; focus on simplifying to a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: When up significant material, don't be obsessed with keeping every pawn. Sacrificing a pawn to trade pieces is often the fastest way to win.
notes.plans: Play Bb4 to force a bishop trade, even if it costs the d4 pawn. After trades, White has two rooks against one rook and queen, which is easily winning.

notes.explains: In the position with Bc2 and Qd3 battery, the idea is similar to a top-level game (Navara vs. Koleopoulos). White played f4 to open the e5 pawn, unleashing the bishop's potential. The bishop on c2 is not bad; it has huge potential energy.
notes.teaches: A bishop that seems blocked can become game-winning if you can open the diagonal. Kinetic vs. potential energy: look for pawn breaks that activate your pieces.
notes.plans: Play f4 to break open the center, then use the battery for a decisive attack.

notes.explains: When considering Qe2, ask the Sam Shanklin question: 'Is Qxc4 actually a threat?' It is not, because Bxa6 would pin the queen to the rook, and after Qxa6, Qxa8 wins the queen. So Black's best defense is Bb7, not protecting the c4 pawn.
notes.teaches: Don't assume a threat is real without concrete calculation. Question every assumption; sometimes the obvious threat is a trap. This enriches tactical vision.
notes.plans: If Black plays Bb7, then White can play g2 or other moves. The key is to recognize that the c4 pawn is not actually hanging.

notes.explains: After h4 g4, White plays Ng5+ forking the king and attacking e6 and f4. Black's king is exposed, and White threatens multiple pawns.
notes.teaches: When the enemy king is exposed, look for knight forks and double attacks. The knight on g5 attacks e6 and f4, creating multiple threats.
notes.plans: Capture on e6 or f4, or play Qh5 to intensify the attack.

notes.explains: White captures on e6, winning a pawn and opening lines. Black's position is falling apart.
notes.teaches: When you have the initiative, take material that also opens lines. Capturing on e6 removes a defender and opens the e-file.
notes.plans: Continue attacking with Qh5 or hxg5, aiming to break through Black's kingside.

notes.explains: White takes on f4, winning another pawn. Black's pieces are undeveloped and the king is exposed.
notes.teaches: Keep taking material if it doesn't slow your attack. Each capture weakens Black's defenses.
notes.plans: Play g6 to attack h7 and further open the kingside.

notes.explains: White plays g6, attacking h7 and threatening to open the h-file. The pawn on g6 also eyes promotion.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is close to promoting, it becomes a huge threat. Here, the g-pawn is only stopped by the rook on h8.
notes.plans: Sacrifice the queen on h7 to remove the rook and promote the pawn.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the queen on h7, forcing the king to take, then the pawn promotes with check. This is a classic idea: remove the defender of the promotion square.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is one step from promotion, look for ways to eliminate the defender. Queen sacrifices on h7 are a common motif in many openings.
notes.plans: After promotion, defend accurately and use the extra material to win.

notes.explains: After promoting, White has a queen and rook against Black's scattered pieces. White plays Nc3 to defend the e4 pawn and prepare further attacks.
notes.teaches: After winning material, don't rush; consolidate. Defend your pawns and coordinate your pieces. Black's king is exposed and his pieces are far away.
notes.plans: Use the queen and rook to attack Black's king, while the knight and bishop support. Avoid perpetual check by finding a safe square for the king.

notes.explains: White plays Rh7+, threatening Qg7#. Black's queen is overloaded, defending g7 and other squares.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is overloaded, use your pieces to create multiple threats. The rook on h7 ties the queen to defense.
notes.plans: Sacrifice on f4 to open the floodgates, then deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the knight on f4, then the bishop, to deflect the queen from g7. After Bxf4, if Qxf4, Qg7 is checkmate. Black's queen cannot defend g7 and f4 simultaneously.
notes.teaches: Sacrifice on a single square to overload the defender. Here, sacrificing on f4 forces Black's queen to abandon g7, allowing checkmate.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, deliver checkmate with Qg7 or a queen maneuver.

notes.explains: White's Be3 and Bxb6 removes Black's dark-squared bishop, but weakens the kingside pawn structure. The key is to exploit the weaknesses on f2 and g3.
notes.teaches: When your opponent weakens their kingside, prioritize rapid development and target the weakened squares.
notes.plans: Play Ng4 to attack the e3 pawn, then Qf3 to pile pressure. Avoid slow moves like h5 that don't address the immediate threat.

notes.explains: After …Nxe5? Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qd5+, White forks the king and knight, winning the knight and the game. This is a classic combination: sacrifice a bishop to expose the king, then deliver a decisive fork.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and their pieces are undeveloped, look for sacrifices that open the king and create forks or double attacks.
notes.plans: Play Qd5+ to win the knight on e5. Black's king is hopelessly exposed, and White has a winning material advantage.

notes.explains: Qe5 forks the rook on h1 and pawn on b2. The rook is undefended, and the pawn on e5 is also a target.
notes.teaches: After winning material, look for forks that target multiple undefended pieces or pawns. Strike while the iron is hot.
notes.plans: Capture b2, then c2 and a2. Avoid taking on c2 first if it allows the opponent's king to defend the rook via g3.

notes.explains: Black chooses not to take on c2 immediately because keeping the c2 pawn blocks the h2 rook from defending the queenside. This makes pushing the a-pawn easier.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, consider how pawns can block enemy pieces from defending. Sometimes it's better to leave a pawn to restrict the opponent's rook.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn to promote. If the opponent sacrifices a knight for the pawn, the resulting endgame is winning due to the outside passed pawn.

notes.explains: Pushing the a-pawn creates a passed pawn. The opponent's knight is poor at stopping outside passed pawns because of its limited range.
notes.teaches: Knights are bad at stopping outside passed pawns. Use this to your advantage in endgames by creating a passed pawn far from the knight.
notes.plans: Push the pawn to a2, then promote. If the opponent tries to stop it, trade rooks and use the king to support the pawn.

notes.explains: When in doubt, choose the simplest winning continuation. Avoid flashy moves unless you are certain they work.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, simplicity is key. Don't risk a complicated line that could give counterplay; instead, consolidate and convert.
notes.plans: Play Qa1 to defend the a-pawn, then push a2. If the opponent plays Bf5, don't premove; calculate to avoid traps.

notes.explains: Pushing a2 threatens promotion. The opponent cannot stop it without losing material.
notes.teaches: In endgames with a passed pawn, push it as quickly as possible. The opponent's pieces will be tied down.
notes.plans: After a2, if the opponent plays Bf5, simply promote. If they ignore, promote and win.

notes.explains: Black must be careful not to premove a2=Q if the bishop on f5 can capture. Always check for counterplay.
notes.teaches: Even in winning positions, respect your opponent's resources. Calculate before every move, especially when promoting.
notes.plans: Play Qxa2 or simply push the pawn after dealing with the bishop. The simplest is to trade queens and win the endgame.

notes.explains: Taking the bishop with the queen simplifies to a winning rook endgame. Black has an extra pawn and a safer king.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, simplify by trading pieces. This reduces the opponent's counterplay and makes conversion easier.
notes.plans: After Qxa2, Black has a winning rook endgame. Push the passed pawn and use the king to support it.

notes.explains: After Qxg5, Black's king is cut off. Rh1 forces ...Kg8, then Nh5 threatens both Qxg7# and Nf6#. Black's only defense is a meaningless check.
notes.teaches: In mating attacks, cutting off the king's escape and coordinating pieces (queen, rook, knight) is decisive. Look for double threats.
notes.plans: Execute the mate: Nh5, then meet any check by moving the king, as mate is unstoppable.

notes.explains: Black's setup with pawns on d5, f5, and e6 (a Maróczy Bind shifted over) makes it hard for White to free himself. Black's strategy is to maintain the clamp and slowly improve.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage and a clamped center, avoid opening the position prematurely. Instead, make improving moves like Re8 (preventing e5) and centralize knights.
notes.plans: Black can consider Ne4, c6, or even g6, but the most flexible is Re8. Later, the queen can lift to e6 and h6 to start a kingside attack.

notes.explains: White's Ba3 is a good idea, aiming to trade off Black's powerful bishop on d6. Black should avoid c5 (which opens the center) and instead play c6 to maintain the clamp.
notes.teaches: When your opponent tries to trade a key defender, consider reinforcing your structure rather than opening lines. c6 protects d5 and keeps the position closed.
notes.plans: Black plays c6, then can develop the knight via a6-c7 or move the queen to e6 to free d7 for the knight. The queen lift to h6 is a long-term attacking idea.

notes.explains: White's c4 is too late; Black has already improved his position. Black now launches a kingside attack with Qe6 and Qh6, exploiting White's weakened king safety.
notes.teaches: Positional play and attacking are not mutually exclusive. Once you have a positional grip, you can transition to a direct attack on the king.
notes.plans: Black plays Qe6 (opening d7 for the knight), then Qh6, followed by Ndf6 and Ng4, targeting h3 and f3. The knight on f3 is White's only defender.

notes.explains: White's g3 weakens h3, allowing Black to play Qh3 and then Ng4, creating a deadly threat. The knight on f3 is overloaded, and Black can sacrifice on h2 or simply play Ng5 to distract it.
notes.teaches: When attacking, look for weaknesses created by defensive moves. g3 weakens h3, and the knight on f3 becomes a critical defender that can be overloaded.
notes.plans: Black plays Qh3, then Ng4, threatening Nxh2. If White defends with Re1, Black can play Ng5, overloading the f3 knight. The immediate threat is Nxf3 followed by Qxh2# or similar.

notes.explains: Black plays Ng5, threatening Nxf3 and then Qxh2#. White's knight on f3 is the only defender; if it moves, Black crashes through. White's position is hopeless.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, identify the key defender and find ways to eliminate it. Here, Ng5 forces the knight to move or be exchanged, leading to mate.
notes.plans: Black continues with Nxf3+ if allowed, then Qxh2#. If White avoids the trade, Black can play Rh6 and Nxh2, or simply take on f3 anyway.

notes.explains: After White takes on g5, Black recaptures with the f-pawn, opening the f-file. Qxg5+ forces Kh1, then Qh6 renews the threat. White's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which pawn recapture opens lines for your attack. fxg5 opens the f-file and gives Black a passed pawn.
notes.plans: Black continues with Rh6 and Nxh2, or simply Qxh2# if possible. The attack is unstoppable.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the knight on h2, forcing Kxh2, then Qxh2#. This is a classic sacrifice to remove the king's pawn shield.
notes.teaches: When the king is exposed, a knight sacrifice on h2 can be decisive if the queen is nearby to deliver mate.
notes.plans: Black plays Nxh2, and after Kxh2, Qxh2# is mate.

notes.explains: Black's Bg4 pins the knight and attacks e4, but White can ignore the pin tactically.
notes.teaches: When a diagonal is open, check for tactical shots like Nxe5, exploiting the loose bishop.
notes.plans: If Black plays Bg4, White can play d5 and then Nxe5, winning a piece after the smoke clears.

notes.explains: Black develops passively; White can consider f4 to occupy more center, but must bring pieces to support the center.
notes.teaches: Occupying more center requires bringing pieces to supervise it; don't overexpand without development.
notes.plans: Play f4, then develop with Bc4, castling, and prepare to open the f-file.

notes.explains: White opens the f-file; Black's knight on f6 blocks it, so White shouldn't rush f5.
notes.teaches: When a file is open but blocked, don't force it open immediately; improve your pieces first.
notes.plans: Consider d5 to leave Black's pieces biting on granite, then develop the bishop and queen.

notes.explains: White has an open f-file and pressure; Black's knight on f6 blocks the file. White can play d5 to close the center and leave Black's pieces passive.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's pieces are passive, you can afford to make prophylactic moves like h3 to prevent knight g4.
notes.plans: Play h3 to stop Ng4, then maneuver the queen to g3 to create threats against h6 and e5.

notes.explains: White's queen on g3 threatens Bxh6 and attacks e5; Black must be careful not to blunder with Ng6.
notes.teaches: When you have multiple threats, don't focus on just one; be aware of all your attacking possibilities.
notes.plans: If Black plays h6, consider taking on e6 first to avoid the knight h5 counterplay.

notes.explains: White takes on e6 first to avoid the knight h5 defense; now Bxh6 is strong because Black can't play Nh5 without losing the knight.
notes.teaches: When calculating captures, consider the order: taking a defender first can prevent counterplay.
notes.plans: After Bxh6, White threatens Qg7#; Black must give up material to avoid mate.

notes.explains: White has a winning attack; Black's king is exposed and White's pieces coordinate well.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, bring all your pieces into the attack; don't rush, but look for the most forceful continuation.
notes.plans: White can play Rf5 threatening Qh5+ and mate; Black's only defense is to give up material.

notes.explains: White's attack breaks through; Black's king is chased into the open and loses material.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive attack, keep the pressure on; don't allow counterplay.
notes.plans: White should continue checking and capturing until the attack is decisive.

notes.explains: After dxe5 and Qxd8, the exchange variation arises. White's knight on d5 looks strong but is not immediately dangerous. Black cannot play c6 because Nc7 traps the rook. The knight attacks c7, so Black must defend it.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, a centralized knight can be more of a mirage than a threat if the opponent can challenge it. Look beyond the immediate outpost to the long-term control of central squares.
notes.plans: Play Na6 to defend c7 and prepare to challenge the knight on d5 with c6 later. If Bg5, respond with Rd6 to unpin the knight and protect f6.

notes.explains: White retreated the bishop to b2, which is not the most challenging move. White should have played Be3 to restrict Black's knight on a6 and prepare c5. Now Black can proceed with the plan.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, every tempo matters. White's passive bishop move allows Black to execute his plan without hindrance. Always consider the most active square for your pieces.
notes.plans: Black can now play Nb4 or Ndc5 to reroute the knight toward d4. The immediate Nb4 is tempting, but after Rc1, the knight has no good follow-up. Better to play Ndc5, threatening Nd3 fork and preparing to go to e6 and then d4.

notes.explains: Black plays Nd7, a typical King's Indian maneuver. This move covers c5, opens the diagonal for the bishop on g7, and prepares to reroute both knights toward d4. The knight on f6 was awkward and needed to be repositioned.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, don't hesitate to move a piece multiple times to improve its effectiveness. Nd7 is a regrouping move that enhances coordination and prepares future centralization.
notes.plans: Black will continue with Ndc5, then Ne6, and finally Nd4. The knight on d4 will dominate the board. Meanwhile, Black can also consider trading dark-squared bishops to weaken White's control of d4.

notes.explains: White plays g4, a typical pawn storm move, but here it is a mistake because the queens are off. It creates a permanent weakness on f4 without any attacking prospects. Black can now target f4 with a knight.
notes.teaches: Pawn storms are only effective when the king is exposed and the position is open. In endgames or closed positions, advancing pawns creates weaknesses that the opponent can exploit. Always consider the downside of pawn moves.
notes.plans: Black can now aim to get a knight to f4 via d3 or e6. The knight on d4 can later move to f4, or the other knight can go to f4 via g5 or e6. The weakness on f4 becomes a long-term target.

notes.explains: Black plays Ndc5, threatening Nd3+ and preparing to reroute the knight to e6 and then d4. The knight on b4 also supports this maneuver. Black is systematically improving his pieces.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, piece improvement is a long-term process. Each move should have a clear purpose, and you should be willing to spend tempos to get your pieces to ideal squares.
notes.plans: Black will play Ne6 next, attacking the bishop on g5 and forcing it to move. Then Nd4 will be established. After that, Black can double rooks on the d-file and consider trading dark-squared bishops.

notes.explains: Black achieves the long-awaited knight on d4. This knight dominates the board, controlling key squares and restricting White's pieces. It is a major strategic victory.
notes.teaches: Centralizing a knight in a closed position is a huge achievement. A knight on d4 controls eight squares and often cannot be easily dislodged. Celebrate small victories and build on them.
notes.plans: Black will now solidify the knight by doubling rooks on the d-file and preparing to trade dark-squared bishops. The knight on d4 is a permanent outpost that will eventually win material or create decisive threats.

notes.explains: Black plays Rcd8, doubling rooks on the d-file and threatening Nxc2+ forking the king and rook. This increases the pressure on White's position. White must be careful to avoid tactical tricks.
notes.teaches: Doubling rooks on an open file is a classic way to increase pressure. Always look for tactical threats like forks when your pieces are centralized.
notes.plans: Black will continue to improve the position, possibly playing Bf6 to trade dark-squared bishops or rerouting the knight on b4 to f4. The pressure will eventually force White to weaken further.

notes.explains: White plays Bf1, a passive move. Black now has a choice: continue with Nc5 to head for f4, or play Bf6 to trade dark-squared bishops. Both are good.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a passive move, you have the luxury of choosing among several good plans. Evaluate which plan is most effective and proceed.
notes.plans: Black can play Nc5, heading for e6 and then f4, or play Bf6, threatening to trade bishops and weaken White's control of d4. The knight on d4 is already strong, so Black can afford to be flexible.

notes.explains: Black plays Nc5, heading for e6 and then f4. This knight will target the weak f4 square created by White's g4 move. The knight on d4 remains a permanent outpost.
