notes.teaches: When you have a weak square in the opponent's camp, reroute a knight to exploit it. The knight on c5 can go to e6 and then f4, or directly to d3 and then f4.
notes.plans: Black will play Ne6 next, then Nf4, creating a powerful knight on f4 that attacks the pawn on g2 and restricts White's pieces.

notes.explains: White plays b4, attacking the knight on c5. Black can simply retreat to e6, maintaining the threat to go to f4. White's queenside expansion does not address the central weaknesses.
notes.teaches: Don't be distracted by your opponent's flank operations. If your central control is strong, you can ignore flank pawn moves and continue with your plan.
notes.plans: Black will play Ne6, then Nf4. The knight on f4 will be very strong. Black can also consider Bf6 to trade bishops, further weakening White's control of d4.

notes.explains: Black retreats to e6, maintaining the threat to go to f4. The knight on d4 is still strong. Black is patiently improving the position.
notes.teaches: Patience is key in closed positions. Don't rush; make small improvements and wait for your opponent to weaken further.
notes.plans: Black will play Nf4 next, creating a powerful knight. After that, Black can consider trading bishops or doubling rooks on the d-file.

notes.explains: White plays Ng3, a decisive mistake. This allows Black to trade dark-squared bishops with Bf6, after which the weak squares on d4 and f4 become indefensible. White should have taken the knight on d4.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a strong knight on d4, you must consider trading it. Allowing Black to keep the knight and trade bishops is fatal. Always evaluate which pieces are most important to trade.
notes.plans: Black will play Bf6, forcing the trade of bishops. After that, the knight on d4 is even stronger, and Black can target the f4 square with the other knight.

notes.explains: Black plays Bf6, forcing the trade of dark-squared bishops. This is a decisive improvement because White's best defensive piece is removed, leaving the weak squares d4 and f4 completely exposed.
notes.teaches: Trading your opponent's best piece is a fundamental strategic goal. Here, the dark-squared bishop was White's main defender of the weak squares. Once it's gone, Black's knights dominate.
notes.plans: After the trade, Black will have a knight on d4 and another heading to f4. The position becomes a technical win.

notes.explains: Black plays Nc2+, forking the king and rook. This is the tactical payoff for the positional pressure. The knight on d4 was perfectly placed to exploit the alignment of the king and rook on the d-file.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong positional advantage, always be alert for tactical opportunities. The knight on d4 not only controls squares but also creates tactical threats like forks.
notes.plans: After Nc2+, Black will win the exchange. The resulting endgame is easily winning due to the extra material and Black's dominant knights.

notes.explains: Black wins the exchange and a pawn. The position is now a technical win. Black has a rook and two knights against White's rook and bishop, with a dominant position.
notes.teaches: Once you have a material advantage, simplify to a winning endgame. Here, Black can trade rooks and use the extra pawn to win.
notes.plans: Black will play Rd2+ to force rook trades, then use the knights to pick off White's pawns. The endgame is straightforward.

notes.explains: Black plays Rd2+, forcing the trade of rooks. This simplifies to a winning endgame where Black's knights dominate White's bishop.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, trade pieces to reduce counterplay. Here, trading rooks leaves Black with a material advantage and no risk.
notes.plans: After the rook trade, Black will use the knights to attack White's pawns and promote a pawn.

notes.explains: Black wins the rook and now has a decisive material advantage. The knights will easily pick off White's remaining pawns.
notes.teaches: Once you have a material advantage, use your pieces to target the opponent's weaknesses. Here, the knights can attack the pawns on the kingside.
notes.plans: Black will play Ne4 or similar to attack the f-pawn, then win more pawns. The game is over.

notes.explains: Black plays Qb6 attacking b2. White should not defend b2 with b3 because that blocks the b3 square for the knight. Instead, ignore the pawn and continue development.
notes.teaches: If Black captures on b2, opening the b-file with Rb1 gives White a strong attack due to Black's poor development. Intuitively, this is bad for Black, so you don't need to calculate.
notes.plans: Play Nbd2, then Nb3, and later Rc1, targeting the d4 pawn at leisure.

notes.explains: White takes on d4 with the f-knight, not the b-knight. This keeps the b-knight on b3 to potentially jump to c5, and prepares a kingside pawn push with f4-f5.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which knight to use based on future plans: the b-knight stays for queenside pressure, the f-knight clears the way for f4.
notes.plans: Play Be3, then consider f4-f5 to attack Black's kingside. The d4 square is controlled by the knight.

notes.explains: If Black plays Nxe5, White has the brilliant move Nc6, attacking the queen and threatening the knight. The queen cannot protect the knight without walking into an x-ray.
notes.teaches: Look for double attacks and x-ray tactics when the opponent's pieces are poorly coordinated. Even if you miss the best move, simpler continuations like Qh5 still give White a strong attack.
notes.plans: After Nc6, Black's queen must move, and White can capture on a7 or continue the attack.

notes.explains: Black captures on a2. White can ignore this pawn and play Qe2, preparing to shift the queen to g4 to target g7, or play f4 to start a kingside pawn storm.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a pawn for long-term positional pressure and attacking chances is a key concept. The a2 pawn is irrelevant for the next 20 moves; White's initiative is worth more.
notes.plans: Play f4, then f5, opening lines on the kingside. The queen on e2 can later go to g4.

notes.explains: White launches a demolition sacrifice: sacrificing a piece to destroy Black's king cover. After f4-f5, White opens the e-file and delivers a quick checkmate.
notes.teaches: A demolition sacrifice is used to rip open the pawn shield around the king. Once the king is exposed, the remaining pieces can deliver a decisive attack.
notes.plans: After f5, capture on e6, then play Qe6+ followed by Bd4+ and Qf6+ etc., forcing mate.

notes.explains: The attack from f4 to checkmate took only seven moves. White's intuition to sacrifice the a2 pawn and then the exchange was justified by the overwhelming attack.
notes.teaches: When you have the initiative, you don't need to calculate every line. Intuition, built from pattern recognition, tells you that the attack is worth the material.

notes.explains: If Black plays c4, White should not be afraid. c4 takes pressure off the d4 pawn, allowing White to focus on kingside play. The closed center gives White time to attack.
notes.teaches: In the Steinitz, c4 actually benefits White because it diverts Black's resources from attacking d4. White can then invest tempi in a kingside assault.
notes.plans: Develop with Bd3, then prepare f4-f5. The center is closed, so White's attack is not easily countered.

notes.explains: If Black plays Bc5, White has a powerful attacking continuation: Rxc5! This sacrifices the exchange but opens lines. After Nxc6 (double attack on queen), White captures on g7 and has overwhelming compensation.
notes.teaches: Positional sacrifices like the exchange can be justified by long-term pressure. Even if you are down material, if your opponent is passive and uncoordinated, you have full compensation.
notes.plans: After Nxg7, drop the knight back to f5 and build up against Black's king. The attack may take several moves but is crushing.

notes.explains: Black has castled queenside and is pushing kingside pawns to create a mating attack. White's knight on h1 is trapped, and Black's bishop on d6 is powerful. The key is to open lines without allowing White counterplay.
notes.teaches: When attacking, coordinate pieces to exploit weaknesses. Here, Black uses the g2 square as a hook to tie down White's pieces, then switches to the e-file when White defends.
notes.plans: Black should continue pushing the h-pawn to open the h-file, while keeping the e-file closed to restrict White's rooks. If White plays f4, Black can occupy the e3 square with a rook.

notes.explains: Black plays Nd4 to defend the e3 square, preventing White's knight from jumping there after h3. This ensures that h3 will be a crushing move, as the knight cannot escape to e3.
notes.teaches: Before executing a pawn break, check if the opponent has a defensive resource that could neutralize it. Here, Nd4 eliminates the knight's escape square, making h3 decisive.
notes.plans: After Nd4, Black plays h3, threatening mate on g2. White must respond with Nh4, after which Black can eliminate the knight with Be7, forcing f4, then take on h4 and occupy the e-file.

notes.explains: Black has sacrificed material to create a mating attack. White's king is exposed, and Black's rook on h2 ties down White's pieces. The immediate threat is Rh1#.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, use a rook to create a 'hook' that ties down the defender. Here, the rook on h2 prevents White from moving the f2 rook, as it would allow mate.
notes.plans: Black should continue to press the attack, possibly by bringing the queen to the h-file or opening the center. White's only defense is to block with the rook on f2, but Black can then infiltrate on the e-file.

notes.explains: Black has won material and is converting the advantage. The queen and rook coordinate to create mating threats, while White's king is exposed. Black's pawns on the queenside are also a threat.
notes.teaches: In converting a winning position, avoid unnecessary risks. Use the queen to control key squares and prevent counterplay. Here, Black's queen infiltrates and forces mate.
notes.plans: Black should continue to harass the white king with checks, while advancing the queenside pawns. The immediate plan is to deliver checkmate or win more material.

notes.explains: Black has pushed the h-pawn to h4, creating a potential mating square on g2. White's knight is trapped on h1, and Black's bishop on d6 is powerful. The position is ripe for a breakthrough.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are passive, pushing pawns to create weaknesses is effective. Here, h4 threatens h3, which would open the h-file and create mate threats.
notes.plans: Black should play Nd4 to prevent White's knight from escaping to e3, then play h3. After White's knight goes to h4, Black can eliminate it with Be7, forcing f4, then take on h4 and occupy the e-file.

notes.explains: Black plays Bxg3, sacrificing the bishop to open the h-file. After fxg3, Black has Rxh2+ and Reh8, creating a decisive attack. The sacrifice is sound because White's king is exposed and Black's rooks dominate.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it is worth sacrificing a piece to open lines against the enemy king. Here, the bishop sacrifice removes a defender and opens the h-file, allowing Black's rooks to deliver mate.
notes.plans: After Bxg3, Black plays Rxh2+ and Reh8, threatening Rh1#. White must give up material to avoid immediate mate, but Black's attack is overwhelming.

notes.explains: Black's queen and rook coordinate to deliver checkmate. The queen chases the white king across the board, while the rook on h2 prevents escape. The final checkmate is Qa4#.
notes.teaches: In a king hunt, use checks to drive the king to a mating net. Here, the queen's checks force the king to the edge, where the rook and queen deliver mate.
notes.plans: Black should continue checking until the king is trapped. The rook on h2 controls the h-file, while the queen covers the a4 square for mate.

notes.explains: Black's final move Qa4# delivers checkmate. The queen is supported by the rook on h2, and the white king has no escape squares.
notes.teaches: Always look for the most efficient checkmate. Here, Qa4# is a classic mate with queen and rook against a lone king.

notes.explains: Black plays Bc5, a sideline that is tactically flawed due to the center fork trick Nxe5, winning back the piece after forking the bishop and knight.
notes.teaches: Recognize the center fork trick: a temporary sacrifice on e5 to fork the bishop on c5 and the knight on e5, regaining material.
notes.plans: After Nxe5, if black recaptures with Bxd4, white plays c3 to trap the bishop or simply develops with Be3, preparing to exploit the lead in development.

notes.explains: After the center fork trick, black's best response is Bd6, keeping the bishop and maintaining a playable position, though white has a development advantage.
notes.teaches: When facing the center fork trick, prefer Bd6 to preserve the bishop and avoid tactical disasters.
notes.plans: White continues developing with d3 and Nf3, aiming to consolidate the extra pawn and central control.

notes.explains: Black plays Qf6, a waste of time. White responds with Nd5, attacking the queen and forcing it back, gaining tempo.
notes.teaches: A prematurely developed queen can be harassed by a knight, gaining time and space.
notes.plans: After Nd5, black's queen retreats to d8, and white can play f4, now safe because the bishop on e3 blocks checks, winning the g7 pawn.

notes.explains: White plays Bb5+ before capturing on h8, taking away the king's escape square and ensuring a forced checkmate.
notes.teaches: In mating attacks, first cut off the king's escape routes before delivering the final blow.
notes.plans: After Bb5+, Kd7, then Qxh8, and black cannot prevent mate on e8 or d8.

notes.explains: White has a massive attack but must not rush with Rh8+; instead, cover the king's only escape square f7 with g6, then deliver mate.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king has only one escape square, block it with a quiet move before initiating the mating sequence.
notes.plans: Play g6, forcing black to capture, then Qh5+ and Rh8#.

notes.explains: Black plays Bxf2+, a common panic move. White can simply play Kxf2 or d4, and the king is safe after manual castling.
notes.teaches: Bxf2+ is not scary; white gets the bishop pair and central control, and the king can find safety on g1.
notes.plans: After Bxf2+, play d4, develop pieces, and castle manually with Kf1-g1.

notes.explains: Black plays Qh4, threatening check. White can simply play g3, forcing the queen back to f6, and then develop with Nd3 or Nd5.
notes.teaches: Queen sorties to h4 are easily parried with g3, gaining time.
notes.plans: After g3 Qf6, play Nd5 or Nd3, developing with tempo.

notes.explains: In the Four Knights English, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 Bb5 Bc5, the center fork trick Nxe5 is met by Bb4, not Bd6, because Bd6 allows a trap with c5.
notes.teaches: Opening principles are not absolute; in specific variations like the Four Knights English, the correct response to Nxe5 is Bb4, not Bd6.
notes.plans: After Bb4, white plays d4 exd4, and black recaptures with Nxe4, leading to sharp play.

notes.explains: White plays Bc4 and Nf3, but black has not played e5, so the fried liver threats are nullified. Black plays e6, blocking the bishop and preparing development.
notes.teaches: Pawn structures determine the effectiveness of attacking ideas; keeping the pawn on e7 neutralizes Bc4+Nf3 threats.
notes.plans: Black develops with Nf6, Be7, O-O, and can later grab the e4 pawn if safe.

notes.explains: Black plays h6, kicking the knight, then captures the e4 pawn. White has no compensation because black's pawn structure is solid.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's attack is harmless, grabbing a free pawn is safe if you have a solid pawn structure.
notes.plans: After Nf3, black plays Nxe4, then develops with Be7, O-O, and consolidates the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays Nd7, a retreating move that attacks the bishop and prepares d4. White errs with Bc3, allowing d4 and Bb5, winning the knight.
notes.teaches: Retreating moves can be strong if they carry a threat; do not judge moves by direction alone.
notes.plans: After Nd7 Bc3, play d4, then Bb5, winning the knight on c5.

notes.explains: Black simplifies with an intermediate pawn capture on c3, leading to mass exchanges and a technically winning endgame.
notes.teaches: Calculate a few moves ahead to find the most clinical simplification that minimizes counterplay.
notes.plans: After bxc3, Nxc5, then Bxc5, and black is up a piece with a simple win.

notes.explains: Black plays Bc5, threatening Qd4 to force a queen trade, but must be aware of white's mating threats. Black intercepts with Qd4.
notes.teaches: Even when winning, always check for opponent's threats; a queen trade can neutralize counterplay.
notes.plans: After Bc5, if white threatens mate, play Qd4 to block and trade queens.

notes.explains: Black plays Ne5, attacking the queen on f3 and winning the bishop pair after Qxb5.
notes.teaches: In the Bowdler Attack, Ne5 is a strong response, winning the bishop pair and leaving the queen misplaced.
notes.plans: After Ne5 Qxb5, black has the bishop pair and can develop with e6, Bb7, and queenside expansion.

notes.explains: Black plays a6, preparing b5 and Bb7, a typical Sicilian setup. White's e5 is less effective with the knight still on g8.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, a6 and b5 are common to gain space and activate the bishop on b7.
notes.plans: Black continues with b5, Bb7, and develops the kingside, aiming for queenside expansion.

notes.explains: Black plays Nh6, defending f7 and heading to f5. This is a multi-purpose move that develops and prepares an outpost.
notes.teaches: When the opponent plays e5, a knight can often go to h6 and then f5, using the pawn as a shield.
notes.plans: After Nh6, black can play Nf5, putting pressure on e5 and g7.

notes.explains: White wins a pawn with Nxd5. Black's position is collapsing due to lack of development. White now has a centralized knight and a material advantage.
notes.teaches: When your opponent is underdeveloped, open the center and create threats. A centralized knight in an open position is a powerful attacking piece.
notes.plans: Use the knight to create forks and further material gains, then convert the advantage in the endgame.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, sacrificing a pawn to open lines and exploit white's poor development. After Qxe5 f6, the queen is forked, and white's position collapses.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a pawn to open lines against an underdeveloped opponent can be decisive.
notes.plans: After e5 Qxe5 f6, white must retreat the queen, and black gains the initiative with open files.

notes.explains: Black plays Kf7, a safe square that avoids checks and prepares to double rooks on the e-file.
notes.teaches: In open positions, the king can often find safety on f7 or e7, especially when the opponent has no attacking pieces.
notes.plans: After Kf7, black doubles rooks on the e-file and targets the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays e4, opening the diagonal for the bishop and creating a path for the knight to f3. This move exploits White's weak dark squares and the pinned knight.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's pieces are tied down, a central pawn break can be devastating. Here, e4 forces White's bishop to a passive square and gives Black a decisive outpost.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Nf3, threatening ...Qh3 and ...Rxe4. The knight on f3 is a monster, and White cannot defend all threats. The game will end quickly.

notes.explains: Black's setup with e6 and g6 creates dark-square weaknesses on the kingside. White's h4 is a provocative move that exploits these weaknesses by threatening to open lines or create a stronghold on g5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent creates a complex of weaknesses (like dark squares), open the position and create tension to exploit them. A pawn push like h4 can provoke further weaknesses or set up attacking ideas.
notes.plans: If Black plays h5, White can occupy g5 with a bishop or knight. If Black castles, White can play hxg6 and open the h-file for a mating attack. If Black plays h6, White can continue with h5 and g4 to blast open the kingside.

notes.explains: After Black plays h5, White's g5 forces Nh7, then h6 dislodges the bishop. Black's king is exposed, and White's queen on d2 threatens Qg5#. The key is to notice that g5 is the only mating square and to prepare it with a battery.
notes.teaches: When the enemy king is short of squares, identify the potential mating squares and find a way to deliver a piece there. Sometimes a quiet move like Qd2, building a battery, is more effective than a flashy sacrifice.
notes.plans: White's plan is to play Qg5 with checkmate. Black can delay with ...f6, but then Bg5 is still deadly. The attack is unstoppable.

notes.explains: Black allowed h5 and then White played h6, attacking the bishop on g7. The double threat of hxg7 and h7 is devastating because Black cannot contain all the weaknesses.
notes.teaches: In positions with a pawn on h5, the pawn can be used to dislodge the defender of the kingside (h6) or to open the h-file (hxg6) after castling. These are two key ideas in such structures.
notes.plans: White will play hxg7 or h7, opening lines or promoting. Black's position collapses due to the multiple threats.

notes.explains: After the sequence, White's queen on d2 threatens Qg5#. Black's only try is ...f6, but then Bg5 is still mate. The attack is clean and winning.
notes.teaches: When you have a mating threat, look for the simplest way to deliver it. Don't overcomplicate with sacrifices if a quiet move like Qd2 sets up an unstoppable threat.
notes.plans: White plays Qg5 next move, checkmate. Black cannot prevent it.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...f6 to block the mate, White simply plays Bg5, renewing the threat. Black's position is hopeless.
notes.teaches: When a mating threat is blocked, look for another piece to deliver the same mate. The idea of transferring the mating piece to the key square is common.
notes.plans: White will play Bg5, and Black cannot stop Qg5# or Bxf6.

notes.explains: After Bg5, if Black takes, White recaptures with check and then mates. The attack is straightforward.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the simplest recapture leads to a winning attack. Don't overlook basic checks and captures.
notes.plans: White plays Qg5+ and then mates. Black's king has no escape.

notes.explains: The final checkmate: Qh6#. The attack succeeded because White exploited the dark-square weaknesses created by Black's e6 and g6 setup.
notes.teaches: A well-prepared pawn storm can lead to a decisive mating attack. The key is to identify the weaknesses and commit to the attack with precise moves.
notes.plans: White delivers checkmate. The game is over.

notes.explains: Black's best response to h4 is probably h5, accepting the weakness on g5 but avoiding a direct attack. Even so, White gets a strong initiative.
notes.teaches: When facing a provocative pawn push like h4, the lesser evil is often to accept a small weakness (like h5) rather than allowing a devastating attack. Sometimes you must choose the least bad option.
notes.plans: Black will try to defend the kingside, but White's pressure on the dark squares remains. Black's position is difficult but defensible.

notes.explains: After Bg5, Black's position is hopeless. The attack is unstoppable.
notes.teaches: When you have a winning attack, don't hesitate. Play the most forcing moves to convert.
notes.plans: White will play Qg5# or Bxf6 next. Black cannot prevent mate.

notes.explains: Bd3 is inaccurate because it allows Black to play e5 with tempo, and White may have to retreat the bishop to c2, losing time.
notes.teaches: In the London System, the bishop belongs on d3 only after h3 to prevent ...e5 forks; otherwise, it's a target.
notes.plans: Black should play Nc6 and then e5, or Re8 to provoke a decision.

notes.explains: Black has achieved e5 in a favorable version. White's setup is toothless; Black has a comfortable position.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, the e5 break is a key pawn lever. When achieved without concessions, Black equalizes easily.
notes.plans: Continue with h6 to ask the bishop a question, then develop the bishop to e6 and complete development.

notes.explains: h6 is a useful waiting move that asks the bishop to declare its intentions. If White takes on f6, Black gets the two bishops. If the bishop retreats to h4, Black can consider g5 later.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is on g5, h6 is a flexible move that can provoke weaknesses or gain the two bishops.
notes.plans: After h6, develop the bishop to e6, then play Qe7 and Rd8, preparing to meet Ne4.

notes.explains: White puts pressure on the knight on f6, but it is well defended by queen and bishop. Black does not need to panic or play g5 yet.
notes.teaches: A pinned knight is not necessarily weak if it has sufficient defenders. Do not rush to break the pin unless the pressure becomes unbearable.
notes.plans: Continue with Re8 to bring the rook into play, and wait for White to castle before considering g5.

notes.explains: Once White castles queenside, the risk of playing g5 decreases because White's king is not on that side. The weaknesses created by g5 are less dangerous.
notes.teaches: The safety of a pawn advance like g5 depends on where the opponent's king is. After short castling, g5 is safer if White has castled long.
notes.plans: Now play g5, forcing the bishop to g3, then prepare f5 with Nd5.

notes.explains: Nd5 is a strong move. The knight is well protected and cannot be easily attacked. It prepares f5 and also opens the possibility of c4 and Nb4.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, a knight on d5 is often an ideal outpost, supporting the f5 break and controlling key squares.
notes.plans: Play f5 immediately, threatening to trap the bishop on g3 with f4.

notes.explains: White allows f5, which is a mistake. Black can now push f4, trapping the bishop on g3. White's bishop is lost.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a bishop on g3 and you have a pawn on g5, the f4 push can trap the bishop. Always be alert to such tactical motifs.
notes.plans: Push f4, and if White takes on f4, recapture with the e-pawn to keep the bishop trapped. If White moves the bishop, take on e4 with advantage.

notes.explains: White blunders by taking on c5. Black can win a piece by first taking on e4, then after White recaptures, taking on e5. If White plays fxe4, Black takes on f3 first, attacking the queen, then takes on g7.
notes.teaches: When your opponent blunders, stay alert for further mistakes. Calculate concrete lines; often the best move is not the most obvious capture.
notes.plans: Take on e4, then on e5, winning a piece. If White recaptures with the pawn, take the knight on f3 first, then the bishop on g7.

notes.explains: Black is two pieces up. The win is straightforward.
notes.teaches: With a decisive material advantage, simplify and avoid unnecessary risks. Trade pieces if it leads to a winning endgame.
notes.plans: Trade queens if possible, then use the extra material to promote a pawn or attack the king.

notes.explains: The Armenian Variation (Nfd7) is a good response to the London System. It blocks the bishop but accelerates e5 and allows f5 later. After e5, Black can play f5, creating a pawn wedge.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, Nfd7 is a flexible move that prepares both e5 and f5. It may look awkward but is theoretically sound.
notes.plans: After Nfd7, play e5, then f5, and later return the knight to f6 to open the diagonal for the bishop. White will attack on the queenside, Black on the kingside.

notes.explains: If White plays Bxf6 before retreating to g3, Black cannot immediately play f5 because White can play e4, blocking the pawn. The difference is crucial.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, White can sometimes prevent f5 by exchanging on f6 and then playing e4. Black must be aware of this prophylactic idea.
notes.plans: If White plays Bxf6, Black should recapture and then consider h5 or other breaks, but f5 may be delayed.

notes.explains: After g5, if White plays Ng5, Black must play Bd5 to prevent Qf3, which would put deadly pressure on the f6 knight. Then White can maneuver the knight to g3 and f5, a strong positional idea.
notes.teaches: Even after sacrificing a piece, positional maneuvers matter. Not every move must be tactical; improving piece placement is key.
notes.plans: Black should aim to trade the knight on f5 or neutralize it. White should route the knight to f5 via g3.

notes.explains: Black plays d5, opening the center. White avoids capturing on d5 because it would expose the king on the e-file. Instead, White keeps the center closed and pushes e6.
notes.teaches: When your king is on the same file as an open center, avoid opening lines that give your opponent counterplay. Keep the position closed to maintain your attack.
notes.plans: Push e6 to create a passed pawn and open lines against the black king.

notes.explains: White captures on f8, winning the exchange. Black recaptures with the rook. White now castles queenside, despite having pushed a4, because the pawn is protected and the king is safer on that side.
notes.teaches: Don't let rigid rules (like 'don't castle into a weakened pawn') prevent you from making the best move. Evaluate each position on its own merits.
notes.plans: Use the extra exchange to continue the kingside attack, targeting the weakened f7-pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays c5, attacking the knight on d4. White retreats the knight to b3, then later to e4, exploiting the pin on the d5-pawn (the queen on d8 is x-rayed by White's queen and rook).
notes.teaches: When a pawn is pinned, you can place a knight on a square defended by that pawn, because the pawn cannot capture. Look for such tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: Centralize the knight on e4, then capture the d5-pawn to open lines.

notes.explains: White plays Ne4, attacking the pinned d5-pawn. Black defends with Bb7. White now considers a fork: Nc5 attacks the bishop and rook, but Black can defend with Rc7. However, this trade weakens Black's control of d5.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a tactical sequence that doesn't win material immediately is still good because it weakens your opponent's position. Look for ways to improve your pieces and create long-term threats.
notes.plans: Trade the bishop on e6 for the rook on c7 via Nc5, then capture the d5-pawn with the knight.

notes.explains: Black plays Nd3+, an interception tactic to disrupt White's defense of the knight on d5. White captures with the bishop, and after exchanges, White wins a second pawn.
notes.teaches: Be alert for intermediate moves (zwischenzüge) that can disrupt your plans. Calculate carefully before capturing.
notes.plans: Consolidate the material advantage, then target the black king with the remaining pieces.

notes.explains: Black plays Qc6, attacking the rook on d3 and threatening Qc1#. White defends by moving the rook to d2, avoiding the checkmate and maintaining pressure.
notes.teaches: Always be aware of your opponent's counterplay, especially checkmate threats. Sometimes the best defense is to move a piece to a safe square while maintaining your attack.
notes.plans: Trade rooks or force the black rook away, then continue the attack with the knight and queen.

notes.explains: White plays Bd4, contesting the powerful g7-bishop. Black's bishop is the only well-developed piece, and trading it will leave the black king exposed.
notes.teaches: Identify your opponent's strongest piece and find a way to neutralize it. Trading it off can cripple their defense.
notes.plans: After the bishop trade, use the knight and queen to deliver checkmate or win more material.

notes.explains: Black plays Qe6, supporting the rook. White now looks for a fork with Nc7, attacking queen and rook. Black cannot avoid losing material.
notes.teaches: In positions with a centralized knight, always look for forks. The knight's mobility makes it a powerful tactical weapon.
notes.plans: Play Nc7, winning the exchange or more. Then simplify to a winning endgame.

notes.explains: White plays Nc7, forking queen and rook. Black captures the rook on e2, but White recaptures, winning a knight and two pawns. The game simplifies to a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify to an endgame where your extra material can be converted. Keep pieces active and create passed pawns.
notes.plans: In the endgame, create a passed pawn on the queenside using the pawn majority. Use the king and rook to support the pawn's promotion.

notes.explains: Black plays Nh5, but White can now play Bxh6, opening the h-file. If Black recaptures, White has Ng5+ and a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent blockades with a knight, look for sacrifices to open lines. The knight on h3 supports g5 and a potential Ng5.
notes.plans: White can take on h6, then follow up with Ng5, forcing weaknesses.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the bishop to open the h-file and bring the knight to g5 with tempo. Black's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: In a kingside attack, sacrificing material to open lines is often worth it if you can bring pieces quickly to the king.
notes.plans: White will continue with Qxh6 or O-O-O, bringing more pieces into the attack.

notes.explains: White captures on e5, opening both the e-file and f-file. Black's king is completely exposed, and White's queen and rook deliver mate.
notes.teaches: Once files are opened against an exposed king, the attack is often unstoppable. Use your queen and rook to deliver checks and force mate.
notes.plans: White plays Qf7+ followed by Qg7#. Black's king has no escape squares.

notes.explains: The Danish Gambit sacrifices one or two pawns (here c3 offers a second pawn after …exd4) to gain a lead in development and the initiative.
notes.teaches: Gambits require a mentality ready to sacrifice material for rapid development and attacking chances. Prioritize piece activity over pawns.
notes.plans: Develop quickly with Bc4, Nf3, and castle, aiming bishops at the kingside.

notes.explains: White plays Bc4, not recapturing the pawn, maintaining the gambit mentality. Black's knight on e4 is undefended and the king is still in the center, making the knight a tactical target.
notes.teaches: A piece in the center is not automatically good if it is undefended and the opponent's king is exposed. Avoid forcing it away; instead, prevent Black from stabilizing it with d5.
notes.plans: Develop Nf3, castle, and consider Qb3 to control d5 and threaten f7.

notes.explains: Black's a6 is a waste of time; he should have played d5 immediately to attack the bishop and secure the knight. Violating opening principles (control center, develop) without good reason is punished.
notes.teaches: If you are not controlling the center or developing, you need a very good reason. Preparing b5 is not sufficient.
notes.plans: White should play Qb3, building a battery with the bishop and threatening f7, while also controlling d5.

notes.explains: After Bxf7+ and Rxe1, Black can play c4, intercepting the queen's protection of the bishop. This is a common tactical resource: a pawn move that breaks the connection between pieces.
notes.teaches: When a piece is pinned or under attack, look for intermediate moves (like c4) that disrupt the opponent's coordination. This is a form of 'desperado' – if you will lose a piece, get as much material as possible in return.
notes.plans: If Black plays c4, White should capture the knight on e4 (taking something) rather than losing the bishop for nothing.

notes.explains: After …Kf7, both queens are hanging. This is a highly tactical situation. The key is to move your queen with check (e.g., Qb3+ or Qd5+) so that after the king moves, you can capture the opponent's queen.
notes.teaches: When both queens are en prise, look for a check that moves your queen away safely. This is a common tactical motif.
notes.plans: Play Qd5+ (or Qb3+) to force the king to move, then capture the queen on e4.

notes.explains: Black's king is on f6, exposed. White has a rook and queen active. The goal is to hunt the king, often by sacrificing pieces to lure it further into the open.
notes.teaches: In a king hunt, consider sacrificing material (like a rook) to force the king into a mating net. Look for checks and threats that restrict the king's escape squares.
notes.plans: Play Rg4+ (rook lift) to check the king. After Kf5, consider Rg5+ or Qf7+ leading to mate.

notes.explains: Rg4+ is a rook lift that checks the king. The king cannot go back to f7 (queen covers) or f6 (bishop covers), so it must go to f5. Now White has a faster mate than Rg5+.
notes.teaches: When hunting the king, don't automatically play the most obvious check. Look for a sacrifice that forces the king into a worse position. Here, the rook on g4 can be a lure.
notes.plans: After Kf5, play Qf7+ (forcing the king to g5 or e5) then Qg5# or similar. Alternatively, Rg5+ leads to mate in a few moves.

notes.explains: After Nf3, Black has a strong unorthodox idea: ...g5, deflecting the bishop from f4 to weaken control of e5, then ...Nxe5 to deflect the knight and win material.
notes.teaches: To increase pressure on a defender, consider removing defenders (like deflecting a piece) rather than just adding attackers. ...g5 is a deflection sacrifice that opens up tactical possibilities.
notes.plans: Play ...g5. If Bxg5, then ...Nxe5, deflecting the knight. After Nxe5, Bxd2+ forces White to lose the queen or suffer decisive material loss.

notes.explains: After Qc2, Black plays ...Nb4, a surprising knight sacrifice. If Qxe4, then ...d5 wins the queen due to the pin on the c2 square. If White avoids, Black gets a strong attack.
notes.teaches: Knight sacrifices on b4 can be powerful when the queen is overloaded. The idea is to exploit the queen's duty to defend c2 and the e4 pawn.
notes.plans: Play ...Nb4. If Qxe4, then ...d5 wins the queen. If White plays something else, Black has a strong initiative with the knight on b4 and threats against the king.

notes.explains: After …Bf5, Black threatens ...Bxc2 and ...Qxb2, and White's king is exposed. The b2-pawn is hanging, and White cannot trap the knight on a1.
notes.teaches: In these sharp lines, the b2-pawn is a constant weakness. Black's threats against the king and the b2-pawn often lead to a decisive attack.
notes.plans: Play ...Bxc2 or ...Qxb2 depending on White's response. The key is to keep the king in the center and exploit White's lack of development.

notes.explains: After …Qxb2, White's king is exposed and Black has multiple threats. The knight on b4 is safe because White cannot trap it without losing material.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is in the center, look for tactics that combine pawn grabs with checks and threats. The exposed king often makes such tactics decisive.
notes.plans: Continue attacking the king with moves like ...Bf5 or ...Rd8. The material advantage and king safety ensure a win.

notes.explains: After …Bf5, Black threatens ...Qc1# and ...Qxa1. White is completely lost. The knight on b4 is still safe, and Black's pieces dominate.
notes.teaches: In these lines, the knight on b4 is a monster. It cannot be easily dislodged and supports a devastating attack. Always consider such outposts.
notes.plans: Play ...Qc1# or ...Qxa1 depending on White's move. The game is effectively over.

notes.explains: After …Qxa1+, Black wins the rook. White's king is still exposed, and Black has a decisive material advantage.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify by trading pieces while keeping the king safe. Here, taking the rook is clean and winning.
notes.plans: Trade down to a winning endgame. Keep the king safe and avoid counterplay.

notes.explains: After …Qxh1, Black has a queen and two pawns for a rook. The game is easily winning.
notes.teaches: In these sharp lines, the material imbalance often favors the side with the queen. Use the queen's power to create threats and win more material.
notes.plans: Activate the queen and coordinate with the remaining pieces. Avoid unnecessary risks.

notes.explains: After Qf7, Black is lost. The queen infiltrates and threatens mate. The game is decided by White's superior piece activity.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, use your queen to infiltrate the opponent's position and create mating threats. Keep the king safe.
notes.plans: Play Qf7, threatening Qg7#. If Black defends, continue with Rg6 and other threats.

notes.explains: After Qf7, Black's king is trapped. White has a forced mate or wins material. The technique is straightforward.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, always look for the fastest and safest way to win. Here, Qf7 is decisive.
notes.plans: Play Qg7# or win the rook on g8. The game is over.

notes.explains: Black takes on c3, but white recaptures with the knight, maintaining a strong center and good piece activity.
notes.teaches: Recapturing with the knight is better than with the pawn because it keeps the pawn structure intact and the knight can later move to e4 or d5.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to b2, then consider pushing b4 or playing f4 to open the center.

notes.explains: Black plays Qa6, a strange move trying to prevent b5, but the queen is offside and can be harassed.
notes.teaches: Don't place the queen on a6 in this setup; it becomes a target and hinders black's development.
notes.plans: Play a4 to reinforce b5, then continue with Bb2 and prepare b4.

notes.explains: White plays Qe1 to avoid the pin and prepare to chase the bishop with h3. This is a flexible move that also supports the center.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is pinned, moving the queen out of the pin can be a good way to neutralize it without weakening your pawn structure.
notes.plans: After Qe1, play h3 to force the bishop to decide, then continue with Bb2 and b4.

notes.explains: Black's bishop moves to f5, where it eyes e4. White must be careful not to allow e4, but it's not immediately possible due to defenders.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop lands on f5, watch for the e4 break. Count attackers and defenders before allowing it.
notes.plans: Continue development with Bb2, and if black tries e4, be ready to capture or counterattack.

notes.explains: White develops the bishop to b2, completing the fianchetto setup. The bishop eyes the long diagonal and pressures e5.
notes.teaches: The bishop on b2 is powerful in this setup, especially after the knight on c3 moves, creating a battery with the queen.
notes.plans: Consider moving the knight to e4 or d5, then play Qc3 to create a battery threatening mate on g7.

notes.explains: White plays b4-b5, opening the position. Black captures on b5, but white recaptures with the bishop, threatening Qc3 with mate threats.
notes.teaches: In this setup, the b4-b5 break is a key plan to activate the bishop. Even if material is temporarily sacrificed, the initiative and threats can be overwhelming.
notes.plans: After Bxc4, play Qc3 threatening mate on g7, forcing black to weaken with f6 or lose material.

notes.explains: White plays Qc3, creating a battery with the bishop on b2. Black must respond to the mate threat on g7.
notes.teaches: Building a battery on the long diagonal is a powerful idea when the opponent's king is castled kingside. It forces weakening moves like f6.
notes.plans: After black defends, continue pressuring the weakened dark squares, possibly with Rc1 or doubling rooks.

notes.explains: Black plays f6 to block the diagonal, but this weakens the e6 pawn and dark squares. White can exploit this.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their pawn structure to block a diagonal, look for ways to exploit the new weaknesses, especially on the same color complex.
notes.plans: Play Bb3 or Bd3 to target e6, or consider opening the center with d5.

notes.explains: White places the bishop on d5, dominating the board and threatening e6. Black's position is collapsing.
notes.teaches: A centralized bishop on a strong outpost can be decisive. It restricts the opponent's pieces and creates multiple threats.
notes.plans: Continue pressure on e6, possibly with Rfe1 or Qd3, and prepare to break through.

notes.explains: White plays Qd3, threatening Qxe6+ and further pressure. Black is helpless.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and pawns are weak, concentrate your pieces on the weak points. A queen and bishop duo can be lethal.
notes.plans: Capture on e6 or play Re6 to double rooks, forcing resignation.

notes.explains: White captures on e6, winning a pawn and maintaining a crushing attack.
notes.teaches: Once you have a decisive advantage, simplify by capturing material while keeping the initiative.
notes.plans: After Rxe6, continue with Re1 or Qd5+ to force mate or further material gains.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with Qe8#, exploiting the weak dark squares and exposed king.
notes.teaches: The fianchetto bishop setup can lead to a swift mate when the opponent weakens their kingside. Always look for mating patterns.

notes.explains: Black has a blockading knight on d5, and after the trade on d6 we reach an IQP position where Black controls the square in front of the isolated pawn.
notes.teaches: In IQP structures, the side opposing the pawn wants to blockade it with a knight and then trade off minor pieces to make the pawn harder to defend.
notes.plans: Complete development efficiently, then build pressure on d4.

notes.explains: Developing the light-squared bishop to g4 pins the knight and is a natural way to develop outside the pawn chain, keeping the bishop active.
notes.teaches: When possible, develop bishops outside your pawn chain to maintain their activity and control over central squares.
notes.plans: After Bg4, Black will play e6, Be7, and castle, keeping the blockade on d5.

notes.explains: Black has completed development with a solid setup: knight blockading d5, bishops placed actively, and king castled kingside.
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, the side with the blockade should aim to trade minor pieces to increase pressure on the isolated pawn.
notes.plans: Bring a rook to d8, then consider trading knights and bishops to leave White with fewer defenders for d4.

notes.explains: Black plays g6 to blunt White's queen on d3 and prevent any immediate mate threats on h7. The weakness of the dark squares is not exploitable because White has no dark-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: Whether a pawn move like g6 creates a weakness depends entirely on the opponent's remaining pieces. If the opponent lacks the bishop to exploit the dark squares, the move is safe.
notes.plans: Continue pressuring d4; after White's response, Black will trade knights on d5 and then capture the isolated pawn.

notes.explains: After trading knights on d5, Black recaptures with the queen to keep the d-file open. With three attackers on d4 and only two defenders, Black wins the isolated pawn.
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, once you have a blockade and have traded off minor pieces, the pawn becomes vulnerable. Counting attackers and defenders is key to deciding when to capture.
notes.plans: After winning the pawn, Black must convert the extra pawn in the endgame by improving piece activity and creating passed pawns.

notes.explains: Kg7 is a multi-purpose move: it defends against potential back-rank mates and takes the sting out of Rc8 because after Rc8 Black can capture and White's recapture is not check, giving Black time to trade queens.
notes.teaches: King moves can be prophylactic, preventing tactical ideas like checks that would allow the opponent to recapture with tempo. Always consider how the king's position affects tactical sequences.
notes.plans: After Kg7, Black will continue to improve the position, possibly moving the queen to f6 to clear the d-file for the rooks.

notes.explains: Black moves the queen to f6, clearing the d-file for the rooks and also eyeing the b2 pawn. This improves the queen's activity while preparing to double rooks.
notes.teaches: In positions with an extra pawn, improving your pieces without forcing events is often best. Patience and small improvements lead to opportunities.
notes.plans: After Qf6, Black will play b6 to defend the a7 pawn and then slowly increase pressure, waiting for White to make a mistake.

notes.explains: Black plays h5 with the plan to advance to h4, clamping down on White's kingside pawns and potentially taking away escape squares from White's king. This is a typical GM move that improves the position without risk.
notes.teaches: Advancing a pawn to restrict the opponent's pawns and king can be a powerful long-term improvement, especially in endgames where pawn mobility matters.
notes.plans: After h5, Black will continue to improve piece placement and wait for White to weaken further.

notes.explains: After White's inaccurate a5, Black captures and then plays Rc5, attacking the b2 pawn and creating threats. White's position collapses under pressure.
notes.teaches: When you have an extra pawn, keep the pressure on. Eventually the opponent's position may crack, leading to further material gains.
notes.plans: Black will now win more pawns and then convert the advantage with accurate technique.

notes.explains: Black plays Qa1, threatening checkmate on h1 and also protecting the a2 pawn. This is a precise move that maintains the initiative and keeps White tied down.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, look for moves that create multiple threats (mate, material gain) while also covering your own weaknesses.
notes.plans: After Qa1, Black is up three pawns and will convert by pushing the a-pawn and activating the king.

notes.explains: Black plays Rd6, preparing to bring the rook to a6 behind the a-pawn. In rook endgames, rooks belong behind passed pawns.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, place your rook behind your passed pawn to maximize its power and tie down the opponent's rook to defense.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn, bring the king to the queenside, and create a second passed pawn on the kingside.

notes.explains: Black pushes the a-pawn all the way to a2, forcing White's rook to stay on the first rank. The king on f5 is safe from checks and supports the pawns.
notes.teaches: When converting a rook endgame with a passed pawn, advance the pawn as far as possible while keeping your king active and safe from checks.
notes.plans: After a2, Black will bring the king to the queenside and create a second passed pawn on the kingside to win.

notes.explains: Black trades knights and plays Bh6 to target the weakened e3-pawn after f3. This is an unconventional but logical way to pressure White's center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens a pawn (here e3), redeploying a bishop to attack it can be more effective than routine development, even if it means moving a fianchettoed bishop.
notes.plans: Black will continue pressuring e3 with ...Qb6 or ...Bxg2 ideas, while preparing queenside expansion with ...b5 to discourage White from castling queenside.

notes.explains: Black plays b5 preemptively, gaining space on the queenside and preparing to open lines if White castles queenside. This move gains a tempo if White castles queenside.
notes.teaches: In opposite-side castling positions, every tempo matters. Starting your attack early, even before the opponent commits their king, can be crucial.
notes.plans: If White castles queenside, Black will open the b-file with ...b4 and ...c5. If White castles kingside, Black will continue with ...Bb7 and ...e5.

notes.explains: Black opens the queenside with b4 and c5, forcing White to recapture on c3. This prevents White from castling queenside safely, as the b-file is now open.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, opening lines can be more effective than a direct attack. Here, Black opens the b-file to target the king.
notes.plans: Black will now redeploy the knight to d7 to chase the bishop and prepare ...e5, opening the center while White's king is vulnerable.

notes.explains: Black plays Bb7, a patient preparatory move. It protects the d5-pawn before pushing e5, preventing White from exploiting the d5 weakness after the center opens.
notes.teaches: Before executing a central break, ensure your pawns are protected. A seemingly passive move like Bb7 can be essential to avoid tactical refutations.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with ...e5, opening the center. The bishop on b7 will support the d5-pawn and later become active on the long diagonal.

notes.explains: Black strikes in the center with e5 after White's g4. This is timely because White's kingside attack is not yet coordinated, and Black opens lines to exploit White's exposed king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent launches a pawn storm, countering in the center can be more effective than defending passively. The center break often disrupts the attack.
notes.plans: After ...e5, Black will open the center with ...dxe5 or ...exd4, activating the rooks and bishops. The knight will later target weak points like g4.

notes.explains: Black plays Re8, maintaining the tension. There is no need to capture immediately; the rook supports the e5-pawn and prepares to recapture if White takes.
notes.teaches: In complex positions, keeping the tension can be better than resolving it. Patience forces the opponent to make the first concession.
notes.plans: Black will wait for White to commit. If White castles kingside, Black will target the g4-pawn with ...Nf6. If White does nothing, Black will eventually push ...e4.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6, attacking the g4-pawn. This is possible because White's bishop cannot capture on e5 due to tactical lines: ...Nxg4, Bxg7, Qxh4 with mate threats.
notes.teaches: When attacking a pawn, always check if the opponent's counter-capture leads to tactics. Here, the threat of ...Qxh4 forces White to defend passively.
notes.plans: Black will win the g4-pawn, then use the open h-file and central control to launch a decisive attack. The knight will later go to g4 or e5.

notes.explains: Black captures the g4-pawn with the knight. This is safe because White's counterplay is insufficient; the knight is well-placed to attack e3 and later f3.
notes.teaches: Winning a pawn is good, but ensure the resulting position gives you active play. Here, the knight on g4 is a powerful outpost that ties down White's pieces.
notes.plans: Black will target the e3-pawn with ...Nxe3 or ...Qc7, and later bring the queen to the kingside. The open h-file and central pressure will decide the game.

notes.explains: Black plays Qc8 instead of the more natural Rc8. This subtlety avoids a tactical line where White's rook checks on d8 after ...Nxe3, winning material.
notes.teaches: In complex positions, every move must be calculated precisely. A seemingly equivalent move can have a hidden tactical flaw. Always check for checks and captures.
notes.plans: Black will recapture on c5, then use the queen and rook to pressure White's weak pawns. The knight on g4 will continue to threaten e3 and f2.

notes.explains: Black's attack culminates in winning material. The knight on f3 is unstoppable, and White's king is exposed. Black simplifies to a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: A successful attack often ends not with checkmate but with winning material. Use the king's vulnerability as a springboard to gain a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: Black will convert the extra material by activating the rooks and pushing the queenside pawns. The king is safe, and White has no counterplay.

notes.explains: Black has a slight advantage: White's e5-pawn is isolated and blockaded, but Black must avoid tunnel vision on that pawn alone.
notes.teaches: Don't fixate on one weakness; combine threats on multiple fronts to overstretch the opponent's defense.
notes.plans: Play ...b4 to attack the c2-pawn, then reroute the knight to c6 to pressure e5, and look for tactical opportunities like ...c4.

notes.explains: Black reroutes the knight to c6 to attack the e5-pawn, while the rook and king alignment on the f-file hints at a tactical idea with ...Bc5.
notes.teaches: Rerouting pieces to target weaknesses is a common theme; always be alert to tactical patterns like aligned king and rook.
notes.plans: Play ...c4 to open lines, then ...Bc5 exploiting the f2-rook, forcing White into a defensive bind.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the exchange with ...Bxf2, winning the queen and a rook due to the fork on d4. White's position collapses.
notes.teaches: Pressure creates tactical opportunities; when the opponent is overextended, sacrifices can be decisive.
notes.plans: Convert the material advantage by simplifying when convenient, but keep queens on if the king is exposed.

notes.explains: Black is up an exchange and a pawn. The conversion requires vigilance: avoid back-rank mates and choose between attacking or trading.
notes.teaches: When converting, combine attacking and simplifying methods flexibly; don't dogmatically stick to one plan.
notes.plans: Trade rooks if possible, keep queens on to threaten the king, and always check for back-rank weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black chooses Qc7 over Qc6 to keep the queen active and maintain mating threats against White's exposed king.
notes.teaches: In endgames with exposed kings, keeping queens on can accelerate the win; don't trade automatically.
notes.plans: Use the queen to create mating threats, then trade down when safe.

notes.explains: Black trades rooks to simplify, then prepares to trade queens or continue the attack as needed.
notes.teaches: Evaluate each trade: if it brings you closer to a won endgame or removes defensive pieces, it's good.
notes.plans: Trade queens when the king is safe, otherwise keep them to exploit the exposed king.

notes.explains: Black trades queens into a rook endgame up a pawn. The conversion is straightforward with active rook.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, activity matters more than pawns; keep the rook active and king safe.
notes.plans: Use the rook to attack White's pawns and support the passed pawn.

notes.explains: Black wins a second pawn and the game is decided. The rook endgame is easily winning.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, keep pressure and avoid unnecessary risks; the extra pawns will convert.
notes.plans: Advance the passed pawns and use the king to support them.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Ng4, threatening ...Ne5. White can consider Qc2 to support e4 and prepare development of the dark-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: When the opponent threatens a knight outpost, reinforcing the center with Qc2 is a solid response that also connects rooks.
notes.plans: Continue with Rc1, then b3 and Bb2, or consider trading the light-squared bishop for Black's fianchetto bishop to ease development.

notes.explains: Black retreats the knight to d7, which makes it harder for Black to play ...e6 later. White now has a choice for the light-squared bishop: keep it on c4, move to f1, or try Bb5 to induce ...a6 then retreat.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, you can use provocative moves like Bb5 to gain a tempo or force a weakness, even if you plan to retreat.
notes.plans: Play Bb5, then after ...a6, retreat to f1 to keep the bishop and prepare a4 to fix the a-pawn.

notes.explains: White plays a4 to fix the a5 pawn and prevent Black from playing ...a4 to block b3. Now the rook can go to a3 and then to d3 to pressure the center, or simply play b3 and Bb2.
notes.teaches: Fixing a pawn with a4 prevents Black from using it to hinder your queenside expansion. The rook can be rerouted via a3 to d3 for central pressure.
notes.plans: Play Ra3, then after ...e6, trade on e6 and play Rd3 to attack d6. Alternatively, if Black doesn't play ...e6, proceed with b3 and Bb2.

notes.explains: Black trades bishops on a6. White should accept because keeping the bishop would allow ...Nb8-c6-a5, attacking the weak a4 pawn. After Bxa6, White's rook on a3 can go to d3.
notes.teaches: When a fianchettoed bishop is under attack, consider trading it if the alternative allows the opponent to target a weakness. Flexibility in rook placement is key.
notes.plans: Play Bxa6, then Rxa6, then Rd3 to pressure d6. Follow up with b3 and Bb2.

notes.explains: White's rook on d3 pressures the d6 pawn. Black has two center pawns but they are weak and require constant defense. White's plan is to trade Black's dark-squared bishop and then attack the king.
notes.teaches: Having more center pawns doesn't matter if they are weak and your pieces are passive. The rook on d3 is more useful than on b1 because it attacks the center.
notes.plans: Play b3, then Bb2 to trade bishops. After the trade, White can use the e-file and the weakened dark squares around Black's king to create mating threats.

notes.explains: Black pushes d5, opening the center. White recaptures and now the e-file is open. White's plan is still to trade the dark-squared bishops and use the e-file for attack.
notes.teaches: When the center opens, the importance of trading the opponent's fianchettoed bishop increases because it exposes the king. The e-file becomes a highway for your rooks.
notes.plans: Play Bb2 to trade bishops, then use the e-file and the weakened dark squares to create threats.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Qe7 instead of ...d5. White continues with b3 and now has the option of Bb2 or first improving the knight with Nf3, threatening to go to g5 or trade on e5.
notes.teaches: Patience is key. Instead of rushing to trade, improve your pieces first. The knight on f3 is more flexible than on g3, and it can later go to g5 or support a trade on e5.
notes.plans: Play Nf3, then after ...Nd7, decide whether to trade on e5 or play Rd1 to increase pressure on d6.

notes.explains: Black plays c4 to trade knights. White recaptures and plays Qe2, attacking the knight. Black blunders with ...Rb2, allowing Qxc4 and then Qxf2+ Kh2, when the rook on g3 defends g2.
notes.teaches: Always check if your opponent's move creates a tactical opportunity. Here, Black assumed Qxd4 was impossible, but the queen fork wins material.
notes.plans: After Qxc4, Black's best is ...Ne5, but White is better with a pawn up and pressure.

notes.explains: The Benko Gambit is an underrated opening that gives Black serious queenside counterplay when it works. However, White can avoid it with Nf3 or play the main line with Nc3, Bxa6, e4, which is considered better for White.
notes.teaches: Even if a gambit is theoretically dubious at the highest level, it can be very effective at club level. The key is to understand the typical attacking ideas: pressure on the b-file, the fianchettoed bishop, and the a6-c4 pawn structure.
notes.plans: If playing the Benko as Black, be prepared for White's avoidance lines. If playing White, the Nc3/Bxa6/e4 line is a reliable way to get an advantage.

notes.explains: Black's ...Rb2 is a blunder because Qxc4 leaves the queen on f2 check defended by the rook on g3. Black resigns.
notes.teaches: In time pressure, players often make false assumptions. Always double-check if your opponent's queen can be captured or if there are checks.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Bc4, Black should not panic. The threat to f7 is not immediate because d6 is already played. Developing with Nc6 is flexible, and e6 can wait.
notes.teaches: Against early Bc4 in the Sicilian, develop naturally without rushing to defend f7. The pawn on d6 already covers e5, so Nc6 is safe.
notes.plans: Continue development with Nf6, then consider e6 to challenge the knight on g5 if White plays Ng5.

notes.explains: When White plays Ng5 and Qh5, the knight on g5 is undefended except by the queen. Black can kick the queen with g6, then fork or pin to win the knight.
notes.teaches: Always check if an attacking piece is defended. If the defender can be chased away, the piece may become vulnerable.
notes.plans: Play g6, then after Qg4 play d5 forking queen and knight, or after Qh4 play Be7 followed by h6.

notes.explains: Black is up two pieces and two pawns. The simplest plan is to trade pieces and simplify. The idea of Nxe4 (or similar) to land a piece on e4, then d5 wins back material with interest.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, look to trade pieces and simplify. In Sicilian positions with Bc4, watch for sacrifices to plant a piece on e4.
notes.plans: Play Nxe4, then after dxe4, d5 wins back the piece. Continue developing and trade down.

notes.explains: With a huge material advantage, the traditional plan is to create a passed pawn and push it. Here, open files allow rook trades to ease the process.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, create a passed pawn and advance it. Use rook trades to clear the path.
notes.plans: Play Rfb8 to create luft, then trade rooks and push the d-pawn. Place bishops to cover squares in front of the pawn.

notes.explains: After e4 Nc6, White can play d4 (independent) or Nf3 (transposing to Ruy Lopez/Italian). A solid positional approach is c3, making the center 'bite on granite', then develop with Bd3, Nbd2, and later Nf1-g3.
notes.teaches: Against the Nimzowitsch, a solid setup with c3, Bd3, and Nbd2 controls the center without overextending. The pawns act as bodyguards for the bishop.
notes.plans: Play c3, Bd3, Nbd2, O-O, then Re1 and consider a4 to pressure Black's queenside if he plays b5.

notes.explains: Black's pawn on b5 is a weakness. White can play a4 to pressure it, potentially opening files for the rook. If Black takes on a4, Qxa4 gives White a strong position.
notes.teaches: In positions with a fixed pawn chain, look to attack the base of the chain. A pawn that sticks out like a sore thumb can be targeted.
notes.plans: Play a4, threatening to capture or open the a-file. If Black plays bxa4, recapture with the queen. Then consider Bb5 to build a battery with Qa4.

notes.explains: After a4, Black played f6, which weakens the light squares. White noticed a check on b3, which becomes relevant if Black captures on b2. The move Bb5 builds a battery and prepares a7 to trap the knight.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a weakening move like f6, note new tactical possibilities (e.g., checks on b3). Always look for ways to exploit weaknesses.
notes.plans: Play Bb5, threatening Qa4 and a7. If Black plays Na6, Bxa6 Rxa7 wins the pawn. If Black misses this, capture on b5 and continue.

notes.explains: White is up a piece and has a strong center. The move c4 glues the bishop and ties down Black's pieces. Later, Rook d3 attacks the weak d6 pawn, and the game simplifies.
notes.teaches: When ahead, use pawns to defend your pieces permanently ('pawns are the best defenders'). Target opponent's weak pawns to increase pressure.
notes.plans: Play c4 to secure the bishop, then Rd3 to attack d6. After winning the pawn, trade down and push the passed pawn.

notes.explains: After e4 Nf6 e5 Nd5, White can play d4, but Black often plays d5 leading to sharp lines similar to the Scandinavian. White can avoid theory with Nf3 and develop naturally.
notes.teaches: Against Alekhine's, playing Nf3 and developing solidly avoids the sharp theoretical lines. Don't give Black what he wants if you're not prepared.
notes.plans: Play Nf3, then c3 to support d4, Bd3, and develop with Nbd2. Consider a4 only if necessary; prophylaxis should be purposeful.

notes.explains: Black's pawn on b5 is a weakness. White plays a4 to strike at it. After Black plays Nc4, axb5 wins the knight. The move Bb5 was found by noticing the light-square weaknesses after c5.
notes.teaches: When your opponent weakens a complex of squares, look to place your bishop on that color. Use the queen to create a battery and pressure.
notes.plans: Play a4, then after Nc4, axb5 wins a pawn. Continue with Bb5 and Qa4 to maintain pressure. If Black plays Na6, consider a7 to trap the knight.

notes.explains: After winning material, White plays c4 to glue the bishop and prevent counterplay. The queen on b6 exerts an x-ray on the king; instead of playing Kh1 (symptom), White plays Qa7 (cause) to eliminate the threat.
notes.teaches: When dealing with a threat, ask if you can target the cause (the attacking piece) rather than just the symptom (the check). This often leads to more effective moves.
notes.plans: Play c4 to secure the bishop, then Qa7 to neutralize the queen's x-ray. After exchanges, push the passed pawn.

notes.explains: Black's a6 is a waste of time; we punish it by pushing d5, claiming central space and blocking the knight from c6.
notes.teaches: When the opponent wastes time with non-essential pawn moves, strike in the center to gain space and restrict their pieces.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, aiming to keep the d5 pawn solid without needing c4.

notes.explains: Black wants to play f5; by putting the bishop on d3 we discourage that advance and keep an eye on the kingside.
notes.teaches: Place bishops on diagonals that hinder the opponent's natural pawn breaks.
notes.plans: Continue development, preparing to bring the knight to g3 via d2-f1-g3, a typical Ruy Lopez maneuver to handle the bishop pin.

notes.explains: The knight on g3 eyes f5 and also covers h5, so when we play h3 the bishop must either capture or retreat, ending the pin.
notes.teaches: Use knight maneuvers to neutralize bishops pinning your knight; the g3 square is often ideal for both attack and defense.
notes.plans: After h3, we can consider queenside expansion with b4 or a4 to undermine Black's pawn chain, exploiting the undefended rook on a8.

notes.explains: With the rook on a8 undefended, we threaten a4-a5 winning the b5 pawn. Black cannot move the knight because the rook is loose.
notes.teaches: Always look for undefended pieces; they create tactical threats that can force concessions or win material.
notes.plans: After a4, if Black defends b5, we can drop the bishop back to c2 or b3 and complete development with castling, then bring the knight to f5.

notes.explains: The knight on f5 is a powerful outpost, pressuring g7 and supporting a future bishop to g5. Black's position is solid but we are accumulating pressure.
notes.teaches: Establish knights on strong outposts like f5; they can dominate the position even without immediate threats.
notes.plans: Follow up with Bg5, then bring the other knight to h2 and g4 to target the f6 knight, and prepare f4 to open lines.

notes.explains: The knight on h2 prepares to go to g4 to trade off the defender on f6, while also supporting the f4 break. The f2 pawn will be pushed to open the f-file.
notes.teaches: When you need more attacking force, redeploy pieces that are doing little; here the knight goes from g3 to h2 to g4, and the f-pawn will open lines.
notes.plans: Play Ng4, then f4 (after moving the king if needed), and bring the queen to f3 to join the attack.

notes.explains: Black plays g6, creating a weakness on h6. The knight can now go to h6, and the dark squares around the black king become vulnerable.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens the side you are attacking, immediately note the new weaknesses (like h6) and target them.
notes.plans: Plant the knight on h6, then look for ways to deliver a 'lobster pincer' checkmate (knight on h6, queen on h4/g4, bishop on g5).

notes.explains: We chase the knight away from h5 with g4, preparing to deliver the 'lobster pincer' mate (Nh6+ and Qh4). The pawn move is safe because Black has no pieces to exploit the king exposure.
notes.teaches: Attack with pawns in front of your own king when the opponent has no counterplay; the pawn advances can drive away defenders and open lines.
notes.plans: After g4, Black's knight must move; then we can play Qh4 and Nh6+ leading to mate or win of material.

notes.explains: We trade the bishop for the knight on f6, winning the queen after Qxd8? because the knight on f5 covers e7. The attack converts to a material advantage.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is the only defender, removing a key defender can win material or force a decisive attack.
notes.plans: After Bxf6, if Black recaptures with the queen, Nxe7+ forks king and queen; if Black avoids that, we remain up a piece with a strong attack.

notes.explains: The combination wins: after Bxf6, the queen is forked; Black avoids immediate loss but ends up in a mating net. The attack is clinical.
notes.teaches: Precision in attack means choosing the most forcing continuation; even when up material, look for the quickest win.
notes.plans: Execute the sequence: Bxf6, then Nxe7+ forking king and queen, then capture on g6 and deliver mate.

notes.explains: The game ends in a forced checkmate. The attack succeeded because we accumulated pressure slowly and then struck precisely.
notes.teaches: Do not rush the attack; build up slowly, then when the moment comes, calculate the forcing sequence to the end.

notes.explains: The entire game illustrates a typical attacking plan in the Alapin: d5 wedge, knight to f5, bishop to g5, knight transfer to h2-g4, then f4 and queen to f3/h4.
notes.teaches: Memorize this attacking sequence: Nf5, Bg5, Nh2, Ng4, Qf3/h4, f4. It is a recurring pattern in many Sicilian and Ruy Lopez positions.

notes.explains: Extra material is like having more players on a soccer field; it doesn't automatically win the game. You still need to create scoring chances (attacks).
notes.teaches: Don't panic when you sacrifice a pawn; if you have a lead in development or attacking chances, the material deficit may be irrelevant. Focus on activity.

notes.explains: The 'lobster pincer' checkmate pattern: knight on h6, queen on h4/g4, bishop on g5, with the knight delivering check and the queen delivering mate.
notes.teaches: Recognize common checkmate patterns; they often recur in similar attacking setups.

notes.explains: After Nc3, Black often plays Bb4 pinning the knight. White can play a3, threatening to win the bishop because the rook on a1 is not hanging (Black has no pieces developed to exploit it).
notes.teaches: A move like a3 can be strong even if it looks like it hangs a rook, because the opponent lacks the coordination to take it. Always consider the opponent's development before assuming a tactic works.
notes.plans: Play a3, and if Bxc3+, recapture with bxc3, opening the b-file and giving White a strong pawn center.

notes.explains: Black takes on c3, and White recaptures with the pawn. This ruins White's queenside pawn structure, but the knight on d6 (after Nd6+) will be a monster, completely paralyzing Black's development.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid to ruin your pawn structure if it gives you a powerful outpost for a knight. The knight on d6 in the Sicilian can be worth more than a clean pawn structure.
notes.plans: Play Nd6+ Kf8 (or Ke7), then Qd6, and Black cannot develop his kingside pieces. White will castle kingside and attack.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6, trying to develop. White can now play Nd6+ and then Qd6, or even play Bc4 and castle, building up pressure slowly. The knight on d6 is a permanent blockade.
notes.teaches: When you have a dominant knight on a weak square, you don't need to rush. Develop your other pieces and increase the pressure.
notes.plans: Play Bc4, O-O, then f4 to open lines. Black's pieces are stuck and White's attack will be overwhelming.

notes.explains: After Qd6+, Black's king is stuck in the center. White has a huge advantage. The game ended quickly with a checkmate after Qd6+ Kf8? (a blunder) but even with Ke8, White is winning.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, look for immediate checks and mating threats. The queen and knight can create a deadly attack.
notes.plans: If Ke8, White can play Bc4, O-O, and then f4, breaking open the center. Black's king will be exposed.

notes.explains: White fell into the trap: after dxc5, Black trades queens and wins a rook with Bxc3+. White is down material and Black has a winning position.
notes.teaches: Always check if a pawn capture leads to a tactical sequence. In the Grünfeld, taking on c5 can be deadly if the bishop on f4 is undefended.
notes.plans: Black is up a rook. Develop quickly, castle, and use the extra material to win.

notes.explains: Black is up a rook. White has some compensation with the two bishops and a pawn, but Black's position is winning. Black should develop and consolidate.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplify by trading pieces and avoid unnecessary risks. Develop your pieces and get the king to safety.
notes.plans: Play Nc6, O-O, and then bring the rook to d8 or c8. The extra rook will decide the game.

notes.explains: White plays Nf3, trying to develop. Black should now play Bg4 or Nc6, developing with tempo. The bishop on a1 is safe for now.
notes.teaches: In the Grünfeld, even when winning, keep developing. Don't let White's pieces become active.
notes.plans: Play Bg4, pinning the knight, then Nc6, O-O, and eventually push e5 or f5 to open lines.

notes.explains: White plays Rc1, threatening to trap the bishop on a1. Black can save it by playing Bb2 or Bg7, but Black is still winning.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, don't be greedy; consolidate. The bishop on a1 can retreat to b2 or g7.
notes.plans: Play Bb2, then Nc6, O-O, and use the extra rook to attack.

notes.explains: After e4 d6 d4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 f4, Black's setup with a6 and e6 is suboptimal. White should continue developing with Nf3 and Bd3, ignoring b5.
notes.teaches: In the Austrian Attack, rapid development and central control are key. Don't fear Black's queenside expansion; it only helps your kingside attack.
notes.plans: Play Nf3, Bd3, O-O, Qe1, then consider e5 to close the center and target f6.

notes.explains: The game followed a typical Austrian Attack plan: e5 closed the center, Ne4 targeted f6, g4 evicted the knight, and Nf6+ won a piece. The rest was a smooth conversion.
notes.teaches: A well-executed kingside attack in the Austrian Attack can lead to a quick win. Key ideas: close the center, target f6, use pawn storms, and combine tactics.
notes.plans: After winning material, activate all pieces and look for mating threats. Avoid unnecessary queen trades if the attack continues.

notes.explains: After winning a piece, White coordinated the rooks and bishop to deliver checkmate. The final position shows a classic back-rank mate with Rf8#.
notes.teaches: Even in the endgame, look for mating attacks. A rook and bishop can work together to trap the king.

notes.explains: The key concept in this game was exploiting the d6 square. Black's combination of g6 and e6 created a permanent hole on d6, which White targeted with Bf4 and later Nd6.
notes.teaches: Never combine g6 and e6 without a solid plan to defend d6. The d6 square is a critical weakness in many openings, especially the Sicilian and Kings Indian setups.
notes.plans: Develop with Bf4 to pressure d6, then use knights to occupy the hole. If Black doesn't play d6, punish it immediately.

notes.explains: In the second game, Black played g6 and e6 early, creating a hole on d6. White responded with Bf4, targeting d6. Black failed to play d6 in time, leading to a quick collapse.
notes.teaches: When your opponent creates a hole on d6, immediately pressure it with bishops and knights. Delay in patching the hole can be fatal.
notes.plans: Play Bf4, then Nbd2 to prepare Nc4 and Nd6. If Black doesn't play d6, take on c5 and occupy d6.

notes.explains: After Bf4, Black played e6, creating a hole on d6. White played Nbd2 to prepare Nc4, threatening Nd6. Black's position quickly became untenable.
