notes.teaches: When you have an extra pawn, you can often use it to open lines and trade queens, leaving the opponent's king exposed. This is a recurring idea in the QGA, Blackmar-Diemer Gambit, and c3 Sicilian.
notes.plans: After e5 dxe5, Black plays Qxd1+ and gets a comfortable endgame with a lead in development.

notes.explains: The order of moves matters: playing Nf3 first prevents Black's ...e5 push, while e3 allows it but is more flexible. The e3 e5 line is very theoretical.
notes.teaches: Move order can be crucial in the opening. Understand the differences between similar lines to choose the one that suits your style.
notes.plans: If you want to avoid theory, play Nf3 first. If you want to play ambitiously, play e4.

notes.explains: White plays Qh5 attacking the knight on e5. Black defends with Bd6, renewing the threat of Ng3.
notes.teaches: Buttress key pieces to maintain threats; here Bd6 protects the knight and keeps pressure.
notes.plans: Play Qf6 to force the queen back, then relocate queen to h4. Alternatively, g6 attacking the queen first is more precise.

notes.explains: Black plays Qe7, putting king and queen on the same file. White wants to open the e-file for a skewer.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen and king share a file, aim to open that file with a pawn trade.
notes.plans: Castle to prepare Re1, then take on d4 after Black moves the knight from f6.

notes.explains: White castles, then after Ng4, takes on d4, leaving the knight on g4 stranded with no squares, winning it.
notes.teaches: When a piece is misplaced, punish it by cutting off its retreat squares.
notes.plans: Develop Nc3, centralize with Nd5, and pile up on Black's kingside weaknesses.

notes.explains: White centralizes the knight to d5 and piles up on h6. Simplicity is key: bring all pieces in patiently.
notes.teaches: After winning material, complete development and accumulate pressure patiently rather than forcing tactics.
notes.plans: Deploy the last rook to the h-file, then look for tactical blows like Bxf7 when the f-file opens.

notes.explains: Bxf7 distracts the rook onto f7, then a discovered check via Ng5 picks off the rook. The king is encircled.
notes.teaches: Combine a discovered check with a vulnerable piece on the opened file to win material.
notes.plans: Take on g5 next move, leading to checkmate.

notes.explains: Knight to b4 is a 'glue move' that defends b2, supports the bishop, and ties White's position together.
notes.teaches: A glue move coordinates multiple defensive and offensive tasks with one piece.
notes.plans: After prophylaxis (g3 to stop Nf4), complete development by castling, then exploit Black's weakened f-pawn push.

notes.explains: Black pushes f5, weakening the diagonal to c4. White takes on f5, and when Black recaptures, a discovered check wins the knight due to the overloaded rook defending both knights.
notes.teaches: An f-pawn push by a castled king weakens key diagonals; exploit with checks that overload defenders.
notes.plans: After winning the knight, harass the king with checks like Bc4 or Bg6, forcing it to e7 for a fork.

notes.explains: Bc4 gives check, exploiting the overloaded rook on f5 that also defends the other rook. Black loses material.
notes.teaches: When a piece defends two others, a check can overload it and force a win.
notes.plans: Capture the knight, then continue harassing the king with queen and bishop battery.

notes.explains: f6 is an exception to 'never play f6' because it prepares e5 with tempo and opens lines for Black's bishops.
notes.teaches: Weigh the pros and cons: f6 weakens the kingside but gains central space and development when the opponent has undeveloped pieces.
notes.plans: Play e5, develop bishop to d6, queen to b6, and bishop to e6 to support the knight on d5.

notes.explains: Black has a strong pawn center and active pieces. White's pieces are passive. Black prepares e4 with f5.
notes.teaches: When you have central control, expand with pawn pushes like f5 to prepare e4, even if it weakens your kingside slightly.
notes.plans: Play f5, then e4, using the queen on b6 to guard d4.

notes.explains: Black captures on e2 with the pawn, attacking the rook. White must move the rook to d2, then Black plays e3, forking king and rook if White takes.
notes.teaches: Calculate concretely: a pawn capture that attacks a rook can lead to a fork if the rook moves to a vulnerable square.
notes.plans: After e3, White gives up the bishop to avoid worse. Black is up a piece and can triple on the d-file.

notes.explains: Black pushes e3, cementing a passed pawn and threatening to advance. White's pieces are passive.
notes.teaches: A passed pawn supported by pieces is a huge asset; advance it and trade down to a winning endgame.
notes.plans: Trade queens by forcing the queen away, then put rooks on the d-file and support the e-pawn.

notes.explains: White recaptures on e5 with a knight, maintaining the attack. Black's king is still in the center.
notes.teaches: In open positions, knights are often better than bishops because they can fork and control key squares.
notes.plans: Continue with Re1, h3 to prevent ...Bg4, and then target the black king with queen and bishop.

notes.explains: White sacrifices a bishop to open the king's position, then uses a double check to force mate.
notes.teaches: Double checks are extremely powerful because the king must move; use them to deliver mate or win material.
notes.plans: After Nd8+, Black cannot block; Qf7# follows next move.

notes.explains: A complex tactical sequence where White sacrifices a rook to expose the black king and win the queen.
notes.teaches: When attacking a castled king, look for sacrifices that open lines and force the king into the open.
notes.plans: After winning the queen, White should consolidate and convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: White has a queen and rook against a rook and bishop, but Black's pawns are weak. White should win.
notes.teaches: In queen endgames, keep the king safe and use checks to improve your position.
notes.plans: White can play Qc7+ to force the king to the back rank, then infiltrate with the queen.

notes.explains: After b3, Black's most principled response is …e5, occupying the center and fighting for an advantage.
notes.teaches: Against flank openings, occupy the center with pawns and then support them with piece development, rather than overextending with too many pawns.
notes.plans: Develop pieces naturally, aiming for a solid center and good piece activity.

notes.explains: After White fianchettoes the bishop to g2, Black plays ...c6 to create a pawn chain (c6-d5-e5) that blunts the bishop's influence on the long diagonal.
notes.teaches: Against a fianchettoed bishop, building a pawn chain on the same color can neutralize its power; the knight can later develop via d7 to f8-g6.
notes.plans: Play ...c6, then ...d5, develop the knight to d7, and later maneuver it to g6 via f8.

notes.explains: Black plays ...a5 to clamp down on the queenside, preventing White's typical expansion with b4 and c4.
notes.teaches: Grab space on the queenside to restrict your opponent's plans, even if the pawn is not immediately defended.
notes.plans: Continue development, castle kingside, and prepare to challenge White's center.

notes.explains: White plays Nc3, which is inconsistent with the Hippo setup. Black can immediately play ...d4, gaining space and asking the knight a question.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes an inconsistent move, punish it by grabbing more central space.
notes.plans: Play ...d4, then follow up with ...b5 to trap the knight on a4 if White plays Na4.

notes.explains: White plays Na4, and Black immediately wins a piece with ...b5. This is a common blind spot even for strong players.
notes.teaches: Always be alert for knight traps involving pawn advances like b5 or g4; even grandmasters can miss them.
notes.plans: After ...b5, the knight is trapped; Black wins a piece and the game is effectively over.

notes.explains: After winning a piece, Black focuses on attacking the weak e3 pawn. The knight goes to d5, attacking e3, and the queen can join via g5.
notes.teaches: Once you have a material advantage, identify the weakest target and attack it with coordinated pieces. Don't rush to develop every piece if the opponent has no threats.
notes.plans: Play Nd5, then Qg5 to pressure e3; take the pawn when possible.

notes.explains: Black chooses to capture the bishop on e4 instead of the rook, because the bishop is White's main attacking piece and removing it leaves the king vulnerable.
notes.teaches: When already up material, prioritize eliminating the opponent's active pieces over gaining extra material. The law of diminishing returns applies: the first piece is most valuable.
notes.plans: Take the bishop, then open the center with ...exd4 to expose the king.

notes.explains: Black plays ...f6 to blunt White's bishop battery on the long diagonal, similar to the earlier ...c6 idea.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid of mate threats if they are easily parried; use pawn moves to block dangerous diagonals.
notes.plans: After ...f6, continue with ...Be5, threatening c5 and setting up a decisive attack.

notes.explains: Black uses a windmill mechanism (rook on g2, king on h1/h2) to win White's queen and pawns.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, use tactical motifs like the windmill to convert efficiently without giving the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: Play Rxg2+ Kh1, then Rg2+ Kh2, and capture the pawn on g3, then move the rook to g2 to win the queen.

notes.explains: If White had played the correct setup (e3, Ne2, Nd2), Black would have played ...Re8, ...Nd7-f8-g6, and later ...Qd7 and ...h5 to pressure the kingside.
notes.teaches: Against passive setups, you can afford to expand on the kingside even after castling, because White has no counterplay.
notes.plans: Maneuver the knight to g6, play Qd7, and push the h-pawn to create weaknesses.

notes.explains: If White plays Ne4, Black should capture on e4. After Bxe4, White's bishop is awkward because it blocks the f3 square and is vulnerable to ...f5.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's piece becomes a target, don't rush to attack it with pawns if it allows the piece to retreat to a good square. Instead, develop and let the awkwardness persist.
notes.plans: Play ...Nd7, then ...f5 to trap the bishop if White doesn't retreat, or simply improve your position.

notes.explains: Black plays ...e6 instead of ...e5 to avoid giving White a d5 outpost. The bishop on c8 is temporarily obstructed, but that's acceptable.
notes.teaches: A move can be good despite obstructing a piece if it serves a higher purpose, like preventing a strong outpost. The bishop can be developed later via b7 or d7.
notes.plans: Play ...Bb4 to pressure e4, then develop the queenside bishop to a6 or b7.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Bb4, pinning the knight and attacking e4. White's bishop on b5 is misplaced.
notes.teaches: Develop with threats to exploit your opponent's poorly placed pieces.
notes.plans: After ...Bb4, Black can consider ...Bxc3+ to ruin White's pawns, or simply continue development.

notes.explains: Black captures toward the center with ...bxc6, opening the a6 diagonal for the bishop and giving Black a central pawn majority.
notes.teaches: When capturing, prefer to capture toward the center to maintain pawn structure and open lines for your pieces.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to a6 to prevent White from castling, then target the weak pawns on c3 and e4.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Qa5, activating the queen and preparing ...Ba6. The queen also eyes the c3 pawn.
notes.teaches: Develop with a dual purpose: activate your queen while preparing to bring out a passive bishop.
notes.plans: Play ...Ba6, then ...Rb8 to put pressure on the b-file.

notes.explains: Black castles, avoiding complications from the line ...Bxc3 Bxc3 Nxe4 Bxg7 Kxg7 Qg4+ etc., which is risky and unnecessary when Black already has a good position.
notes.teaches: When you have a solid advantage, avoid unnecessary complications. Choose the safe, practical continuation.
notes.plans: Castle, then continue with ...Rb8 and ...Ba6, aiming to open the position.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Rb8, activating the rook and x-raying the queen on a5 through the b-pawn. This sets up tactics like ...Rxb3 if White's queen moves.
notes.teaches: Lateral x-rays with rooks are powerful; activate your least active piece and look for hidden tactical possibilities.
notes.plans: After ...Rb8, if White plays c4, Black can trade queens and enter a winning endgame. Otherwise, infiltrate with ...Rb2.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Qe5+, gaining a tempo and forcing White to block with the queen. After the trade, Black wins another pawn on c2.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, simplify to a winning endgame. Don't hesitate to trade queens if it leads to a clear win.
notes.plans: Trade queens, then capture on c2, and use the extra pawns to win the endgame.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Rb2, infiltrating the second rank. The rook is well placed and supports further advances.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, rooks belong on the seventh rank (second rank for Black). Infiltrate and create threats.
notes.plans: Double rooks on the second rank, then target the g2 pawn or create a mating net.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Ba6, activating the bishop and threatening to take on c4. White cannot capture due to ...Rb1#.
notes.teaches: Involve your remaining pieces; the bishop on a6 is powerful because it pins the rook to the back rank.
notes.plans: Play ...Ba6, then ...Rfb8, and if White plays Nc5, take on c4 with the bishop, deflecting the rook and mating.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Rbb2, doubling rooks on the second rank and threatening ...Rxg2#. White is forced to take on c4, allowing mate.
notes.teaches: Double rooks on the second rank create irresistible mating threats. Force your opponent to make concessions.
notes.plans: Play ...Rbb2, then after ...Bxc4, play ...Rb1# or ...Ra1#.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Bg4, pinning the knight. White responds with h3, asking the bishop to declare its intentions.
notes.teaches: When your piece is pinned, you can often ask the pinning piece to commit with a pawn move like h3. If it retreats to h5, you have the option to play g4 later.
notes.plans: Play h3, then if ...Bh5, consider g4 when it is advantageous, but don't rush; castle first.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Nd4, and White responds with g4, which is now strong because it gains space and prepares Qf3 and Bg5.
notes.teaches: Wait for the right moment to play g4; it is most effective when the knight is on d4, as it also threatens to trap the bishop and creates attacking chances.
notes.plans: Play g4, then Qf3 and Bg5, putting pressure on Black's kingside.

notes.explains: White plays Bg5, threatening to take on f6 and then Nd5. Black blunders with ...Qe7, allowing Nd5 with a fork on c7 and e7.
notes.teaches: Always be alert for knight forks; when a knight reaches d5, it often creates devastating threats.
notes.plans: Play Nd5, and if ...Qe7, the queen is forked; if ...Qd8, then Nxf6+ and Bxf6 wins material.

notes.explains: White plays Nd5, forking queen and bishop. Black's queen is lost.
notes.teaches: When you have a knight on a strong outpost, look for tactical blows that exploit the opponent's loose pieces.
notes.plans: Capture the queen and convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: In the famous Winter-Capablanca game, Capablanca played ...g5 to imprison White's bishop on g3. The key detail is that ...Nxg5 is not a threat because of ...Nxd5, leaving the bishop undefended.
notes.teaches: When imprisoning a bishop, ensure that your opponent cannot free it with a sacrifice. Check concrete tactics before committing.
notes.plans: After ...g5, White's bishop is trapped; Black can then open the queenside and win with the extra piece.

notes.explains: In the speedrun game, Black had an uncontested bishop on c5 and White's pawn on g4 was vulnerable, so the Capablanca plan was not directly applicable.
notes.teaches: Pattern recognition is useful, but always adapt to the concrete specifics of the position. Do not apply a plan blindly if the conditions are different.
notes.plans: Instead of imprisoning the bishop, White played Bg5 and later Nd5, winning material.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Accelerated Grand Prix Attack
notes.explains: After winning a pawn and simplifying, Black's queen is safe in the center because there are multiple retreat squares. The queen should not fear being trapped as long as evacuation routes exist.
notes.teaches: A queen in the center is rarely trapped if you have planned retreat squares. Don't panic—calculate the escape routes.
notes.plans: Consolidate by developing the kingside and trading down to a winning endgame.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Accelerated Grand Prix Attack
notes.explains: Black's ...h5 is prophylactic, preventing h3 and gaining control of kingside squares. After ...h4, Black has a powerful attack with ...Nh6 sacrificing a pawn for initiative.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like ...h5 can prevent White's pawn breaks and create attacking chances. Sacrificing a pawn for development and initiative is often worth it when the opponent is undeveloped.
notes.plans: Play ...h4, then ...Nh6 (sacrificing the h5 pawn), followed by ...Qh4, ...Ng4, and a kingside assault.

notes.explains: Black's ...c5 is an inferior way to challenge the center. White's main advantage is development, not the d5 pawn. White should develop actively with Bb5+ and prepare Re1+ to exploit Black's lagging development.
notes.teaches: In the Fantasy Variation, White's biggest asset is development. Don't focus on the d5 pawn; use it to open lines and deliver a quick checkmate or win material.
notes.plans: Play Bb5+ to force ...Nc6, then Re1+ winning material. If Black plays ...c4, continue with d6 and Qd4 to exploit the loose bishop on g4.

notes.explains: After d6 Qb6, Qd4 is a winning move because it attacks the loose bishop on g4 and the pawn on g7, while also defending the d6 pawn. Black has multiple hanging pieces and no good defense.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has undefended pieces, look for centralizing queen moves that create multiple threats. Undefended pieces are the raw material for combinations.
notes.plans: After Qd4, if Black captures on f3, trade queens and recapture the bishop; if Black moves the bishop, capture on g7 or continue the attack.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...Bxf3 first, White can still play Qd4, attacking g7, e7, and f3. Black has no good move because all pieces are hanging. The simplest win is to trade queens and win the bishop on e7.
notes.teaches: Even when the opponent tries a tricky move order, a central queen can create a 'triple attack' that leaves the opponent helpless. Look for forcing sequences that exploit multiple loose pieces.
notes.plans: Play Qd4; if Black's bishop moves, capture on g7; if Black trades queens, recapture and win the e7 bishop.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...Bc6 to eliminate White's bishop, White should capture on g7 first (Qxg7) because the rook is trapped. Then White wins a piece.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to trade off your attacking piece, calculate the immediate threats first. Capturing a trapped rook can be more important than recapturing.
notes.plans: Play Qxg7, then if Rg8, Qxg8#; if Rf8, continue with Bg5 and win.

notes.explains: After ...Bc6, Qxg7 wins because the rook on h8 is trapped. If Black plays ...Qb6, White has the deflection promotion e8=Q, winning.
notes.teaches: In endgames, look for deflection promotions and trapped pieces. A queen promotion with check can be a decisive tactical blow.
notes.plans: Play Qxg7; if ...Rg8, Qxg8#; if ...Qb6, promote to queen with check, deflecting the queen.

notes.explains: The bishop sacrifice on h6 is a typical attacking idea against the Philidor. After ...gxh6 Qxh6, Black's king is exposed. The key is to open the center with ...d5 exd5 cxd5, then use the knights and rooks to deliver checkmate.
notes.teaches: In the Philidor, a bishop sacrifice on h6 can be devastating if Black's king is stuck in the center. Open the center to bring your pieces into the attack.
notes.plans: After the sacrifice, play ...d5 to open lines, then use the knight on d5 and rook on e1 to create mating threats.

notes.explains: The move ...Ne5 is a deflection: it tempts the bishop to capture, removing the defender of d8, allowing ...Ne7+ and ...Rxd8#. If ...Nxe5, then ...Ne7+ is checkmate because the queen x-rays the bishop.
notes.teaches: Deflection tactics often involve sacrificing a piece to lure a defender away from a critical square. Look for x-ray attacks and back-rank mates.
notes.plans: Play ...Ne5; if Bxe5, then ...Ne7+ and ...Rxd8#; if ...Nxe5, then ...Ne7+ is mate.

notes.explains: The computer shows the sacrifice is unsound if Black defends correctly with ...Bf8, kicking the queen, and then ...d5 at the right moment. However, in practice, the attack often succeeds because the defense is difficult to find.
notes.teaches: Even unsound sacrifices can be practical weapons below master level. The key is to create complications that are harder for the opponent to defend than for you to attack.
notes.plans: If the sacrifice is refuted, White can play prophylactically with Bb3 and slow maneuvering, maintaining a small advantage.

notes.explains: Black has traded knights to eliminate White's active knight on e5 and now develops the bishop to c6, putting pressure on g2 and forcing White to react.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a well-posted knight, exchanging it efficiently (here Nbd7) can be better than chasing it with the queen, which would allow White to support it with d4.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with e6 to block the bishop on c4, then Bc6, and castle kingside.

notes.explains: Black plays e6 to make the bishop on c4 'bite on granite' – it no longer attacks anything important. Castling is then natural.
notes.teaches: When facing a bishop on c4, playing e6 is a solid way to neutralize it; g6 would leave the bishop active on the long diagonal.
notes.plans: Black will complete development with Be7 and O-O, then consider queenside expansion or central breaks.

notes.explains: Black plays a6 to prevent both Nb5 and Bb5, keeping the light-squared bishop on c6 where it is a key piece pressuring g2.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like a6 can be important to preserve a well-placed bishop. Don't fear Nb5 – the bishop can drop back to b8 and remain effective.
notes.plans: Black will continue with b5 to restrict White's pieces and prepare queenside expansion.

notes.explains: b5 gains space on the queenside and restricts White's minor pieces, especially the knight on a3 and the bishop on b3.
notes.teaches: When you have a space advantage, expanding with pawns can suffocate the opponent's pieces. But avoid overextending – keep the pawn chain solid.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with Bd6, preparing kingside play or a Greek Gift sacrifice.

notes.explains: Bd6 develops the bishop, aims at h2, and sets up potential kingside attacking ideas. The bishop on c6 and the bishop on d6 create a battery against White's king.
notes.teaches: When in doubt, default to reasonable developing moves. Bd6 is natural and keeps the tension, preparing tactics like the Greek Gift sacrifice.
notes.plans: Black will consider h5 to anchor the g4 square for a knight, then possibly play Ng4 or the Greek Gift sacrifice Bxh2+.

notes.explains: h5 prepares the Greek Gift sacrifice by anchoring the g4 square for the knight, and also threatens Ng4 directly. It is a classic preparatory move before sacrificing on h2.
notes.teaches: The Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh2+ followed by Ng4+) often requires preparation: the g4 square must be controlled. h5 is a standard way to secure that square.
notes.plans: Black will play Bxh2+ if White allows, or else continue with Ng4 and then Qc7 to set up a mating net.

notes.explains: Black plays Qc7 to keep the queen near the kingside, preparing a mating attack. The queen on c7 supports the idea of Bh2+ and Bg1, threatening mate from two directions.
notes.teaches: In a kingside attack, keep your queen close to the action but not exposed. Qc7 is safer than Qh4 because it avoids White's defensive resources like d5.
notes.plans: Black will play Bh2+ and Bg1, threatening mate on h2. If White defends, Black can play ...gxh3 and ...Qh2#.

notes.explains: Black plays Bh2+ and then Bg1, threatening mate on h2 from both the bishop and the knight. This is a classic mating pattern: the bishop on g1 and knight on g4 combine to threaten ...Qh2#.
notes.teaches: The bishop on g1 and knight on g4 create a deadly mate threat. This pattern is common in many games – recognize it and look for ways to set it up.
notes.plans: After White defends (e.g., Nxg4), Black recaptures with hxg4 and then ...gxh3, threatening ...Qh2#. White's only defense is to give up material or allow mate.

notes.explains: After hxg4, Black plays gxh3, opening the h-file and threatening Qh2#. White cannot prevent mate without losing material.
notes.teaches: When you have a mating attack, keep adding pressure. Opening lines (here the h-file) is often decisive. The threat of mate forces the opponent to give up material or get mated.
notes.plans: Black will play Qh2# if White does not block. If White plays g3, then ...h2#. Otherwise, Black can take on g2 and then deliver mate.

notes.explains: Black sacrifices the exchange (rook for bishop) to keep the attack going. After ...Bxd5, Black has two pawns for the piece and a continuing attack. The king is exposed and Black's pieces are active.
notes.teaches: In a sacrificial attack, material is secondary to king safety and piece activity. Two pawns for a piece is often sufficient compensation if the attack persists.
notes.plans: Black will activate the rook on a8 via ...Kf8 and ...Re8, bringing more pieces to the attack. White's king is stuck in the center and vulnerable to checks and discovered attacks.

notes.explains: Black plays Kf8 to tuck the king away safely and prepare to bring the rook on a8 into the game via e8. This is a typical defensive/offensive maneuver: secure the king and activate the rook.
notes.teaches: When your king is safe, you can focus on activating all your pieces. Kf8 is a useful move to avoid forks (like Bf5+) and to connect the rooks.
notes.plans: Black will play Re8, putting pressure on the e-file and supporting the attack. The rook on e8 is a powerful piece even if not immediately threatening anything.

notes.explains: Black plays c4 to open lines against White's king. The pawn break is decisive because it creates threats like Ba4+ and allows the rook to join the attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, pawn breaks like c4 can open files and diagonals for your pieces. Look for ways to expose the king further.
notes.plans: After c4, Black will play Ba4+ and then Rxb3 or other captures, winning material. The attack is overwhelming.

notes.explains: Black uses checks and threats to drive the king to a4, then plays Rb8 threatening ...Rxb3+ and mate. The king is exposed and Black's pieces coordinate perfectly.
notes.teaches: In a king hunt, use checks to force the king into a worse position. Then bring in all your pieces to deliver the final blow. The b-file becomes the main avenue of attack.
notes.plans: Black will play Rxb3+ or Qxb3+ followed by mate. White's king has no escape.

notes.explains: Black simplifies to a winning endgame by trading rooks. With a queen and pawns against a queen, Black's extra pawns and active king decide the game.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage and are short on time, simplifying to a winning endgame is a practical approach. Trade pieces but keep the pressure.
notes.plans: Black will push the passed pawns and use the queen to create threats. White's king is exposed and cannot stop the pawns.

notes.explains: After Nf5, Black's position is critical. The knight on f5 attacks g7 and d6. Black's only defense is to play g6, but then White can play Qe2, threatening Qxe7# and winning material.
notes.teaches: A knight on f5 in the Philidor can be devastating. Combine it with a queen move like Qe2 to create mating threats and exploit pinned pieces.
notes.plans: Play Qe2, threatening Qxe7#. If Black plays d5 to defend the knight, simply castle to break the pin, then capture the bishop on e7 and win the knight.

notes.explains: Black's knight on c4 is pinned by Qe2. Black's only try is d5, but after 0-0 White breaks the pin and wins the bishop on e7. Then Nxd5+ wins the knight.
notes.teaches: When a piece is pinned to the king, look for ways to break the pin while maintaining the threat. Castling can be a powerful unpinning move.
notes.plans: Castle, then capture the bishop on e7 with the queen, followed by Nxd5+ winning the knight.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 Nc3 (without c4), Black should play d5 or transpose to the Pirc. If White plays e3, it's unambitious. Black's instinct should be to play c5, challenging the center.
notes.teaches: Against a passive London setup with e3, Black should immediately strike with c5 to undermine White's center and create dynamic play.
notes.plans: Play c5, and if dxc5, recapture with the knight or queen, aiming for rapid development and pressure on the queenside.

notes.explains: After c5, White often plays b4 to hold the pawn, but this weakens the queenside. Black can then play a5, opening lines and putting pressure on the a4 knight.
notes.teaches: When White tries to cling to a pawn with b4, counter with a5 to open the a-file and target the advanced knight.
notes.plans: Play a5, then after bxa5, open the diagonal for the bishop and prepare Ng4 to attack h2.

notes.explains: After the queenside opens, Black can play Ng4, threatening Nxh2. White's knight on f3 is the only defender; if it can be removed, the attack crashes through.
notes.teaches: Combine pressure on the queenside with a kingside attack. Use the knight to target h2 and force weaknesses.
notes.plans: Play Ng4, then if White plays h3, Ne5 to deflect the knight. If White takes, recapture with the queen and continue the attack.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, Black has a knight on e5 and White's king is exposed. Black can play Qh5, threatening mate on h2. White's best defense is f4, but then Black's knight retreats to e5, dominating the light squares.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, even after queen trades, the attack can continue with the remaining pieces. The knight on e5 is a powerful outpost.
notes.plans: Play Qh5, then after f4, retreat the knight to e5 and target the light squares. Consider sacrificing the knight on h4 to expose the king.

notes.explains: Black's knight on e5 is a monster. White's bishop is under attack, and Black can play Nxh4, sacrificing the knight to open the king. The dark-squared bishop joins the attack.
notes.teaches: When you have a dominant knight, look for sacrifices to rip open the king's position. Every piece can become a killer.
notes.plans: Play Nxh4, then after gxh4, Qxh4+ and bring the bishop to h6 with devastating effect.

notes.explains: Black's attack is overwhelming. The bishop on h6 threatens mate, and White's king is exposed. The game ends quickly.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, never underestimate the power of the dark-squared bishop. It can deliver the final blow.
notes.plans: Play Bh6, threatening Qg3# or Qf2#. White has no adequate defense.

notes.explains: Ng5 threatens Nxh7 and Qh5. Black's kingside is defenseless. The knight sacrifice on f6 is thematic to open the king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is short of defenders, a knight sacrifice on f6 can rip open the castled position. Follow with queen and bishop for mate.
notes.plans: Play Ng5, then if Black plays h6, Nxf6+ gxf6, Qh5 with unstoppable mate threats. If Black plays Nf6, Nxf6+ and the same idea.

notes.explains: After Qh5, Black cannot prevent mate on h7. The only try is Qxd4+, but after Kh1, Black's queen is out of play and mate follows.
notes.teaches: In such attacking positions, don't be distracted by checks. Simply move the king and continue the threat.
notes.plans: Play Qh5, and if Qxd4+, Kh1. Then Qxh7# is unstoppable.

notes.explains: After …cxd5, Black has a knight developed, controls the center, and White has moved the queen three times—a clear violation of development principles.
notes.teaches: In the opening, prioritize piece development over pawn moves. Moving the same piece repeatedly wastes time and hands the initiative to the opponent.
notes.plans: Continue developing with ...Nc6 or ...e5, aiming to complete kingside castling and activate the bishops.

notes.explains: Playing Bg4 attacks the queen and provokes f3, which weakens White's kingside. The bishop is safe because the knight on c3 defends it, and if White plays Nf3, Black pins the knight.
notes.teaches: Provoking weaknesses is a powerful concept: place a piece where it can be attacked, force a weakening pawn move, then retreat. The two tempi spent are worth the structural damage.
notes.plans: After f3, retreat the bishop to f5, eyeing the weakened light squares. Black can follow up with e6 and develop the other bishop.

notes.explains: Qa5+ forks the bishop on c4 and the king. If White plays Nc3 to defend, the knight is pinned and attacked by the pawn on d5—a classic case where a pawn attacking a pinned piece leads to material loss.
notes.teaches: Always look for tactical opportunities like forks. When a pinned piece is attacked by a pawn, the defender is often in trouble because the pawn cannot be captured by the pinned piece.
notes.plans: Capture the knight on c3, then the bishop on c4, leaving White's kingside shattered. Black will be up a piece with a winning position.

notes.explains: After winning the piece, Black should not look for flashy continuations. Instead, complete development with e6, Bc5, and castle. The position is winning; simple, solid moves preserve the advantage.
notes.teaches: When you have a big material advantage, avoid unnecessary complications. Focus on finishing development, securing the king, and trading down to a technically winning endgame.
notes.plans: Play e6, develop the bishop to c5 or d6, castle kingside, and then start targeting White's weak pawns.

notes.explains: After trading queens, Black is up a piece and several pawns. Even in the endgame, complete development: bring out the bishop and centralize the king. Playing f6 prevents the bishop from being trapped on g7.
notes.teaches: Never neglect development, even in the endgame. A piece left on its starting square is a liability. Use pawn moves like f6 to give the bishop a safe square.
notes.plans: Play Bd6 or Bc5, then centralize the king to d7 or e7. Target White's weak pawns and trade down to a winning pawn endgame.

notes.explains: In the endgame, Black spots that White's king and rook are on the same diagonal. The bishop can maneuver to c4 to skewer the rook. When facing an unexpected check, remember the three defenses: capture, block, or move the king.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to tactical motifs like skewers, even in simplified positions. When surprised by a check, pause and consider all three ways to meet it.
notes.plans: Play Bc4, skewering the rook. After the rook moves, capture it. Then mop up White's remaining pawns.

notes.explains: …f6 is a terrible move because it weakens the kingside and doesn't develop. White can immediately exploit it with Nxe5, winning a pawn and more.
notes.teaches: Never play f6 in the opening unless absolutely necessary. It weakens the king's position and neglects development. The Damiano Defense is a classic example of how to punish such moves.
notes.plans: Play Nxe5, and if Black recaptures with ...fxe5, then Qh5+ wins the rook. If Black doesn't recapture, White is up a pawn with a better position.

notes.explains: After winning the rook, White should not rush to capture everything. Instead, complete development: bring out the knight, castle, and centralize. The position is winning; simple moves suffice.
notes.teaches: When you have a decisive material advantage, focus on development and king safety. Don't get greedy; consolidate your position before launching further attacks.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to c3 or d2, castle kingside, and then advance the center pawns. Black's king is exposed, so any further attack will be easy.

notes.explains: Black's king is exposed and White has a crushing attack. The game ends in a quick checkmate. This demonstrates the consequences of weakening the kingside early.
notes.teaches: A single bad move like f6 can lead to a swift defeat. Always prioritize king safety and development in the opening.
notes.plans: Deliver checkmate with the queen and bishop coordination.

notes.explains: After e4 c6 f3 d5 e5 e6 Nf3 Bg4, the correct move is Bc4, targeting f7 and threatening Bxf7+ followed by Nxe5. Black cannot take the knight because …Bxf3 Qxf3 gives White a massive attack on f7.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, prioritize active piece development and immediate threats over material. The bishop on c4 creates a tactical threat that forces Black to defend precisely.
notes.plans: After Bc4, if Black plays …Nf6?, White wins with Bxf7+ Kxf7 Nxe5+ (forking king and bishop) and regains the piece with a winning attack.

notes.explains: Black's Nd4 is an old sideline aiming to disrupt normal Ruy Lopez play. White should not panic; the knight is a target.
notes.teaches: Against early knight sorties, the simplest approach is often to challenge or capture it, but here Bc4 is the principled retreat, keeping pressure on e5.
notes.plans: Develop with d3, then Nbd2, and later consider f4 to build a kingside attack.

notes.explains: After Nxd4 exd4, White's bishop retreats to c4 (not a4) to keep an eye on f7 and support d3. Black's d4-pawn is isolated and weak.
notes.teaches: In the Bird, White's bishop belongs on c4 to maintain pressure; the d4-pawn is a long-term weakness that Black must defend.
notes.plans: Play d3, develop the knight to d2, and later target the d4-pawn with moves like Re1+ and Bg5.

notes.explains: d3 is solid, protecting e4 and preparing development. Black's best is d5, challenging the center.
notes.teaches: When the center is fluid, solidifying with d3 is often better than committing to e5, which would allow ...d5 with tempo.
notes.plans: After ...d5, capture on d5, then Re1+ to exploit Black's uncastled king.

notes.explains: Re1+ is natural, forcing Black to block with Be7 or Be6. This gains time and keeps the king in the center.
notes.teaches: Checking with the rook when the opponent's king is exposed is a standard way to gain tempo and disrupt coordination.
notes.plans: After ...Be7, play Bg5 to trade dark-squared bishops, leaving Black with a bad bishop on e6.

notes.explains: Bg5 is a positional move, aiming to trade bishops. After ...f6 or ...Be6, White gets a favorable exchange.
notes.teaches: Trading your opponent's good bishop (here the dark-squared one) can leave them with a passive piece, especially when the center is open.
notes.plans: After ...Be6, capture on e7, then develop Nbd2 and target the d4-pawn.

notes.explains: After the trade, Black's queen is on e7, and the d4-pawn is weak. White should now play Nd2, but Bxd5 was even stronger, doubling Black's pawns and leaving a monster knight on d5.
notes.teaches: When you have a choice between a good positional move and a decisive one, calculate carefully; here capturing on d5 gives a nearly winning advantage.
notes.plans: If Nd2, then ...0-0-0 is possible, but White can still press with Nb3 and target d4.

notes.explains: Black's queenside castling is risky but sharp. White missed the chance to take on d5 earlier; now the position is complex.
notes.teaches: When your opponent castles into an attack, you must act quickly but accurately; slow buildup can be punished if you miss tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: Play Nb3 to pressure d4, then consider a4 to open lines on the queenside.

notes.explains: Black's c5 weakens d5 but also opens lines. White's knight on b3 is passive; rerouting it to d2 or c1 is better.
notes.teaches: Knights on the rim are grim; if a knight has no future on b3, redeploy it to a better square like d2 or c1.
notes.plans: Play Nbd2, aiming for c4 or e4, and keep the tension on the queenside.

notes.explains: Black's Nf4 is a mistake; it opens the e-file and allows White's queen to become active. The correct move was Rh6, defending and preparing counterplay.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, do not give up key squares without compensation; Nf4 weakens control of e6 and invites White's rook to e5.
notes.plans: Play Re5! immediately, attacking the knight and threatening to win the bishop on e6.

notes.explains: Re5 is a brilliant move, attacking the knight and threatening to capture on e6. The rook is untouchable due to the pin on the knight.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move is to place a piece en prise if capturing it leads to a decisive advantage. Here Re5 exploits the overworked knight.
notes.plans: If the knight moves, capture on e6 and ruin Black's pawns; if ...Bxc4, recapture and then build up slowly with Ra1, Nc1-d3, and eventually b4.

notes.explains: After …Ne6, White has a positional advantage. Black's pieces are passive, and White can slowly improve.
notes.teaches: When you have a static advantage (better pawn structure, active pieces), do not rush; improve your worst piece and then break through.
notes.plans: Play Ra1, then Nc1-d3, and finally b4 to open lines on the queenside.

notes.explains: After improving all pieces, b4 is the decisive pawn break, opening the b-file and creating threats.
notes.teaches: When all pieces are optimally placed, use a pawn break to create new invasion points. Here b4 forces weaknesses in Black's camp.
notes.plans: After ...cxb4, play Nxb4 threatening Nc6+; if ...Nxb4, then Rxb4 and double on the b-file.

notes.explains: White has won a pawn and has a strong attack. Black's queen is active but White's rooks dominate.
notes.teaches: In the attack, keep pieces coordinated; here the rook on b1 and the queen on f3 work together to threaten mate.
notes.plans: Play c5 to open the diagonal, then Re7 or Nf6 to deliver mate.

notes.explains: White's attack is overwhelming. Black's king is exposed, and White has multiple threats.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is trapped, use checks and threats to force mate or win material.
notes.plans: Play Qf4+ and then Nb4 to cut off the queen's defense, leading to mate on b7.

notes.explains: White has won a pawn and has a winning endgame. The extra pawn and active rook ensure victory.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, simplify by trading queens and use your extra pawn to promote.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn, trade rooks if possible, and promote.

notes.explains: Black's d6 is passive, blocking the bishop and giving White everything it wants. The Vienna Gambit aims for Black to take the pawn, giving White central control with d4 and opening the f-file for attack.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing the f-pawn in the Vienna Gambit gains central space and opens lines against Black's king. The open f-file is a double-edged sword but can be a powerful attacking avenue.
notes.plans: Develop pieces naturally, aiming to build an attack. Do not go pawn-hunting prematurely.

notes.explains: After Nc3 Nc6, Bb5 is a Ruy Lopez-style move putting pressure on e5. Black's Bd7 is a reasonable response.
notes.teaches: In the Vienna, developing the bishop to b5 can be strong, but avoid immediate pawn grabs like Bxc6 then Nxe5, as Black can reply Qd4 forking the knight and king.
notes.plans: Instead of capturing, retreat the bishop to c4 or a4, preparing to castle and attack.

notes.explains: After Bc4 Be6, trading bishops on White's terms is good. Bb3 (or Bxe6) is a typical way to recapture with the a-pawn, improving the pawn structure.
notes.teaches: Trading on your own terms means forcing the opponent to capture your piece in a way that benefits your structure or activity.
notes.plans: After Bxe6 fxe6, White can play positionally with Nxe5 or aggressively with Ng5. The e6 pawn is a target.

notes.explains: After Ng5, Black's fxe5 allows d4 with tempo, then Ng6. White's center is strong, and the knight on e6 is a powerful outpost.
notes.teaches: When you have a central pawn majority and an outpost, use pawn breaks like d5 to secure the outpost and restrict the opponent's pieces.
notes.plans: Play d5 to cement the knight on e6, then follow up with Bg5 hitting the knight on f6. Black's position is paralyzed.

notes.explains: In the position with a knight on e6 and Black's king stuck in the center, White can win with simple tactics. Nxd5 (or exd5) opens lines, and the f-file becomes deadly.
notes.teaches: When you have a huge positional advantage, look for tactical finishes. The open f-file and exposed king lead to quick checkmates.
notes.plans: Nxd5 exd5, then Qh5+ or Qf3, with threats of mate. Black's king is helpless.

notes.explains: If Black accepts the gambit with exf4, it's a mistake. Unlike the King's Gambit, White's knight on c3 supports e5, chasing the knight back to g8.
notes.teaches: In the Vienna, exf4 is bad because White can play e5, forcing the knight back and gaining a huge lead in development. Develop with Nf3 and d4 to recover the pawn.
notes.plans: Play Nf3 (not d4 immediately to avoid Qh4+), then d4. White will win back the pawn with a big development advantage.

notes.explains: In some sharp lines, White can sacrifice more material for a devastating attack. For example, after exf4 d6 d4, White can play Bc4 and later sacrifice a knight on f7 or similar.
notes.teaches: When you have a development lead, sacrifices to expose the king are often justified. Look for patterns like bishop g5 distracting the knight, then knight f7+ winning the queen.
notes.plans: Continue the attack with piece sacrifices, forcing the king into the open. Castle with check and deliver mate.

notes.explains: The best response to the Vienna Gambit is d5, countering in the center. This leads to theoretical lines where Qf3 is strong.
notes.teaches: Meet flank attacks with central counterplay. d5 is a principled move that challenges White's center.
notes.plans: In the d5 line, White plays Qf3, creating threats. Black must be careful.

notes.explains: After Black plays d6 and develops passively, White has a clear positional advantage. Black's bishops are passive, White has more central control and active pieces.
notes.teaches: The Vienna Gambit can lead to a positional edge even without tactics. Compare piece activity and central control to assess the advantage.
notes.plans: Continue developing, possibly with Kh1 to avoid Qd4 tricks, then slowly improve the position.

notes.explains: In the game, after Bc4 Be6, White traded bishops and later played Ng5. Black's Qd7 allowed fxe5, and then White sacrificed the exchange with Rxf6 to remove the defender of h5.
notes.teaches: When calculating sacrifices, look for the defender of a key square. Removing the defender can enable a decisive queen check or fork.
notes.plans: After Rxf6, if Kd8, Qf8+ wins the rook. If Ke7, Qf7? is a mistake; instead Qf6+ forks king and rook. Always check intermediate moves like bishop checks on c5.

notes.explains: After the exchange sacrifice, White must be careful of Black's counterplay on the diagonal. Bc5+ is an intermediate move that can be dangerous.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, always consider intermediate checks and captures. They can turn the tables.
notes.plans: If Bc5+, White can play Qf3 or Rf2 to consolidate. Two pieces for a rook is a material advantage.

notes.explains: After Nxc5 d4, White played d5 to secure the e6 outpost for the knight. This is game over; Black has no moves.
notes.teaches: When you have a knight outpost, support it with pawn advances to make it permanent. The knight on e6 paralyzes Black's position.
notes.plans: If Black moves the bishop, Nxg7 wins. Otherwise, simply improve pieces and deliver mate.

notes.explains: In the final position, after Kf7 g6, the fastest win is to remove the defender of g6 with a sacrifice, then check and win the rook.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, look for the most direct tactical finish. Removing the defender is a common motif.
notes.plans: Play a move like Bxg6+ hxg6, then Qxg6+ Kf8, and Qf6+ winning the rook.

notes.explains: White's f4 is a flank move that does not develop. Black should strike in the center with d5.
notes.teaches: Against flank pawn moves, the typical response is to challenge the center immediately.
notes.plans: After d5, if White takes, Black recaptures with the knight after Nf6 to avoid the queen being chased by Nc3.

notes.explains: After exd5, Black plays Nf6, not Qxd5, because Nc3 would chase the queen. If White defends with c4, Black gets compensation for the pawn.
notes.teaches: Recapturing with the knight avoids losing time and keeps the queen safe. The pawn on f4 becomes a long-term weakness.
notes.plans: Black aims to develop quickly and exploit the d4 outpost and White's weakened kingside.

notes.explains: Black has three advantages: lead in development, White's weak king (due to f4), and the d4 outpost for a knight.
notes.teaches: Compensation for a pawn can come from multiple factors: development, king safety, and positional outposts.
notes.plans: Complete development, castle, and later maneuver a knight to d4.

notes.explains: Ng2 is a mistake; White should have played d3 or Nf3 to defend the pawn. Now Black can win back the pawn with Bxc4.
notes.teaches: When behind in development, avoid moving pieces multiple times; prioritize defending key pawns.
notes.plans: Capture on c4 and maintain pressure.

notes.explains: Black trades on f1 to prevent White from castling. If White recaptures with the knight, castling is blocked; if with king or rook, castling is lost forever.
notes.teaches: Exchanging to ruin the opponent's king safety is often worth it, even if the material is equal.
notes.plans: Prepare castling for Black; choose bishop development carefully.

notes.explains: Be7 is better than Bd6 because it avoids a potential check on e2 and keeps the d3 square accessible for the queen or knight. The bishop on e7 also defends the knight on f6.
notes.teaches: Choose developing squares that avoid interference with your own pieces and maintain flexibility.
notes.plans: Castle and then bring the queen to d7 and rook to d8 to pressure d3.

notes.explains: White plays d3, which becomes a target. Black can pile up on it with Qd7 and Rfd8. Nb4 is too committal; keeping the knight on c6 allows Nd4 if White plays Rf3.
notes.teaches: When attacking a weak pawn, bring pieces to bear without committing to a specific square too early; keep options open.
notes.plans: Play Qd7 and Rfd8 (not Rad8, to keep the a-rook for e8 if needed).

notes.explains: White plays Rf3 to defend d3, but Black centralizes the knight with tempo on the rook. This is better than Nb4 because it doesn't commit the knight prematurely.
notes.teaches: Centralizing with tempo is a powerful way to improve your position while forcing the opponent to react.
notes.plans: Continue pressure with Rd8; later move the knight to f5 to increase the threat on d3.

notes.explains: Black moves the knight to f5, threatening c4. If White captures c4, Black wins a piece; if not, Black gets a powerful passed pawn on d3.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is under pressure, advancing it can create decisive threats if the opponent cannot capture.
notes.plans: Play c4, creating a passed pawn on d3 and undermining the knight on e4.

notes.explains: White plays g4 to attack the knight, but Black captures because the queen x-rays the g4 pawn. If White recaptures, Nxe3+ wins the queen.
notes.teaches: Look for x-ray attacks and discovered checks; a pinned piece can still deliver a discovered check if it moves along the pin line.
notes.plans: After Nxg4, Black wins material and the game.

notes.explains: Black plays Ne3+ with discovered check, winning the queen. The knight move must be chosen carefully; Ng3+ would be bad because Qxg3 or Rxg3 gets out of check.
notes.teaches: When delivering a discovered check, ensure the moving piece does not hang or allow the opponent to escape cheaply.
notes.plans: Win the queen and convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: In the endgame after ...Nxe4 and ...Qh1+, Black can force a win by trading queens and using the extra piece. The king is safe on g7, and the bishop on g5 pins the queen.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, simplify by trading pieces while maintaining a material advantage and king safety.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Bxg5, ...Qxg5, and then pushes the passed pawns.

notes.explains: Black plays Qh5, attacking h2 and maintaining the threat on d3. The bishop on e7 is crucial because it guards f6, preventing a knight fork.
notes.teaches: In endgames, keep pieces coordinated and watch for counterplay; a well-placed defender can neutralize threats.
notes.plans: Capture the d3 pawn and then the c4 pawn, simplifying further.

notes.explains: Black wins the d3 pawn and White's position collapses. The rook trade simplifies the position.
notes.teaches: When ahead, trade pieces to reduce counterplay; capturing with the rook instead of the pawn can force favorable trades.
notes.plans: Continue capturing pawns and promote the passed pawn.

notes.explains: Black's capture on d4 is inaccurate because it allows White's knight to develop to its natural square c3, gaining a big center and quick development.
notes.teaches: In the c3 Sicilian, Black should avoid exchanging on d4 early; instead, keep tension to restrict White's knight to the clunky d2 square.
notes.plans: White will continue developing, aiming to control the center and exploit Black's slow development.

notes.explains: If White plays h4 immediately, Black can respond with h5, slowing down White's pawn storm. White should avoid this by first playing Bh6 to prevent h5, or by playing g4 to prepare h4-h5.
notes.teaches: In a pawn storm, be aware of moves that block your advance. Sometimes you need to prepare h4 with g4 or a bishop trade to prevent Black from playing h5.
notes.plans: White should consider g4 first, then h4-h5, ensuring the h-file opens on White's terms.

notes.explains: White plays g4 to prevent Black from taking on h5 with the knight. If Black had taken, the knight could go to f4, cutting off the queen's access to h6 and disrupting the attack.
notes.teaches: When calculating pawn advances, consider the opponent's knight jumps. g4 can be a useful prophylactic move to secure the h5 square.
notes.plans: After g4, White will play h5, opening the h-file, then trade bishops and bring the queen to h6.

notes.explains: White opens the h-file and brings the queen to h6, putting pressure on Black's king. Black defends by bringing the knight to f8 and the rook to g8.
notes.teaches: After opening a file, bring your queen and rooks to the attack. Patience is key; the opponent may defend well, so you need to accumulate more pieces.
notes.plans: White can consider bringing the rook to the h-file via d2, or reposition the bishop to g5 to target the knight defending h7.

notes.explains: White drops the bishop back to g5 instead of trading it. The king is now in the corner, so the main defender is the knight on f8 (protecting h7). The bishop on g5 targets that knight and prepares Qh2, threatening to eliminate the defender.
notes.teaches: Be flexible in your attacking plans. The same piece can have a different purpose as the position evolves. Here, the bishop is no longer needed to trade; it's better used to target the knight.
notes.plans: White will play Qh2, threatening Qxh7#. If Black defends, White can bring the rook to d2 and then to h2, or use the knight via h3-g5.

notes.explains: White plays Qh2, threatening Qxh7#. The queen is safer here than on h6 because it's less exposed, and it still exerts deadly pressure.
notes.teaches: The queen can be just as effective on h2 as on h6, and it's often less vulnerable. Look for safe squares that still maintain the threat.
notes.plans: White will now bring the rook to h2 via d2, or use the knight to join the attack.

notes.explains: Black defends by trading the knight for the bishop, then bringing the knight back to f6. White's queen is forced to retreat to h4, and the attack seems to stall.
notes.teaches: When your opponent defends well, don't panic. You may need to bring in more pieces, like the rook or the other knight, to rebuild the attack.
notes.plans: White can play Rd2, preparing to double rooks on the h-file, or consider a pawn break like b4 to create new weaknesses.

notes.explains: White plays Rd2, preparing to bring the rook to h2. This is a methodical way to add more firepower to the attack.
notes.teaches: When the queen alone isn't enough, bring your rooks into the attack. Doubling on the h-file can create decisive threats.
notes.plans: White will play Rdh2, threatening Qxh7#. Black may need to give up material to avoid checkmate.

notes.explains: White plays b4, a pawn break on the queenside. This doesn't trap the knight but opens lines and frees the b3 square for the knight, which can later go to c5 or d3.
notes.teaches: Even when attacking on one side, you can use pawn breaks on the other side to create new avenues for your pieces or weaken the opponent's structure.
notes.plans: After b4, White may play Nb3 or a5 to further pressure Black's queenside, while maintaining the kingside threats.

notes.explains: White plays Bd3, developing the bishop and defending the f3 pawn. This also prepares to swing the queen to h5 or f5, keeping the pressure on Black's king.
notes.teaches: In an attack, don't neglect defensive moves. Protecting your own king and key pawns is essential to maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: White will continue to pressure Black's king, possibly with Qf5 or Qh5, while Black tries to counter on the queenside.

notes.explains: White plays Rf2, preparing to infiltrate to f7. This is a flexible move that threatens to trap Black's queen or create new mating threats.
notes.teaches: Be flexible with your rook lifts. Sometimes the h-file isn't the only target; the f-file can also be decisive.
notes.plans: White will play Rf7, attacking the queen and threatening checkmate. Black may have to give up material.

notes.explains: White plays Qh5, preventing Black's queen from moving and threatening Qxh7#. This forces Black to give up material to avoid checkmate.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is a key defender, pinning or blocking it can be a decisive tactic.
notes.plans: White will capture on h7 or f7, winning material and eventually checkmating.

notes.explains: White's d3 is a passive but not terrible move; the most principled response is e5, occupying the center. After Nd2, Black develops naturally with Nf6, and when white plays c4, it's a one-move threat that creates a hole on d4. Black should not panic or try to refute it immediately.
notes.teaches: Against offbeat openings, avoid the mindset of needing to crush them in five moves. Play principled chess, develop naturally, and trust that the positional advantages (space, development, weak squares) will accumulate.
notes.plans: Occupy the d4 outpost with a knight, keep the center closed with ...e5, and prepare to attack on the kingside once white's king is stuck in the center.

notes.explains: Black plays Bd6 instead of the more active Bc5 because Bc5 is vulnerable to Nb3, which can lead to the bishop being trapped or forced to give up the bishop pair. Bd6 is solid: it defends the e5 pawn and supports the center.
notes.teaches: Don't automatically put bishops on the most active square if they become targets. A 'bad' bishop that defends good pawns is often valuable. Think of the bishop and pawn as a unit.
notes.plans: Follow up with Nf4, targeting the d4 square, and later drop the knight back to e6 to double-attack d4, preventing white from freeing themselves with d4.

notes.explains: Black plays Bg4, pinning the knight and preventing white's natural Ne4. The immediate idea is to later drop the bishop back to e6, but when white blunders with Nxe4, Black must be flexible and capture the knight, winning a pawn and ruining white's kingside structure.
notes.teaches: Be flexible: have a plan, but if an opponent's mistake gives you a concrete advantage, change your plan to cash in immediately. A tactical motif like Nxd4 hitting the knight twice is often decisive.
notes.plans: After Bxf3, bring the queen to h4 and h3 to threaten checkmate, while preventing white from consolidating with Rg1 because of the hanging f2 pawn.

notes.explains: After Rg2, Black should not play forcing moves like Nh4 (which allows Rg3) or vague moves like h5. Instead, the priority is king safety: castle queenside to avoid checks and connect rooks. Then play on the other side of the board, lifting the rook to g6 and threatening Rg4 followed by Rh4 mate.
notes.teaches: When the attack stalls, don't force it. Improve your position: get your king safe, bring in reinforcements, and look for quiet moves that set up unstoppable threats. Avoid one-move-itis.
notes.plans: Castle queenside, then play Rg6, Rg4, and Rh4, threatening Qxh2#. If white defends, use the extra material to push pawns and simplify.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Najdorf Variation, English Attack
notes.explains: In the Najdorf, white's Nb3 is a known but bad move. Black should immediately play d5, undermining the e5 pawn. White cannot capture because of tactical issues: exd5? Nxd5 wins a piece due to the pin on the knight. This is a concrete refutation.
notes.teaches: Knowing a few moves of theory in sharp openings like the Najdorf can give you a massive advantage at club level. When your opponent plays a dubious move, look for the most direct refutation: undermine the center or attack the overextended piece.
notes.plans: After d5, if white plays Bg5, Black can play Nxe3? No, because of Bxf7+! But Black has Bb4+ recovering the queen. So Nxe3 is winning. Simplify by trading queens and win a piece.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Najdorf Variation, English Attack
notes.explains: After the queen trade, Black has Bc5, threatening to win the exchange. White's king is stuck in the center. Black should not rush; instead, pile up on the c2 pawn with Rc8 and later play b5 to open lines. The attack is straightforward.
notes.teaches: When you win material in the opening, don't relax. Your opponent may have compensation in development. Keep the pressure on, use your extra pieces to attack, and avoid unnecessary complications.
notes.plans: Play Rc8, Nb4 (threatening Nxd3+ due to the pin on c2), then capture the c2 pawn, bring the other rook in, and open the b-file with b5. The king is exposed, so checkmate follows quickly.

notes.explains: After white's a3, Black plays Ne4, threatening Bxc3+ if white captures. White's best is to avoid taking, but if white does, Black gets a rook and a strong attack. Black should not grab material immediately; instead, play Nxc5, keeping the bishop on g7, and later eliminate white's dark-squared bishop to dominate the dark squares.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, the dark-squared bishop on g7 is a monster. Sometimes it's better to keep it and go for positional pressure rather than grab material. The spirit of the opening is piece activity and attack, not pawn-grabbing.
notes.plans: Play Nxc5, then Ne4, threatening to take on d2. After white's rook moves, play d6 and Bg4, targeting the c4 pawn. Eventually trade bishops and push the a-pawn, using the extra pawn and bishop pair to win.

notes.explains: Black is up a rook and a pawn. In time pressure, the key is to avoid unnecessary complications. Identify the only real danger (the knight jumping to c6) and block it with Rfc8. Then simplify by trading pieces and pushing the a-pawn. Anticipate white's threats and keep the position stable.
notes.teaches: When converting a winning position in time pressure, prioritize safety over flashy tactics. Identify your opponent's only counterplay and neutralize it. Keep the position simple and use your material advantage.
notes.plans: Play Rfc8 to block Nc6, then trade bishops and push the a-pawn. If white tries to create counterplay, use the extra material to simplify into a won endgame.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 f4, White's f4 is reasonable but not best. Black can play d5 or e5. If e5, Black gets the f5 square for the bishop. The main line is exd5 Qxd5, but that develops White's queen early. Better is Nf6 preparing to recapture on d5 without allowing Nc3 with tempo.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, avoid taking back with the queen if it allows the opponent to develop with tempo. Prepare the recapture with a knight move.
notes.plans: Play Nf6, then after Nc3, take on d5, and if White plays c4, occupy the d4 outpost with the knight.

notes.explains: If White plays c4 to defend the d5 pawn, it weakens the d4 square and doesn't develop. Black can sacrifice the pawn for compensation: two pieces developed vs zero, weak king safety for White (due to f4), and a powerful knight outpost on d4.
notes.teaches: A move that threatens a piece is not automatically good if it doesn't develop. Compensation for a pawn can include development lead, king safety, and outposts.
notes.plans: Sacrifice the pawn with e6, then after dxc6 Bxc6, enjoy development lead, weak White king, and the d4 square.

notes.explains: In the position after e4 c5 f4 e5 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3 Bf5 c3 d4 cxd4 exd4 Nb5 Bb5 Bxb5+ Nge7 e6, Black played Nd5. White's key mistake was Nxd4, opening the diagonal for Black's bishop. Better was Ne1 or d3 to keep the position closed.
notes.teaches: When your king is exposed, avoid opening lines for the opponent's pieces. Sometimes a retreat is necessary to keep the position solid.
notes.plans: Instead of Nxd4, play Ne1 or d3 to keep the center closed and only be slightly worse.

notes.explains: White's bishop on d3 is inaccurate because it leaves the d4 pawn undefended. Black can attack it with Nbd7 and then e5, or with Nc6 and then e5. The idea is to target the d4 pawn before White can consolidate.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, look for ways to attack White's center pawns, especially if they are not well defended.
notes.plans: Play Nbd7, then e5 to attack d4, or Nc6 followed by e5.

notes.explains: After Nbd7, Black can play Nc5 to put pressure on e4. White may try to take on c5, but Black can sacrifice the pawn to open lines. The key is to activate the queen and rook for an attack.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you can sacrifice a pawn to open lines and activate your pieces for a king attack.
notes.plans: Play Nc5, and if White takes, open the f-file and play f5, then Qh4 with attacking chances.

notes.explains: White's bishop h6 is a blunder because it leaves the bishop undefended (only protected by the queen). Black can play Qh4+ (after moving the knight from f6) to win the bishop.
notes.teaches: Always check for undefended pieces and look for queen checks that can win material.
notes.plans: Play Qh4+ to win the bishop.

notes.explains: If White plays e5 prematurely after d6, Black can take on e5, forcing the king to move, and then reactivate the bad bishop with f6.
notes.teaches: A bad bishop can be reactivated by pawn breaks like f6, opening the diagonal.
notes.plans: Take on e5, then play f6 to activate the bishop.

notes.explains: To trade a bad bishop, you can play Bh6, forcing White to take, then recapture with the queen, winning a piece and getting rid of your worst piece. This is a positional combination.
notes.teaches: Use tactics to improve your position, such as trading a bad piece for a good one.
notes.plans: Play Bh6, and if White takes, recapture with the queen.

notes.explains: White sacrificed a pawn to expose Black's king in the center. However, Black's bishop on d6 (after ...Bd6) becomes a rock that blocks the d-file and neutralizes White's attack. White overestimated the d-file and underestimated the solidity of Black's setup.
notes.teaches: When calculating compensation for a pawn, consider not only king safety but also the opponent's defensive resources. A well-placed piece (like Bd6) can shut down your main attacking line.
notes.plans: White should have played c3 earlier to create a pawn chain and then slowly prepare Ba6 or Bb4, avoiding the premature pawn sacrifice.

notes.explains: Black's Bd6 is a perfect defensive move: it blocks the d-file, protects the king, and cannot be easily dislodged. White's attack stalls because the main artery to the king is closed.
notes.teaches: A single well-placed defensive piece can nullify an attack. Look for such consolidating moves (like Bd6) that simultaneously defend and restrict the opponent.
notes.plans: White should try to activate the rooks and create other threats, perhaps by playing f4-f5 or g4 to open lines, but Black's position is solid.

notes.explains: Black has three connected passed pawns and is winning. However, in time pressure, Black allowed White's queen to become active. Black should have traded pieces (e.g., ...Rd1) or dropped the queen back to eliminate counterplay.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplify by trading pieces, especially queens, to reduce the opponent's counterplay. Don't let the opponent generate activity.
notes.plans: Black should play ...Rd1 or ...Qd8 to neutralize White's threats and then push the passed pawns.

notes.explains: Black played ...d6 to prevent White's e5 clamp. This is crucial because allowing e5 gives White a strong grip on d6 and dark squares, as seen in the classic Petrosian game.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, if White plays Bc4 and f3, Black must be careful not to allow e5. Playing ...d6 early prevents the clamp and keeps the position flexible.
notes.plans: Black can later play ...d5 to challenge the center, even if it costs a tempo, because White's setup is passive.

notes.explains: Black played ...Ra8 as a 'healthy waiting move'. It x-rays the queen, creates a square for the bishop on f8, and waits for White to commit to a plan. It does not create weaknesses like h6 would.
notes.teaches: A waiting move is healthy if it improves your position without creating weaknesses. Use it when you are unsure of the best plan and want to see the opponent's intentions first.
notes.plans: After White's response, Black can choose a plan (e.g., ...b5, ...Ba6, or ...d5) based on White's setup.

notes.explains: After White's f3 (a mistake), Black exploited the weak d3 pawn by playing ...c4, then taking with the bishop to pin White's queen to the rook, winning the exchange. This was concrete calculation, not general principles.
notes.teaches: When a pawn becomes weak, calculate concrete captures. Sometimes taking with a piece (here the bishop) is better than with the queen because it creates a pin or other tactical advantage.
notes.plans: After winning the exchange, Black should continue to develop and activate pieces, avoiding unnecessary material giveaways.

notes.explains: Black is up material but should not give it back unnecessarily. For example, playing ...Rc5? allows ...Qxf7+ and Black's advantage shrinks. Only sacrifice material if it's necessary to win.
notes.teaches: When you are winning, don't voluntarily give back material unless it forces a quick win. Simplify by trading pieces, but keep your extra material.
notes.plans: Black should continue to consolidate, trade pieces, and push for a win without unnecessary risks.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Be7, the natural developing move Bc4 is threatened by ...Nxe4 followed by d5 forking bishop and knight.
notes.teaches: When a fork threatens your bishop, retreat it to b3 to avoid the tactic without weakening your pawn structure.
notes.plans: Continue development with Bf4, but be aware of Black's plan to push c5-c4 trapping the bishop. Instead, play Bd5, attacking the rook and preparing to meet c5 with a favorable exchange.

notes.explains: After Bd5, Black played b5 threatening c5-c4. Bd5 blocks the pawn chain and attacks the rook, so if c5, the bishop is well-placed and can be recaptured with a knight to create an outpost.
notes.teaches: Place your bishop in front of the enemy pawn chain to avoid being trapped and to maintain activity.
notes.plans: If Black plays c5, recapture with the knight to centralize it. Then aim to attack with Qg4 and Bh6, exploiting the g-file.

notes.explains: After Nxd5, the knight is centralized. Black's bishop on e7 moved to f6, weakening the g7 square. Qg4 targets g7 and creates a pin.
notes.teaches: Centralize your pieces and look for attacking chances against the king. A pin on the g-file can be decisive.
notes.plans: Play Bh6 to exploit the pin. If Black defends with Ng6, retreat; otherwise win the exchange. Then simplify by trading rooks and win the endgame.

notes.explains: After winning the exchange and some pawns, White has a winning endgame. The plan is to create a passed pawn on the f-file using the pawn majority, then use it as a decoy to win other pawns.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, identify your pawn majority and create a passed pawn. Use the passed pawn to tie down the opponent's king, then bring your king to collect other pawns.
notes.plans: Push g4 and f5 to create a passed f-pawn. Then use the passed pawn to distract Black's king while White's king captures pawns on the queenside.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 Be3 Nf6 Bc4 O-O Bb3, White played Nxc6? which opens the b-file and helps Black prepare d5.
notes.teaches: Avoid trading knights on c6 in the Accelerated Dragon as it gives Black easy play with ...bxc6 and ...d5. Instead, keep the tension with Nc3 or other moves.
notes.plans: Develop with Nf6, fianchetto the bishop, and aim for d5 to challenge White's center.

notes.explains: After bxc6, Black played Qb6 to prevent White from castling, exploiting the weakened f3 pawn. White's f3 is a common mistake that weakens the dark squares and allows Qb6.
notes.teaches: Prevent the opponent from castling by placing your queen on b6, especially when f3 has been played. Use the time they spend dealing with the queen to expand in the center.
notes.plans: Play e5 to close the queen's diagonal and then expand with e4. If White tries Be3, play Ng4 to disrupt it and attack b2.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 d5 exd5 e4 Qe2 Nf6 Nc3 Be7 d3 O-O dxe4 Nxe4, Black played Bg4 pinning the knight. The knight is defended by a pawn on g2, so the pin is not dangerous.
notes.teaches: A pin is dangerous only if the pinned piece is not defended by a pawn. If it is, you can often ignore it or counterattack the pinning piece.
notes.plans: Develop with Nc3 and Qe2 to protect the knight and prepare to unpin with g4 if needed. Then play Bd3 to develop kingside and prepare Re1.

notes.explains: After Qe2, Black played f5? attacking the knight. White can retreat but instead played Bd3, blocking the c1 bishop but prioritizing kingside development and the threat of Re1.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must violate development principles to address immediate threats. Here, getting the rook to e1 is more important than developing the queenside bishop.
notes.plans: Play Bd3 to protect the knight and prepare Re1. Then exploit Black's king stuck in the center with Bc4 and Ng5, threatening f7.

notes.explains: After Bd3, Black played f6, weakening the e8-h5 diagonal. White played Bc4, attacking f7, and then Ng5, threatening checkmate with Nxf7 if Black doesn't defend properly.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, look for checkmate patterns. Here, a double check with Nf6+ is devastating because the king has no escape squares.
notes.plans: Play Bc4 to attack f7, then Ng5. If Black plays f6, take with gxf6 and then Nxf6#. If f5, take with Qxf5 and then Nxf6+ with double check and mate.

notes.explains: Black develops bishops to e7 and b6, which are invulnerable squares. Be7 prevents Ng5, and Bb6 reinforces the knight. This is solid and avoids tactics like Bg4 which would allow Nxe5.
notes.teaches: Place bishops on squares where they are not easily attacked and serve defensive roles. Avoid advanced bishop placements that create tactical vulnerabilities.
notes.plans: Continue improving position, possibly with a5 to prevent b4, then Qd7 to connect rooks.

notes.explains: f6 is safe here because White has no bishop on the a7-g1 diagonal, and Black's own bishop can reposition. It reinforces e5 and prevents Ng5.
notes.teaches: f6 is not always weakening; evaluate what it actually weakens. If the opponent cannot exploit the diagonal, it can be a solid defensive move.
notes.plans: Play Qd7, eyeing h3 and preparing potential sacrifices.

notes.explains: f5 reopens the bishop's diagonal, attacks h4, and defends the bishop on g4. It also prevents Nxe5 tactics.
notes.teaches: When defending a piece, consider moves that also create counterplay. f5 serves multiple purposes.
notes.plans: Continue pressuring White's kingside.

notes.explains: Bf6 defends the e5 pawn with the least valuable piece, freeing the rook for other tasks. This is more flexible than immediately playing Re8.
notes.teaches: Accomplish defensive tasks with the least valuable piece possible, keeping rooks and queen for more important duties.
notes.plans: Follow with Re8, completing development, then consider breaks like f4 or e4.

notes.explains: Black takes on g4 to prevent White from occupying e4 with a knight. Although it gives up the bishop, it avoids a strong knight outpost.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must part with a good piece to deny the opponent a key square. Evaluate the trade concretely.
notes.plans: Play Nd4, attacking the queen and starting active play.

notes.explains: f4 is a concrete attempt to break White's kingside defense, even though it gives up the e4 square. The attack should be worth the concession.
notes.teaches: When you sense the time is right, press the attack even if it means sacrificing a positional plus. Trust your feeling after improving your pieces.
notes.plans: After f4, aim to open the f-file by moving the bishop from f6.

notes.explains: Nf5 is the only logical square, pressuring White's kingside and threatening sacrifices like Bxh4.
notes.teaches: When attacking, place knights on squares that maximize pressure on the opponent's king.
notes.plans: Consider rook lifts or further sacrifices to break through.

notes.explains: After Nxg3 and Nxh4, Black wins a pawn and exposes White's king. The attack has paid off.
notes.teaches: When the attack yields material, take it and continue pressing. An exposed king is a long-term asset.
notes.plans: Consolidate and exploit the weakened king position.

notes.explains: After Nf4 forces Bxf4, Black recaptures with the pawn, attacking the knight on g3. The bishop retreats to d8 again, staying out of the rook's way.
notes.teaches: After a trade, reassess the position. New ideas (like rook lifts) become possible. Retreat bishops to keep them safe and not block rooks.
notes.plans: Prepare to lift the rook to h6 or target the d3 pawn.

notes.explains: b6 prevents Nc5, which would fork the rook and queen. This allows the rook lift to h6.
notes.teaches: Identify your top priority (rook lift), find the obstacle (Nc5), and make it disappear with a prophylactic move.
notes.plans: Play Rh6, then continue the attack.

notes.explains: Be7 repositions the bishop to a better diagonal, preparing to bring the rook to d8 to pressure d3.
