notes.teaches: Don't hesitate to reposition pieces to improve their activity. The bishop is still useful from e7.
notes.plans: Play Rd8, targeting the weak d3 pawn.

notes.explains: c4 provokes d4, which isolates the knight on e4 by removing its pawn support. Black then redirects pressure onto the knight.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you provoke a pawn move to weaken the opponent's piece support. Then shift your attack to that piece.
notes.plans: After d4, play Re8 to x-ray the knight, then maneuver to create a pin or win the knight.

notes.explains: Bxa3 exposes the attack on the knight on e4. It's a discovered attack, not a sacrifice, as the knight is undefended.
notes.teaches: Look for discovered attacks when a piece moves away. Even if it seems risky, calculate concretely.
notes.plans: Follow up by doubling rooks or taking the knight.

notes.explains: Kh8 is prophylaxis against knight checks on f6, but it walks into backrank issues. Better to play h6 first for luft.
notes.teaches: When playing prophylactically, also consider new weaknesses created. Always create luft when the backrank is vulnerable.
notes.plans: Push the h-pawn to promote, while defending the c4 pawn.

notes.explains: Push the h-pawn, as it is far from White's knight and has good promotion chances. The d-pawn is blockaded.
notes.teaches: In pawn races, push the pawn furthest from the opponent's pieces. A single passed pawn can be very powerful.
notes.plans: Continue pushing h-pawn to promotion, while keeping the king safe.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 d6 d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Be7, White has a choice. The natural Bc4 is less accurate because the c3 knight blocks the c2 pawn push, which is important in Italian-style setups. Better is Bb5+, forcing ...Bd7 and then Bc4, transposing to a favorable Morphy-like line.
notes.teaches: In the Philidor, White should aim to trade the light-squared bishops to weaken Black's kingside and gain a lead in development. The move Bb5+ is a key idea to achieve this.
notes.plans: After Bb5+ Bd7 Bxd7+ Nxd7, White can play 0-0 and then push e5 to open the center, exploiting Black's lagging development.

notes.explains: In a position where Black has played ...Bg4 pinning the knight, White's best response is Bb5, not fearing Bxf3 because recapturing with gxf3 opens the g-file and reinforces e4. The doubled f-pawns are not a weakness here; White's king is safe and the open file gives attacking chances.
notes.teaches: Don't fear doubled pawns if they come with concrete benefits like open lines or central control. Pawn structure is secondary to activity and initiative.
notes.plans: After gxf3, White can play Qxd4 or take on f6 first, then follow up with 0-0-0 and a kingside attack.

notes.explains: When White has a dynamic advantage (lead in development, better piece activity), it's crucial to press it immediately rather than playing slow positional moves. Here, instead of natural moves like Bg5 or Rd1, the aggressive Qg3 hitting g7 and b7 exploits Black's undeveloped kingside.
notes.teaches: Distinguish between static and dynamic advantages. With a dynamic advantage (initiative), seek direct threats and force the opponent to react, not allowing them to consolidate.
notes.plans: After Qg3, if Black defends g7 with ...Bd6, then Qxg7 Rg8 Qh6 keeps the queen active and the knight on f6 is unsupported. If Black plays ...Qe7, White can target the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: When ahead in development and attacking, the queen often works best on the sidelines (e.g., Qh3) rather than centrally. Central queen positions are vulnerable to harassment and trades, which the defending side wants. Here Qh3 keeps the queen safe, prevents Black from castling, and keeps the f-pawn free to advance.
notes.teaches: The queen is a supporting actress, not the star of the attack. Place it on the flank where it is less exposed and can support pawn advances and piece coordination.
notes.plans: After Qh3, if Black plays ...Qe5, then f4 drives the queen back. Then Bc5+ Kh1 and the knight on h5 becomes a target. White can trap it with e5, cutting off its retreat.

notes.explains: When the opponent's knight is on h5 with only one escape square (g7), White can trap it by playing e5, cutting the connection between the queen and the knight. Then Black must either weaken with ...g6 or lose the knight.
notes.teaches: Look for knights on the rim that are short of squares. A knight on the edge can often be trapped by advancing a pawn to take away its only retreat.
notes.plans: After e5, if Black plays ...g6, White can continue with Rd1, threatening Qd7# and also preparing g4 to push the knight back. The rook on d1 also prevents ...Qd5 counterplay.

notes.explains: Against the London, Black's most combative response is d4 d5 Bf4 c5, immediately attacking the center. After c3 (a common mistake), Black plays …cxd4 cxd4 Qb6, exploiting the unprotected b2 pawn. White is already worse and must play accurately to avoid losing a pawn or getting a bad position.
notes.teaches: The London's weakness is the b2 pawn. By playing ...c5 and ...Qb6, Black puts immediate pressure on White's queenside and forces White to defend passively.
notes.plans: After Qb6, White's best is Qd2, but then Black continues with ...Nc6 and ...e5, opening the center while White's queen is awkward on d2. Black should aim for rapid development and tactical blows.

notes.explains: In the London with c3, after d4 d5 Bf4 c5 c3 cxd4 cxd4 Qb6 Qd2 Nc6, Black should play ...e5 as soon as possible. This opens lines for the bishops and exploits White's awkward queen on d2. The move ...e5 is more effective than slow moves like ...e6.
notes.teaches: When you have a dynamic advantage (better development, opponent's queen misplaced), open the center immediately to maximize your piece activity. Don't give the opponent time to consolidate.
notes.plans: After ...e5, if White takes dxe5, Black recaptures with ...Nxe5, threatening ...Nf3+ or ...Bc5. If White plays e3, Black can continue with ...Bc5 and ...Nge7, putting pressure on d4.

notes.explains: In a sharp position from the London, Black has the idea of playing ...g5 to attack the bishop on f4. This is a common motif in many openings (e.g., Jaenisch Gambit). The threat is ...h5 trapping the bishop. White often cannot avoid this without serious concessions.
notes.teaches: The ...g5 push to attack a bishop on f4 is a recurring idea. It forces White to either retreat (losing time) or allow the bishop to be trapped, often leading to a strong attack for Black.
notes.plans: After ...g5, if White plays Bg3, Black follows with ...h5, threatening ...h4. White may try f3, but then ...Nxg3 hxg3 creates weaknesses. Black should aim to open the h-file and attack the king.

notes.explains: After Black's ...e5 break, White may play dxe5, leading to a position where Black can sacrifice the exchange on c3 for a strong attack. For example, ...Nxe4 Qc2 Nb4!? is a surprising idea: the knight on b4 threatens ...d5 and ...Nc2+, and White's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, look for piece sacrifices to open lines and expose the enemy king. A knight sacrifice on b4 can disrupt White's coordination and create lasting threats.
notes.plans: After Nb4, if White plays Qd2, Black can play ...d5, opening the center. If White plays Qb1, Black can play ...Bf5, threatening ...Nc2+. The initiative is worth more than material.

notes.explains: Against the Smith-Morra Gambit (e4 c5 d4 cxd4 c3), Black's best practical response is …d5, declining the gambit. This is rare but very effective if White is not booked up. After exd5 Nf6, Black gets a good version of the Caro-Kann Panov, where Black's pieces are active and White's extra pawn is weak.
notes.teaches: Declining the gambit with ...d5 can be safer than accepting, especially if you know the resulting positions. It transposes to a favorable Caro-Kann structure where Black has easy development.
notes.plans: After …Nf6, if White plays Nf3, Black can play ...Bf5 (or ...Bg4) with good play. If White plays dxc6, Black recaptures with ...Nxc6 and has a lead in development. Black should aim to complete development and target White's central pawns.

notes.explains: In a line of the Smith-Morra where Black plays ...d5 and White plays c4, Black can play ...e5, opening the center. If White takes en passant, Black gets a massive lead in development. The key idea is ...e5, using tactics to favor Black.
notes.teaches: When White tries to defend the extra pawn with c4, Black should strike in the center with ...e5. This is a typical counter in many openings, exploiting White's overextended pawns.
notes.plans: After ...e5, if White plays dxe6, Black recaptures with ...Bxe6, with active pieces. If White plays fxe6, Black plays ...Bxe6, and White's king is exposed. Black should aim to castle quickly and attack.

notes.explains: In a position where Black has a knight on c2 and White's king is on d1, Black's best move is ...a6, not ...Nxa1. The move ...a6 is prophylaxis: it prevents White's queen from going to b7 with tempo and also stops ...Bb5 ideas. After ...a6, the knight on c2 is safe and Black can later retreat it with ...Nb4, threatening ...Bc2 and ...Bb1.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move is a quiet prophylactic move that prevents the opponent's counterplay. Don't rush to grab material if it gives the opponent dangerous counterplay.
notes.plans: After ...a6, Black can play ...Nb4, threatening ...Bc2+. White must waste time moving the rook, and Black's attack continues. The knight on a1 would be trapped after Qb7, so ...a6 is essential.

notes.explains: In the French Advance (e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Qb6 a3), White plays a3 to prevent ...Bb4 and prepare b4. The idea is to secure the c5 square for the knight via Na4, forcing Black's queen to move. This is a standard plan to gain space on the queenside.
notes.teaches: In the French Advance, White's main plan is to support the d4 pawn and then expand on the queenside with b4. The move a3 is prophylactic, preventing Black's bishop from pinning the knight.
notes.plans: After a3, White can play Na4, forcing ...Qa5+ (or ...Qc7), then Bd2 and Bd3, followed by 0-0. The knight on a4 can later go to c5, putting pressure on Black's position.

notes.explains: After White has established a knight on c5, Black may try to exchange it with ...Bxc5. White should recapture with the rook, not the pawn, to keep the queenside open and maintain pressure. The rook on c1 supports the knight and later can double on the c-file.
notes.teaches: When recapturing on a strong outpost, prefer the rook over the pawn if it keeps the file open and maintains attacking chances. A pawn recapture may close the position and reduce your advantage.
notes.plans: After Rxc5, White can double rooks on the c-file, play a4 to undermine Black's pawns, and eventually break through with b5. Black's position becomes cramped and passive.

notes.explains: In a position reminiscent of Alekhine–Nimzowitsch, White can play Rc2 to prepare doubling rooks on the c-file. This is prophylactic: it prevents Black's knight from jumping to f5 (which would attack the pawn on d4) and also prepares Qa1, which protects d4 and allows doubling.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves like Rc2 can serve multiple purposes: they prevent the opponent's ideas while improving your own piece coordination. Think about what your opponent wants to do and stop it.
notes.plans: After Rc2, White can play Qa1, then double rooks on the c-file. Black is completely tied down. Eventually, White can play a4 to break Black's queenside pawns and create passed pawns.

notes.explains: Black takes the f4 pawn and then plays d5 to open the center, exploiting White's weakened kingside after f4. The idea is to open lines to attack the exposed king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their kingside, open the center to exploit it. Don't recapture the gambit pawn immediately with the queen (allowing Nc3), but develop with Nf6 to support the pawn and keep the queen safe.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, aiming to return the pawn for positional advantages like the two bishops and a solid center.

notes.explains: Black plays Be6 to neutralize White's bishop on c4, which was x-raying the knight on f6 and pressuring f7. This is a typical development move that also asks White what he wants to do.
notes.teaches: Neutralize opponent's active pieces with simple developing moves. Don't fear passive-looking moves if they improve your position and reduce the opponent's threats.
notes.plans: Contest the center with c5 or Nc6, using the c-pawns as bargaining chips to eventually undouble them and gain a strong pawn structure.

notes.explains: Black plays Nc6, which appears to ruin the pawn structure but is actually a flexible move. The doubled c-pawns can be pushed to contest the center and later undoubled, turning a weakness into a strength.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are not always bad; they can be used as a bargaining chip to gain central control or be undoubled later. Think dynamically about pawn structures.
notes.plans: Push c5, and if White takes, recapture with the bishop, then play Qxd4 to force queen trade and correct the pawn structure, leaving Black with a solid endgame edge.

notes.explains: After trading queens, Black has an extra pawn and the two bishops. The key is to activate pieces and restrict the opponent's knight. Playing f6 prevents the knight from centralizing on e5, a prophylactic idea.
notes.teaches: In endgames, first activate your pieces, then restrict the opponent's best squares. Prophylaxis means asking what the opponent wants and preventing it.
notes.plans: Play g6 to stop the knight from reaching f5, then a5 to hinder queenside expansion. Centralize the bishop to d5 and slowly improve the position.

notes.explains: Black continues the boa constrictor style: f6, g6, a5, and Bc6-d5. Each move improves a piece or restricts White. The king is brought to g7 to activate it for the endgame.
notes.teaches: Gradually improve your position by making small, purposeful moves. Don't rush; squeeze the opponent by limiting their options while enhancing your own.
notes.plans: Eventually break with c4 to open the position, exploiting the greater activity of Black's pieces. Trade rooks and promote the pawn.

notes.explains: Black prepares the decisive pawn break c4. Since Black's pieces are more active, opening the position will magnify that advantage. The break leads to a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are more active, look for a pawn break to open lines and convert the advantage. The principle is: active pieces need open positions.
notes.plans: Play c4, trade rooks, and promote the passed pawn. Prevent opponent's counterplay (e.g., rook b1 to stop the b-pawn).

notes.explains: Black plays h6, a pointless move that weakens the kingside and allows White to occupy the center. White responds with natural development, gaining a strong position.
notes.teaches: Don't make unnecessary pawn moves in the opening; they waste time and can create weaknesses. Develop pieces and control the center.
notes.plans: Exploit the weak h6 by building an attack. Play Qb3 to pressure f7 and b7, then consider tactics like Bxf7+ to win material.

notes.explains: White has a strong position after Qb3. Black's bishop on g4 is a mistake because it leaves both f7 and b7 undefended. White can exploit this with a tactic like Bxf7+.
notes.teaches: In the opening, watch for undefended pieces and tactical shots. A move like Bg4 can be punished if it leaves key squares unprotected.
notes.plans: Consider Bxf7+ first (if it wins material), then take on b7. Alternatively, play d5 to open the center and increase pressure.

notes.explains: With opposite-side castling, White must attack the black king quickly. The plan is to open the h-file with h4-h5 and then sacrifice on h6 to break through.
notes.teaches: In opposite-side castling, attack is paramount. Open files against the enemy king and use piece sacrifices to accelerate the attack.
notes.plans: Play e5 to force the queen to a bad square, then take on h6. Avoid traps like Bxh6? which loses a rook. Instead, use the rook lift and knight outpost on c5.

notes.explains: White avoids the trap Bxh6? because it loses a rook after ...gxh6 Rxh6? Qf4+ and ...Qxh6. Instead, White first plays e5 to force the queen to f4, then takes on h6 safely.
notes.teaches: Always double-check calculations; don't stop early. Look for opponent's counter-resources before committing to a sacrifice.
notes.plans: After e5 and Bxh6, open the h-file and double rooks for a checkmate attack. Use the knight on c5 to block counterplay.

notes.explains: White improves the knight to c5, a strong outpost that blocks Black's counterplay on the c-file and supports the attack. The queen stays on c2 to guard the knight.
notes.teaches: Look for outposts for your knights, especially in attacking positions. A well-placed knight can both support the attack and defend against counterplay.
notes.plans: Double rooks on the h-file and deliver checkmate on h7. The knight on c5 prevents Black from activating his rook.

notes.explains: After the sequence, White has a choice: Nxc6 wins a pawn but gives Black activity. It's better to avoid such 'cashing in' and instead maintain positional pressure.
notes.teaches: Don't be seduced by a flashy tactic that wins material if it allows the opponent to activate their pieces. Calculate deeper to see if the gain is worth the loss of initiative.
notes.plans: White should prefer developing moves like Bg2 or castling, keeping the tension and exploiting Black's weak pawns and passive pieces.

notes.explains: After castling, White has a pleasant position with active pieces and Black's queenside is weak. White should consider prophylactic moves like b4 to prevent Black's knight from reaching d4 via c5.
notes.teaches: Prophylaxis is key: anticipate your opponent's best square for a piece and prevent it. Here, b4 stops ...c5 and ...Nc6-d4.
notes.plans: White plays b4, then develops the bishop to e3, and prepares f4 to control the center and restrict Black's pieces.

notes.explains: Black's a5 is a good move, forcing a3 and creating a potential outpost on b5. White must be careful not to allow Black counterplay. The position remains better for White due to space and activity.
notes.teaches: When your opponent creates a weakness, consider whether it can be exploited. Here, a5 opens the a-file but also gives Black the b5 square; White must weigh the trade-offs.
notes.plans: White continues with Rfd1, aiming to occupy the d-file with a rook on d6, while keeping an eye on Black's queenside counterplay.

notes.explains: After the rook trade on a1, White has two open files (a and d). The a-file is less important because Black's rook on a2 is just an irritant. White focuses on the d-file, where there are real targets.
notes.teaches: When there are two open files, prioritize the one that leads to weaknesses in the opponent's position. Don't fear giving up a file if the other offers more concrete threats.
notes.plans: White plays Rfd1 and then Rd6, doubling rooks on the d-file to pressure the knight on d7 and the pawn on d5.

notes.explains: White's rook on d6 is a powerful outpost, attacking the knight and the pawn on d5. Black's last chance to create counterplay was ...c5, but he missed it.
notes.teaches: An outpost on an open file can be a decisive advantage. Use it to tie down enemy pieces and create multiple threats.
notes.plans: White doubles rooks on the d-file and prepares f5 to increase pressure on the kingside, eventually forcing a breakthrough.

notes.explains: After Qd4, White attacks both the rook on d6 and the pawn on b6. Black cannot defend both, so White wins a pawn and creates a passed d-pawn.
notes.teaches: Double attacks are a fundamental tactic. Look for moves that threaten multiple targets, especially when the opponent's pieces are tied down.
notes.plans: White captures the b6 pawn, then uses the passed d-pawn to win the game, while keeping the king safe from Black's potential rook activity on the a-file.

notes.explains: In the endgame, White activates the king to support the passed pawn. The king on d5 protects the pawn and helps create breakthroughs like b5.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, the king becomes a powerful piece. Use it to support passed pawns and create threats, often by centralizing it.
notes.plans: White pushes b5 to force the knight back, then advances the d-pawn (now on b7) to win a piece or promote.

notes.explains: The final phase: after b7, Black's king cannot approach due to the rook's x-ray. White promotes the pawn and wins.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, cutting off the enemy king is crucial. Use your rook to block the king's path to the passed pawn, ensuring promotion.
notes.plans: White promotes the b-pawn, using the rook to shield the king and the x-ray to prevent the black king from interfering.

notes.explains: After f4, Black should immediately open the center with …d5, exploiting the weakening of the f4-square and the e5-pawn's loss of support.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a weakening pawn move like f4, strike in the center to exploit the weaknesses created.
notes.plans: Follow up with ...Nc6 and ...Bf5, targeting the weakened f5-square.

notes.explains: After …Nf6, Black offers a gambit. White cannot easily defend the d5-pawn; if c4, Black has ...e6 with strong compensation.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and the opponent has weakened squares, sacrificing a pawn can give lasting positional compensation.
notes.plans: Black aims to develop quickly, target f4, and occupy the d4-outpost with a knight.

notes.explains: Black has three key advantages: a lead in development, the weakness of f4 (making White's kingside unsafe), and the d4-square as a permanent outpost for a knight.
notes.teaches: When evaluating compensation for a pawn, consider development, opponent's pawn weaknesses, and potential outposts—especially central squares for knights.
notes.plans: Black will aim to get a knight to d4, either by eliminating White's knight on f3 or after it moves.

notes.explains: After …Bg4, Black pins the knight. A common idea is ...Nxe4, sacrificing the knight for two pawns and White's light-squared bishop, then ...d5 to break the center.
notes.teaches: When facing an Italian-style setup, the ...Nxe4 sacrifice can eliminate White's central control and key bishop, giving Black lasting compensation.
notes.plans: If White accepts the sacrifice, Black plays ...d5, opening lines and gaining the two bishops.

notes.explains: In this sharp line, Black sacrifices a piece for two pawns and a strong center. The key is to follow up with ...Nf6 and ...e5, then fianchetto the c8-bishop to b7, creating 'Horwitz bishops' aimed at White's king.
notes.teaches: When you have two bishops and a pawn center, coordinate them by fianchettoing the remaining bishop to the long diagonal.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Nf6, ...e5, ...Be7, O-O, and ...Bb7, with pressure on the kingside.

notes.explains: Black has two bishops and a solid pawn center. The light-squared bishop is particularly strong because White's light-squared bishop is gone, making the long diagonal uncontested.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop of the same color as your fianchettoed bishop is missing, your bishop gains extra power on the long diagonal.
notes.plans: Black will fianchetto the c8-bishop to b7, then pressure the kingside with ...Qd7 and ...Rae8.

notes.explains: After …Qc7, Black has two bishops and a better pawn structure. The key is to avoid opening the e-file prematurely before castling.
notes.teaches: In positions with an exposed king, be cautious about opening files that lead to your king before you have castled.
notes.plans: Black will castle, then play ...Bf6 and ...Rfd8, putting pressure on the d-file.

notes.explains: Black has a slight edge due to the bishop pair and better pawn structure. The position is equal but pleasant for Black.
notes.teaches: When you have a small positional advantage, don't force matters; simply improve your pieces and wait for the opponent to create weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Rad8, ...b6, and ...Bc6, then consider ...Qxb3 or ...d5 to increase pressure.

notes.explains: Black wins a pawn but must be careful not to cling to it. The rook on b3 is active, and Black can double rooks on the d-file.
notes.teaches: When up material, don't be afraid to give back a pawn to activate your pieces and coordinate them for an attack.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Rbd3, ...Rd2, and infiltrate with the rooks, while White's king is exposed.

notes.explains: Black's rook on d2 is active, and White's kingside pawns are fixed. Black can stop ...g4 by ...h5 or by meeting g4 with ...fxg3 en passant.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, fixing the opponent's pawns and preventing counterplay is key. Use your rook to control the seventh rank.
notes.plans: Black will play ...h5 to fix the kingside pawns, then bring the king to the center and advance the queenside pawns.

notes.explains: Black has a winning rook endgame. The rook is active, and White's pawns are weak.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, activity matters more than pawn count. A rook on the seventh rank can create decisive threats.
notes.plans: Black will advance the queenside pawns and use the rook to attack White's pawns from behind.

notes.explains: Recapturing with the pawn keeps the queen battery on f7 and gives the dark-squared bishop a powerful square on a3.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, recapturing with the pawn can preserve attacking potential and open lines for other pieces.
notes.plans: Play Ba3+ to disrupt Black's kingside and force d6, then develop with Rd1.

notes.explains: After Rd1, Black plays Nxe4, attacking the rook and defending d6. White must find the best response.
notes.teaches: When the attack stalls, look for ways to transform the advantage into a different form, such as a favorable endgame.
notes.plans: Consider f3 to kick the knight, or the stronger Bishop d5, which attacks b7 and keeps pressure.

notes.explains: White takes on d6 with the rook, keeping the initiative and threatening discoveries. The e5 pawn is a sitting duck.
notes.teaches: When the direct attack fades, transform into a position with a lasting advantage: an extra pawn and active pieces.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to f3, castle, and then use the rook on d6 to create threats, eventually winning the e5 pawn.

notes.explains: After castling, White has a rook on d6 and needs to keep the initiative. Ng5 is natural, threatening Ne6 and Nf7.
notes.teaches: In endgames with active rooks, look for knight maneuvers that create forks and threats.
notes.plans: Play Ng5, then after Rd8, avoid taking on d8; instead play Nf7, forking rook and bishop.

notes.explains: After Nf7, Black takes on d6. Recapturing with the knight is better than with the bishop because it forks the rook on h8 and opens the f-file for the rook.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which piece gives more activity and future threats. The knight recapture paves the way for Rf7 infiltration.
notes.plans: Take on g7 with the rook, then take on b7 with the knight, winning two pawns and creating a strong attack.

notes.explains: White wins two pawns and has a rook on the seventh rank. Black tries to counter with Rf8, but the bishop prevents that.
notes.teaches: When up material, consolidate by improving your king's safety and centralizing it, as in the 'Russian school' approach.
notes.plans: Move the king to e3 to avoid back-rank mates, then pick off Black's remaining weak pawns.

notes.explains: White centralizes the king to e3, avoiding any back-rank tricks and preparing to push pawns.
notes.teaches: In winning endgames, improve your king's position before rushing to capture more material. Safety first.
notes.plans: Trade knights to reach an opposite-colored bishop endgame, then push the c-pawn and win more pawns.

notes.explains: White wins a third pawn and gets connected passers. The simplest plan is to push the c-pawn.
notes.teaches: In endgames with connected passers, push them supported by pieces; don't rush, but keep the pressure.
notes.plans: Play c4, then c5, c6, etc., while the knight and bishop defend each other.

notes.explains: White is up four pawns and can push pawns freely. The king can come to d4 to support.
notes.teaches: When massively ahead, simplify by trading pieces and pushing pawns; avoid unnecessary risks.
notes.plans: Push c5, c4, etc., and use the king to shepherd pawns to promotion.

notes.explains: This is the Carlsbad structure, a classic imbalanced pawn formation arising from the Queen's Gambit Declined. Black's setup with c6, Be7, Nbd7, and later Ne6 and b6 is standard, aiming to reinforce d5 and prepare c5 counterplay.
notes.teaches: In the Carlsbad, Black's key ideas are to solidify the d5 pawn, develop pieces harmoniously, and prepare a timely c5 break to challenge White's center and create queenside counterplay.
notes.plans: Black will complete development with Bb7, then push c5 to create tension. After exchanges, Black aims to activate the knight on c5 and pressure White's queenside.

notes.explains: After the c5 break and exchanges, Black has a knight on c5 and a pawn on a4, while White has a rook on d1. Black's position is solid but White's rook activity and potential kingside attack (with f4-f5) require careful defense.
notes.teaches: In the Carlsbad, after c5, Black must be alert to White's plans of f4-f5 and kingside expansion. Black's counterplay often involves pushing the a-pawn and using the knight on c5 to pressure White's queenside.
notes.plans: Black will push the a-pawn to create a passed pawn, while keeping the king safe. The knight on c5 can be used to block or trade, and Black should aim to simplify to a drawn rook endgame.

notes.explains: After Nd2, Black has a winning idea: g5, attacking the bishop. If the bishop takes on g5, Nxe5 is crushing. If it retreats to g3, h5 traps it. The knight on d2 is overloaded.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's knight is overloaded (defending multiple pieces), pawn storms like g5 and h5 can be used to exploit the lack of coordination.
notes.plans: Play g5, and if Bxg5, Nxe5 wins material. If Bg3, h5 threatens to trap the bishop. White's position collapses.

notes.explains: After g6, Black is ready to fianchetto. White's best is the computerish f3 to prepare e4, but most London players won't know this. Black gets a fantastic position.
notes.teaches: The fianchetto setup against the London gives Black a harmonious, active position. White's lack of development makes it hard to counter.
notes.plans: Continue with Bg7, O-O, and then target the d6 pawn or prepare a central break.

notes.explains: After the trade, Black's queen is on d7. White should choose a good square for the queen. Qd3 is fine, offering lateral mobility and covering light squares.
notes.teaches: In positions with a weak pawn (d6) and an outpost (d5), place the queen on a flexible square like d3, where it can support the center and switch to attack.
notes.plans: Castle queenside to bring a rook to d1, piling up on the d6 pawn. Then look for ways to increase pressure without rushing to capture the knight on f6.

notes.explains: White has built up pressure on d6. Black plays Qg4, forking the bishop on g5 and the pawn on g2. White can defend the bishop with f4, sacrificing the g2 pawn. This is a sound sacrifice because Black's queen will be trapped on the kingside.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is attacked and you can defend it with a pawn, consider sacrificing the g2 (or b2) pawn to open a file against the enemy king. The queen often gets trapped.
notes.plans: After f4, if Black takes on g2, play Rg1, chasing the queen. The queen has few squares and White's attack will be devastating.

notes.explains: After Qh3, White threatens both trapping the queen with Rd2 and a mating attack. Black is helpless. The key idea was to double on the h-file and create multiple threats.
notes.teaches: When the enemy queen is stranded on the kingside, use rook lifts and queen maneuvers to create unstoppable threats. The queen cannot escape because the rook on d1 controls d4.
notes.plans: Play Rd2 to trap the queen, or if Black tries to escape, continue the mating attack. The position is completely winning.

notes.explains: Black plays h6, but White simply plays Rd2, trapping the queen. The queen has no escape squares. Black resigned shortly after.
notes.teaches: When the queen is trapped, don't overcomplicate. Simply play the move that traps it, even if it seems slow. Winning the queen is decisive.
notes.plans: After Rd2, the queen is lost. White will convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: If Black had played c4 to open an escape diagonal for the queen, White can still win in many ways. The simplest is Bxf6, then Nd5, threatening Qh8# and taking away the e7 escape square.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to create an escape route, look for a combination that takes away the escape squares and delivers mate or wins material. Here, Nd5 is a classic centralizing move that also blocks the king's escape.
notes.plans: After Bxf6, Bxf6, play Nd5, threatening Qh8#. The king is trapped and White wins.

notes.explains: After Nd5, Black is completely lost. The knight takes away the e7 escape square, and Qh8# is threatened. Black's queen is also under attack.
notes.teaches: In king hunts, the first priority is to take away the king's escape squares. A knight on d5 often does this job perfectly.
notes.plans: If Black tries to run, continue checking and chasing the king until mate. White is up material anyway.

notes.explains: If Black plays h6 instead of taking on g2, White can save the bishop with h3. If Black then takes on g2, the rook on g1 chases the queen, and White can later take on h6.
notes.teaches: When your bishop is attacked by a pawn, consider moving a pawn to defend it (h3) rather than retreating or exchanging. This keeps the pressure on.
notes.plans: After h3, if Qxg2, Rg1, Qh5, g4, Qh4, Bh4, maintaining the bishop and continuing the attack.

notes.explains: After Bh4, the bishop is safe and White still has all the pressure. The queen is misplaced on h4.
notes.teaches: By defending the bishop with a pawn, you maintain the pin and keep the initiative. The opponent's queen often ends up on a bad square.
notes.plans: Continue building up pressure, possibly with g5 or doubling rooks on the g-file.

notes.explains: The teacher shows a game he lost as a 1600 where he tunnel-visioned on capturing the d6 pawn and traded his bishop for the knight on f6, only to lose to a counterattack. The lesson is to keep perspective and not rush.
notes.teaches: Avoid tunnel vision. Just because a pawn is weak doesn't mean you should immediately grab it. Consider the opponent's counterplay and keep your pieces active.
notes.plans: In the example, White should have played Be3 or Kb1 instead of Bxf6. Keep the bishop and maintain the attack.

notes.explains: The teacher reiterates that the bishop on d3, though seemingly modest, has great potential energy. It can become a hero if the center opens up (e.g., after e5).
notes.teaches: A piece on a modest square can still be very powerful. Don't judge a piece only by its immediate activity; consider its potential after pawn breaks.
notes.plans: In the game, White could have played e5, opening lines for the bishop on d3 and the queen, leading to a winning attack.

notes.explains: Black fell into the trap: dxc3 allows Qd5, attacking f7 and the knight on c3. White can win a piece.
notes.teaches: Always check if a fork or attack can be defended by a single move that defends both targets simultaneously.
notes.plans: Avoid dxc3; instead play Nf6 or d3 to keep the pawn.

notes.explains: After a tactical sequence, White has a queen on d4 and Black has a rook on g8. Black is down material but has counterplay.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, keep your composure; even if you miss a move, you can still find resources if you stay calm.
notes.plans: Black should look for ways to exploit White's exposed king and uncoordinated pieces.

notes.explains: Black played Nc6, attacking the queen and forcing it to move. White's queen is active but Black's pieces are developing.
notes.teaches: Develop with tempo when possible; attacking the opponent's queen gains time.
notes.plans: Black should continue developing, targeting White's king and open files.

notes.explains: Black has developed the bishop to f5, eyeing the queenside. White's queen is on e3, defending the d3 pawn.
notes.teaches: Piece activity and coordination matter more than material in dynamic positions.
notes.plans: Black can consider ...Qe7+ to force White's king to move, or ...d5 to open lines.

notes.explains: Black gave a check on e7, testing White's response. White can play Be3 or Qe4. Qe4 is strong, forcing queen trade and an equal endgame.
notes.teaches: When up material, trading queens can simplify to a winning endgame. A queen trade is especially safe when you are up a piece or more.
notes.plans: If White plays Qe4, Black should trade queens and play the endgame with an extra pawn and active pieces.

notes.explains: Black played Nc4, attacking the bishop on e3 and threatening to win the d3 pawn. White's king is still in the center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is uncastled, use that as a target. Activate your pieces and create threats.
notes.plans: Black should continue to pressure White's king and pawns, possibly with ...d5 or ...Qe5.

notes.explains: Black played d5, opening the bishop and threatening the queen. White castled, but Black has a strong initiative.
notes.teaches: Prioritize development and activity over material. A pawn push that opens lines for your pieces is often worth the temporary material loss.
notes.plans: Black should look for tactical blows like ...Ne5 forking queen and bishop, or ...Qe5 threatening mate.

notes.explains: Black played Ne5, forking the queen and bishop. White's queen must move, and Black wins a piece.
notes.teaches: Forks are powerful; always look for them when pieces are undefended or loosely placed.
notes.plans: Black should win the piece and then simplify to a winning endgame.

notes.explains: Black captured the bishop on g4, winning a piece. White's queen is active but Black is up material.
notes.teaches: When you are up material, the simplest path to victory is often to trade pieces and enter an endgame.
notes.plans: Black should trade queens and then use the extra piece to win the endgame.

notes.explains: Black played Qe5, threatening mate and forcing White to weaken the kingside. Black is up a piece and has an open h-file.
notes.teaches: Use threats to induce weaknesses. You don't need a pawn storm when you already have an open file for your rook.
notes.plans: Black should bring the rook to the h-file and deliver mate or win more material.

notes.explains: Black played Re4, threatening to trade rooks and then push the passed pawn. White's knight is passive.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, rook activity is paramount. Trading rooks can simplify to a won pawn endgame.
notes.plans: Black should trade rooks, then push the c-pawn to create a passed pawn, using the king to support it.

notes.explains: Black played Rc4, attacking the c-pawn and preparing to push the passed pawn. White's knight is tied down.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, coordinate your pieces to support the passed pawn. Use your rook to attack enemy pawns.
notes.plans: Black should push the c-pawn, using the rook to protect it and the king to support.

notes.explains: Black captured the c3 pawn, now having a rook and two pawns for a knight. The passed pawn on c4 is ready to advance.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, convert by creating passed pawns and using your king actively.
notes.plans: Black should push the c-pawn, using the rook to shield the king from checks.

notes.explains: Black played Rc2, attacking the knight on d2 and threatening to win it. White's pieces are uncoordinated.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, target the opponent's weakest piece. Use your rook to attack and restrict.
notes.plans: Black should win the knight or force a favorable trade, then promote the passed pawn.

notes.explains: Black captured the knight on d2, now having a rook and two pawns vs rook. The win is straightforward.
notes.teaches: Once you have a decisive material advantage, simplify to a basic endgame and use standard techniques to win.
notes.plans: Black should push the passed pawn, using the rook to block checks, and promote.

notes.explains: Black played c5, creating a passed pawn. White's king is far away, and Black's king can support the pawn.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, a passed pawn supported by the king is a decisive advantage. Push it and use the rook to block checks.
notes.plans: Black should advance the c-pawn, using the rook to shield the king from checks, and promote.

notes.explains: After e3 d5, Black chooses d5 over e5 to avoid a reversed French where White gains a tempo. The setup with c6 and Bd6 reinforces the center and prepares a flexible development.
notes.teaches: Against offbeat first moves, focus on sound central control and flexible development rather than overreacting. A solid center with c6 and Bd6 is a reliable setup.
notes.plans: Black aims to complete development, castle, and later expand on the queenside with a5, while keeping the bishop on c8 for potential activation.

notes.explains: Black avoids the immediate e4 push because it leads to messy complications. Instead, Qd7 simply attacks the weak f5 pawn, which is hard to defend. White's king is uncastled, and the pawn on f5 is a permanent weakness.
notes.teaches: When a direct tactical approach is unclear, look for simple, concrete moves that target opponent's weaknesses. Attacking an undefended pawn can be more effective than forcing complications.
notes.plans: After Qd7, Black will capture the f5 pawn, then target the d3 pawn. The bishop on d6 and knight on f4 support a future e4 break, opening lines against White's king.

notes.explains: After White plays Bb2, Black plays e4, opening lines and trapping the bishop on b2 because the e2 square is defended twice. White is forced to give up the bishop for insufficient compensation.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is poorly placed, a pawn break can trap it. Always check if the opponent's pieces have safe retreat squares before committing to a plan.
notes.plans: Black wins the bishop and then converts the extra material. The open e-file and active pieces ensure a decisive attack.

notes.explains: After winning material, Black simplifies to a winning endgame. The extra pawn and active king ensure victory. White's pawns are weak and Black's king can penetrate.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, simplify to a clearly winning endgame. Keep queens on if the opponent's king is exposed; trade if the endgame is technically winning.
notes.plans: Black will advance the passed e-pawn and use the king to support it, while White's scattered pawns are easy targets.

notes.explains: White plays b3 (the Keres or Nimzowitsch variation) to fianchetto the bishop. Black can counter by developing Nc6 and then playing e5, shutting down the bishop's diagonal. This weakens d5 but is worth it because White's bishop becomes passive.
notes.teaches: When your opponent fianchettos early, consider blocking the bishop's diagonal with a pawn advance like e5, even if it creates a weakness. The trade-off is often favorable if the bishop is neutralized.
notes.plans: After e5, Black can complete development with Nf6, Bb7, or use the 'Batmanic' setup: fianchetto the kingside bishop and bring the knight to e7 to support f5 later.

notes.explains: After …h6, Black's move is a waste of time that creates a hook on g6. White can exploit this with g4, opening the g-file and threatening to push further to g5, disrupting Black's kingside development.
notes.teaches: When your opponent wastes a tempo with a weakening pawn move like h6, you should immediately look for ways to punish it by opening lines or creating threats on that side of the board.
notes.plans: Play g4 to open the g-file, then follow up with Qf3 and Rg1 to build an attack against Black's king.

notes.explains: After …c5, Black weakens the b5 square. White exploits this by playing Nb5, threatening Nc7. The knight on b5 also frees the c-pawn, allowing White to later challenge the center with c4.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a pawn move that weakens a square, you should immediately look to occupy that square with a knight. Additionally, moving the knight from c3 allows you to use the c-pawn to contest the center, a key idea in d4 openings.
notes.plans: Play Nb5, then follow up with Bd6 to attack the rook and force it to f7, where it blocks Black's coordination. Then consider c4 to challenge Black's center.

notes.explains: After exf4, a common mistake is to play d4 immediately, which allows Qh4+ and forces the king to move. Instead, develop the knight to f3 first to prevent that check.
notes.teaches: In the Vienna, don't play d4 before Nf3 because it opens the door to Qh4+. Always prioritize preventing that check.
notes.plans: Play Nf3, then develop naturally.

notes.explains: After castling, e5 is effective. If Black plays d5, White can simply take on f6 and then on g7, ruining Black's pawn structure. The key difference from earlier is that White's king is safe.
notes.teaches: A move that was premature earlier can become strong once the king is secure. Compare positions before committing.
notes.plans: Take on f6, then g7, then target the f4 pawn.

notes.explains: Black's king is on g7 with a ruined pawn structure. White is down a pawn but has overwhelming compensation: Black's king is exposed and his pieces are passive.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid to sacrifice a pawn for long-term pressure when the opponent's king is vulnerable and your pieces are active.
notes.plans: Develop the rook to e1, then play d4 and target the f4 pawn. Black's king will remain weak.

notes.explains: If Black plays Ng4 instead of d5, White can play h3, and after Nh7, Nd5 forks the bishop and the f4 pawn. This is a good example of how a move that was previously dismissed (Nd5) becomes ideal when circumstances change.
notes.teaches: Don't permanently discard a move just because it was bad in one position. Re-evaluate as the position evolves.
notes.plans: Play Nd5, forking bishop and pawn, then win back the pawn with an attack.

notes.explains: After Nd5, Black gives a check on c5. White can simply block with d4, gaining time and central space. Black's pieces are pushed to the side, and White has a crushing position.
notes.teaches: When you have a fork or a threat, look for ways to improve your position with tempo. Blocking a check with a pawn can be very powerful.
notes.plans: Play d4, then take on f4 and continue the attack.

notes.explains: White plays Kh1 to eliminate the pin on the d4 pawn and avoid any back-rank issues. It's a patient, prophylactic move that keeps all advantages without forcing anything.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the best move is a quiet waiting move that removes your opponent's counterplay. Don't feel obliged to play the most aggressive move every time.
notes.plans: After Kh1, White can take on f4 and then build up pressure with moves like Rf3 or Qd3.

notes.explains: White takes the f4 pawn, restoring material equality. Black's king is still exposed, and White's pieces are centralized.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and a weak enemy king, simple recaptures can maintain pressure without needing sacrifices.
notes.plans: Continue with moves like Nxb6, then axb6, then d5 to open the center.

notes.explains: Black plays dxe5, and White recaptures with the knight, centralizing it beautifully. The knight on e5 is a powerful outpost, eyeing f7 and g6.
notes.teaches: Centralize your knights; they become extremely dangerous when they can't be easily chased away.
notes.plans: Follow up with Nxb6, then axb6, then d5 to open lines against the black king.

notes.explains: White plays d5, striking in the center and opening lines. Black's king is exposed, and White's pieces are perfectly coordinated for an attack.
notes.teaches: When you have a development lead and the opponent's king is weak, open the center with pawn breaks to maximize your attacking chances.
notes.plans: After d5, White threatens Bxh6 and other tactical blows. The attack is overwhelming.

notes.explains: White plays Bxh6, sacrificing a bishop to open the h-file. Black's king is now extremely vulnerable, and White's pieces swarm around it.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and your pieces are well-placed, look for sacrifices that open lines. Simple tactics like this can be decisive.
notes.plans: After gxh6, play d6, threatening Qd3 and mate threats. The attack is unstoppable.

notes.explains: White plays d6, threatening Qd3 and keeping the knight alive. This is a classic example of checking both move orders: d6 first is better than Nxg6 because it maintains more threats.
notes.teaches: When you have a sequence of two moves, always check both orders. One may be significantly stronger.
notes.plans: After d6, Black's best is Qf6, but White can then play Bf4 or other consolidating moves, keeping the extra pawn and attack.

notes.explains: White plays Bf4, consolidating and keeping the extra pawn. The attack is still strong, and Black's king is permanently weak.
notes.teaches: After a successful sacrifice, don't rush. Consolidate your material advantage while maintaining pressure.
notes.plans: White can follow up with Qd2, Rf3, or other moves to increase the pressure. The position is winning.

notes.explains: White plays Rf1+, setting up a discovered check. The king is forced to move, and White can then capture the rook on a8 or deliver mate.
notes.teaches: In positions with a discovered check, don't rush to move the checking piece. First bring in reinforcements to make the threat even stronger.
notes.plans: After Kf7, White can play Rxf7+ or Rf8+ with mate threats.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with R1f7#, a classic double-check mate. The rook on f8 delivers check, and the rook on f1 covers the escape square.
notes.teaches: Always look for the most forceful continuation. When you see a good move, look for a better one—here, mate is better than capturing the rook on a8.

notes.explains: Black captures the rook on h1, winning a rook for a pawn. White's king is exposed and Black has a decisive material advantage.
notes.teaches: When converting a material advantage, keep your pieces active and your opponent's king unsafe. Avoid unnecessary risks.
notes.plans: Black will evacuate the queen to a safe square, then continue attacking with the remaining pieces while White's king is stuck in the center.

notes.explains: In the Slav, after d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 dxc4 a4, White stops b5. Black should not cling to the pawn but develop freely.
notes.teaches: Don't waste moves defending a gambit pawn; instead, develop pieces to active squares.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to f5, outside the pawn chain, and prepare natural development.

notes.explains: After a4, the bishop belongs on f5, exploiting the weakness created by f4 (if White played f4).
notes.teaches: Identify weaknesses created by opponent's moves and place pieces to exploit them.

notes.explains: When White plays Nh4 to trade the bishop on f5, leaving the bishop there is better than retreating to g6. After Bxf5 exf5, Black gets a pawn on f5 that controls e4 and creates a kingside pawn mass.
notes.teaches: Accept doubled pawns if they bring positional gains like central control and pawn chains.
notes.plans: Play g6 to defend f5, then continue development.

notes.explains: After White plays a4, Black should play a5 to prevent White from pushing a5 and to cement the bishop on an outpost.
notes.teaches: Prevent opponent's pawn breaks that would create weaknesses in your structure.

notes.explains: With the bishop on an outpost and White's bishop locked behind pawns, Black's pieces are more active. Opening the center with c5 favors Black.
notes.teaches: When your pieces are more active, open the position to exploit that activity.
notes.plans: Play c5, then bring rook to c8 anticipating the file opening.

notes.explains: Black improves the queen to d5, increasing pressure on the center and preparing tactics.
notes.teaches: Make marginal improvements to your pieces; centralize the queen when safe.
notes.plans: Continue pressure on d4, consider g6 to secure back rank.

notes.explains: After White plays a5, the knight on b5 becomes undefended and the queen on d3 is vulnerable. Black exploits this with c4, attacking the knight and queen simultaneously.
notes.teaches: Look for undefended pieces and vulnerable queens to create double attacks.
notes.plans: Play c4, then capture the knight if White doesn't defend properly.

notes.explains: After winning a pawn, Black should not grab the pawn immediately but find the best intermediate move. Here, taking on a6 is better than taking on f2 because it avoids tripled pawns.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, look for the most accurate move, not the most obvious capture.
notes.plans: Take on a6, then consolidate and simplify.

notes.explains: With a passed pawn, Black wants to trade rooks to reach an endgame where the pawn is strongest.
notes.teaches: In endgames, simplify by trading pieces to make passed pawns more powerful.
notes.plans: Play b5 to chase the rook, then queen b6 and rook a7 to trade the second pair of rooks.

notes.explains: Instead of promoting immediately with c2, Black first takes on f2 to bring the queen back to f6, preventing counterplay and perpetual check.
notes.teaches: Be careful when promoting; ensure your king is safe and opponent has no perpetual check.
notes.plans: Play g4, then c2, promoting the pawn.

notes.explains: The semi-Slav (e6) blocks the bishop on c8, leading to complex lines. The Slav with Bf5 is simpler and solid.
notes.teaches: Choose openings that suit your style; the Slav offers solid development without early complications.

notes.explains: The bishop on b4 (or similar outpost) should not be traded for a less active bishop, as it upholds weaknesses behind it (pawns on a5 and c5).
notes.teaches: Don't trade an active piece for a passive one; outposts protect pawn weaknesses.
notes.plans: Keep the bishop, pressure d4 with c5.

notes.explains: After Nxe4, Black should not play Bf5 because of Nh4 attacking the bishop and the pawn chain. Instead, play f5 to defend the knight with a pawn, following the Pillsbury idea.
notes.teaches: Pawns are the best defenders of pieces; use them to hold a strong outpost.
notes.plans: Castle, then look for tactics like e5 to open lines.

notes.explains: With the knight on e4 defended by f5, Black can play e5, exploiting the undefended knight on g5 (type two undefended piece) and the x-ray of the rook on f1.
notes.teaches: Identify type two undefended pieces (protected by only one piece) to create tactics.
notes.plans: Play e5, opening the center and attacking the knight.

notes.explains: If White plays f3, Black can take on d4 with devastating effect because the king is exposed.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their king's safety, open lines to exploit it.
notes.plans: Take on d4, then continue the attack.

notes.explains: Type one undefended piece: no defender. Type two: defended by exactly one piece (not a pawn). Awareness of these helps avoid blunders.
notes.teaches: Categorize undefended pieces to spot tactics and avoid mistakes.

notes.explains: f3 is a serious weakness; it weakens e3 and g3. Black retreats the bishop to f5 or d7, and may provoke g4.
notes.teaches: Provoke weaknesses like f3; the bishop can retreat and later be redeployed.
notes.plans: Retreat to f5, and if g4, drop back to g6.

notes.explains: Black avoids trading on g3 because it would open the e-file and remove support from d5. Instead, retreat the bishop to g6 to preserve the pawn chain.
notes.teaches: In pawn chains, avoid trades that weaken your structure or open lines for the opponent.
notes.plans: Keep the bishop on g6, complete development, and consider Qb6 later.

notes.explains: Qb6 is a typical Caro-Kann idea: it pressures d4, supports the knight, and eyes b2. It's often strong because the c-pawn is already pushed.
notes.teaches: Always consider Qb6 in the Caro-Kann; it's a multi-purpose queen move that can be played at the right moment.
notes.plans: Complete development first (Bd6 or Be7, O-O), then play Qb6.

notes.explains: f4 is a strong idea (Botvinnik-like) aiming to disrupt the pawn chain with f5. Black must react accurately.
notes.teaches: f4-f5 is a typical plan to break the Caro-Kann pawn chain; Black should not panic but find a prophylactic response.
notes.plans: Play h6 to see White's reply; if Bh4, consider prophylaxis like Nh5 or moving the bishop to h7 to take the sting out of f5.

notes.explains: By moving the bishop to h7, Black takes the sting out of f5: the bishop is no longer attacked, and f5 no longer threatens anything immediately.
notes.teaches: Type 2 prophylaxis: allow the threat but make it harmless by removing the target or creating counterplay.
notes.plans: After f5, Black can castle or play g5 to trap the knight on g3.

notes.explains: White traded bishop for knight, giving Black the two bishops. Black castles, now threatening d4. The immediate Bxd4? fails due to Qxd4 and the pin, but after O-O, Black is fine.
notes.teaches: Don't rush to capture; sometimes simple moves like castling maintain the pressure.
notes.plans: Play Qb6, pressuring d4 and b2.

notes.explains: Qb6 is perfectly timed: it attacks the bishop on d3, pressures d4, and threatens b2. White is forced to trade on c6, giving Black the two bishops and a great center.
notes.teaches: Qb6 is a powerful multi-purpose move in the Caro-Kann; it can force favorable trades and create queenside pressure.
notes.plans: After Bxc6 bxc6, Black has the two bishops and can push e5 or play Rc8.

notes.explains: Black captures on b2, and if White plays Rb1, the queen is not trapped because the bishop on h7 guards b1. Even if Rb1 were possible, the queen can escape.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid to capture b2; the queen is often safe, and the material gain is worth it.
notes.plans: After Qxb2, consider Qb5 to offer a queen trade and open the c-file for the rook.

notes.explains: Qb5 is a strong follow-up: it offers a queen trade, aims at the knight on e2, and if the queen trades, the c-file opens for Rc8 attacking c3.
notes.teaches: Weaponize the queen trade: offer it to open lines or improve your piece activity.
notes.plans: If queen trades, play Rc8 and target the backward c3 pawn. Otherwise, keep the queen on b5 and look for tactics.

notes.explains: e5 opens the center for the two bishops and puts more pressure on White's position. White cannot play c3 because the c-pawn is gone.
notes.teaches: With two bishops, open the center to maximize their power.
notes.plans: Continue with Rc8, Bg5, and target the knight on e2.

notes.explains: Bg5 restricts the knight on e2 and threatens to win it. The idea is to dislodge the rook from e1, e.g., by Bf2 or Bc2, winning the knight.
notes.teaches: When a piece is defended by another, look for ways to dislodge the defender (e.g., bishop check on b3 or f2).
notes.plans: Play Bf2 after the rook moves, winning the knight.

notes.explains: White collapses with Nh5, leaving the knight on e2 hanging. Black takes it first, then the rook, with a back-rank mate threat.
notes.teaches: In time pressure, choose the most clinical move; taking the knight first removes all counterplay.
notes.plans: Capture the knight on e2, then the rook on e1, and enjoy a winning material advantage.

notes.explains: After Bg5, the queen is trapped. Black loses a queen for a minor piece. The conversion is straightforward: avoid unnecessary trades, keep the initiative, and use the extra queen to win more material.
notes.teaches: When converting a material advantage, don't rush to simplify. Keep your active pieces and look for ways to increase pressure. Every move should have a purpose, like threatening to win more pieces.
notes.plans: Play h4 to threaten h5 and activate the rook. Consider sacrificing the exchange on h6 to open lines, then use the queen and rook to pick off Black's knights. Always check for undefended pieces after opponent's pawn moves.

notes.explains: White has a queen for a knight and a pawn. The game is winning. The key is to avoid stalemate traps and continue attacking. Playing h6 from the other side is a good way to win more material.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, stay alert for counterplay like stalemate. Keep attacking and use your material advantage to create threats. Don't give the opponent chances to escape.
notes.plans: Play h6 to attack the rook, then take on c4. If the opponent doesn't resign, continue simplifying while maintaining the material advantage. Always calculate before capturing to avoid blunders.

notes.explains: Black fianchettoes the bishop to g7, preparing to attack the d4 pawn and support the f5 break.
notes.teaches: Fianchettoing the bishop is a flexible way to develop while keeping pressure on the center.
notes.plans: After castling, Black will aim for Bg4 and f5 to open lines against White's king.

notes.explains: Black plays Bg4, threatening to trade for the knight on f3 and also eyeing the d4 pawn. White cannot take on d5 because Nxd4 wins a pawn.
notes.teaches: When calculating tactics, consider if the opponent's capture leaves a hanging piece or allows a counter-capture.
notes.plans: Black will continue with f5 to open the diagonal for the bishop on g7 and increase pressure on White's position.

notes.explains: Black achieves the ideal setup: fianchettoed bishop, Bg4, and the f5 break. The pawn on f5 opens the dark-squared bishop's diagonal and creates attacking chances.
notes.teaches: In IQP positions, the side with the pawn break should execute it when ready, as it activates the pieces and creates targets.
notes.plans: Black will continue to press on the kingside, possibly with moves like Qd7, Rf6, and doubling rooks.

notes.explains: Black plays Rf6, preparing to double rooks and also threatening Bxf3 followed by Rxh2+ if White takes on e6. The move also eyes the f-file.
notes.teaches: Rook lifts to the sixth rank can be powerful for both attack and defense, especially in closed positions.
notes.plans: Black will look for tactical opportunities, such as Bxf3 and then Rxh2+ if the king is exposed, or simply increase pressure.

notes.explains: Black retreats the rook to f8, maintaining pressure on the f-file and preparing to double rooks or play f4.
notes.teaches: Sometimes a retreat is necessary to regroup and prepare the next phase of the attack.
notes.plans: Black will aim to play f4, opening the diagonal for the bishop on g7 and creating threats against White's king.

notes.explains: Black plays f4, opening the diagonal for the bishop on g7 and creating a direct threat against White's king. The pawn on f4 also restricts White's pieces.
notes.teaches: A pawn break like f4 can open lines for the bishop and create mating threats, especially when the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: Black will continue with Qe6, threatening mate on h3, and possibly Rf6-f7 to increase pressure.

notes.explains: In a Caro-Kann structure, Black can flip the order of development: first Bg6, then Nf5, to avoid ...f5 breaking the center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent threatens to break your pawn center with f5, you can 'flip' the piece order: put the bishop on g6 first, then the knight on f5, so that ...f5 is no longer dangerous.
notes.plans: Develop with Bg6, then Nf5, castle, and prepare central breaks or kingside attack.

notes.explains: White plays Qf3 early, which is not a threat. Black should not rush to play d5 immediately, as that might justify the queen's placement. Instead, prepare d5 with e6.
notes.teaches: Don't play a central break just because you can. Sometimes it's better to prepare it with a move like e6, ensuring a more robust pawn center and avoiding giving the opponent's pieces activity.
notes.plans: Play e6, then d5, develop pieces, castle, and only then look for active play.

notes.explains: White's bishop on f3 is trapped by the pawn on g4 and has no retreat squares, while Black's bishop on c5 is safe and Black is up two pawns.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for tactical ways to win more material or force a decisive simplification. Always check for trapped pieces before playing a quiet move.
notes.plans: Play Bc5 to protect the pawn on c5 and maintain the trap on the bishop. White's bishop is lost, so the game is effectively over.

notes.explains: Black has doubled rooks on the e-file and is up two pawns. The queen trade would be favorable for Black, but there is a more concrete winning move: g4 traps the bishop on f3.
notes.teaches: Before playing a solid move like Qe6, always check for more forcing alternatives. Pattern recognition from similar positions can help you spot tactics like trapping a bishop.
notes.plans: Play g4 to trap the bishop on f3, winning a piece. After that, consolidate the extra material and simplify.

notes.explains: Black has developed the bishop to f5 with tempo, completing development. The pawn on c6 is defended by the bishop on f5, and Black's pieces are active.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, prioritize completing development with tempo. Use your extra material to create threats and force your opponent to defend.
notes.plans: Play Re7 to double rooks on the e-file and protect the pawn on c6. Then look for ways to trade queens or create further threats.

notes.explains: Black has played d6 and c6, creating a solid pawn chain that restricts White's bishop on f3. The bishop is 'biting on granite' and has no active role.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's bishop is poorly placed, you can restrict it with pawn moves. A bishop that is blocked by its own pawns or opponent's pawns becomes passive.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to f5 with tempo, then double rooks on the e-file. The bishop on f3 is harmless, so focus on activating your pieces.

notes.explains: After the exchange of rooks, Black has a queen and knight against White's queen and bishop. Black is up two pawns but needs to consolidate. The move d6 is natural, but first Black should consider more active options like Nc6 to pressure the knight on d4.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for moves that create threats and force your opponent to defend, rather than just solidifying. Active play can accelerate your consolidation.
notes.plans: Play Nc6 to attack the knight on d4. If White captures, Nxc3 hangs, so White must retreat or castle. Then Black can take on d4 and win a second pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays Nc6, attacking the knight on d4 and threatening to win it. White cannot capture because Nxc3 would hang the knight on c3. This forces White to deal with the threat, giving Black time to consolidate.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, use your pieces to create multiple threats. This forces your opponent to defend and gives you time to improve your position.
notes.plans: After White's response, capture on d4 with the knight or queen, winning a second pawn. Then consolidate by playing d6 and developing the remaining pieces.

notes.explains: Black has just played g5 to chase the bishop and win the pawn on e4. The decision to weaken the kingside with g5 is justified because White's king is uncastled and the knight on d4 is hanging, giving Black time to consolidate.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you must violate general principles (like king safety) when concrete calculation shows you can get away with it. Look for tactical justifications: hanging pieces, uncastled king, or other weaknesses that buy you time.
notes.plans: After Bg3, take on e4 with the knight. If White recaptures, take with the rook, attacking the knight on d4. White must defend, giving Black time to develop and consolidate.

notes.explains: Black plays Re8, putting pressure on the e4 pawn. White cannot easily defend it because the knight on f3 is pinned by the bishop on c5. This is a typical idea in the Stafford Gambit and similar openings.
notes.teaches: In open games, putting a rook on an open file against a weak pawn can create immediate pressure. If the pawn is defended only by a piece that can be pinned, the pressure can be very effective.
notes.plans: If White does not defend the pawn adequately, Black can capture on e4. If White plays f3 to defend, Black can strike in the center with d5, opening up the position.

notes.explains: Black castles early, which is ambitious and flexible. It prepares to put pressure on the e4 pawn with Re8, and also keeps the option of playing d5 in one move if White misplays.
notes.teaches: Castling early can be a flexible move that prepares multiple plans. It is often better than committing to a specific pawn structure like d6, as it keeps options open.
notes.plans: After castling, Black will play Re8 to pressure the e4 pawn. Depending on White's response, Black may play d5, d6, or Nc6.

notes.explains: Black plays Bc5, inviting White to take on e5 and transpose into the Stafford Gambit. White declines by playing d4, leading to a position similar to a Scotch but with the knight on c6 not yet developed.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, you can often invite your opponent to take a pawn by developing a piece with tempo. If they decline, you still get a good position with active pieces.
notes.plans: Black will continue development with O-O, Re8, and pressure on the e4 pawn. The bishop on c5 is well-placed, eyeing the kingside and the pawn on f2.

notes.explains: White plays d4, which is a solid move but leads to a position where Black has good development and pressure on the e4 pawn. The position is similar to a Scotch but with Black having the bishop on c5 already developed.
notes.teaches: In open games, central pawn advances like d4 are natural, but they can also give the opponent targets. Black's pieces are already active, so White must be careful not to fall behind in development.
notes.plans: Black will develop the bishop to c5, castle, and then put pressure on the e4 pawn with Re8. The knight on f3 is pinned, making the e4 pawn vulnerable.

notes.explains: Black recaptures with the d-pawn, keeping the center open and maintaining the option to develop the bishop to c5. This is a typical recapture in the Stafford Gambit.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which pawn structure gives you better piece activity. Here, dxc6 opens lines for the bishop and queen, while keeping the center fluid.
notes.plans: Black will play Bc5 next, putting pressure on the f2 pawn and preparing to castle. The open d-file can also be used later.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6, inviting the Stafford Gambit. This is a sharp line where Black sacrifices a pawn for quick development and attacking chances.
notes.teaches: The Stafford Gambit is a risky but practical weapon at the club level. Black gets active pieces and potential kingside attacks, but must know the tactical nuances.
notes.plans: If White takes on e5, Black will play Nc6, attacking the knight and regaining the pawn with interest. If White declines, Black can still play a normal game.

notes.explains: After bxc3, White has the two bishops, a solid pawn structure, and the e4 pawn is well defended. Black's bishop pair is gone, and White is already better.
notes.teaches: When your opponent gives up the bishop pair early, recapturing with the pawn can preserve structure and give you long-term advantages.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, then consider Bg5 to pressure f6 and threaten e5, exploiting Black's lack of development.

notes.explains: Bg5 threatens e5, which would win material because Black's knight on f6 is pinned and Black lacks defensive resources. If Black plays d6, e5 still wins. If Black moves the queen, Bxf6 leaves Black with a shattered kingside.
notes.teaches: A pin is especially dangerous when the pinned piece defends a key square (like e5) and the opponent cannot easily break the pin with a pawn or piece.
notes.plans: Play e5 as soon as possible to exploit the pin and win material.

notes.explains: After Bxf6 gxf6, White plays Qh5 threatening Qxh6#. Black's only defense is g6, but then Bxg6 wins. The g-file is open and Black's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's kingside pawns are compromised, look for immediate mating threats by bringing the queen to h5 or h6.
notes.plans: Deliver checkmate by opening lines to the king, not just winning material.

notes.explains: In the Marshall Attack, Black sacrifices a pawn for attacking chances. The key is to keep the queen on the kingside (here on h5) and prepare rook lifts. White's a4 is a standard Ruy Lopez idea to challenge Black's queenside.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, do not trade queens unless forced; keep the pressure on the king. The h-pawn push (g5) can be safe if it prevents White from blocking the attack.
notes.plans: Black should continue attacking with moves like f5 or g5 to open lines, while White consolidates with moves like a4 and Nf1.

notes.explains: In this sharp line, Black's attack is very dangerous. White must be precise. The move g5 is a typical idea to prevent White's rook from going to h4 and to keep the queen on h3. Pushing the h-pawn is often safer than it looks, especially if the h-file remains closed.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid to push pawns in front of your king if it serves the attack. The h-pawn push can be safe if the opponent's heavy pieces cannot access the h-file.
notes.plans: Black should continue to probe with queen and rooks, looking for sacrifices to open the king. White must defend accurately and try to consolidate.

notes.explains: Black's attack culminates in a forced checkmate. The key move was …Qh3+ forcing the king to f4, after which g5+ and Rg2+ drive the king to the queenside where it is mated. This shows the power of coordinated heavy pieces.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, look for forcing sequences that drive the enemy king into a mating net. Even if you are down material, a sustained attack can win.
notes.plans: Execute the mating sequence accurately; every check must be precise.

notes.explains: Against the Smith–Morra Gambit, declining the pawn with Nf6 is a solid alternative to accepting. It attacks e4 and forces White to either transpose to an Alapin Sicilian with e5 or play a less aggressive setup.
notes.teaches: Declining a gambit can steer the game into calmer waters, especially if you are not fully booked up on the sharp main lines.
notes.plans: If White plays e5, the knight retreats and the game transposes to an Alapin Sicilian. If White avoids e5, Black can safely capture the pawn later.

notes.explains: When White plays Bd3 instead of the typical Bc4, the gambit is less dangerous because the bishop is passive, staring at the d4 pawn. Black can take the pawn with a comfortable version of the gambit.
notes.teaches: In gambits, the placement of a single piece can drastically change the evaluation. A passive bishop reduces White's attacking potential.
notes.plans: Black should develop naturally with Nc6, d6, and fianchetto the dark-squared bishop. There is no urgency to play e5, which would weaken the d5 square.

notes.explains: With a4-a5 and Nc3, White chases the queen away from b5. If the queen goes to b4, Ra4 traps it. The queen must abandon b7, and White wins a pawn.
notes.teaches: Use pawn advances and piece pressure to exploit the queen's vulnerability as a defender. The queen is a poor defender because it can be chased away easily.
notes.plans: After Ra4, Black's queen goes to d6 or e7, and White takes on b7, gaining a pawn and a strong initiative.

notes.explains: After Bxb7, Black plays Rb8 attacking the bishop. Instead of retreating to f3, White should play Qf3, which defends the bishop and threatens Bc6+ and Bf4 with tempo.
notes.teaches: Always look for the most active continuation. Retreating is often passive; consider moves that maintain or increase the initiative, even if they leave a pawn undefended (c2 is unimportant).
notes.plans: Play Qf3, threatening Bf4 and Bc6+. Black's queen is overloaded, and White's development advantage is decisive.

notes.explains: Qf3 defends the bishop and prepares Bf4 and Bc6+. Black's queen is tied to defending b7, and White's pieces are more active.
notes.teaches: When you have a threat, consider if you can make a preparatory move to make the threat even stronger. Don't rush to play the threat immediately if a setup move increases its power.
notes.plans: Play Bf4 (or Rc4 first) to attack the queen, then Bc6+ winning material. Black's position collapses.

notes.explains: After Qxb7, Black's queen goes to d8. White can play Bf4, pinning the queen to the king on the d-file. This is stronger than immediate checks because it creates a lasting bind.
notes.teaches: When the king and queen are on the same file, look for pins and tactics. A pin can be more devastating than a check because it paralyzes the opponent.
notes.plans: Play Bf4, then consider Rc1 or Nd5 to increase pressure. Black's queen is trapped, and White will win material.

notes.explains: Rc1 prepares Nd5, threatening smothered mate on c7 and attacking the queen. The king and queen on the same file make this tactic possible.
notes.teaches: When you see a potential knight fork or smothered mate, look for a preparatory move like Rc1 to make the threat unstoppable. The threat is stronger than the execution.
notes.plans: Play Nd5, forcing Black to give up the queen or be mated. After exd5, Rxc7 is mate.

notes.explains: Qf3 is a good centralizing move. The queen supports the bishop and avoids being a target. It's better than keeping the queen on d5 where it blocks pieces.
notes.teaches: The queen is a supporting actress: from a safe, central square, it supports other pieces and creates threats without being exposed. Avoid placing the queen in the thick of things unless necessary.
notes.plans: Play Rd1 or Re1 to activate the rook, then push the queenside pawns. Black has no counterplay.

notes.explains: Black plays Rd8, attacking the bishop. White can defend with Bd5 or simply play d5, defending the bishop and threatening to advance. The simplest is to trade rooks or play Qf6, threatening mate on f7.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, simplify when possible. Don't keep tension unnecessarily; trade pieces to reduce counterplay.
notes.plans: Play Qf6, threatening Qxf7#. If Black takes the rook, Qxf7+ and Qf6#. Alternatively, take on c7 and then push pawns.

notes.explains: Qf6 threatens Qxf7#. Black must give up material to avoid mate. This is a clean finish.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for direct mating threats to end the game quickly. Don't allow the opponent to complicate.
notes.plans: After Qf6, if Black plays Rxd1+? then Qxf7+ and Qf6#. Otherwise, take on f7 and then on c7, winning easily.

notes.explains: Black blocks with gxf6, but White simply recaptures with Bxf6, and Black is helpless. White is up a queen and several pawns.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, don't overcomplicate. Simple captures and threats are often best.
notes.plans: Play Bxf6, then activate the rook and push pawns. The win is trivial.
