notes.explains: In the Advanced French, White closes the center with d5. This is a sound strategy but requires deep positional understanding. Black often attacks the base of the pawn chain (d4) with moves like c5 and Qb6.
notes.teaches: When the center is closed, the main plan is to attack the base of the pawn chain (the pawn that supports the chain). This is called undermining.
notes.plans: Black should play c5 to attack d4, and if White defends with c3, Black can continue with b5-b4 to undermine further.

notes.explains: This is the traditional main line of the Alapin. White has an isolated queen pawn (IQP) but active pieces and the bishop pair. Black has castled and the position is balanced.
notes.teaches: In IQP structures, the side with the pawn should seek dynamic play and avoid piece trades, while the opponent should aim to blockade and trade down.
notes.plans: White can consider Qg4 to pressure g7, or Rd1 to support d4. The key is to maintain tension and avoid premature exchanges.

notes.explains: Black brings the queen out early after …d5, which allows White to develop with tempo by attacking the queen.
notes.teaches: Avoid bringing the queen out too early in the opening; it gives the opponent free development and a lead in development.
notes.plans: Continue developing naturally with d4, knights before bishops, and centralize pieces.

notes.explains: White avoids the standard c3 in the French Advance, playing Nf3 and Nc3 to accelerate development. The key is to maintain control over the e5 square, which is the central battleground.
notes.teaches: In the French, the e5 pawn is a double-edged sword: it gives White space but also creates a target. White's compensation for the pawn comes from piece activity and control of the e5 outpost.
notes.plans: Develop naturally with Bd3, castle, and then reinforce the e5 knight with moves like Re1, Bf4, and Ndf3. Avoid premature captures that relinquish control of e5.

notes.explains: A common mistake is playing Bb5 to pin the knight on c6. This pin is not dangerous because the knight is defended by a pawn, and Black can easily break it with a6 or Bd7.
notes.teaches: To assess a pin, check if the pinned piece is defended by a pawn and whether you can bring more attackers. A pin defended by a pawn is usually harmless.
notes.plans: Instead of Bb5, play Bd3, aiming at the kingside where Black will likely castle. This bishop is more useful for the attack.

notes.explains: When Black plays g4, White can consider capturing on c6 to open lines. After bxc6, White takes on d6 with the queen, not the knight, because the knight recapture would allow Black to play Ne5 and activate.
notes.teaches: In tactical sequences, choose the recapture that maintains pressure. Here, Qxd6 keeps the knight on e5 and threatens Qxd4, exploiting Black's weak pawn structure.
notes.plans: After Qxd6, White has a clear advantage. The plan is to target Black's weak pawns and use the active pieces to create threats.

notes.explains: After Qxd6, White should not rush to take on c4 with the rook. Instead, Qxd4 is better, forking the queen and pawn. If Black trades queens, the pawn structure is ruined.
notes.teaches: Always calculate one move deeper. A natural capture like Rxc4 might look good but can allow counterplay (c5 opening a diagonal). Look for moves that combine attack and defense.
notes.plans: Play Qxd4, and if Black recaptures, White wins a pawn. Then consolidate with Nb3, targeting the c5 pawn and preparing to win more material.

notes.explains: In a similar position, White considered Nxc6 allowing Qxf2+. This is not dangerous because after Kh1, the open f-file benefits White's attack. Black's king is exposed and White has threats like Qh5 and Rf1.
notes.teaches: Don't fear captures with check if they open lines for your attack. Calculate the resulting position: if your pieces are active and the opponent's king is vulnerable, the check may be harmless.
notes.plans: After Kh1, White threatens Qh5 and Rf1. Black's lack of development means the attack is decisive. This shows the power of initiative over material.

notes.explains: In a sharp Sicilian position, White played f5 to break Black's pawn chain. Even though it looks like a blunder (allowing Rxc8 and Bxc2+), White calculated further: Qe3, Kxa1, and then Bb5+ followed by Qh6#. The attack is worth more than the rook.
notes.teaches: When sacrificing material, calculate until the threats are exhausted. A sacrifice that opens the enemy king is often correct, even if it involves a check or capture of your piece.
notes.plans: After f5, if Black takes the rook, White's attack is unstoppable. The king on a1 is safe, and the bishops deliver mate. This illustrates the importance of deep calculation.

notes.explains: After queens are traded, the position is symmetrical and equal. White has an easier time castling short, while Black's king is stuck in the center.
notes.teaches: In queenless middlegames, pawn structure becomes more important because of the increased chance of transitioning to a pawn endgame.
notes.plans: Black should develop actively, aiming for ...Bg4 to pin the knight and avoid ...Nc6 due to Bb5 annoyance.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on h5 is vulnerable to harassment by ...Nd4, threatening to capture and ruin Black's structure. Keeping the bishop on the g4-d1 diagonal is crucial.
notes.teaches: When a piece is attacked, consider whether retreating to a square that maintains its activity is better than exchanging or moving to a passive square.
notes.plans: Black should play ...Bc8, allowing ...Nd7 and then redevelop the bishop. This is a damage control move that avoids immediate harassment.

notes.explains: After ...Bc8, Black's knight can develop to d7, and the bishop will later come out. White's g4 was a mistake, allowing Black to equalize.
notes.teaches: In queenless positions, you can take time to develop pieces without immediate threats, as long as you avoid creating weaknesses.
notes.plans: Black will play ...Nd7, ...Bd6, and eventually ...e6 to activate the bishop, neutralizing White's slight initiative.

notes.explains: In this rook vs. bishop and knight endgame, piece activity is everything. Black's pieces are more active, and White's rook is passive.
notes.teaches: When you have two minor pieces against a rook, activity decides the result. Use your pieces to create threats and trap the rook.
notes.plans: Black can trap the rook on h5 with ...Bf4, ...Bh6, and the king walking to g8. This is a brutal idea that wins material.

notes.explains: Black's king is active and the pawn on f6 is a passed pawn. White's knight on d4 is passive, tying down White's king.
notes.teaches: In knight endgames, fixing weaknesses with pawn moves (like ...a4) can create a target that the opponent cannot defend due to passive pieces.
notes.plans: Black's plan is to fix the a2 pawn with ...a4, then maneuver the knight to c3 to win the pawn and promote. White's passive pieces cannot prevent this.

notes.explains: Black's b5 is a mistake; it weakens the queenside without sufficient development. White should now open the center with e4, as Black's pieces are poorly placed.
notes.teaches: When your opponent neglects development and makes pawn moves, you should seize the center and open lines to exploit their lack of coordination.
notes.plans: Play e4, then castle, and later strike with d5 to open the center and target Black's weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black's Ng4 is a 'fishing pole' idea, threatening h2 if White plays h3. White should not play h3; instead, open the center with d5 to exploit Black's misplaced knight.
notes.teaches: When a knight leaves the center, it relinquishes control of central squares. Strike immediately with a pawn break to open lines and activate your pieces.
notes.plans: Play d5, open the e-file, and target the weak b5 pawn. Avoid h3 as it plays into Black's trap.

notes.explains: After d5, Black plays e5, which allows White to take on e5 and win a pawn. White's bishop on b2 becomes active after the pawn trade.
notes.teaches: In hypermodern setups, the fianchettoed bishop gains power once the central pawns are traded or advanced. The pawn on d4 is temporary; its exchange opens lines for the bishop.
notes.plans: Take on e5, then play Bc6 to attack the rook and secure an outpost. Follow up with Nbd2-c4 targeting d6.

notes.explains: White plays Bc6, attacking the rook and placing the bishop on a strong outpost. This move also prepares to target the d6 pawn.
notes.teaches: Place pieces on outposts where they are safe and exert pressure. Anticipate your opponent's development (here, Black will fianchetto) and start your plan early.
notes.plans: Follow up with Nbd2-c4, targeting d6. If Black castles, consider h3 to trap the knight on g4.

notes.explains: White plays h3 only after Black's king has moved to f8 (or castled), ensuring the knight on g4 is trapped. This is a safe way to win the knight without allowing the fishing pole trap.
notes.teaches: Timing is crucial: only play h3 when the knight cannot be sacrificed for a dangerous attack. If the king is still on e8, h3 can be met with ...Nxf2 or other tricks.
notes.plans: After h3, Black's knight is lost. Continue to target d6 with Bc1-a3 or other means.

notes.explains: White plays g3 to chase the queen away, then Nxd6 wins a pawn and traps the queen. The knight on d6 is devastating because it attacks the queen and threatens discoveries.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is active, you can often drive it away with a pawn move like g3, then exploit the resulting weaknesses. A knight fork or discovery can win material.
notes.plans: After Nxd6, play Ba3 to threaten a discovered attack on the queen. The queen has only one safe square (Qb6), but then Nc4 or other moves win it.

notes.explains: White plays Ba3, threatening a discovered attack on the queen. Black's queen is trapped; after Qc3, Ne4 wins the queen.
notes.teaches: Use bishops to create discovered attacks against a trapped queen. Coordinate your pieces to maximize pressure on the opponent's most valuable piece.
notes.plans: Win the queen, then simplify and convert the material advantage. Push the d-pawn and centralize the queen.

notes.explains: Black blunders with Na7, leaving the pawn on b5 undefended. White can win a pawn, but there is a better move: d5! This piles pressure on the knight, opens the bishop, and wins the pawn in a much stronger version than immediate Nxb5.
notes.teaches: When an opponent's piece is undefended and under attack, look for a move that increases the pressure rather than capturing immediately. d5 here is more forcing and leaves Black's pieces passive.
notes.plans: Play d5, then after Black's response, capture on b5 with the bishop or knight, maintaining a dominant position.

notes.explains: After b4, White plays Qa4+ instead of capturing on a7. This check wins the pawn on b4 while attacking both queenside minor pieces. Black is forced to defend passively with Qb8, leaving a disastrous position.
notes.teaches: When a pawn is hanging, consider if a check or other forcing move can win it in a better way. Qa4+ wins the pawn while keeping the initiative.
notes.plans: After Qb8, prevent Black from castling by playing Nb5, trading knights to land the bishop on b5, pinning the knight on d7 and keeping the king in the center.

notes.explains: White plays Nb5, trading a good knight for Black's bad knight on a7. This seems to violate positional principles, but the concrete goal is to prevent Black from castling. After the trade, the bishop lands on b5, pinning the knight on d7 and trapping the king in the center.
notes.teaches: Concrete tactical goals can override general positional principles. Here, preventing castling is more important than preserving a good knight. Always prioritize the most forcing plan.
notes.plans: After Nb5 Nxb5 Bxb5, Black's king is stuck in the center. Follow up with Rc1, targeting the pinned knight and preparing a decisive attack.

notes.explains: Black plays Qc7, protecting the knight and preparing to castle. However, the queen becomes vulnerable. White has a crushing tactical sequence: Bb6! uses the pin on the d7 knight, forcing the queen back, and then Rc1 wins material.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is tied to defending a piece, look for a move that exploits the pin. Bb6 attacks the queen and the pinned knight simultaneously, winning at least a piece.
notes.plans: After Bb6 Qb8, capture on d7 with the bishop, forcing the king out, then deliver checkmate with Rc1+ and Rc7.

notes.explains: White captures on d7, transforming the pin into a direct attack on the king. After Kxd7, Rc1+ forces the king to the c-file, where it will be checkmated. This is the fastest path to victory.
notes.teaches: When you have a pin, consider capturing the pinned piece if it exposes the enemy king. This can transform a material advantage into a mating attack.
notes.plans: After Rc1+, Black's king is forced to c6 or c7, and White delivers mate with Rc7 or Bc6.

notes.explains: Black retreats the bishop to g6 instead of trading, keeping the tension and threatening f5 to trap the bishop. White must respond with Nh4 to avoid losing the bishop.
notes.teaches: Sometimes maintaining the tension is better than trading; a threat like f5 can force the opponent into awkward moves.
notes.plans: After Nh4 Nxg6 hxg6, Black gets the pawn cube structure and can continue with Nb6 or Nf8.

notes.explains: After hxg6, Black has the pawn cube (pawns on f6, g7, h7). This structure is very safe for the king and allows Black to push f5 and g5 for attack without weakening.
notes.teaches: The pawn cube is a resilient structure: you can advance two pawns for attack while the king remains secure behind the remaining pawn.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to b6 or f8, then consider Bc7 and Qd6 to create a battery on the h2-b8 diagonal.

notes.explains: Black plays Bc7 and Qd6, creating a battery on the h2-b8 diagonal. If White plays g3 to block, then Rxe3 wins a pawn because the f2-pawn is overloaded (defending g3 and the bishop).
notes.teaches: A queen-bishop battery can create tactical threats; look for overloaded pawns that defend multiple pieces.
notes.plans: After Rxe3, Black wins a pawn and maintains pressure. If White avoids g3, Black can continue with Nd5 or other improving moves.

notes.explains: Black executes the tactic Rxe3, exploiting the overloaded f2-pawn. White cannot recapture because f2 defends both g3 and the bishop.
notes.teaches: When a pawn defends two pieces, capturing one can overload it; always check for such tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: After Rxe3, Black is a pawn up with a strong attack. Continue with fxe3 Qxe3+ and then bring the rook to the e-file.

notes.explains: Black has won a pawn and now must be flexible in converting the advantage. Instead of playing Rxe3 again (which would allow Kg2), Black drops the rook back to e8 or e4 to prepare for White's counterplay like c5.
notes.teaches: When attacking, be flexible; don't force a continuation if the opponent can escape. Look for ways to consolidate and take more pawns.
notes.plans: If White plays c5, Black can take on d4 with the rook, ending up with two extra pawns in an endgame. Otherwise, improve piece placement.

notes.explains: Black plays Re4, preparing to meet c5 with Rxd4, winning another pawn. This is a precise way to convert the advantage.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, look for moves that secure material while preventing counterplay. Re4 both attacks d4 and prepares to capture if White pushes c5.
notes.plans: After c5 Rxd4, Black has two extra pawns and a winning endgame. If White doesn't play c5, Black can improve further.

notes.explains: White plays c5, and Black captures on d4 with the rook, winning a second pawn. The resulting endgame with two extra pawns is winning despite opposite-colored bishops.
notes.teaches: In opposite-colored bishop endgames, extra pawns are often decisive, especially if they are passed or can create multiple threats.
notes.plans: Black will have a material advantage and can aim to trade pieces or create passed pawns.

notes.explains: Black wins the queen for a rook and bishop, but more importantly, the pawn cube remains intact and Black has a winning endgame.
notes.teaches: Even after heavy exchanges, the pawn cube provides king safety and can be useful in the endgame for creating passed pawns.
notes.plans: Black will use the extra pawns and the active rook to win the endgame.

notes.explains: The pawn cube (pawns on f6, g7, h7) is a recurring theme. It allows Black to push pawns for attack without weakening the king, and even in endgames it can be useful.
notes.teaches: The pawn cube is a versatile structure: it provides king safety, supports pawn storms, and can be a asset in endgames due to its solidity.
notes.plans: In the middlegame, use the cube to launch an attack with f5 and g5. In the endgame, use the extra pawns to create passed pawns.

notes.explains: Black voluntarily gives up central space, allowing White to build a broad pawn center. In return, Black develops pieces harmoniously and prepares to strike at the center with ...e5 or ...c5. White's center can become overextended if he pushes pawns without proper piece coordination.
notes.teaches: Hypermodern openings cede the center early to undermine it later. The key is not to fear a big pawn center; if the opponent overextends, counterstrikes in the center can be devastating.
notes.plans: Black aims to play ...e5 or ...c5 to challenge White's center, often following up with piece pressure on the central pawns.

notes.explains: In the King's Indian, Black often fianchettoes the kingside bishop to g7, putting pressure on the dark squares and the center. White's classical approach (e.g., four pawns attack) can be met with precise counterplay.
notes.teaches: The fianchettoed bishop is a long-range piece that supports central breaks and can become a powerful attacking piece.
notes.plans: Black develops with ...g6, ...Bg7, ...d6, and ...Nf6, then chooses between ...e5 or ...c5 to challenge White's center.

notes.explains: Bc4 against the Sicilian is often ineffective because Black can play ...e6, blunting the bishop's diagonal. Black does not need to rush ...d5; simple development is fine.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, Bc4 is a common mistake. Black can neutralize it with ...e6, and the bishop becomes a target rather than an attacker.
notes.plans: Black develops naturally: ...Nc6, ...Nf6, ...Be7, ...O-O, and later ...d5 or ...b5 with queenside play.

notes.explains: A pawn on h3 near the enemy king is a 'hook' – a target for sacrifice. By sacrificing a piece on h3, you can open the h-file and expose the king.
notes.teaches: Look for 'hooks' – advanced pawns near the opponent's king. Sacrificing to open lines is a typical attacking idea.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Qd7 and then ...Bxh3, opening the h-file. The queen and rook join the attack along the h-file.

notes.explains: After e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3, the queen is attacked and must move. White gains time and development. Black's early queen sortie often leads to a development deficit.
notes.teaches: The Scandinavian Defense gives White a lead in development if Black is not careful. White should develop naturally and exploit Black's misplaced queen.
notes.plans: White plays d4, Nf3, Bc4/Bd3, O-O, and aims to build a strong center while Black catches up in development.

notes.explains: With a lead in development, White can sacrifice a pawn (d4) to open lines and expose Black's king. The queen on f3 pressures f7 and h7, and the bishop on d3 targets h7.
notes.teaches: A development lead justifies temporary pawn sacrifices to open the position. The attacker should seek direct threats against the king.
notes.plans: White plays Qf3, Bd3, and considers Qh3 to provoke weaknesses like ...g6, then opens the h-file with a pawn sacrifice.

notes.explains: White played Bg5, which is an unusual developing move. It weakens the b2 pawn because the bishop leaves the pawn chain. This makes the pawn break c5 attractive, as it keeps the diagonal open for Black's bishop and prepares Qb6, attacking the undefended b2 pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop moves outside the pawn chain, look for pawn breaks that open lines to exploit weaknesses, like the b2 pawn. The move c5 can be a better choice than e5 when it targets an undefended pawn.
notes.plans: Black can consider c5 followed by Qb6 to pressure b2. The immediate Qb6 is not necessary, but the threat is unpleasant for White.

notes.explains: White played d5, opening the long diagonal for Black's bishop. Black can exploit this by playing Ng4, threatening to take on g5. Since White's knight is not developed, the e4 square is available for Black's knight.
notes.teaches: When the opponent opens a diagonal, look to exploit it with piece play. An undeveloped knight leaves key squares like e4 unguarded, allowing tactical threats.
notes.plans: Black plays Ng4, threatening Nxg5. If White responds Bh4, Black can take on b2, winning a rook.

notes.explains: After White played Bh4, Black took on b2. Instead of immediately taking the rook, Black should consider improving the position first. The queen is the worst defender because it is easy to dislodge. Black can play Nc3, attacking the queen and forcing it away from defending the rook, then take the rook with a better position.
notes.teaches: Avoid automatic moves. When winning material, take time to see if a zwischenzug can improve your position. The queen is a poor defender because it can be chased away.
notes.plans: Play Nc3 first, attacking the queen. After the queen moves, take the rook on a1. This leads to a better version for Black than immediately taking the rook.

notes.explains: After taking the rook, Black's bishop on a1 is trapped. White wants to castle and attack it. Black must accept losing a minor piece. The correct choice is to give up the knight, not the bishop, because the bishop is the key attacking piece in the King's Indian. Black should sacrifice the knight for maximum compensation, preferably taking a central pawn (d5) rather than a flank pawn (a2).
notes.teaches: When you must lose a piece, keep the one that is more important for your attack. In the King's Indian, the dark-squared bishop is crucial. Sacrifice the knight for the best available pawn, preferably a central one.
notes.plans: Play Nxd5, taking the central pawn. Then play d6 to prevent White's d6 threat. Black is up the exchange and winning.

notes.explains: Black is up material but must continue developing. The knight can go to a6, heading for b4 or c7. Knights on the rim are often bad, but here a6 is a transit point to a better square. Don't be afraid of temporary awkwardness if the piece has a clear destination.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, don't rest on your laurels. Continue developing. A knight on the rim can be acceptable if it is passing through to a good square.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to a6, aiming for b4 or c7. Then develop the bishop to f5, pinning White's queen and rook.

notes.explains: Black has a permanent pin with the bishop on f5 pinning the queen to the rook. To exploit this, Black should attack the pinned knight. The move d5 is a typical way to attack the piece in front of the pin. However, White's bishop on c4 can pressure the d5 pawn. The prophylactic move c4 is better: if White takes on c4, Black plays Rc8, creating a second pin on the same file, and then d5 is safe.
notes.teaches: When you have a pin, attack the pinned piece with a pawn. But consider potential counterplay against the pawn; use prophylactic moves to remove defenders before executing the breakthrough.
notes.plans: Play c4 first. If Bxc4, then Rc8 pins the bishop to the queen. Then d5 attacks the knight, winning material.

notes.explains: White has a lead in development, but Black is up material with a solid center. A development advantage is not intrinsically winning; it must be converted into something tangible like a material advantage or a mating attack. Here, White cannot transform his lead because Black's material advantage and solid center neutralize it.
notes.teaches: Categorize advantages: material is intrinsic (gold), while development and space are transformative (cash). A lead in development must be converted to win; otherwise, it is meaningless against a material advantage.

notes.explains: Black immediately plays d5, challenging the center and exploiting the weakness created by f4.
notes.teaches: Against the Grand Prix Attack (f4), the immediate d5 is the critical response, undermining White's center.
notes.plans: After d5, Black aims to recapture with the knight (Nf6) to put pressure on the d5 pawn on favorable terms.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6 instead of recapturing with the queen, keeping the tension and preparing to gambit the pawn.
notes.teaches: Recapturing with the knight allows Black to play e6 next, forcing a trade and gaining compensation through control of d4 and pressure on White's weak f4 pawn.
notes.plans: Black will play e6, trade on d5, and then develop with active moves like Bc5 or Bd6, targeting the f4 pawn.

notes.explains: After the trades, White has a weak pawn on f4 and a bad bishop on f1, while Black has strong central control and active piece play.
notes.teaches: The f4 pawn becomes a long-term weakness; White's king safety is compromised because castling kingside doesn't fully solve the issues.
notes.plans: Black should develop actively, targeting the f4 pawn with moves like Bd6 and Qc7, piling up pressure.

notes.explains: White's a3 is a non-developing move that ignores the threats; Black can immediately punish by playing Bd6, attacking the f4 pawn.
notes.teaches: When the opponent wastes time, seize the initiative with active development and direct threats.
notes.plans: Play Bd6, then Qc7 to pile up on f4, and consider castling kingside to bring the rook into play.

notes.explains: Black captures the f4 pawn, opening the diagonal for the bishop and gaining material while maintaining pressure.
notes.teaches: Taking free pawns is good, but ensure it comes with additional benefits like opening lines or creating threats.
notes.plans: After capturing, castle kingside to activate the rook and prepare further attacks, possibly with Ng4 targeting h2.

notes.explains: Black castles kingside, x-raying the queen and reinforcing control over d4. The rook on d8 adds pressure.
notes.teaches: Castling kingside in such positions is aggressive because it brings the rook to the d-file and supports central dominance.
notes.plans: Follow up with Ng4, threatening Bxh2 and aiming for e3 to create mating threats.

notes.explains: Ng4 creates threats of Bxh2 and the knight can go to e3, intensifying the attack on White's king.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, look for knight maneuvers that create immediate threats and force weaknesses.
notes.plans: If White plays Bxf4, then Qd2, Black can play Nd4 to distract the knight on f3, followed by Be3+ and Qh2#.

notes.explains: White tries to trade queens with Qd2, but Black has a tactical refutation: Nd4, distracting the knight on f3.
notes.teaches: When the opponent offers a queen trade, consider if you can use it to create a decisive tactical blow.
notes.plans: Play Nd4; if Qxd4, then Nxe2+ wins the queen. If not, Be3+ forces checkmate.

notes.explains: Nd4 exploits the weak d4 square tactically: it distracts the knight on f3, allowing Be3+ and Qh2#.
notes.teaches: A weak square can be used not only for positional outposts but also for tactical decoys to remove defenders.
notes.plans: After Nd4, if Nxd4, then Be3+ forces checkmate. If Qxd4, then Nxe2+ wins the queen.

notes.explains: White's alternative g3 creates weaknesses on the kingside; Black can respond with h5-h4 to open lines.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens their kingside, consider a pawn storm to exploit the exposed king.
notes.plans: Play h5, then h4 to open the h-file and launch an attack.

notes.explains: a6 prepares b5, attacking the base of White's pawn chain (c4). This is a thematic plan against a pawn chain: undermine the base.
notes.teaches: When facing a pawn chain, attack its base to weaken the entire structure. Here b5 targets c4, the base of White's c3-d4-e5 chain.
notes.plans: After b5, Black will open lines and activate pieces, while White's center becomes vulnerable.

notes.explains: After the trade on b5, White no longer has a pawn chain. The d5 pawn becomes weak, and the a-file opens. Black can target the a2 pawn.
notes.teaches: After a pawn trade, reassess the new weaknesses. The open a-file and the weak d5 pawn are key targets.
notes.plans: Bring the rook to a8, move the knight from a5 to b7 to pressure a2, and double rooks on the queenside.

notes.explains: c4 is a strong move that targets the b3 pawn and opens the a-file. It also solves the problem of the passive knight on a5 by allowing it to capture on c4.
notes.teaches: When attacking the queenside, identify specific targets (like a2) and bring pieces to bear. c4 is a typical pawn break to open lines and activate pieces.
notes.plans: After c4, Black can capture with the knight, opening the a-file and threatening Rxb2.

notes.explains: The knight on c4 is powerful, eyeing d3 and f2. Black's pieces are all coordinated on the queenside, creating immense pressure.
notes.teaches: An attack on the queenside works like a kingside attack: bring pieces in, identify weaknesses, and pile up pressure. Here, the a2 pawn is a concrete target.
notes.plans: Continue pressure with moves like Nd3, threatening f2 and preparing to win material.

notes.explains: Sacrificing the knight on f4 is necessary to play c3, which wins material. The queen is overloaded, unable to defend both f4 and the rook.
notes.teaches: Transforming an advantage often requires sacrificing a well-placed piece for a greater goal. Always look for the best execution, not just the first capture.
notes.plans: After Nxf4, play c3, winning the knight on c3 or the rook on b1.

notes.explains: After Rxc1, Black wins a piece and the pawn on c3 is a passer. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: Don't rush; look for the most precise tactical sequence. Here, capturing on c1 sets up a fork and leaves Black up material.
notes.plans: Promote the c-pawn or simply convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: The game illustrates a Benko Gambit-style attack in the King's Indian. Black sacrifices a pawn on b5 to open lines and generate lasting queenside pressure.
notes.teaches: The Benko Gambit idea can arise from the King's Indian: sacrifice the b-pawn to open the a- and b-files, then activate pieces against the opponent's queenside weaknesses.
notes.plans: Typical follow-ups include Ba6, Qa5, and doubling rooks on the b-file.

notes.explains: After Qb6, if White plays d5, Black's knight goes to a5. This knight may look misplaced but is part of a plan to pressure c4 with b5.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, the knight on a5 is a common motif to support the b5 break. It's not a mistake if it serves a concrete plan.
notes.plans: Prepare b5 with a6, then open the queenside.

notes.explains: White's queen on d2 made it harder to defend against b5. A better setup might have been Qc2 and Rc1, or dropping the bishop back to e2 to discourage b5.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, White must be careful about queen placement. The queen on d2 can be vulnerable to tactics and does not help defend the queenside.
notes.plans: White should consider prophylactic moves like Be2 or Qc2 to hinder Black's b5 break.

notes.explains: After Rb1, White had the resource Qxd3, threatening mate on c8. Black must respond with Rxc1, distracting the rook from c8, and then capture the bishop on h6.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to counter-resources. Here, Qxd3 creates a mating threat, but Black has a precise defense that wins material.
notes.plans: Black's defense involves Rxc1 to remove the rook from the c-file, then capturing the bishop.

notes.explains: The knight sacrifice on b5 opens the position. After capturing on g7, White wins two pawns and has a winning attack.
notes.teaches: Sacrificing a knight to destroy the opponent's pawn structure and expose the king is a common tactical motif in open Sicilian positions.
notes.plans: White should keep queens on the board to maintain attacking chances, then double rooks on the d-file and look for checkmate.

notes.explains: White is two pawns up with a strong knight. The king is safe, and the passed pawns will decide.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, avoid unnecessary complications. Simplify if possible, but keep attacking chances if the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: Bring the rook to the d-file, create threats, and promote the passed pawn.

notes.explains: Black's setup with Nge7 and ...Nxd4 is standard, aiming to replace knights and castle kingside. The fianchetto of the bishop is not necessary; Be7 is fine.
notes.teaches: In the Taimanov Sicilian, Black often exchanges knights on d4 and develops naturally with Be7 and O-O. The fianchetto of the bishop is optional.
notes.plans: Black should aim for quick development and castling, then decide on queenside expansion.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Nbd7, allowing White to immediately push f4, entrenching the knight on e5. Black's position becomes difficult.
notes.teaches: When the Pillsbury knight is established, Black must undermine it immediately with ...c5 or ...g5, or risk being overrun.
notes.plans: White can now consider f5 to trap Black's bishop on e6, or castle queenside to prepare a direct attack.

notes.explains: White plays f5, attacking the bishop on e6. This wins a piece for two pawns, but also removes the powerful knight from e5.
notes.teaches: Sometimes tactical gains outweigh positional advantages; winning a piece for two pawns is often good in an open position.
notes.plans: After fxe6, recapture with the rook, then play d5 to gain tempo and open the center.

notes.explains: White castles queenside, deploying the rook quickly. Black has three pawns for the piece, but White's two bishops and open center give a strong initiative.
notes.teaches: When ahead a piece in an open position, castling queenside can be safe and activate the rook faster than kingside.
notes.plans: Use the bishops to control diagonals and open files, targeting Black's king.

notes.explains: White plays Rhe1 to chase the queen away, then Bf5 to attack the rook and put pressure on Black's knights. Controlling the e-file is key.
notes.teaches: In open positions with a material advantage, controlling open files and activating pieces is more important than defending pawns.
notes.plans: After Bf5, Black's pieces are tied up; White can aim to trade on e6 and dominate the e-file.

notes.explains: Black plays Rd6, which is a blunder because the rook becomes trapped after Bg3. The game ends quickly.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to loose pieces and potential traps; a trapped rook can decide the game immediately.
notes.plans: Play Bg3, winning the rook. If Black tries Qc5, respond with Nxb5 to trade queens and win a pawn.

notes.explains: White plays Nxb5, attacking the queen and threatening to trade queens while winning a pawn. This is the most clinical continuation.
notes.teaches: When winning, look for moves that simplify while maintaining a decisive advantage. Trading queens when up material is often good.
notes.plans: After Qxb5, Bxd6 wins a rook. Black resigns shortly.

notes.explains: Black's ...c5 challenges the knight on d4. White's knight retreats to f3, and Black develops naturally. The position is dynamically balanced.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, ...c5 is a typical pawn break to challenge White's center and open lines. Black should prioritize development and king safety before launching an attack.
notes.plans: Black can consider ...a5 to prevent b4, then ...Qb7 and ...Rfe8, preparing ...f5 or ...e4 to create kingside threats.

notes.explains: White's passed pawn on b7 is powerful, but Black's rook on b8 and bishop on c6 defend. White sacrifices a piece to break through, leading to a rook endgame where White has a pawn advantage.
notes.teaches: In endgames, a passed pawn can be worth a piece if it forces concessions. Calculation of forcing sequences is crucial to convert the advantage.
notes.plans: White should aim to activate the king and create a second passed pawn. Black must defend accurately and seek counterplay with the king.

notes.explains: Black has a strong knight on f4 and pressure on the c-file. White's king is on the queenside, and Black can consider ...b4 to open lines. The position is sharp with mutual chances.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, Black often attacks on the queenside with ...b5-b4, while White attacks on the kingside with g4-g5. Piece activity and pawn breaks are critical.
notes.plans: Black can play ...b4 to open the b-file and create threats against White's king. White should continue with h4 and Bh3, aiming for a kingside attack.

notes.explains: Black plays ...b4, opening the queenside. White's knight on d4 is strong, but Black's rooks are active. The position is double-edged.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, ...b4 is a typical pawn break to create weaknesses in White's queenside pawn structure. Black should follow up with ...a5-a4 to gain space.
notes.plans: Black can play ...a5 and ...a4, then ...Ra8-a6-b6 to pressure b2. White should counter with h4 and Bh3, aiming for a kingside attack.

notes.explains: After a series of exchanges, White has a pawn on b4 and Black has a rook on a4. White's king is active, and Black's pawn on b4 is weak. The endgame favors White due to the better pawn structure.
notes.teaches: In endgames, an active king and better pawn structure are often decisive. Black should have avoided the pawn weakness on b4.
notes.plans: White can play Kc4 to attack the b4 pawn, then create a passed pawn on the queenside. Black should try to activate the rook and create counterplay.

notes.explains: Black's Bb4+ pins the knight and threatens d5, but White's bishop on b2 eyes g7. Blocking with Nbd2 is natural but clogs the center; Kf1 is more aggressive, keeping the diagonal open.
notes.teaches: When deciding between blocking a check with a piece or moving the king, consider which option preserves your attacking potential. Here, Kf1 avoids blocking the bishop's diagonal and keeps the queen's mobility.
notes.plans: White aims to complete development and maintain pressure on g7, possibly with Qb3 or e5 later.

notes.explains: Black's f6 blunts the bishop but creates permanent weaknesses on the kingside, especially the diagonal a2-g8. The knight on g8 is undefended (type 2 undefended piece).
notes.teaches: Pawn moves that weaken the king's pawn shield are often irreversible. Exploit such weaknesses by targeting undefended pieces and building pressure along the weakened diagonals.
notes.plans: Play Qb3, attacking f7 and the undefended bishop on b4, forcing Black to respond and further disrupt his development.

notes.explains: After Qb3, Black trades bishop for knight with check, then White recaptures with the king. White's king is safe in the center because Black has no pieces developed to attack it. White now has a lead in development and pressure on the kingside.
notes.teaches: Moving the king early can be acceptable if the opponent cannot exploit it. Here, the king on d2 is safe and actually helps control key squares, while White's pieces are active.
notes.plans: White will castle kingside, then push e5 to open lines and exploit Black's weak f6 pawn.

notes.explains: White plays e5, opening the position. Black cannot capture the bishop on e5 because of the pin along the e-file (Re1 would skewer the queen). White's bishop on e5 is well-placed, but its job is done; it can now be redeployed.
notes.teaches: A piece that has fulfilled its purpose (here, preparing e5) can be repositioned to a more active square. Don't cling to a piece's current location if it can do more elsewhere.
notes.plans: Play Ba3, targeting f8 and preventing Black from castling, while preparing to bring the knight to d6 via c4.

notes.explains: Black plays b6, preparing to fianchetto the bishop and castle. White's knight wants to reach d6, but the bishop on c4 is in the way. White needs to move the bishop to a square that keeps pressure on the diagonal and clears c4 for the knight.
notes.teaches: When planning a piece maneuver, consider intermediate moves that improve your position. Here, Bd5 centralizes the bishop and keeps the diagonal, while allowing the knight to go to c4 and then d6.
notes.plans: Play Bd5, then Nc4, aiming for Nd6. If Black takes on e5, White recaptures with the bishop and supports the knight with Bxc5.

notes.explains: The knight reaches d6, a powerful outpost. Black cannot easily dislodge it. White's pieces are active, and Black's king is stuck in the center. The knight on d6 controls key squares and restricts Black's pieces.
notes.teaches: An outpost knight, especially one that cannot be attacked by pawns, is a huge asset. It restricts the opponent's pieces and often leads to a decisive advantage.
notes.plans: White will continue to pressure Black's position, possibly with Rfd1 to x-ray the king, and look for tactical blows like Bxc6 or discovered checks.

notes.explains: White plays Rfd1, x-raying the king on e8. This is a preparatory move: it sets up tactics like discovered checks or pins. The choice of rook matters: putting the f-rook on d1 leaves the a-rook free to go to c1 if the king moves to c7.
notes.teaches: When placing a rook on an open file, consider where the other rook will go. Anticipate the opponent's likely response and place your rooks accordingly to maximize their activity.
notes.plans: If Black takes on e5, White can recapture and then use the discovered check. If Black moves the king to c7, White can play Rac1 to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: Black moves the king to c7 to escape the x-ray. White responds with Rac1, now x-raying the king again. The queen on e7 is also under pressure. White's pieces are perfectly coordinated.
notes.teaches: X-ray attacks (aligning a piece with the opponent's king through another piece) are powerful. By placing rooks on d1 and c1, White creates multiple threats and keeps the king in the crosshairs.
notes.plans: White will look to open lines, e.g., by Bxc6 or by playing a discovered check. The immediate threat is Nb5+ or Nd6+? Actually, the knight is already on d6; White can consider moves like Bxc6 or Qb3 to increase pressure.

notes.explains: White plays Nb5+, forcing the king to the b-file. This clarifies the situation: the king cannot go back to d8 because of the rook on d1. The knight check also opens up possibilities for discovered attacks.
notes.teaches: A check can force the opponent's king to a worse square, especially when combined with x-ray threats. Always consider checks that restrict the king's options.
notes.plans: After the king moves to b8 or b7, White can play Bxc5, opening the b-file and threatening discovered check. The queen on e7 is x-rayed by the rook on c1, so Black must be careful.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the bishop on c5 to open the b-file and create a discovered check threat. Black captures, but now White's queen and rook are aligned against the king. The pawn on b6 is gone, so the b-file is open.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you need to sacrifice material to open lines for an attack. Here, the bishop sacrifice removes the b-pawn, allowing a devastating discovered check or a direct attack on the king.
notes.plans: White can now play a discovered check by moving the knight, e.g., Nd6+ or Nc7+. The queen on e7 is also under attack, so Black's position is critical.

notes.explains: Instead of immediately playing a discovered check, White plays Nd4, improving the knight and x-raying the queen on e7. This is a patient move that maintains the tension and avoids premature complications.
notes.teaches: When the immediate tactical blow doesn't work (e.g., the discovered check leads to a defense), it's often better to improve your pieces and keep the pressure. Potential energy can be more valuable than cashing in too early.
notes.plans: White threatens Bxc6, attacking the queen and threatening checkmate on c7. Black must respond, and White can then win the queen or deliver mate.

notes.explains: Black plays Re8, threatening checkmate on e1. White responds with h3, creating luft for the king and preventing back-rank mates. This is a necessary prophylactic move.
notes.teaches: Always be aware of back-rank threats. Creating luft (a pawn move to give the king an escape square) is often essential before launching a final attack.
notes.plans: After h3, White can continue the attack with Bxc6, winning the queen or delivering checkmate. Black's threats are neutralized.

notes.explains: White plays Bxc6, attacking the queen and threatening checkmate on c7. Black's queen is overloaded: it must defend c7 and cannot capture the bishop because of the x-ray from the rook on c1.
notes.teaches: An overloaded piece cannot defend two threats simultaneously. Here, the queen on e7 must defend c7 and cannot capture the bishop on c6 because that would lose the queen to the rook on c1.
notes.plans: After Bxc6, Black's queen is lost. White will capture the queen and then convert the material advantage.

notes.explains: White wins the queen for a rook and bishop, leaving Black with a rook and two pieces for the queen. However, White's remaining pieces are active, and Black's king is exposed. White can continue the attack.
notes.teaches: Even after winning the queen, the game isn't over. Keep attacking the exposed king and use your queen's mobility to pick off pawns and create threats.
notes.plans: White will play Qg3 or g6, threatening checkmate and forcing Black to give up more material. The king is safe on h2, and White's pawns are solid.

notes.explains: After Bb5+ and Bxc6, Black's bishop is pinned and the queen's contact with d6 is blocked, allowing Qxd6 to win a pawn.
notes.teaches: Intermediate moves like Bb5+ can improve the effectiveness of a capture by creating a pin or blocking defenders.
notes.plans: After Qxd6, Black may try to counter with Qa5+; White can block with Nc3, maintaining the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Black's queen move Qb6 loses another pawn and leaves his king exposed. White is now two pawns up with a dominating position.
notes.teaches: When you are underdeveloped, avoid trading queens if it leaves your king vulnerable or drops more pawns.
notes.plans: White can continue to develop and target Black's exposed king.

notes.explains: Black's king has been forced to f6, a very exposed square. White has many attacking options.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, look for checks and forcing moves, but also consider non-checking moves that bring more pieces into the attack.
notes.plans: e5+ is a natural check, but also consider Ng5+ or even O-O to bring the rook into the attack without rushing.

notes.explains: After e5+ Kxe5, Ng5+ forces fxg5, and then Qg4 threatens mate. If Black avoids the knight capture, Nc4 forks king and queen.
notes.teaches: When you can't find a forced mate, look for forks like Nc4 that win material and simplify the win.
notes.plans: If Black plays Kf6 instead of taking the knight, Nc4 wins the queen. Otherwise, Qg4 leads to a quick mate.

notes.explains: Castling is a powerful non-checking move that brings the rook into the attack. The king is so exposed that White doesn't need to rush.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is in the open, a quiet move that brings another piece into the attack can be more effective than a direct check.
notes.plans: After O-O, White threatens Re1+ and Qf3+ etc. The rook on e1 will be decisive.

notes.explains: Black blunts the bishop with e6 and develops solidly. White's Ng5 threatens nothing and Black can simply play h6.
notes.teaches: When your opponent attacks prematurely, a simple developing move that defends the threat is often best.
notes.plans: Black can play h6 to drive the knight back, then continue development. The position is comfortable for Black.

notes.explains: After the queen trade, Black's king is in the center but safe for now. White has no immediate attack.
notes.teaches: Trading queens can relieve pressure, but be aware of king safety. Here Black's king is not in danger.
notes.plans: Black can continue development with Bd6, Nge7, and eventually castle manually. The doubled pawns on f6 are not a weakness.

notes.explains: White plays Bxf7, but Black can simply recapture with the king. White has no follow-up because his pieces are undeveloped.
notes.teaches: A sacrifice without sufficient development is usually unsound. Make sure you have enough pieces in the attack before sacrificing.
notes.plans: Black recaptures with the king and is fine. White's attack fizzles out.

notes.explains: Black recaptures with the king and is safe. White has no compensation for the sacrificed bishop.
notes.teaches: When your opponent sacrifices, don't panic. Accept if you can defend, and trust your development.
notes.plans: Black is up a piece and can consolidate. The king on f7 is not in danger.

notes.explains: White has a clamp on d5, giving superior central control. Black finds it hard to achieve the d5 pawn break.
notes.teaches: Doubled pawns are not always a weakness; the resulting central clamp and control of key squares can be more important.
notes.plans: White prepares either f4 or d4 pawn breaks, using the pin on the knight to hinder Black's development.

notes.explains: White plays d4 instead of f4 because f4 would allow exf4 and g5 forking the knight and bishop. d4 challenges the center without that risk.
notes.teaches: When choosing between pawn breaks, consider tactical refutations like forks. Compare lines to detect subtle differences.
notes.plans: After d4, White aims to open the center and activate pieces, with ideas like Qd3 connecting rooks and preparing Rfd1.

notes.explains: Black plays b5 to start queenside pressure, threatening b4 and Ba6. White must decide how to respond.
notes.teaches: When facing queenside expansion, consider prophylactic moves that prevent Black's ideas (like a6 supporting b5) before committing to your own plan.
notes.plans: White rejects Rfd1 due to the threat of a6, c5, c4 trapping the bishop (Noah's Ark trap). Instead, White plays f4 to strike in the center.

notes.explains: White plays Na4 to prevent Qb6 and Ba6, which would create nasty pins. The knight on the rim is a concrete necessity, not a general principle violation.
notes.teaches: Concrete calculation overrides general principles. Sometimes a move that looks bad (knight on the rim) is forced to prevent stronger threats.
notes.plans: White plans to advance e5, opening the center and using the knight on a4 to later capture on c5 if it becomes weak.

notes.explains: After a chaotic sequence, White emerges with two knights for a rook and a pawn, but the knight on a4 is trapped. White's compensation includes the passed e7 pawn, a pawn for the exchange, and Black's pieces clustered on the queenside.
notes.teaches: When down material, look for dynamic compensation: a strong passed pawn, piece activity, and opponent's coordination issues.
notes.plans: White centralizes the queen to d5, forcing Black's queen to a passive square, and prepares a rook lift to g3 to attack the king.

notes.explains: White sacrifices the rook with Rxg7+ to expose the king. After Kxg7, Qf6+ forces Kg8, then Nf5 threatens mate on g7. Black must take on f5, but White has a beautiful follow-up.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, follow the principle of checks, threats, and captures. Look for sacrifices that open the king and create mating nets.
notes.plans: After Nf5, if Black takes, White plays Qg4+ and Bf6, forcing mate. If Black plays g6, White sacrifices the knight on e6 to open the f-file, then delivers mate with Qg7.

notes.explains: After Nf3, Black fianchettoes the bishop (g6, Bg7) to clamp down on d4. This is a classic setup against the Closed Sicilian.
notes.teaches: Fianchettoing the bishop in the Sicilian gives multiple pieces control over the d4 square, a key outpost.
notes.plans: Complete development with d6, Nf6, and castle kingside, aiming for an accelerated dragon setup.

notes.explains: White's Qe2 and g4 are premature. Black is already castled with coordinated pieces, while White's king is still in the center and his pieces are uncoordinated. The g4 push creates weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has lagged in development and created weaknesses, look for immediate tactical blows. A pawn storm without proper preparation can backfire.
notes.plans: Consider Nxg4 sacrifice to open lines, or play Rb8 followed by b5-b4 to dislodge the knight and open the b-file.

notes.explains: White played Qd1 instead of accepting the queen sacrifice for three pieces. This is a typical mistake: overvaluing the queen and underestimating the power of three minor pieces.
notes.teaches: Three minor pieces can be stronger than a queen, especially when the opponent's king is exposed and the pieces coordinate well. Evaluate imbalances concretely, not by rote.
notes.plans: Capture the rook with Bxf1, keeping the pieces on dominant squares and heading for a quick checkmate.

notes.explains: In the resulting position, Black can push f5 to open the f-file for the rook. White has no counterplay on the kingside, so Black's king is safe.
notes.teaches: When attacking, involve all available pieces. Opening a file for a rook can be decisive. Don't fear weakening your own king if the opponent has no attacking pieces.
notes.plans: Play f5, opening the f-file, then bring the queen to h4 via e5, and deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: White's best response to the Closed Sicilian is g3 and Bg2, transposing to a standard setup. Instead, Nf3 and Bd2 are too passive.
notes.teaches: In the Closed Sicilian, fianchettoing the king's bishop is essential for a tenable position. Passive bishop development (like Bd2) leaves White without counterplay.
notes.plans: Black should continue developing with d6, Nf6, and castle kingside, aiming for a typical Dragon setup.

notes.explains: After White castles long, Black's bishop on g7 aims at b2. The immediate plan is to open the b-file with b5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent castles into your fianchettoed bishop, a pawn storm on that side (b5-b4) can open lines for a direct attack on the king.
notes.plans: Play b5 immediately. If White takes, play Rb8 and then b4 to dislodge the knight. If White doesn't take, push b4 anyway, then follow with Qa5 or Qb6.

notes.explains: If White responds to the pawn storm with b3, the attack shifts to exploiting the weakened dark squares (like a3 and b4).
notes.teaches: Pawn storms are not rigid; you must adapt to the opponent's defensive moves. When a pawn advance creates weaknesses, redirect your attack to exploit those squares.
notes.plans: Play Qb4 or Qa6, aiming to get the queen to a3 or the knight to b4, threatening checkmate.

notes.explains: Playing a5 instead of b5 is a mistake because White can reply a4, blocking the pawn storm, or a3, wasting Black's time. The pawn storm should aim to open files, not just push pawns.
notes.teaches: Pawn storms must have a clear purpose: opening lines for pieces. Don't advance pawns without a concrete plan; sometimes a single pawn push or a piece sacrifice is more effective.
notes.plans: Prefer b5 over a5. If the knight doesn't take, continue with b4 and then Qa5, putting pressure on the b-pawn.

notes.explains: After b5 b4, if White plays a3, Black can sacrifice with bxa3, threatening to promote on a1. The resulting queen on a1 is powerfully placed.
notes.teaches: Pawn sacrifices can create devastating passed pawns or open lines. Always consider the promotion threat when the opponent's pawn structure is compromised.
notes.plans: Play bxa3, then after Bxa3, the pawn on a2 threatens to queen, and the new queen will dominate the board.

notes.explains: White's g3 is a reverse Modern setup, often leading to a double fianchetto (Hippo). Black should not fear this passive setup.
notes.teaches: Against the Hippo, seize central space and adopt a flexible setup. The recommended response is ...Bd6 and ...c6 to blunt the kingside bishop.
notes.plans: Play ...d5, ...e5, ...Nf6, ...0-0, and later push ...e4 or ...d4 to gain space.

notes.explains: White's f4 is weakening. Black should not mechanically follow the standard setup but adapt: now ...Nc6 supports e5 and prepares ...f6 to solidify the center.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a weakening pawn move, be flexible. Prioritize protecting the e5 pawn over following a preset plan.
notes.plans: Play ...f6, then after exf6 Nxf6, castle kingside. The pawn on f6 will not be weak once the king is safe.

notes.explains: White's d4 is a positional mistake, creating weaknesses on e3 and c3 while blunting the bishops. Black should immediately strike with ...e4.
notes.teaches: When the opponent creates weaknesses, target them concretely. The e3 square becomes a permanent hole for a black knight or pawn.
notes.plans: Play ...e4, then ...Ng4 (or ...Nh5) to exploit e3. If White plays Nh4, trap the knight with ...g5.

notes.explains: White's knight on h4 is trapped by ...g5. The bishop on f5 controls the escape square, so the knight cannot flee.
notes.teaches: When a knight is on the rim, look for ways to trap it with pawns. Concrete calculation is key: if White had castled, ...g5 would be met by Nf5, but here it works.
notes.plans: Capture the knight, then continue the attack with ...Bxh2+ (Greek Gift sacrifice) or simply win material.

notes.explains: After winning the knight, the Greek Gift sacrifice ...Bxh2+ is decisive. The king cannot escape to f1 because the e3 pawn blocks, and the queen joins via h4.
notes.teaches: The Greek Gift sacrifice requires three ingredients: a bishop aiming at h2/h7, a knight that can jump to g4/g5, and the queen able to reach h4/h5. Here it works without castling.
notes.plans: Play ...Qh4+, then ...Qg3, ...e3, and deliver mate. The fastest way is to block the king's escape with ...e3.

notes.explains: In the Owens Defense (e4 b6 d4 Bb7 Bd3), the old line …f5 is tricky. White should play exf5 Bxg2 Qh5+ g6 fxg6 Bg7 (not …Nf6? gxh7+ Kxh7 Qxh7#). Then gxh7+ Kf8 Nh3! (not Nf3? Nf6) and the knight goes to g5, paralyzing Black.
notes.teaches: In the Owens Defense, after …f5, take on f5 and then play Nh3, aiming for Ng5. Do not take the knight on g8; instead, slowly develop the queenside and bring the rook to g1.
notes.plans: Play Nc3, Bd2, O-O-O, and Rg1. Black is paralyzed despite being up a rook. If Black tries ...Qe8, then Qxh7+ and mate follows.

notes.explains: After the Greek Gift, the fastest mate is to play ...e3, blocking the king's only escape square (d2). Then Qf2 is threatened, and if Qd3, ...Rf3 wins.
notes.teaches: When delivering mate, first identify the king's escape squares and block them. Here ...e3 is more efficient than ...Qf2 immediately.
notes.plans: Play ...e3, then ...Qf2+ and ...Rf3# or ...Qg2#.

notes.explains: The final mating net: ...Rf3 threatens ...Qh2# and ...Rg3#. White's pieces are useless.
notes.teaches: In a king hunt, coordinate queen and rook to create multiple mate threats. The rook on f3 covers h3 and g3, while the queen covers h2.
notes.plans: Deliver mate with ...Qh2# or ...Rg3#.

notes.explains: If White tries to defend with Qd2, ...Rg3 threatens ...Qh2# and ...Rxg2. The attack is unstoppable.
notes.teaches: Always look for ways to increase pressure. The rook lift to g3 creates a decisive threat.
notes.plans: Play ...Qh2# or ...Rxg2+ Kxg2 Qf2+ Kh3 Qh2#.

notes.explains: In the Glek System (e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 5.0-0), Black often plays ...Bc5 or ...d5. Against ...a6, White should not play a4 (weakens b4) but continue development with Bg2.
notes.teaches: In the Glek, do not fear ...b5; simply develop. The bishop on b5 is not threatened because ...b5 can be met by Bb3 or Bc2.
notes.plans: Play Bg2, then d3, Nbd2, Re1, and prepare c3 or d4.

notes.explains: Black plays ...Bb4, pinning the knight. White should not play d3 (passive) but simply castle, and if ...Nxe4, recapture with the d-pawn (d3) to open lines.
notes.teaches: When Black pins the knight, do not panic. Castling is fine; if Black captures on e4, recapture with the d-pawn to gain central control.
notes.plans: After ...Nxe4, play d3, then Nxe5, winning the pawn back with a discovered attack on the knight.

notes.explains: After Nxe5, Black cannot play ...Nxe5 because of the discovered attack on the knight on b4. White wins the pawn back and has the bishop pair.
notes.teaches: The move Nxe5 is a standard tactic in the Glek when Black has played ...Bb4. It exploits the loose knight on b4.
notes.plans: After recapturing, White has a pleasant position with the bishop pair and Black's king in the center.

notes.explains: White plays f4, chasing the knight. The idea is to push f5, opening the bishop and preventing Black's bishop from coming to g4 or h3.
notes.teaches: In the Glek, pushing f4-f5 is a common plan to gain space and activate the bishop. It also restricts Black's pieces.
notes.plans: After f5, if the knight goes to d7, continue with f5. If ...Nf6, then Bg5 pins it. Castle kingside and prepare an attack.

notes.explains: Black's knight on c4 is loose. White can attack it with Qe2, threatening Bxb7 and a discovered check. If Black plays ...Be6, then f5 wins the bishop.
notes.teaches: When a knight is on a loose square, target it with queen moves that also create threats. Qe2 attacks the knight and sets up Bxb7.
notes.plans: Play Qe2, then if ...Be6, f5; if ...Nb6, Bxb7 wins the exchange. Simplify if possible.

notes.explains: White wins the exchange and a pawn. The rest is a matter of converting the extra material by trading rooks and picking off pawns.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, simplify by trading pieces, especially rooks. Identify weak pawns and capture them methodically.
notes.plans: Trade rooks, then push the passed pawn. Avoid unnecessary counterplay by keeping the king safe.

notes.explains: White has a rook and two pawns vs a rook. The plan is to trade rooks and then push the passed pawns. Black's pawns are weak.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, active rook and passed pawns are key. Trade rooks when ahead to make the win easier.
notes.plans: Play Rf2, then double rooks on the e-file, or simply pick off Black's pawns. Avoid stalemate when promoting.

notes.explains: In the Glek, if Black plays ...Bc5 (instead of ...Bb4), White should know the center fork trick: after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 5.0-0 Bc5 Bg2, if Black castles, Nxe5 Nxe5 d4 wins the bishop.
notes.teaches: The center fork trick (Nxe5 followed by d4) is a common tactic in the Glek when Black's bishop is on c5. It wins a pawn and the bishop pair.
notes.plans: After d4, Black must play ...Bd6, then dxe5 Bxe5 10.0-0, and White has the bishop pair and central control.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...d6 (instead of ...Bc5), White should play Ne2 (prophylactic) to prepare f4, trapping the bishop on c5. For example: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 5.0-0 Bc5 Bg2 d6 Ne2! and f4 is coming.
notes.teaches: When the bishop is on c5 and Black plays ...d6, the prophylactic Ne2 prepares f4 to trap the bishop. This is a key idea in the Glek.
notes.plans: Play f4, then g4, Ng3, and Nf5, creating a kingside attack. Black's knight on d7 blocks the bishop, but White's initiative is strong.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...a6 and then ...Bb4, White should not fear ...Nxe4 because of the discovered attack. The correct response is to play Bg2 and then d3, recapturing with the d-pawn.
notes.teaches: In the Glek, the move ...Bb4 is not dangerous. Simply develop and if Black captures on e4, recapture with the d-pawn to open lines.
notes.plans: After d3, play Nxe5, winning the pawn back. Then develop with Nc3, Be3, and Qd2, aiming for central control.

notes.explains: If Black plays ...d5 (the main line), White should exchange on d5 and then fianchetto the bishop. For example: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 5.0-0 d5 exd5 Nxd5 Bg2.
notes.teaches: Against ...d5 in the Glek, exchange and fianchetto. This leads to a typical Glek pawn structure with White having the bishop pair and pressure on the long diagonal.
notes.plans: Play Nc3, Re1, and prepare c3 or d4. The bishop on g2 is powerful.

notes.explains: In the Glek, if Black plays ...Bg4, White should not fear it. Simply push h3, and if the bishop retreats to h5, play Qe1 or Kh2, then Nh4, targeting the bishop.
notes.teaches: The pin ...Bg4 is not dangerous in the Glek because White can often ignore it or chase it away with tempo. The bishop on h5 can become a target.
notes.plans: Play h3, then if ...Bh5, play Qe1 or Kh2, then Nh4, threatening Nf5. The bishop on h5 is misplaced.

notes.explains: In the Glek, a common tactical idea is Nxf2 (Desperado sacrifice). White should not fear it because Nxc6 wins a piece. For example: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6 Ba4 Nf6 5.0-0 Bb4 Bg2 Nxe4 d3 Nf6 Nxe5 Nxe5 Bxb4 d6 f4 Nc4 Qe2 Nxf2? Nxc6 wins.
notes.teaches: When a knight sacrifices itself on f2, look for a counter-sacrifice or capture that wins material. Here Nxc6 wins a piece because Black's queen is overloaded.
notes.plans: If Black plays ...Nxf2, simply capture on c6. If Black recaptures, White is up a piece. If Black takes the queen, White has checkmate threats.

notes.explains: In the Glek, if Black plays ...Nc4, White should play Qe2, attacking the knight and threatening Bxb7. This is a common double attack.
notes.teaches: When a knight lands on c4, Qe2 is a strong response, attacking the knight and the b7 pawn. It often wins material.
notes.plans: After Qe2, if Black defends with ...Be6, then f5 wins the bishop. If ...Nb6, then Bxb7 wins the exchange.

notes.explains: In the Glek, if Black plays ...Nf6 and White has f4, a good idea is Bg5, pinning the knight. If Black plays ...h6, retreat to h4, maintaining the pin.
notes.teaches: The pin Bg5 is very effective in the Glek because Black cannot easily break it. The knight on f6 is a key defensive piece.
notes.plans: After Bg5, if ...h6, Bh4. Then prepare f5 or g4 to increase pressure. Black's king is vulnerable.

notes.explains: White's c4 creates a hole on d4. Black should immediately clamp on d4 with Nc6, avoiding e5 which would let White off the hook.
notes.teaches: When White creates a central weakness, occupy it with pieces before committing to a pawn structure.
notes.plans: Follow up with g6, Bg7, and later d6 and e6 to complete the Botvinnik setup (Ne7).

notes.explains: Black can increase control over d4 by trading the light-squared bishop for the knight on f3. Bg4 pins the knight, and after Bxf3, Black removes a defender of d4.
notes.teaches: Control of a key square can be improved by removing defenders, not just adding attackers. A two-move bishop sortie is acceptable when the center is closed and development is otherwise sound.
notes.plans: Play e6 and Ne7 to complete the Botvinnik setup, then consider g5 to carve out the g6 square for the knight.

notes.explains: Black has completed the Botvinnik setup with Ne7 and Bg7. The center is closed, so the usual Sicilian rule against playing both e6 and g6 does not apply because White cannot exploit d6.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, general opening principles (like not playing both e6 and g6) can be safely violated. Focus on piece harmony and control of key squares.
notes.plans: After White's h6 and Bh4, play g5 to gain the g6 square for the knight, then Nf4 to target dark squares.

notes.explains: Black's g5 and Nf4 aim for opposite-colored bishops to emphasize White's dark-square weaknesses. After White plays Bxf4, Black recaptures with the pawn, opening the g-file and giving the queen access to g5.
notes.teaches: Creating opposite-colored bishops in a closed position magnifies the strength of your bishop and the weakness of your opponent's. Always reassess after a trade: new squares become available.
notes.plans: Play Qg5 to pressure the bishop and prepare an attack down the g-file. Castle queenside if needed.

notes.explains: White's Nb5 is met by a6, forcing the knight back. Black's queen on g5 solidifies the dark-square bind and threatens future sacrifices on the g-file.
notes.teaches: When you have a positional advantage, avoid unnecessary pawn-grabbing (like Bxb2) that might open lines for the opponent. Keep the position closed and increase the pressure.
notes.plans: Play Rg8 to build up on the g-file, then Be5 to prevent White from opening the center with e5. Castle queenside and prepare a decisive breakthrough.

notes.explains: Black's attack culminates in Rxg2, crashing through. The king is safe on the queenside, and White's king is exposed. The key was building up piece pressure before striking.
notes.teaches: When you dominate a color complex, the attack often comes naturally. Avoid overly fancy sacrifices unless you are sure they lead to mate; simple pressure is often enough.
notes.plans: After Rxg2, White cannot defend against the threats on the g-file and the exposed king.

notes.explains: In the Closed Sicilian (or similar setups with g3 and Bg2), Black's standard plan is queenside expansion with a6 and b5. This plan is universal: it applies in the King's Indian Attack and other anti-Sicilian lines.
notes.teaches: Against fianchetto setups, Black's typical plan is to expand on the queenside with b5. Remember to play Rb8 first to avoid tactical tricks like e5 when the rook is on f8.
notes.plans: Play a6, Rb8, and b5, then continue with b4 to target the c3 pawn. If White plays f4, avoid b5 immediately because e5 wins a piece; instead, play Ne8 to unpin and prepare b5.

notes.explains: Black's queenside attack with b5-b4 is a typical plan in many Sicilian lines. The key is to maintain the tension and not push b4 prematurely unless White has a pawn on c3.
notes.teaches: When White has a pawn on c3, pushing b4 can be strong. Otherwise, keep the pawn on b5 and maintain the option of bxc3. Use piece play (e.g., Nd4, Qa5) to increase pressure before committing to the pawn break.
notes.plans: After b5, if White plays Be3, consider Nd4. If White plays g4, continue with Qa5 or Ne6-d4. The goal is to create weaknesses on the queenside and eventually open lines.

notes.explains: In the Delayed Alapin (Nf3 d6 c3), Black should avoid the trap Nxc4? which loses to Qa4+. Instead, play Bd7 to reinforce the threat of Nxc4 and discourage d4.
notes.teaches: Against the Delayed Alapin, a simple developing move like Bd7 is sufficient at the club level. The key is to prevent White from playing d4 easily.
notes.plans: After Bd7, if White plays d3, continue with g6, Bg7, and castle. Then expand on the queenside with b5, following the same plan as in the Closed Sicilian.

notes.explains: Black's plan of b5-b4 is effective because White cannot easily push d4. The pawn break b4 targets the c3 pawn and opens lines for the rooks.
notes.teaches: When White cannot play d4, Black's queenside expansion with b5 is a powerful plan. Use moves like Nd7 to reinforce control over d4 and prepare the break.
notes.plans: Play b5, then b4 to open the b-file. If White plays a4, notice the weakening of b3 and consider Nd4 to fork or infiltrate. The key is to create pressure on the queenside while White is passive.

notes.explains: Black's Nd4 exploits the alignment of White's queen and rook on the same diagonal. The threat of c2 forking the rooks forces White to weaken the queenside.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to alignments of enemy pieces. A seemingly well-defended piece can become undefended if you can force a deflection. Use tactical motifs like forks and discovered attacks to increase pressure.
notes.plans: After Nd4, if White plays Qd1, then c2 forks the rooks. If White plays Be3, then Nxc2 wins a pawn. The goal is to win material or create further weaknesses.

notes.explains: After c4, the queen must retreat. Qd7 is best because it keeps the queen active, defending key squares and avoiding the trap Qe4? Nc3.
notes.teaches: When retreating a queen under attack, prefer a square that maintains maximum activity and defensive coverage.
notes.plans: Black will continue developing, aiming to pressure the d4 pawn.

notes.explains: Taking on d1 with the queen is a trap: after dxc5 Qxd1+ Kxd1, Black's bishop on h5 is undefended and White's bishop gets the long diagonal, winning material.
notes.teaches: Do not grab material if it exposes your pieces to a counterattack that loses more. Always consider the opponent's threats after a capture.

notes.explains: The intermediate move Bxf3 before Nd4 is critical. Without it, Black's knight has no good square and White gets a huge initiative with Ne5. By trading on f3, Black secures the d4 outpost for the knight.
notes.teaches: When a piece is under pressure, look for an intermediate exchange that clears the path to a strong square. The knight on d4 becomes an unassailable outpost.
notes.plans: Black will support the knight with e5 and develop the bishop to d6, blockading the d4 pawn.

notes.explains: e5 cements the knight on d4. Trading the bishop for the knight would be disastrous: the knight is the dam holding back White's pieces. Without it, White's forces flood in.
notes.teaches: When a piece is a crucial defender, protect it at all costs. Do not trade it off unless the compensation is overwhelming.
notes.plans: Black will castle, then prepare b5 to undermine White's pawn chain.

notes.explains: Ne8 retreats to avoid Bxf6 ruining the kingside pawn structure. Retreating is fine; the move also opens the f-file for a future f5 break.
notes.teaches: Do not fear retreating moves. They can be the best way to preserve a good structure or prepare an attack. Always check if the retreat leaves anything undefended.
notes.plans: Black will regroup: bishop to e7, knight to d6, then f5 to challenge White's center.

notes.explains: The knight on d6 is an eternal knight: it cannot be dislodged by White's bishop (which is biting on granite) and dominates the position. The bishop retreated to e7 to clear the d6 square for the knight.
notes.teaches: A knight on a strong central outpost that cannot be attacked by enemy pawns or pieces is a decisive advantage. Clear the path for it even if it means a retreat.
notes.plans: Black will play f5 to force White's knight away, then recapture on d6 and launch a kingside attack.

notes.explains: f5 forces White's knight to move, allowing Black to recapture on d6 and cement the blockader. This is a direct way to improve the knight's position while opening lines.
notes.teaches: When you have a strong blockader, use pawn breaks to force enemy pieces away and solidify your own outpost.
notes.plans: After White moves the knight, Black recaptures on d6 and then builds pressure with Rf8, preparing e4 or f4.

notes.explains: d6 is a tactical shot. After …d6, if Nxd6, then …Nxd6 Bxd6 Bxd6 and Black wins a piece because the d5 pawn is no longer an umbrella protecting the bishop. The tactic works because Black's rook on f8 will attack the queen after fxe4.
notes.teaches: When calculating tactics, look for intermediate moves that remove defenders or change the pawn structure. Here, d6 opens lines and exploits the loose bishop.
notes.plans: Black will follow up with Nxf3+ to win a piece.

notes.explains: Nxf3+ is the key tactic. After Kc1 Nxd2 Kxd2 fxe4, Black attacks the queen with the rook on f8. If White takes the queen, Black recaptures with the rook, winning a piece. The tactic works because the f-pawn capture opens the f-file for the rook.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, you can afford to give some back to simplify. Here, sacrificing the knight leads to winning a piece because of the discovered attack on the queen.
notes.plans: After winning the exchange, Black converts by simplifying and using the extra material.

notes.explains: After winning a rook, Black is up material. The game simplifies into an easily winning endgame. Black can give back some pawns to clarify the win.
notes.teaches: When converting a material advantage, simplify the position. Do not fear returning a little material if it eliminates counterplay and makes the win straightforward.
notes.plans: Black will activate the king and push passed pawns.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6, White's most dangerous try is Bg5, threatening to ruin Black's pawn structure with Bxf6. Black can defend with Nbd7 or e6; Nbd7 has seen a resurgence.
notes.teaches: In the Najdorf, Black must be ready to defend against Bg5. The knight on d7 supports the e5 break and can later hop to the c5 or e5 outpost.
notes.plans: Black aims to play ...e5, ...h6 to test the bishop, and eventually uncoil with ...Nc5 or ...Ne5, often sacrificing a pawn for activity.

notes.explains: After Bg5 Nbd7 f4 Qc7 Qf3 h6 Bh4, Black can sacrifice a pawn with …g5!? to gain dynamic play. The idea is to open lines and get the knight to e5 with tempo.
notes.teaches: Sacrifices for initiative are common in sharp Sicilians. The knight on e5 becomes a powerful outpost, and Black's pieces coordinate to attack White's queen and king.
notes.plans: Black plays ...g5, ...Nc5/e5, and ...Bg7, aiming to keep White's king in the center and exploit the weak dark squares.

notes.explains: After winning a piece, Black should not be greedy. Instead of …Qa5+ (which allows Bxd2) or …Qxc2 (which allows Rc1), the queen goes to c6, where it is safe and active.
notes.teaches: When up material, prioritize safety and coordination over immediate captures. A well-placed queen can defend key squares and support further advances.
notes.plans: Black develops with ...Bd7, ...Rc8, and ...Be7, keeping the king in the center until the position clarifies.

notes.explains: Black should fianchetto the bishop to b7 rather than a6, because a6 allows a4 and opens the a-file for White. The bishop on b7 pressures e4 and supports the knight.
notes.teaches: In closed positions, fianchettoing the bishop can be more effective than developing to an open file, especially when the opponent can exploit the open file.
notes.plans: Black completes development with ...Bg7, ...0-0 (or keep king in center), and prepares ...Nc5 or ...d5.

notes.explains: Black should not castle queenside because White can play ...Na7 forking the rook and bishop. Instead, the king stays in the center or moves to d8, which is safe behind the d6 pawn.
notes.teaches: King safety is relative. In open positions, castling is crucial; in closed or semi-closed positions, the king can sometimes remain central if the pawn structure provides cover.
notes.plans: Black moves the king to d8 to avoid pins and then continues with ...Nc5, ...Rc8, and eventually ...e4 or ...d5 breaks.

notes.explains: When White threatens Bb5 pinning the knight, Black can simply move the king to d8, avoiding the pin. This is a minimalist defense that keeps Black's structure intact.
notes.teaches: Sometimes the simplest move is best. Moving the king out of a pin can be more effective than blocking or counterattacking, especially when the pawn structure is solid.
notes.plans: After Kd8, Black can meet ...b4 with ...Nxd3, opening the c-file for counterplay.

notes.explains: Black eventually takes on e4 after moving the king away from the pin. If White recaptures with the queen, Black has a battery against g2 with ...Ng5 and ...Qh1+.
notes.teaches: When up material, opening the position can be beneficial if your pieces are well-coordinated. The battery on the long diagonal can create mating threats.
