notes.plans: Black plays ...Nxe4, ...Ng5, and ...Qh1+ to win the pawn on g2 or force a queen trade.

notes.explains: In the line Bg5 Nbd7 f4 Qc7 Qf3 h6 Bh4 g5 fxg5 hxg5 Bxg5, Black can play …Qc5! forking the knight and bishop. White must defend both, but Black continues with ...g5 attacking the queen.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, concrete calculation is essential. The fork Qc5 is a typical tactical resource after the pawn sacrifice.
notes.plans: After ...Qc5, Black plays ...g5, ...Ne5-g4, and ...Bh6 to prevent White from castling and to dominate the dark squares.

notes.explains: After ...Ne5-g4, Black should not play ...Nfg4 because that leaves the d5 square weak. Instead, ...Neg4 keeps the knight on f6 to defend d5, preventing White from using that square.
notes.teaches: When choosing between two similar moves, consider which squares the opponent gains access to. Defending key central squares can be more important than keeping a knight on an outpost.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Bh6 to stop White from castling, then ...Qb4 attacking b2 and threatening ...Nxe4.

notes.explains: If White plays Nf5 instead of a better move, Black can play ...Qb4, attacking the b2 pawn and threatening ...Nxe4. White's position collapses because the king cannot castle and the queen is overloaded.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, look for ways to open lines and attack with multiple pieces. Overloading the queen is a common theme.
notes.plans: Black captures on e4, then ...Bxh6 or ...Rc8, winning material or delivering checkmate.

notes.explains: In the line where White takes on f6, Black gets positional compensation. For example, after ...Rxb1, ...Nxe4, ...Qxe4, the endgame is horrible for White because Black's pawns are better and the king is safe.
notes.teaches: Material is not everything. Positional factors like pawn structure, king safety, and piece activity can outweigh a pawn deficit.
notes.plans: Black aims to trade down to a favorable endgame with active pieces and a safer king.

notes.explains: If White gives up the dark-squared bishop with Bxf6, Black gets uncontested control of the dark squares and White's king can never castle safely.
notes.teaches: The dark-squared bishop is often White's most important defender in the Najdorf. Exchanging it can leave fatal weaknesses on dark squares.
notes.plans: Black plays ...Bh6, ...Qb6, and ...0-0-0, exploiting the dark-square weaknesses.

notes.explains: After Bg3, Black can play ...gxf4 and then ...e5, creating a powerful pawn chain. White's position is already very bad.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a positional mistake, punish it immediately by seizing space and restricting their pieces.
notes.plans: Black pushes ...e5, ...f5, and ...d5, crushing White in the center.

notes.explains: Black should not play ...d5 prematurely because White can reply with Qxd5, and then ...Qc7? allows Nc7+. Black must finish development and move the king away from the pin first.
notes.teaches: In sharp positions, opening the center before your king is safe can be disastrous. Always consider tactical shots like knight forks.
notes.plans: Black completes development with ...Kd8, ...Rc8, ...Be7, then ...d5 or ...e4.

notes.explains: After e4 c5 d4 cxd4 c3 dxc3 Nxc3, Black's a6 is an improvisation. White should respond with the normal setup: Bc4, aiming for a standard Morra development.
notes.teaches: In gambit openings, stick to the standard developing moves; don't improvise just because the opponent does.
notes.plans: Develop naturally: Bc4, Nf3, O-O, and later push e5 to open lines and create threats.

notes.explains: Black's combination of e6 and g6 (the 'Swiss cheese defense') is a classic mistake. It leaves d6 weak and White can quickly plant a knight there, as shown in the game.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, avoid playing both e6 and g6 unless you have a specific setup that covers the dark squares. The d6 square becomes a permanent weakness.
notes.plans: White should immediately target d6 with e5 and Ne4, aiming to get a knight to d6.

notes.explains: White plays e5 not to keep the pawn, but to sacrifice it to get the knight to d6. After e5 f6, White plays Ne4, sacrificing a second pawn. The knight on d6 will be worth more than the material.
notes.teaches: In gambits, be willing to sacrifice material for positional domination. A knight on a powerful outpost like d6 can outweigh two pawns.
notes.plans: Play Ne4, then Nxd6 (or Nc7) to establish the knight on d6, then bring other pieces to attack.

notes.explains: After the knight reaches d6, White needs to coordinate the other pieces. The idea of b3 and Ba3 is fast (only two moves) and threatens discovered checks along the a3-f8 diagonal, forcing the king to f6.
notes.teaches: Use the 'three-move rule' to evaluate if a plan is too slow: if it takes three or more moves, it's often too slow; two moves is fast enough.
notes.plans: Play b3 and Ba3 to create threats against the black king, forcing it into a vulnerable position.

notes.explains: With the king on f6, White reshuffles knights: Ng5 (retreating the knight from d6) then Nd6+ again, forcing the king back to e7 or f8, both on the a3-f8 diagonal, losing the queen.
notes.teaches: Retreating knights can be part of a regrouping maneuver to force the opponent's king into a worse position. Don't be afraid to move a piece backward if it sets up a stronger threat.
notes.plans: Play Ng5 (the other knight) to give check, then Nd6+ to drive the king onto the diagonal where Ba3 wins the queen.

notes.explains: After winning the queen, White should open the position to bring the queen into the attack. Even if Black gets a fork (e.g., d5), White can sacrifice material because being up a queen allows blasting through.
notes.teaches: When you are up significant material, simplify by opening lines and trading down. Don't be afraid of tactical complications if you have a material advantage.
notes.plans: Play e5 to open lines, then use the queen to deliver checkmate or win more material.

notes.explains: In the final phase, White has a queen and rook against scattered black pieces. The simplest win is to go directly for checkmate with Rfd1 and then queen invasion.
notes.teaches: When winning, choose the most direct and safe plan. Avoid unnecessary captures that give the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: Play Rfd1, then Qf7+ or Qd6 to force mate or win more material.

notes.explains: If Black declines the Morra with Nf6, White can transpose into the Alapin (c3 Sicilian) with e5, which is a solid alternative. This makes the Morra a win-win: if Black accepts, White gets attacking chances; if Black declines, White gets a good positional game.
notes.teaches: Choosing an opening that can transpose into another familiar system gives you flexibility and reduces the amount of theory to learn.
notes.plans: After e4 c5 d4 cxd4 c3 Nf6, play e5 to transpose into the Alapin.

notes.explains: The Morra is not objectively bad; even with perfect play, Black is not better. At club level, opponents often mishandle it by playing as in the Open Sicilian, which leads to quick defeats.
notes.teaches: Don't dismiss gambits as unsound. Many are perfectly playable and can be very effective against unprepared opponents.
notes.plans: Learn a few key ideas and traps, such as the e5 push after Bc4 and Nf6, which can win the queen.

notes.explains: In the famous game against Van Wely, White played Bc4 even though it 'bites on granite' against e6. The idea is that tactics outweigh positional considerations: White later sacrifices a knight on d5 to open lines.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, tactical opportunities can override normal positional rules. Be alert for sacrifices that open up the opponent's king.
notes.plans: After Bc4, Nc6, Nf3, e6, castling, and Black's knight goes to e7, play Bg5 to induce f6, then retreat to e3, and later sacrifice on d5.

notes.explains: After the knight sacrifice on d5, White plays Rxd5, locking in Black's bishop on f8 and opening the e-file. Then f4 opens the position further, and Bg5 prevents castling and sets up a mating attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, use pawn breaks and piece sacrifices to open files and diagonals for a direct attack.
notes.plans: Play f4 to open the e-file, then Bg5 to stop castling, followed by Qd2 and doubling rooks on the e-file.

notes.explains: The final combination in the Van Wely game: Rxc6 blasts through, and after Black recaptures, Bg5 wins because Qe7+ leads to mate. This shows the power of the bishop on the long diagonal.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, look for sacrifices that remove defenders and create unstoppable threats. The bishop on g5 can be decisive.
notes.plans: Play Rxc6, then after dxc6, Bg5 threatening Qe7+ and mate.

notes.explains: The teacher recounts a personal game where he, as Black, played e6 and g6 and was punished by White's Qd6, threatening Nc7. This shows the danger of neglecting the d6 square.
notes.teaches: Always be aware of the opponent's threats to occupy weak squares. A knight on d6 can be devastating, especially if it forks the queen and rook.
notes.plans: If you have a weak square, try to prevent the opponent's piece from landing there, or prepare to trade it off.

notes.explains: In the game, Black played f6, which was the losing move. Better was f5 to prevent Ne4, or g4 to stop the knight from reaching d6. But even then, White's compensation is overwhelming.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, you must be precise. Allowing the opponent to establish a knight on a key outpost like d6 is often fatal.
notes.plans: If Black plays f5, White can play Bg5 and Qd6, still maintaining strong pressure.

notes.explains: After the knight reaches d6, White's b3 and Ba3 is the final nail in the coffin. It threatens discovered checks and forces the king into a mating net.
notes.teaches: When you have a dominant piece, bring your other pieces to support it. A bishop on a3 can be deadly when combined with a knight on d6.
notes.plans: Play b3, Ba3, then use the knight to give check and force the king onto the a3-f8 diagonal.

notes.explains: The knight reshuffling (Ne4, Nfg5, then Nd6+) is a key maneuver to drive the king onto the deadly diagonal. This idea can be hard to see but is essential in such positions.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid to retreat knights to regroup. A temporary retreat can set up a decisive double attack or check.
notes.plans: Play Ne4, then Nfg5, then Nd6+ to force the king to e7 or f8, winning the queen.

notes.explains: The main line of the Morra accepted often involves e6 and a6, with White playing Qe2 and Rd1. This is a standard setup that gives White good compensation.
notes.teaches: In the Morra, a typical plan is to put the queen on e2 and rook on d1, supporting the center and preparing e5.
notes.plans: Develop with Qe2, Rd1, and then push e5 when ready.

notes.explains: White's e5 is a mistake; it gives Black an ideal French setup with the bishop on f5 and knight on c6. Black should not rush with Bf5 but can play Nc6 first.
notes.teaches: When White plays e5 in this structure, Black gets a French-like position with the bishop outside the pawn chain, which is very comfortable. Develop naturally with Nc6 and Bf5.
notes.plans: Play Nc6, Bf5, e6, and then Qb6 to pressure d4.

notes.explains: Black plays e6, completing the French pawn chain. White may try g4, but Black can respond with h5 to prevent overextension.
notes.teaches: In this setup, White's aggressive pawn pushes like g4 are not dangerous if Black responds correctly with h5, creating weaknesses for White.
notes.plans: Continue with Qb6, then develop the knight to f5 via h6 or g6.

notes.explains: Black plays Qb6, pressuring d4. Unlike in the French, the bishop on f5 is already developed. The knight on g8 needs a home; options include Nh6 or Bg6 followed by Nf5.
notes.teaches: Qb6 is a standard French idea to pressure d4. Here, the bishop on f5 is a bonus. The knight on g8 can be developed to f5 via h6 or g6, often after Bg6.
notes.plans: Play Bg6, then Nh6 or Nf5, and later castle kingside or queenside.

notes.explains: Black plays Nh6, not fearing Bxh6 because White's dark-squared bishop is a key defender of d4. If White takes, Black gets the g-file and pressure on b2.
notes.teaches: Do not fear Bxh6 in such positions; White's dark-squared bishop is important for defending d4. Losing it weakens White's structure and gives Black attacking chances.
notes.plans: If White takes on h6, play gxh6, then use the g-file and pressure on b2. Otherwise, continue with Bg6 and Nf5.

notes.explains: Black completes the regrouping: Bg6 vacates f5 for the knight, and Nf5 gives the knight a strong outpost. All pieces are developed except the king.
notes.teaches: When pieces compete for squares, a timely retreat (like Bg6) can free up a better square for another piece. This is a common maneuver in cramped positions.
notes.plans: Castle, then prepare f6 to break open the center and increase pressure on d4.

notes.explains: Black plays f6 to open the center and increase pressure on d4. White's knight on b5 is a target; Black can retreat the queen to b6 or b8, but b6 pins the knight to the pawn.
notes.teaches: f6 is a typical break in French-like structures to challenge the center. It opens lines and increases pressure on the d4 pawn.
notes.plans: After f6, if White takes, recapture with the bishop and target d4. If White doesn't take, consider a6 to drive the knight away or take on e3 later.

notes.explains: Black retreats the queen to b6, pinning the knight to the pawn and reinforcing pressure on d4. The position is ripe for a breakthrough.
notes.teaches: Retreating the queen to b6 pins the knight and adds pressure. Always consider pins to increase the effectiveness of your attack.
notes.plans: Prepare to take on e5 or e3, depending on White's response. The knight on b5 is a liability.

notes.explains: White plays Bd3, a mistake. Black can now win material by taking on e5 or e3. The key is to calculate carefully: after exf5, Bxf5, Bxf5, Qxf5, the knight on b5 is hanging.
notes.teaches: When calculating captures, always note undefended pieces at the end of the line. Here, the knight on b5 is hanging after the sequence, winning a piece.
notes.plans: Play exf5, then after Bxf5, take on e3 or e5, exploiting the hanging knight on b5.

notes.explains: After the sequence, Black wins a piece because the knight on b5 is hanging. White's position collapses.
notes.teaches: Always check for hanging pieces at the end of a tactical sequence. This is a common source of blunders.
notes.plans: Capture the knight or the bishop on e3, winning material.

notes.explains: In the King's Indian, after d5 by White, the c5 square becomes a key outpost for Black's knight. Black often plays a5 to prevent b4, which would chase the knight away, and to gain space on the queenside.
notes.teaches: Prophylaxis: anticipate and prevent your opponent's threats before executing your own plan. Here, a5 stops b4 and prepares the knight's deployment to c5.
notes.plans: Black will aim to put a knight on c5, support it with b6, and then prepare f5 to attack on the kingside. White will counter on the queenside.

notes.explains: A typical kingside attack in the King's Indian involves the maneuver Nh5, aiming for Nf4, followed by f5. But first, Black should support the knight on c5 with b6, a patient preparatory move.
notes.teaches: Patience in attack: don't rush the f5 break; first secure your outpost and improve your pieces. The knight on h5 eyes f4 and can later support the f-pawn push.
notes.plans: After b6 and Nh5, Black will play f5, opening lines against White's king. White may try to counter with a4 or b4.

notes.explains: In the Petrosian Variation, after d5, Black's typical plan is a5, Nc5, b6, and Nh5. White's f3 prevents Nh5, so Black may need alternative preparations like Ne8 or Kh8.
notes.teaches: Flexibility in plan execution: if one path is blocked, find another. The knight can reroute via d7 or e8, or the king can move to h8 to support the f5 break.
notes.plans: Black will still aim for f5, but must adapt the knight's route. White will try to maintain the center and prepare queenside expansion.

notes.explains: If White plays b4 to chase the knight from c5, Black can respond with Bxb4, sacrificing a pawn to open lines and create a powerful outpost on d4 for the knight.
notes.teaches: Sacrificial idea: giving up a pawn for long-term positional compensation, such as a knight outpost and active bishops. This is a typical King's Indian counter.
notes.plans: After Bxb4, Black will play Nxd4, establishing a strong knight. White's king may become exposed, and Black's bishops will target the kingside.

notes.explains: When White takes the pawn on a4 (after a4 by Black), Black can play Rxa4, forcing the queen to move, and then deliver checkmate threats with Qh4 and Ng3. The key is to remove the queen's defense of h5.
notes.teaches: Thinking backwards: to execute a combination, consider what obstacle prevents it and find a way to remove that obstacle. Here, Rxa4 forces the queen away, enabling the mate threat.
notes.plans: Black will play Qh4, threatening Qxh2#. White may try f4 or Kh1, but Black's attack is overwhelming.

notes.explains: In the Maroczy Bind, White has a space advantage and central control. Black's plan is to gain queenside space with a5-a4, then deploy the queen to a5 and attack White's queenside.
notes.teaches: Space advantage: when cramped, counter by expanding on the side where you have more space. Black's queenside expansion is a typical plan in the Maroczy.
notes.plans: Black will play a5, a4, Qa5, and target White's b-pawn. White will try to maintain the bind and attack on the kingside.

notes.explains: When White trades pieces in the Maroczy, it can leave him with a bad bishop (light-squared, blocked by pawns). Black should aim to trade off White's good bishop (dark-squared) and keep the bad one.
notes.teaches: Bishop quality: in closed positions, a bishop that is blocked by its own pawns is 'bad'. Trade your opponent's good bishop and keep your own active one.
notes.plans: Black will seek to exchange dark-squared bishops, leaving White with the light-squared bishop that is hampered by pawns on light squares.

notes.explains: In a standoff between queens (e.g., Qb6 vs Qb3), if your queen is protected by a pawn, you control the standoff and can decide whether to trade. This gives you flexibility.
notes.teaches: Control of tension: when two pieces attack each other, the side whose piece is defended by a pawn has the advantage in deciding the outcome. Use this to maintain pressure or force favorable trades.
notes.plans: Black can keep the queens on to maintain pressure, or trade if advantageous. The pawn defender ensures safety.

notes.explains: When White plays a3 to avoid Nb3, Black can still play Nb3, forking queen and rook. This exploits the weakened b3 square after a3.
notes.teaches: Weak square exploitation: a3 weakens the b3 square, creating a potential fork. Always consider how your opponent's pawn moves create tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: Black will play Nb3, winning material or forcing a favorable trade. White must respond carefully.

notes.explains: In the endgame after trades, Black's knight on c5 and rook on f2 give him a winning advantage. The plan is to attack White's queenside pawns while keeping the king safe.
notes.teaches: Endgame technique: when ahead, target your opponent's weak pawns and activate your rook. Use the knight to control key squares.
notes.plans: Black will play Rf2, attacking the f-pawn, then target the queenside pawns. White's rook becomes passive.

notes.explains: Comparing two similar positions (one from a classical game, one from the current game) reveals that the presence of a knight on c5 or e5 makes a critical difference. Without the knight, White's e-file pressure is decisive; with the knight, Black has counterplay.
notes.teaches: Method of comparison: to understand a position, compare it to a known one and identify the key difference. This helps evaluate imbalances and choose the right plan.
notes.plans: In the current game, Black's knight on c5 gives him queenside counterplay, making White's e-file attack less effective.

notes.explains: Black plays c5, trying to transpose into a Sicilian. White can punish Black's extra pawn moves by pushing d5, creating a Benoni-like structure where Black has wasted tempi.
notes.teaches: When opponent makes many pawn moves, seize the center with d5 to gain space and punish the loss of time.
notes.plans: Play d5 to fix the center and exploit Black's lag in development.

notes.explains: White pushes d5, reaching a Benoni-like structure. Black's a6 and c5 cost time, giving White a lead in development.
notes.teaches: In such structures, White's space advantage and development lead are key. Don't rush to attack; consolidate first.
notes.plans: Defend the d5 pawn with Nc3, and avoid premature moves like Ng5 that drop pawns.

notes.explains: Black plays d6, defending the c5 pawn. White now has a choice between positional (a4) and tactical (dxe6) approaches.
notes.teaches: With a lead in development, the tactical approach (opening the center) is often more punishing. The positional approach (a4) is also good but less direct.
notes.plans: White chooses dxe6 to open the center and attack Black's weakened pawn structure.

notes.explains: White captures on e6, opening the center. Now White considers Ng5 with a specific aim: to eliminate Black's light-squared bishop and attack the weak e6 pawn.
notes.teaches: Ng5 is not just a 'cool' move; it has a concrete goal: trade the bishop on e6 and then target the pawn on e6 with Bc4. Only play such moves when you have a clear follow-up.
notes.plans: Play Ng5, threatening to take on e6. If Black moves the bishop, Bc4 will be crushing against f7.

notes.explains: White plays Ng5, threatening Nxe6. Black should not play h6 because White wants to take the bishop anyway; h6 weakens the diagonal and invites Bg4.
notes.teaches: Don't play weakening pawn moves like h6 when the opponent wants the trade. Instead, develop with Nc6 or consider b5, though risky.
notes.plans: If Black plays Nc6, White takes on c6 and then plays Bc4, targeting the e6 pawn.

notes.explains: White executes the plan: Nxe6 eliminates the bishop, and Bc4 targets the weak e6 pawn. White is clearly better.
notes.teaches: When you have a specific plan, execute it consistently. The e6 pawn is a permanent weakness.
notes.plans: Continue pressuring e6 and develop the rest of the pieces. Black's pawn structure is damaged.

notes.explains: Black blunders with h6, allowing Nxe6 winning a piece. This is a common mistake at lower levels.
notes.teaches: Always consider if your opponent's threat is real. Here, Ng5 threatens Nxe6, and h6 doesn't prevent it; it just loses time.
notes.plans: White takes on e6 and wins a piece. The game is effectively over.

notes.explains: After Nxe6, Black tries Qe7 attacking the knight. White can play Qh5, pinning the pawn on e6 and threatening multiple things.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, look for the most accurate move. Qh5 pins the pawn and keeps the attack going, rather than simplifying immediately.
notes.plans: Play Qh5, then if Qf6, play g5! to open lines and win the queen.

notes.explains: White plays Qh5, pinning the e6 pawn and threatening Nc7+ or simply winning material. Black's position collapses.
notes.teaches: When you have multiple winning moves, choose the one that maintains the most pressure and limits counterplay.
notes.plans: After Qf6, play g5! to open the f-file and win the queen.

notes.explains: White plays g5, attacking the queen and opening lines. If Qe6, Nc7+ wins the queen. This is a typical tactical motif.
notes.teaches: Pawn pushes like g5 can open lines and create decisive threats. Always consider such advances when the opponent's queen is exposed.
notes.plans: After g5, Black's queen must move, and White wins material.

notes.explains: Nc7+ forks king and queen, winning the queen. The game is over.
notes.teaches: Always look for forks and checks that win material. This is a classic knight fork.
notes.plans: Take the queen and convert the endgame.

notes.explains: White wins the queen with Nc7+. The game is effectively over.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, stay alert for tactical finishes. Don't relax until the game is won.
notes.plans: Capture the queen and simplify to a won endgame.

notes.explains: The game ends with White winning a queen. Black's opening play was poor, and White punished it effectively.
notes.teaches: This game illustrates how to punish unusual early pawn moves with principled development and a concrete attacking plan.

notes.explains: White plays Bd3 to prevent Black from developing his bishop to f5. Black's bishop has no good square, and White's position is already excellent.
notes.teaches: In positions where Black has played ...h5, Bd3 is often the most precise move—it stops ...Bf5 and prepares natural development.
notes.plans: Follow up with Nf3 and h3, reinforcing the center and preparing to exploit Black's passive setup.

notes.explains: Black plays Qb6, attacking the d4 pawn. White can play a3, a useful waiting move that also defends the pawn indirectly. If Black takes on d4, White traps the queen with Be3.
notes.teaches: When your opponent's queen is active, look for ways to trap it. Here a3 is both a useful defensive move and a trap—if Black grabs the pawn, the queen gets caught.
notes.plans: Play a3, then h3 to kick the bishop, and if Black takes on f3, recapture with the queen and then Be3 traps the queen on d4.

notes.explains: Black falls into the trap: after Qxf3, Black takes the d4 pawn, and Be3 traps the queen. Black's queen is lost, giving White a decisive advantage.
notes.teaches: Don't settle for winning a piece when you can win the queen. Always look for the most punishing continuation.
notes.plans: After trapping the queen, simplify and convert the material advantage. Keep pressure on Black's weaknesses.

notes.explains: Black tries Ng5 to create counterplay, but White simply retreats the queen to e2, keeping the trap intact. Black's queen is still trapped.
notes.teaches: When your opponent tries to complicate, stay calm and find the simplest refutation. Don't panic and give up your advantage.
notes.plans: Continue to exploit the trapped queen; eventually Black will have to give up material.

notes.explains: White castles queenside, and the position is winning. Black's queen is still trapped, and White has a huge material advantage.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplify and trade down. Keep your king safe and avoid unnecessary risks.
notes.plans: Use the extra queen to attack Black's weakened pawns and king. The knight on d6 is a strong outpost.

notes.explains: White grabs the a7 pawn, winning material. Black's position collapses.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for direct captures that maintain or increase your lead.
notes.plans: Continue to attack Black's weaknesses; the knight on d6 is a powerful outpost.

notes.explains: White plays Nc5, threatening mate on b7. Black's knight on b6 is the only defender; once it moves, mate follows.
notes.teaches: When looking for mate, identify the key defensive pieces and target them. Here the knight on b6 is the main obstacle to Qb7#.
notes.plans: If Black moves the knight, play Qb7#. Otherwise, continue pressuring the knight.

notes.explains: Black plays Rb8, but White takes on b7 with checkmate. The game ends.
notes.teaches: Always be alert for checkmate patterns. Here the queen and knight combine for a simple mate on b7.

notes.explains: The king on d1 is vulnerable. Black should develop with Nf6, not rush to capture on d3, and aim to trade on favorable terms.
notes.teaches: Develop pieces before capturing pawns, especially when the opponent's king is exposed.
notes.plans: Play Nf6, developing and threatening e4. If White takes, recapture with the knight after trading queens.

notes.explains: Bd2 unpins the knight and reinforces e4, forcing Black to trade on d3. After Bxd3, Black can castle, and the f4 pawn becomes a long-term weakness for White.
notes.teaches: A pawn that looks supportive can become a target once the opponent's king is safe and the position opens.
notes.plans: Take on d3, castle, then target the f4 pawn.

notes.explains: After castling, Black should immediately challenge the knight on e5 with Nbd7, aiming to trade it off before White can solidify it.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a well-placed knight, trade it off quickly before it becomes a permanent outpost.
notes.plans: Play Nbd7, threatening to exchange on e5.

notes.explains: Black is up the exchange. The immediate priority is to activate the rook on a8 and bring it into play. The queen can wait; moving the rook to e8 is a low-hanging fruit.
notes.teaches: When ahead material, activate all pieces before rushing with the queen. Look for simple improvements.
notes.plans: Play Rae8, putting the rook on an open file.

notes.explains: White has two bishops on the d-file, but they cannot both move at once. Black can safely play Rae8, and when the bishop on d2 moves, the queen can go to c7 or a5.
notes.teaches: Don't fear doubled pieces on a file if they block each other; you can wait for them to move before committing your queen.
notes.plans: Wait for the bishop to move, then place the queen on c7 or a5.

notes.explains: The position offers multiple good plans. One strong idea is to trade pieces with Nf5, aiming to exchange on d5 and simplify. If White avoids the trade, Black should not fear threats to h7; g6 is a simple defense.
notes.teaches: When ahead, simplify by trading pieces. Don't be afraid of mating threats if you have a simple defensive move like g6.
notes.plans: Play Nf5, threatening to trade on d5. If White doesn't take, continue with g6 to defend h7.

notes.explains: After Nxd5, White recaptures with the rook. Black should not automatically recapture with the pawn; instead, look for a better move: Rxe1+ forces a rook trade, and then Qxd5 wins a pawn.
notes.teaches: Always look for checks and captures that improve your position before making automatic recaptures.
notes.plans: Play Rxe1+ first, then Qxd5.

notes.explains: Black is up a pawn and has a winning endgame. White plays Qh3, threatening h7. Black must create luft; g6 is better than h6 because the bishop on d3 controls h7.
notes.teaches: When making luft, consider which squares the opponent's bishop controls. g6 is often safer than h6 against a bishop on the long diagonal.
notes.plans: Play g6 to block the bishop's diagonal.

notes.explains: Black can win the a2 pawn with Qa5+ followed by Qxa2. But first, activating the rook with Re8 is even better; it creates a hidden threat of Qa1# if the d2 square is controlled.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, activate all pieces before grabbing pawns. A rook on an open file can create mating threats.
notes.plans: Play Re8, threatening Qa1# after controlling d2. Then pick up the a-pawn.

notes.explains: White cannot prevent the mate threat. If White plays Qh6, then Re2 controls d2, forcing Bxe2 and Qa1#. Other defenses also fail.
notes.teaches: When you have a coordinated attack, look for quiet moves that set up unstoppable threats.
notes.plans: After Re8, if Qh6, play Re2, then Qa1#.

notes.explains: After Bxf7+, Black's best is Kd7, but then Ba3 boxes in the king. White has a winning attack with all pieces active while Black is undeveloped.
notes.teaches: Recognize patterns from other openings (like the Italian) where a bishop sacrifice on f7 followed by a check from a3 or g5 leads to a decisive attack.
notes.plans: White will continue with Qe6 or other moves to deliver checkmate, exploiting Black's lack of development and exposed king.

notes.explains: Black blunders the bishop on b4. White must recapture correctly: Nxb4, not Bxb4, because Bxb4 allows the queen to pin the knight on b4 after ...Nxb4.
notes.teaches: When recapturing, consider which piece leaves the opponent's queen less active. Taking with the knight avoids a pin.
notes.plans: After Nxb4, White is up a piece and should continue developing with e4 and Bc4.

notes.explains: White has a large lead in development and an extra piece. Black's queen is still active but White can aim to trap it.
notes.teaches: When up material, simplify by completing development. Don't rush to trap the queen if it risks losing time.
notes.plans: Play Bd3, castle, and consider trapping the queen by covering escape squares like e6 and b2.

notes.explains: White develops the bishop to d3, preparing to castle. Black's queen has limited squares; White can consider trapping it.
notes.teaches: To trap a queen, methodically identify all escape squares and cover them with pieces without creating new escape routes.
notes.plans: Play Nd4 to cover e6, then consider Qc1 to cover b2, followed by Ra1 to trap the queen.

notes.explains: White covers b2 with Bf5, then plays Ra1, trapping the queen. Black resigns.
notes.teaches: Trapping a queen often requires multiple pieces cooperating. Cover all escape squares before springing the trap.
notes.plans: After Ra1, the queen has no safe square; Black must resign or lose the queen.

notes.explains: Black plays Bxe5, the better move. White should push e3 (or e4) to restrict the bishop and prepare development.
notes.teaches: In queenless middlegames with a material imbalance, central pawn pushes can restrict enemy pieces and open lines for your rooks.
notes.plans: Play e3, then develop with Be2, 0-0, and double rooks on the b-file.

notes.explains: White plays g4, a computer novelty, threatening g5 to drive away the knight and preparing Bg2. This is crushing.
notes.teaches: When the opponent is paralyzed, a pawn storm can accelerate the attack without allowing counterplay.
notes.plans: Play g5, then Bg2, followed by Nc4 and h3, maintaining the bind.

notes.explains: White methodically covers all queen escape squares and traps it. The queen had only a2 as a safe square, which White covered with Bf5.
notes.teaches: To trap a queen, first identify all escape squares, then cover them one by one without creating new escapes.
notes.plans: After Ra1, the queen is trapped; Black resigns.

notes.explains: Black resigns as the queen is trapped. White is up a piece with a winning position.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage and the opponent's pieces are uncoordinated, patience and piece cooperation will convert the win.
notes.plans: White will capture the queen and then win with the extra material.

notes.explains: After Nb5 and Nd6+, White gets a monster pawn on d6 that cramps Black's position. Black's dark-squared bishop is gone, so the d6 pawn is hard to attack.
notes.teaches: A knight on d6 supported by a pawn is a powerful outpost. Don't be afraid to sacrifice a pawn if you get such a strong positional trump.
notes.plans: Defend d6 with Bf4 after eliminating the knight on c6 (Nxc6). Then Black's lack of dark-squared bishop makes d6 a permanent weakness.

notes.explains: Black castles, which opens the h-file for White's attack. The pawn on d6 restricts Black's king escape squares.
notes.teaches: When your opponent castles into a weakened kingside, consider rook lifts (e.g., Re3) and queen maneuvers to the h-file. The d6 pawn prevents the king from fleeing to the center.
notes.plans: Play Ng5 to prevent f6 (which would loosen White's grip). Then lift the rook to e3 and bring the queen to g4 or h4 for a mating attack.

notes.explains: After Qg4, Black's best defense is f6, but then g5 is a strong reply, leading to a messy but winning attack for White. The key is that the g6 pawn is crucial; if it falls, Black's king is exposed.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, don't rush; consider prophylactic moves like Re3 to support the e6 pawn and enable doubling on the e-file. The immediate Qg4 was actually winning, but the preparatory Re3 was also good.
notes.plans: After f6, play g5 to open lines. If Black takes on g5, Qxg5 followed by Rh3 creates mating threats. The bishop on f4 covers c1, preventing back-rank counterplay.

notes.explains: In this line, Black's only move to avoid immediate loss is g5, but after Qf5 and Rh3, White threatens mate. Black must find Rf8, but White still has a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When the g6 pawn is captured, the h-file becomes lethal. The d6 pawn prevents the king from escaping to e7, making the mating net effective.
notes.plans: Continue with Rh3 and Qh5, threatening Qh7#. If Black defends, consider sacrificing the knight on e6 to open lines.

notes.explains: The engine shows that even in complex lines, White maintains an advantage. The bishop on f4 is crucial for covering c1, preventing Black from forcing a draw by repetition.
notes.teaches: Never rush a move. In this position, a3 (threatening Qxd5) was even stronger than Bf4, winning a pawn and simplifying. Always consider if you can improve your position before committing to a 'natural' move.
notes.plans: If you have time, look for ways to win material without compromising your attack. Here, a3 followed by Qxd5 would have been clean.

notes.explains: Black's Qb6 attacks b2. White can defend with Rb1, a solid working-person's move. There's no need to be fancy.
notes.teaches: Simple, solid moves are often best. Rb1 defends the pawn and prepares to develop the knight. Don't overcomplicate when a straightforward move works.
notes.plans: Play Rb1, then Nc3, Be2, and castle.

notes.explains: Black castles, preparing d4. White can preemptively restrict the queen with Na4, threatening to trap it. The queen's only squares are a5 and c5; taking them away traps it.
notes.teaches: Look for ways to trap the opponent's queen in the middlegame. Identify the queen's escape squares and try to cut them off.
notes.plans: Play Na4, then if the queen goes to a5, play b4 to trap it. If the queen goes to c5, play b4 as well.

notes.explains: Na4 attacks the queen and threatens b4, trapping it. Black must play Bd6 to create an escape square, but then White can capture and simplify.
notes.teaches: When you see a potential queen trap, commit to it. Even if the opponent finds a defense, you often gain time or material.
notes.plans: After Bd6, capture on d6 with the knight or bishop, then continue developing. White remains up a pawn with a solid position.

notes.explains: White plays exd5, thinking to win a pawn, but Black's bishop on b5 is undefended. Black can play Nxd5, and after the exchanges, Black wins a pawn because the bishop on b5 is hanging.
notes.teaches: When the opponent captures a pawn, check if any of their pieces are undefended. A simple recapture may win material if a piece is hanging.
notes.plans: Play Nxd5, and if White recaptures, capture the bishop on b5. Black ends up a pawn up.

notes.explains: After the exchanges, Black is up a pawn. White may try b5 to create counterplay, but Black can defend with Bd7 and maintain the extra pawn.
notes.teaches: When you win a pawn, consolidate by defending it and neutralizing the opponent's counterplay. Don't panic; just develop and keep the extra material.
notes.plans: Play Bd7, defending the pawn and preparing to castle. Then activate the rooks and push the queenside pawns.

notes.explains: Black plays f6, a move that looks weakening but is justified because White has no light-squared bishop to exploit the diagonal. Black's bishop can go to e6 to cover the weakness.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you can play 'ugly' moves like f6 if the opponent lacks the piece to punish it. Evaluate the opponent's remaining pieces before making such concessions.
notes.plans: Play f6 to solidify the e5 pawn and prepare to develop the bishop to e6. The king is safe enough because White's dark-squared bishop is gone.

notes.explains: White captures on f6, but Black can recapture with the pawn and then take on b5. The queen on b7 is annoying, but Black can retreat the queen to b8, threatening to trade queens or attack b5.
notes.teaches: When your queen is attacked, consider retreating to a square that also creates threats. Qb8 attacks b5 and offers a queen trade that favors you.
notes.plans: Play Qb8, and if White moves the queen, capture on b5. If White trades queens, recapture with the rook and Black's position is solid with an extra pawn.

notes.explains: Black's queen on b8 is well placed. White's threats are limited. Black should now focus on undermining the b5 pawn with c6 or a6, but must choose carefully to avoid counterplay.
notes.teaches: When deciding between two similar moves (a6 vs c6), calculate the opponent's best response. Here, c6 is better because a6 allows Rc1 skewering the bishop.
notes.plans: Play c6, attacking b5. If White plays Rc1, Black can capture on b5 and the skewer is avoided. After winning the pawn, activate the rook and push the a-pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays c6, undermining b5. White's best try is Rc1, but Black can simply capture on b5 and the rook on c1 doesn't skewer anything because the bishop is defended.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, look for the simplest way to convert. c6 wins a pawn cleanly without allowing counterplay.
notes.plans: After cxb5, Black is up two pawns. Then activate the rook to the c-file and push the a-pawn. The rook on c7 is annoying, but Black can chase it away with Bf8.

notes.explains: Black plays Bf8, attacking the rook on c7. The rook must move, and Black will capture it, leaving Black with a rook and two pawns vs a bishop and pawn. The a-pawn is a decisive passed pawn.
notes.teaches: In the endgame, prioritize activating your pieces and attacking the opponent's most active piece. Here, Bf8 chases the rook away and wins material.
notes.plans: After the rook moves, capture it. Then push the a-pawn, using the rook to support it. The bishop cannot stop both pawns.

notes.explains: Black captures on a3, winning a second pawn. The rook on c1 is passive. Black's rook on a8 is well placed behind the passed a-pawn.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, keep taking material if it doesn't compromise your position. Bxa3 is safe and increases the advantage.
notes.plans: Push the a-pawn. The rook on a8 supports it. White's rook and bishop cannot coordinate to stop it. Promote the pawn or win the rook.

notes.explains: Black pushes the a-pawn. White's rook on a1 is tied to the pawn. Black's rook on a8 is ideally placed. The win is straightforward.
notes.teaches: In rook vs bishop endgames with passed pawns, the rook is superior. Push the pawn and use the rook to support it. The bishop cannot defend against both the pawn and the rook.
notes.plans: Continue pushing the a-pawn. If White's rook leaves a1, the pawn promotes. If White's bishop tries to block, the rook captures it.

notes.explains: White is up a piece and plays Be3, unpinning and threatening to trade bishops. Black's bishop on g4 is attacked and must move or be exchanged.
notes.teaches: When up material, complete development first before committing to a conversion plan.
notes.plans: Trade pieces to simplify, especially queens, to reduce Black's counterplay.

notes.explains: Black captures on e3. White must decide whether to recapture with the knight or the pawn. Taking with the knight attacks the queen, forcing a queen trade.
notes.teaches: When converting a material advantage, choose the recapture that forces further simplification, especially queen trades.
notes.plans: Recapture with the knight (Nxe3), then after Qd7? Nxg4, or if Qc8, Nxg4 wins material.

notes.explains: After forcing the queen trade, White is up a piece. Now White should continue simplifying by trading rooks and centralizing the king.
notes.teaches: In a winning endgame, trade pieces but not pawns; bring the king to the center.
notes.plans: Play Rd1 to threaten rook trade, then centralize the king with Kf1 or h3 to create luft.

notes.explains: White plays Rd1, threatening to trade rooks. Black's knight is misplaced and White can win a pawn.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, active rooks and king centralization are key. Use multi-purpose moves like Kf1 (luft, king centralization, prevents back-rank mates).
notes.plans: Play Kf1, then take the free pawn on d4 or attack Black's pawns.

notes.explains: After trading rooks, White's king moves to f1, creating luft and centralizing. Black's king is passive.
notes.teaches: In king and pawn endgames, bring the king forward before pushing pawns. Use the pawn as a decoy to win opponent's pawns.
notes.plans: Centralize the king, then push the queenside pawns or use them to distract Black's king.

notes.explains: If Black had played Nf6 instead of Nc6, White would need to handle the fork threat on d5. The queen is overloaded defending both the knight on d5 and the bishop on g4.
notes.teaches: When your opponent attacks two pieces, look for moves that create new threats or exploit overloaded defenders. Consider intermediate moves that gain tempo.
notes.plans: Play Nf3-d4, attacking the bishop on g4 and defending the knight on d5? No, that leaves d5 undefended. Better: play Bf4, attacking c7 and threatening the rook, then after Black responds, capture on g4.

notes.explains: If Black plays e4, attacking the knight on d5, White must find a way to avoid losing a piece. The knight cannot move without losing the bishop on g4.
notes.teaches: When you cannot save both pieces, look for counterplay: e4 creates weaknesses. Play Bf4 attacking c7, then if Black takes the knight, Bxc7 wins the rook. But beware of intermediate moves like f6 blocking the check.
notes.plans: After Bf4, if Black takes the knight, recapture with the pawn (dxe4) to attack both the bishop and rook simultaneously, gaining a tempo.

notes.explains: In the line where Black plays e4, White can play Bf4, then after Nxf4? dxe4 attacks the bishop on g4 and the rook on a8. Black cannot defend both.
notes.teaches: When making an intermediate move, try to do it with tempo so the opponent cannot solve the original threat. Capturing with a pawn can create two threats at once.
notes.plans: Play dxe4, threatening both the bishop and rook. Black must lose material.

notes.explains: If Black plays e4 and White plays Bf4, Black might not take the knight but instead play something else. White should still look for drawbacks in Black's move.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a move that seems strong, look for its drawbacks. e4 weakens the d4 square and opens lines for White's pieces.
notes.plans: Consider moves like Ng5 or Bf4 that exploit the weaknesses created by e4.

notes.explains: The concept of tempo: a tempo is a unit of time in chess, equivalent to a move. Gaining a tempo means making a threat that forces the opponent to waste a move.
notes.teaches: Tempo is like a dollar to time's money. You gain a tempo when your move forces the opponent to respond to a threat, effectively giving you an extra move.

notes.explains: After Be3, if Black plays Bxe3, White can recapture with the knight (Nxe3) attacking the queen. Black can avoid the queen trade by playing Bd7, but that is passive.
notes.teaches: When you have a choice of recaptures, consider which one forces further simplification or creates a threat. The knight recapture attacks the queen and may force a queen trade.
notes.plans: If Black plays Bd7, White can centralize the queen and attack d5.

notes.explains: In the endgame, White played Kf1 instead of h3. Kf1 is multi-purpose: it creates luft, centralizes the king, and prevents back-rank checkmate.
notes.teaches: Always look for moves that accomplish multiple goals. Multi-purpose moves are efficient and often the best.
notes.plans: After Kf1, bring the king to the center and push pawns.

notes.explains: In a winning endgame with an extra piece, the plan is to centralize the king, then either promote a pawn directly or use a pawn as a decoy to win opponent's pawns.
notes.teaches: Two fundamental ways to win: 1) Direct promotion using your resources, 2) Decoy: distract the opponent's king with a pawn, then gobble up his pawns.
notes.plans: Bring the king to the center, then push the queenside pawns. If Black's king opposes, switch to the kingside.

notes.explains: In the game, White had a choice between taking the knight or the pawn. Taking the knight first attacks the rook and simplifies.
notes.teaches: When up material, prefer to trade pieces rather than pawns. Simplify to a winning endgame.
notes.plans: Take the knight, then continue simplifying.

notes.explains: At the end of the game, White brought all pieces into the attack rather than rushing for checkmate. This made the win easier.
notes.teaches: When you have a huge material advantage, bring all your pieces into the game before delivering checkmate. Patience prevents blunders.
notes.plans: Play Qe2, then Rf5, etc., to bring the rook and queen into the attack.

notes.explains: The king and queen are the worst defenders because when they are attacked, they must move, abandoning the piece they defended.
notes.teaches: If a piece is defended only by the king or queen, it is vulnerable. Attack the defender to win the piece.

notes.explains: Black played d5, c6, e6, and developed the bishop outside the pawn chain (to f5 or g4). This is a good scheme against the London System.
notes.teaches: In queen's pawn openings, develop the light-squared bishop before playing e6 to avoid locking it in. The move e6 is not bad in the Queen's Gambit, but here we can play more actively.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to f5 or g4, then castle by hand (Rf8, Kg8) if needed.

notes.explains: White played a3 and other non-developing moves. Black should ignore and develop. Castling by hand (Rf8, Kg8) is fine.
notes.teaches: When the opponent wastes time, just develop. Don't be intimidated by pawn moves. Castling by hand is a useful technique when normal castling is prevented.
notes.plans: Play h6 to ask the bishop's intention, then Rf8, Kg8, and later play Qg6 attacking g2.

notes.explains: Black played Qg6, threatening g2. White cannot castle because of tactics. If White plays Bg2, Black can play Bxh3 or other moves.
notes.teaches: When considering a discovered attack, ensure the opponent cannot capture the piece delivering the discovery while simultaneously defending the target.
notes.plans: Play Bh3, forcing g3, then win the exchange.

notes.explains: Black played Bh3, forcing g3, then won the exchange. The attack on the king is decisive.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, open lines and attack with pieces. A pawn sacrifice to open the f-file is often worth it.
notes.plans: After winning the exchange, bring the rook to f8 and deliver checkmate.

notes.explains: In the London System, White often plays Nc3, but this blocks the c-pawn and weakens control of d4. Black can exploit this by playing c5 and putting pressure on d4.
notes.teaches: In queen's pawn openings, Nc3 is often suboptimal because it prevents c3 or c4. Black should target the d4 pawn with moves like c5 and Nbd7.
notes.plans: Play c5 to undermine d4, then Nbd7 to challenge the knight on e5.

notes.explains: Black's …Nf6 is a blunder. White plays Bxf7+ Kxf7 Nxe5+ forking king and bishop, winning two pawns and leaving Black's king exposed. Black's best defense was …Nd7 to cover e5.
notes.teaches: Always consider your opponent's tactical resources. A seemingly natural developing move like Nf6 can be punished by a combination that exploits the weakened f7 square.
notes.plans: White is two pawns up with a shattered black kingside. Continue developing (e.g., Nc3, O-O) and prepare to attack down the f-file or along the a2-g8 diagonal.

notes.explains: After …Ke8 Nxg4, Black plays …Nd7 to block the e5 square. White is two pawns up and can choose between materialistic play (Nc3 protecting e4) or rapid development (O-O). Castling is fine; White should not fear ...Bxc3 because the dark-squared bishop is valuable for the attack.
notes.teaches: When ahead in material, avoid one-move threats that neglect development. Moves like c3 (threatening Qb3) can be tempting but may allow Black to consolidate. Instead, prioritize piece activity and king safety.
notes.plans: Castle kingside, then consider e5 to dislodge the knight on f6, opening lines for the queen and rook. The immediate threat is Qe6# after ...Nxe5 Qxe5.

notes.explains: White plays e5, attacking the knight on f6 and threatening Qe6#. Black cannot defend f6 with a piece because the rook on f1 controls the file. This pawn push uses the central pawn to dislodge Black's only defender, creating a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: Use central pawn advances to open lines and create direct mating threats. When the opponent's king is exposed, every tempo counts—don't waste time on slow maneuvers.
notes.plans: After …Nxe5 Qxe5, Black cannot block the f-file (e.g., ...Qf4? Rxf4). The threat of Qe6# is unstoppable, leading to a quick win.

notes.explains: Black's correct response to Bc4 is …Nd7, covering e5. After O-O, Black can play ...Ngf6 to cover the rook on f1. White then typically plays c3, intending Qb3, creating a battery on the b3-f7 diagonal and attacking b7. Black must be precise to survive the sharp complications.
notes.teaches: In sharp lines, knowing the correct defensive moves is crucial. Black must be willing to enter complex positions where one mistake can be fatal. The Fantasy Variation is a practical weapon because it forces Black to know theory.
notes.plans: White can consider h3 to provoke ...h5? (then g4) or play c3 and Qb3. Black should aim to castle quickly and challenge White's center.

notes.explains: After O-O Ngf6, White's queen should not go to f6 (to cover the rook) because that exposes the queen to tactical ideas. Instead, develop the knight to c3 and prepare c3 and Qb3. The queen belongs on b3, where it attacks b7 and creates a battery with the bishop.
notes.teaches: Avoid using the queen to do a knight's job. The queen is a valuable piece that should not be placed in front of a rook where it can be targeted by discovered attacks.
notes.plans: Play c3, then Qb3. If Black castles, White can consider taking on b7, but must be careful not to fall behind in development. The position remains sharp with mutual chances.

notes.explains: White's c3 prepares Qb3, creating a battery on the b3-f7 diagonal. This is a good idea because it attacks b7 and the f7 square simultaneously. Black must respond accurately, e.g., with ...Bd6 or ...Qc7.
notes.teaches: In the Fantasy Variation, the queen-bishop battery on b3-f7 is a key attacking idea. It pressures Black's queenside and kingside at the same time.
notes.plans: After c3, play Qb3. Black may castle, and then White can consider taking on b7 or continuing development with Bg5. The center remains fluid, and both sides must navigate tactical complications.

notes.explains: After …Bd6 Qb3 O-O, White can consider taking on b7, but this is risky because White is underdeveloped. The pawn on b7 is poisoned; Black gets active play. White should instead continue development with Bg5 or h3.
notes.teaches: Material gain is not always worth the cost of development. When the opponent has active piece play, it's often better to consolidate and maintain the initiative rather than grab a pawn.
notes.plans: Play h3 to prevent ...Bg4 and prepare g4, or play Bg5 to pin the knight. The position remains sharp, and White should aim to keep the pressure without overextending.

notes.explains: White plays h3, threatening g4 to chase the knight on f6. If Black retreats ...Bh5, then g4 traps the bishop. If Black plays ...h5, White can play g4 anyway, opening lines. This is a typical way to gain space and create attacking chances on the kingside.
notes.teaches: In closed positions with a space advantage, use pawn advances to cramp the opponent and create weaknesses. h3-g4 is a common plan to expand on the kingside.
notes.plans: After h3, if Black plays ...Bh5, then g4 wins the bishop. If Black plays ...h5, White can play g4 anyway, opening the h-file. White should continue developing and look for tactical blows.

notes.explains: After …Bh5, White plays g4, trapping the bishop. Black must give up the bishop or allow a decisive attack. This is a direct consequence of the h3-g4 plan.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is pinned to the edge of the board, a pawn advance can trap it. Always be alert to such tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: After g4, Black's bishop is lost. White will be up a piece and can continue the attack. The game is effectively over.

notes.explains: If Black retreats ...Bg6, White can continue with h4-h5, trapping the bishop again. The bishop on g6 is a target, and White can win it with accurate play.
notes.teaches: Once you have a bind on the opponent's piece, keep the pressure on. Use pawn advances to force the issue and win material.
notes.plans: Play h4, threatening h5. Black may try to escape with ...f6, but White's attack is overwhelming. The bishop is doomed.

notes.explains: White plays h4, threatening h5 to trap the bishop. Black cannot prevent it, and the bishop will be lost. This is the culmination of the kingside pawn storm.
notes.teaches: A consistent pawn storm can decisively win material. Once the opponent's piece is trapped, don't give them a chance to escape—push the pawns.
notes.plans: After h4, Black's bishop is lost. White will be up a piece and can convert the win.

notes.explains: After …Bxh5 Rxh5, White has won a piece. Black's kingside is shattered, and White has a rook on the h-file. The attack continues.
notes.teaches: Winning material is good, but don't stop there. Keep the pressure on the exposed king and look for further tactical blows.
notes.plans: White can bring the queen to the h-file or play Qg3, threatening mate. Black's position is hopeless.

notes.explains: White plays Qd2, preparing to double on the h-file or play Qh6. The queen joins the attack, and Black has no defense. The game is over.
notes.teaches: Coordinate your pieces for the final assault. Once the opponent's king is exposed, bring all available pieces to the attack.
notes.plans: Play Qh6, threatening Qxh7#. Black can only delay with ...f6, but White's attack is decisive.

notes.explains: After …f6 exf6 Rxf6, White plays Qh6, threatening Qxh7#. Black's rook on f6 is pinned by the bishop on c4, and there is no defense. The game ends in a few moves.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to create an escape, use the pin to maintain the mating threat. The bishop on c4 is a powerful attacking piece even in the middlegame.
notes.plans: After Qh6, Black's only move is ...Rf7, but then Qxh7+ Kf8 Qh8#. The attack is unstoppable.

notes.explains: White delivers checkmate with Qh8#. The entire sequence from h3 to mate is a model of how to conduct a kingside attack in the Fantasy Variation.
notes.teaches: A well-executed pawn storm followed by piece coordination can lead to a quick checkmate. The Fantasy Variation is a dangerous weapon that rewards aggressive play.
notes.plans: The game is over. White wins by checkmate.

notes.explains: This game illustrates the key ideas of the Fantasy Variation: rapid development, targeting f7, and a kingside pawn storm. Black's early mistake (…Nf6) was punished immediately, but even with correct play (…Nd7), White has a sharp attacking game.
notes.teaches: The Fantasy Variation is a practical and underrated weapon against the Caro-Kann. It leads to sharp, tactical positions where knowledge of the key ideas gives White excellent winning chances. Black must be precise to survive.
notes.plans: If you play the Fantasy Variation, study the main lines after …Nd7, including the h3-g4 plan and the queen-bishop battery. If you face it as Black, be prepared to defend accurately and know the critical defensive moves.

notes.explains: Black played Bc5, which walks into the center fork trick. After Nxe5, Black must play Bd6 to keep the bishop pair; otherwise, White gets a clear advantage.
notes.teaches: The center fork trick (Nxe5) is a common tactical motif when a knight on c3 attacks e5 and Black's bishop on c5 leaves e5 undefended. Always be alert for such forks.
notes.plans: After Nxe5 and Bd6, White has better center control and a vulnerable black bishop on e5. Develop naturally, avoiding premature pawn pushes like f4.

notes.explains: White has a clear advantage due to better center control and the awkward bishop on e5. The move f4 is premature because after Bxc3, dxc3, and d6, the f4 pawn becomes a liability, hindering White's bishop and creating kingside weaknesses.
notes.teaches: Avoid weakening pawn pushes like f4 when they create hooks and impede piece development. Prioritize natural development over aggressive but premature pawn moves.
notes.plans: Play Bd3, then castle kingside, followed by Bg5 to pin the knight on f6. Only then consider f4 to gain space.

notes.explains: White has developed harmoniously with Bd3, castling, and Bg5. The knight on c3 controls d5, and the bishop on g5 pins the knight. Black's bishop on e5 is awkward. The idea of Ne2 to 'pull the chair' is tempting but allows d5, leading to messy complications. Bg5 is simpler and strong.
notes.teaches: When a tactical idea like Ne2 creates unnecessary complications, prefer the solid developing move. Simplicity is often the most accurate way to maintain an advantage.
notes.plans: Prepare f4 to gain space and attack. Black may play h6 or Qe8 to unpin. White can then coordinate rooks with Qd2 and consider f4.

notes.explains: Black played h6 and Qe8 to escape the pin. White plays Qd2, coordinating the queen with the knight and preparing to meet Bxc3 without worry. The queen also eyes the c7 pawn after potential trades.
notes.teaches: Coordinate your pieces behind the scenes. Qd2 connects rooks and supports the knight, making Bxc3 harmless. Always scan for loose pawns after piece trades.
notes.plans: Continue development, possibly with f4 or Rfe1. If Black plays Ng4, chase it with h3. White is better due to space and piece activity.

notes.explains: Black's Ng4 was impulsive; White chased it with h3 and the knight is trapped. Black then blundered with Qe6, giving up the knight. White captures and is up a piece.
notes.teaches: When up material, avoid unnecessary complications. The simplest continuation is often best. Don't be greedy; sacrificing a pawn to eliminate Black's only developed piece and secure your king is a good trade.
notes.plans: After Bxg4, White is up a piece. Simplify by trading pieces, especially queens, to convert the advantage. Use the semi-open f-file for rook activity.

notes.explains: White plays f4 to open lines and trade queens. After exf4, Qxf4, Black plays f6, but White trades on e5 and wins a pawn. White is up a piece and a pawn.
notes.teaches: Use the semi-open f-file to force queen trades and simplify. When ahead, trading queens reduces Black's counterplay and makes conversion easier.
notes.plans: Continue simplifying. Black may play F5 to avoid recaptures. White can then play Bc4+ and push e6 to exploit Black's undeveloped queenside.

notes.explains: White plays Bc4+ and e6, threatening e7. Black's king is exposed and queenside undeveloped. White has a decisive attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed and their pieces are undeveloped, push passed pawns and create direct threats. Be flexible in your approach; there are many ways to win.
notes.plans: Threaten e7, then after Rf8, play Bf7+ to clear d8 for Qd8#. Calculate concretely; don't rely on pattern recognition alone (e.g., Qd8 might be a false friend if Black can defend with Be6).

notes.explains: Black is up a pawn and has played Kg8 to avoid tricks. White's Ng5 threatens nothing serious. Black should continue developing and consolidate.
notes.teaches: When up material, prioritize safety and development. Avoid unnecessary risks. The king on g8 is safe if the h7-e4 diagonal is covered.
notes.plans: Develop with d5 or h6, then complete development. If White plays Ne6, it's harmless; Black can ignore or prevent it with e5. Simplify by trading pieces if possible.

notes.explains: White sacrificed a knight for two pawns and an attack. Black's king is on h8, and White has some threats. Black should consolidate and use the extra piece.
notes.teaches: When under attack with extra material, stay calm and look for simplifying trades. Don't panic; the extra piece will tell.
notes.plans: Play Qd7 or Qe7 to defend and prepare to trade queens. If White offers a queen trade, consider accepting if it simplifies without losing too many pawns. Develop the rooks.

notes.explains: White forced a queen trade and won the exchange. Black is down an exchange but has an extra pawn. The endgame is winning for Black due to the extra piece.
notes.teaches: In endgames with extra material, activate your pieces and create passed pawns. Don't rush; methodically improve your position.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to c6 or e6, then bring the rook to the open file. Use the bishop to target weak pawns. White's king is exposed, so be careful of checks.

notes.explains: Black is up an exchange and a pawn. The knight on c6 is well placed. White's rook on d1 is active, but Black can double rooks on the d-file or push the e-pawn.
notes.teaches: In rook endgames, controlling open files is crucial. Use your extra piece to create threats and force weaknesses.
notes.plans: Play e5 to free the bishop, then Rd8 to challenge the d-file. If White trades rooks, the knight and bishop vs rook endgame is winning. Be patient.

notes.explains: Black weakened the kingside with g5, creating a hook. White can now use this pawn to open lines for an attack. The knight on e4 is strong, but White can target the g5 pawn.
notes.teaches: Pawn hooks on the side you are attacking are invitations to open files. Use them to launch an attack. Here, h4 is the correct way to exploit the g5 pawn.
notes.plans: Play h4 to open the h-file. If Black pushes g4, the diagonal to h6 opens. Then target the h6 pawn with Qd2 and Nxc3 (or Nxe4) to maintain pressure.

notes.explains: White sacrificed a pawn to win the h6 pawn and open the h-file. Black's king is exposed. White has a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When attacking, be willing to sacrifice material to open lines and expose the enemy king. The h-file is a highway to checkmate.
notes.plans: Play Qd2, then Rh4 to bring the rook into the attack. The bishop on h6 and queen can deliver mate. Black's pieces are undeveloped, so the attack should succeed.

notes.explains: White doubled rooks on the h-file. Black's king is trapped on f8. White threatens Rh8+ and mate. Black's pieces are passive.
notes.teaches: In a direct king attack, double heavy pieces on the open file. The threat of penetration is often decisive. Don't give the opponent time to consolidate.
notes.plans: Play Rh8+ to force Kg7, then R1h7+ and Qh6+ leading to mate. Alternatively, sacrifice the queen on h7 for a mating net.

notes.explains: After e5, Black retreats the knight to g8. White must decide how to defend the pawn on e5. Nf3 is a natural developing move but leaves the pawn loose; f4 secures it permanently but weakens the kingside. Both are reasonable, but Nf3 is more positional.
notes.teaches: When choosing between defending a pawn with a developing move or a pawn move, consider the trade-off between solidity and king safety.
notes.plans: White plays Nf3, accepting that the pawn may be lost if Black attacks it, but trusting that the development lead compensates.

notes.explains: White plays Qd5, defending both the pawn on e5 and the pawn on c5 simultaneously. This is better than Qd4 because after Qd4, Black could play ...Nc6 with tempo. Qd5 is safe here because Black has no immediate threats to the queen.
notes.teaches: Early queen development can be effective if it defends multiple pawns and cannot be easily harassed. Compare Qd4 vs Qd5: the latter avoids a tempo-gaining knight move.
notes.plans: White maintains the extra pawn and prepares to develop the bishop to f4 or c4, keeping pressure on Black's position.

notes.explains: Black plays …f6, attacking the pawn on e5. White must calculate carefully. The immediate exf6 Nxf6 attacks the queen, but White can improve by first playing Bc4, threatening the knight on g8 and preparing to recapture on f6 with the bishop or queen.
notes.teaches: When both queens are hanging, look for checks and desperado moves. Here, playing Bc4 first introduces a threat that changes the calculation after exf6.
notes.plans: White plays Bc4, then after ...e6, exf6 Nxf6 Qxc6 is possible, winning two pawns and destroying Black's structure.

notes.explains: Black captures on f4 instead of recapturing with the knight, allowing White to play fxg7, winning a rook. After …Qxg7? Qxg7 Bxg7 Bxg8, White is up a full rook.
notes.teaches: When a pawn reaches the seventh rank and attacks a rook, it can be devastating. Always consider such captures even if they seem risky.
notes.plans: White is up a rook and must consolidate. The immediate threat is ...Qc1+ and ...Qxb2, so White must address that.

notes.explains: After Bxg8, White is up a rook. Black's threats are ...Qc1+ and ...Qxb2. White can meet ...Qc1+ with Ke2, and if ...Qxb2, then Nbd2 connects the rooks. Alternatively, Bxd5! is even stronger: after ...Qc1+ Ke2, if ...Qxh1, then Bxg8 wins the knight and White's attack is decisive.
notes.teaches: When two knights defend each other, they can be overloaded. Here, Bxd5 exploits the fact that the knight on g8 must defend both the queen on h1 and the knight on d5.
notes.plans: White plays Bxd5, forcing a winning position. The king can safely move to e2, and the knight on d2 will connect the rooks.

notes.explains: White is up a piece and has a winning attack. The black king is stuck in the center. White's plan is to bring the queen to d6, then play Ng5, threatening mate on f7. If the king escapes to e8, a queen triangulation forces it back to d8 for a checkmate.
notes.teaches: In a winning position, reverse-engineer the mate: identify the target position (king on d8, knight on g5) and use the queen to force the king there.
notes.plans: Play Qd6, then Ng5. If ...Ke8, then Qe5+ Kf8 (or ...Kd8 leads to immediate mate), Qf6+ Kg8, Qf7+ Kh8, and Qg7#. If no mate is available, consolidate by developing the knight to d2 and activating the rook.

notes.explains: The Budapest Gambit (d4 Nf6 c4 e5) is a reputable gambit where Black sacrifices a pawn for rapid development and initiative. The main line is Ng4, aiming to regain the pawn, while Ne4 is more speculative.
notes.teaches: Choose the more solid gambit line (Ng4) over the speculative one (Ne4) for reliable compensation.
notes.plans: Develop quickly, target White's kingside, and use tactical threats to regain the pawn or launch an attack.

notes.explains: After d4 Nf6 c4 e5 dxe5 Ng4 Nf3 Nc6 Bf4, Black should play Bb4+ (not Bc5, which allows e3). The check develops with tempo and sets up the smothered mate trap.
notes.teaches: Use checks to gain tempo and force the opponent into passive moves, creating tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: After Bb4+, White often plays Nbd2, then Black plays Qe7, and if a3, Ncxe5 threatens Nxd3#.

notes.explains: If White avoids the trap with e3 instead of a3, Black can take the knight on f3 and play d6, leading to a position where Black has the two bishops, harmonious development, and no weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When the opponent avoids a trap, transition into a solid positional setup with good piece play.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to the long diagonal, castle, and prepare rook activity.

notes.explains: Black's knight on c6 pressures the d4 pawn. White's bishop on b5 neutralizes the knight and threatens to ruin Black's pawn structure if he castles long.
notes.teaches: Tailor development to the opponent's moves rather than developing to pre-planned squares. Bishop b5 is better than c4 here because it directly addresses the knight's pressure.
notes.plans: Continue development, aiming to exploit Black's lagging kingside development and misplaced queen.

notes.explains: Black's bishop d7 is a mistake. White can punish with d5, exploiting the lead in development (three pieces developed to two) and Black's uncastled king.
notes.teaches: When ahead in development, open the center to increase the pressure. A pawn push like d5 can be justified if it disrupts the opponent's coordination.
notes.plans: Push d5, forcing the knight back, then continue developing with tempo.

notes.explains: After d5, the knight retreats to b8. White's bishop on b5 now blocks Black's knight from developing to c6. Retreating the bishop to c4 is better than capturing on d7, which would help Black redevelop.
notes.teaches: Retreating moves can be strong if they maintain pressure. Here, bishop c4 keeps the d5 pawn defended and leaves Black's knight stuck on b8.
notes.plans: Play Bc4, then Qe2 to defend the bishop and prepare Be3 and long castling.

notes.explains: White defends the bishop on c4 with Qe2, which also x-rays the king and prepares Be3 and long castling. This is better than b3, which would leave the knight on c3 undefended and vulnerable to b5.
notes.teaches: When defending a piece, prefer moves that also serve other purposes (development, attack). Avoid leaving pieces undefended on squares accessible to the opponent.
notes.plans: Play Be3 with tempo, then castle long and prepare an attack.

notes.explains: Black plays Na6, intending to castle long. White can prevent this with the prophylactic move g4, which threatens Bxa6 or Nxf7 if Black castles. This is a proactive way to stop the opponent's plan.
notes.teaches: Prophylaxis should be active: look for moves that both prevent the opponent's idea and create new threats. Here, g4 stops castling and prepares an attack.
notes.plans: After g4, if Black castles, capture on a6 or f7. If not, continue the attack.

notes.explains: White sacrifices a knight on f7 to expose the king. After Rg8, White can play Qxa6, threatening the rook on g8 and the queen on b7, eventually winning material.
notes.teaches: When ahead in development, sacrifices to open the king are often justified. Calculate forcing sequences to ensure the attack succeeds.
notes.plans: After Qxa6, if Qb7, take the queen and then the rook. The pawn on f7 freezes Black's development.

notes.explains: After winning the exchange, White's knight on d6 is a monster. Black tries to close the gate with Nd6, but White slips through with Ra4-d4, combining with the knight to attack.
notes.teaches: When the opponent tries to block your entry, look for ways to 'slip through the gate' by moving the rook to a different file or rank. The knight on d6 is powerful because it restricts Black's king and pawns.
notes.plans: Play Ra4, then double rooks on the d-file, and promote the e-pawn.

notes.explains: Black's e6 and c6 is a passive setup. White should not play e5 immediately because it closes the center, reducing the impact of Black's poor development. Also, the pawn chain e5-d4 is vulnerable to c5, and the knight on c3 blocks the c3 pawn from defending the base.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes passive pawn moves, keep the center open to exploit their lack of development. Avoid creating a pawn chain that gives the opponent a target (the base).
notes.plans: Develop naturally, aiming to keep the center fluid. Consider c3 to support d4 if needed.

notes.explains: White captures on h6 to double Black's pawns, then plays c3 to solidify the pawn chain. The bishop on d3 is well placed, and the pawn on e5 is strong.
notes.teaches: When you have a pawn chain, use the least valuable piece to defend it. Here, c3 is better than Be3 because it uses a pawn instead of a bishop.
notes.plans: Prepare a kingside attack with h4, aiming for a Greek Gift sacrifice on h7.

notes.explains: White plays h4 to control the g5 square, preparing a Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh7+). If Black prevents with h6, the pawn becomes a hook that White can use to open the kingside with g5 or build a battery with Bc2 and Qd3.
notes.teaches: The Greek Gift sacrifice requires control of g5. h4 is a preparatory move that also creates a hook if Black responds with h6. A hook is a pawn that can be used to open lines against the king.
notes.plans: If Black doesn't prevent, play Bxh7+ and Nxg5+ with a mating attack. If Black plays h6, consider g5 or Bc2 followed by Qd3.

notes.explains: White builds a battery with Bc2 and Qd3, threatening mate on h7. Black's only defense is g6, but then White can capture the h6 pawn with the bishop, shattering Black's kingside.
notes.teaches: A battery (queen and bishop on the same diagonal) can create immediate mating threats. The hook pawn on h6 becomes a target that can be used to open lines.
notes.plans: After g6, play Bxh6, breaking the pawn shield and continuing the attack.

notes.explains: White's c4 is a rare move that weakens d4. Black should not play e5 because it creates a symmetrical weakness on d5. Instead, fianchetto the bishop to pressure d4.
notes.teaches: Avoid creating symmetrical weaknesses. Here, e5 would weaken d5, giving White a target. Instead, develop pieces to control key squares without creating pawn weaknesses.
notes.plans: Play g6, Bg7, d6, and Nf6 (or Ne7), aiming to control d4.

notes.explains: White pins the knight on f3 with Bg4, intending to exchange it and then plant a knight on d5 (the Smyslov idea). This enhances control over d4 and d5.
notes.teaches: The Smyslov idea: exchange a bishop for a knight to gain control of a key square (here d5). Pattern recognition allows you to apply this idea in different positions.
notes.plans: After Bxf3, play Qxf3 and then Nd5, establishing a powerful outpost.

notes.explains: White has a knight on d5, a classic outpost. Black's pieces are passive. White should now activate the queen and rook, and prepare a queenside pawn break with b5.
notes.teaches: Once an outpost is established, activate all pieces to increase pressure. The queen can join the attack, and rooks should be centralized. A pawn break like b5 can open lines.
notes.plans: Play Qa5 to pressure a2 and the knight, then a6 to prepare b5. If White prevents b5, look for other weaknesses like b3.

notes.explains: White blundered with a4, allowing Black to open the a-file and win a rook. The knight on d4 is the decisive piece, as it can jump to c6 or e6. Black's plan is to continue with b5 and activate the rook.
notes.teaches: When you have a powerful outpost, look for tactical opportunities to exploit the opponent's weaknesses. Here, the knight on d4 is a monster that can win material.
notes.plans: Play b5, then bring the rook to the second rank and deliver checkmate or win more material.

notes.explains: Black has a winning endgame with an extra rook. The bishop on d5 is powerful, and Black can promote the b-pawn. The game is decided.
notes.teaches: In winning positions, simplify and avoid counterplay. Use your pieces to support pawn promotion.
notes.plans: Push the b-pawn, use the rook to attack, and force resignation.

notes.explains: After …Nc6, the natural d5 closes the center and lets Black's knight retreat. Taking on c3 with Nxc3 opens the center and leaves Black's knight on e5 unsupported.
notes.teaches: When a central pawn capture opens lines and leaves an opponent's piece without pawn support, it is often better than pushing past. The knight on e5 looks active but is vulnerable to attack.
notes.plans: Develop flexibly with Nc3, keeping options open. Avoid committal moves like Nf3 or f4 until Black's intentions are clearer.
