notes.explains: Black played Bc5 and then dxc3, which is a mistake. The correct response is Nf6, transposing to the Italian after cxd4 Bb4+. Falling for the trap Bxf7+ forces the king out and White picks up the bishop on c5 with Qd5+, leaving Black much worse.
notes.teaches: In the Scotch Gambit, Black should not cling to the extra pawn on d4 with dxc3; instead, develop with Nf6 and accept the pawn sacrifice for active play.
notes.plans: After Bxf7+, Black must choose the safest king retreat. Kf8 is best because Ke8 leaves the king exposed on the e-file and makes d6 a hook for e5.

notes.explains: After Kf8, Black must develop quickly and aim to castle by hand. The immediate plan is to play h6, then Kf7, Rf8, and Kg8, using the bishop on c8 to cover checks on the light squares.
notes.teaches: When the king is exposed, prioritize castling by hand over material. Do not cling to extra pawns if they compromise king safety.
notes.plans: Play h6 to prevent Nxg5, then Kf7, Rf8, and eventually Kg8. Develop the knight to f6 and bishop to g4 or e6.

notes.explains: After Nxf7, Black's king is exposed and White has a strong attack. The knight sacrifice opens lines.
notes.teaches: Initiative and development can justify material sacrifices, especially when the opponent's king is vulnerable.
notes.plans: Continue attacking the king with pieces like Qe2 and O-O-O, exploiting the open files.

notes.explains: d4 opens the center, leading to open positions where piece activity matters most.
notes.teaches: The Scotch Game teaches active development and punishes slow play because the open center exposes weaknesses.
notes.plans: Develop knights and bishops to active squares, aiming to control the center and prepare attacks.

notes.explains: White plays d4, challenging Black's center. This is a natural move in the Alekhine's Defence, leading to open positions.
notes.teaches: In the Alekhine's Defence, White often plays d4 early to challenge Black's pawn on e5. Black's best response is usually ...d6 or ...exd4.
notes.plans: White will continue with d5 or Nc3 depending on Black's response.

notes.explains: d6 is passive because it opens the light-squared bishop but blocks the dark-squared bishop, which can only go to e7.
notes.teaches: When choosing a move, consider how it affects both bishops; blocking one bishop often makes the move suboptimal.
notes.plans: White should continue developing with Nc3 and Bc4, pressuring f7.

notes.explains: Black plays d6, a standard move in the Alekhine's Defence. White now has several options, including the Four Pawns Attack with c4.
notes.teaches: After e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 d6, White can choose the Four Pawns Attack with d5 and then c4. This is a sharp line that requires precise play.
notes.plans: White will play d5 next, gaining space and forcing Black's knight to move.

notes.explains: Developing the knight to c3 is natural; now we need to place the bishop on a good square.
notes.teaches: Bc4 is better than Bb5 because Bb5 can be neutralized by Bd7, while Bc4 maintains lasting pressure on f7.
notes.plans: Play Bc4, targeting f7 and preparing for a potential kingside attack.

notes.explains: g6 is a mistake because it wastes two tempi to fianchetto the bishop, leaving Black underdeveloped.
notes.teaches: In open positions, you cannot afford slow development; prioritize getting pieces out and castling.
notes.plans: Exploit Black's lag in development with aggressive play, like Nxc6 and e5.

notes.explains: Black's d6 is passive; it blocks the bishop and doesn't develop. The main moves are Bc5 or Nf6.
notes.teaches: In the opening, develop pieces actively. Moves like d6 that obstruct your own development are generally inferior.
notes.plans: Prepare d4 with c3 to occupy the center with pawns.

notes.explains: Black plays d6, a passive move that blocks the bishop. White should immediately open the center with d4, exploiting the lead in development.
notes.teaches: Against passive moves like d6, the automatic response is to open the center with d4, taking advantage of the development lead.
notes.plans: Play d4, and after the trade on d4, the queen ends up on d4 with a comfortable advantage.

notes.explains: c3 prepares d4, aiming to build a strong pawn center.
notes.teaches: Occupy the center with pawns when possible. Prepare d4 with c3 rather than playing it immediately if it allows exchanges.
notes.plans: Follow up with d4, then recapture with a piece to maintain central control.

notes.explains: White plays d4 and e4, aiming for a pawn center. Black's response is unusual.
notes.teaches: Occupy the center with pawns. e4 is a natural follow-up to d4.
notes.plans: Develop pieces and maintain the center.

notes.explains: White wins a pawn and exposes Black's king. Black's king is on e7.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, prioritize development and king safety. Don't rush to attack; bring pieces out first.
notes.plans: Castle queenside to avoid counterplay and prepare an attack.

notes.explains: White castles queenside, avoiding Black's potential kingside attack. The king is safe on the queenside.
notes.teaches: Castle to the side where your king is safer. If the opponent has pawns missing on one side, castle to the opposite side to avoid giving them an attack.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to f3, then open the center with d5 or c5.

notes.explains: White advances e5 to clamp down on Black's position, then ignores the d4 pawn and develops with Nf3 instead of defending with c3.
notes.teaches: In the Steinitz Variation, White sacrifices the d4 pawn to accelerate development and maintain the e5 pawn, which restricts Black's pieces.
notes.plans: White will continue developing (Bd3, Re1) and overprotect e5, aiming to build an attack while Black struggles to free their position.

notes.explains: In this position, Black can play e5 even though White has a bishop on b2. If White takes on e5, Black has tactical resources like Ng4 or Nfd7 to regain the pawn or create counterplay.
notes.teaches: A fianchettoed bishop does not automatically prevent the e5 break. Black can often force e5 with tactical tricks, especially if White's pieces are not optimally placed.
notes.plans: After e5 dxe5, play Ng4 or Nfd7 to attack the e5 pawn and the bishop on b2.

notes.explains: When White plays Nc3 instead of Nf3, Black can switch to c5. This exploits the diagonal to b2 and creates tactical threats like Ne4 and Qa5.
notes.teaches: Be ready to change your pawn break based on White's move order. c5 can be more effective than e5 when White's knight is on c3, as it targets the b2 bishop and opens lines.
notes.plans: Play c5, and if White plays d5, follow up with Qa5 and Ne4, pressuring the b2 bishop and the center.

notes.explains: After d5, Black plays Qa5, threatening Ne4 and putting pressure on the d5 pawn. White cannot easily defend because the bishop on b2 is exposed.
notes.teaches: Qa5 is a strong move in such positions, as it pins the knight on c3 and prepares tactical operations like Ne4 or Nxd5.
notes.plans: Follow up with Nc6, then if White plays d5, capture with cxd5 and play Bxc3+ winning a pawn.

notes.explains: If Black plays Nf8 instead of Kh7, the sacrifice on e6 is unsound because Black can defend with N6h7, holding g6. White's attack would be repelled.
notes.teaches: Not every sacrifice is sound. Black's best defense is to bring a knight to h7 to cover g6 and involve the bishops. Recognizing when an attack is premature is crucial.
notes.plans: If Black defends correctly, White should switch plans, perhaps playing d4 to open the center.

notes.explains: After Black plays Nf8, White can switch to d4, opening the center. The e5 pawn is now vulnerable, and White can consider sacrifices on e5 or f7.
notes.teaches: Playing d3 does not mean you cannot later play d4. Be flexible and open the center when it benefits you, especially if the opponent's pieces are poorly placed.
notes.plans: Play d4, and if Black takes, recapture with the knight and put pressure on e5. If Black does not take, consider pushing d5 or sacrificing on e5.

notes.explains: White plays c3 to create a pawn chain that blunts Black's dark-squared bishop on g7. The downside is that the knight loses the c3 square, but it can later develop to d2, similar to the London System.
notes.teaches: When facing the Modern Defense, c3 is a solid, positional setup that limits Black's bishop and allows for slow, patient development.
notes.plans: Develop with Bd3, Nf3, and later Nbd2-f1-e3-g4, aiming to occupy the f6 square.

notes.explains: Black plays d5, which is a strategic mistake because it weakens the dark squares. White should close the center with e5, not capture on d5, to exploit those weaknesses.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens dark squares, closing the center with e5 gives you a clear target and a long-term plan.
notes.plans: Play e5, then develop with Nf3, and later maneuver the knight to f6 via d2-f1-e3-g4.

notes.explains: Black plays c4, further locking the center. This gives White a free hand to attack on the kingside, as Black's dark-square weaknesses become permanent.
notes.teaches: When the center is closed, you can safely maneuver pieces without fear of immediate counterplay. The 'three-move rule' is less relevant in closed positions.
notes.plans: Prepare the knight maneuver Nbd2-f1-e3-g4 to target f6, and eventually attack on the kingside.

notes.explains: f3 looks anti-developmental, but the point is to prepare e2-e4, seizing a massive center. Black's most common reply Nc6 allows White to execute the plan.
notes.teaches: Sometimes violating development principles is justified if it sets up a powerful central pawn duo. The key is to have a concrete follow-up.
notes.plans: Play e4, then after dxe4, interpose d5 to kick the knight, then recapture on e4 with a pawn mass.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, a move the teacher doesn't know. White must choose between dxe5, exd5, or f4. f4 is tempting to chase knights and create a pawn chain, but it weakens the king.
notes.teaches: When facing an unfamiliar move, rely on general principles but stay flexible. f4 is a natural-looking pawn lever, but concrete calculation is needed.
notes.plans: Consider f4 to push e5 later, or exd5 to win a pawn but risk development issues.

notes.explains: f4 is played, but Black responds with Ng4, attacking the queen and threatening to exploit White's weak dark squares. White's king is exposed and development lags.
notes.teaches: A pawn chain is only good if your king is safe and pieces are developed. Here f4 created weaknesses without sufficient compensation.
notes.plans: White must defend against Ng4 threats and try to catch up in development. Options include Qxd5, Be2, or h3.

notes.explains: Black's queen on e7 blocks the bishop and is vulnerable. White has a lead in development and should not rush sacrifices.
notes.teaches: Developing the queen early can obstruct piece development and create targets. Complete development before launching attacks.
notes.plans: Castle, then consider Nxc3 or Rxe1 to exploit the queen's position.

notes.explains: White pushes h4 to dislodge the knight on g3 (or g6 in similar positions). This is a common idea to gain space and open lines.
notes.teaches: Pushing the h-pawn can be used to kick away a knight that blocks a bishop or to create attacking chances, even if it weakens the king's pawn shield. Evaluate concretely, not by dogma.
notes.plans: After h5, if the knight moves, the bishop on f5 becomes active. If the knight captures on h5, recapture with the bishop and attack.

notes.explains: Black's Qb6 pins the pawn on b2 and threatens Nxg5. White must respond carefully; moving the king to h1 is safe.
notes.teaches: When your pawn push is met with a counterattack, don't panic. A king move can defuse the pin and maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: After Kh1, continue with the plan to dislodge the knight or sacrifice on h7.

notes.explains: Black played b5 early, sending the bishop to b3 where it wants to go anyway. The problem is that Black's kingside is not developed, so White can open the center with d4 and then play Ng5 with extra force.
notes.teaches: Don't chase the bishop to b3 before you've developed your kingside. The priority is kingside development (Nf6, Be7, castling) before playing b5.
notes.plans: White should play d4 to open the center, then consider Ng5 now that the center is tense. Black should aim to finish kingside development and castle before pushing b5.

notes.explains: After d4, the center is tense. Ng5 becomes stronger because if Black plays d5, White can capture e5 and open the center, exploiting Black's lack of development.
notes.teaches: Revisit moves that were previously ineffective when the position changes. A move like Ng5 may become good after a preparatory move like d4.
notes.plans: White should consider Ng5, threatening f7. Black should respond with d5 to close the center, but White can then take on e5 with advantage.

notes.explains: Black played Bg4, pinning the knight. White can respond with f3, forcing the bishop to h5, but then White has Bxf7+ winning a pawn and exposing the king.
notes.teaches: When your opponent pins a knight, consider intermediate moves like Bxf7+ before dealing with the pin. Don't automatically retreat or defend.
notes.plans: White should play Bxf7+ first, then f3 to drive the bishop away. Black should consider moving the bishop to d7 instead of h5 to avoid helping White's attack.

notes.explains: If Black plays Nf6 on move 4, White usually castles. Black should then play Be7, not d6, to avoid Ng5 ideas.
notes.teaches: Prioritize kingside development (Be7) before pushing d6. This prevents White from playing Ng5 with tempo.
notes.plans: Black will castle, then play b5 and d6. White will play Re1 or d3.

notes.explains: Black has completed kingside development and castled, then played b5 and d6. The position is solid and Black is out of the opening woods.
notes.teaches: The correct order in the Ruy Lopez is: develop kingside, castle, then play b5 and d6. This avoids many tactical pitfalls.
notes.plans: Black can consider c5 or other breaks. White will play c3 or d4.

notes.explains: In the Exchange Variation, after White takes on c6 and e5, Black should play Qd4, threatening the knight and the e4 pawn. This is a strong move that gives Black the initiative.
notes.teaches: In the Exchange Variation, Qd4 is a good move that attacks two targets and forces White to defend. It leads to a favorable endgame for Black.
notes.plans: After Qd4, White usually plays Nf3, then Qxe4, and after Qe2, Black trades queens and has a better endgame with the king in the center.

notes.explains: Black has developed, castled, and placed a rook on e8. White's king is still in the center and Black has a clear advantage.
notes.teaches: In the Exchange Variation, Black gets a comfortable endgame with active pieces and a vulnerable white king. This is a good line for Black to know.
notes.plans: Black will continue to pressure the e-file and look for ways to exploit the king's position.

notes.opening: Ruy Lopez, Exchange Variation, Fishing Hook Trap
notes.explains: Black plays Bg4, pinning the knight. This is a trap: if White plays h3, Black can play h5, and if White takes the bishop, Black has Qh4 with a mating attack.
notes.teaches: The Fishing Hook Trap is a sharp line where Black sacrifices a bishop for a devastating attack. White must know the correct response (d3) to avoid losing.
notes.plans: White should play d3, ignoring the pin. Black can then play Qf6 or other moves, but the position is complex.

notes.explains: White plays d3, ignoring the pin. This is the correct response, avoiding the trap. Black can then play Qf6 or other moves.
notes.teaches: When faced with a pin, sometimes the best response is to ignore it and continue development. d3 is a solid move that prevents the trap.
notes.plans: Black can play Qf6, Be7, or other moves. The position is roughly equal.

notes.explains: Black takes on e4, entering the Open Ruy Lopez. This is a sharp line that requires precise play from both sides.
notes.teaches: The Open Ruy Lopez is a legitimate but dangerous line for Black. It requires good knowledge of theory to avoid early problems.
notes.plans: White will play d4 or Re1. Black must be ready to defend the e4 pawn or counterattack.

notes.explains: Black plays b5 and d5, challenging the center. This is a theoretical line. Black must be careful not to fall into traps.
notes.teaches: In the Open Ruy Lopez, Black often plays b5 and d5 to counterattack. This requires precise calculation.
notes.plans: White can play c3 or Nbd2. The position is complex.

notes.explains: Black has played the Closed Ruy Lopez, a solid and classical setup. Both sides have developed harmoniously.
notes.teaches: The Closed Ruy Lopez is a reliable system for Black. It focuses on solid development and slow buildup.
notes.plans: Black can play Na5, c5, or other breaks. White will play d4 or a4.

notes.explains: White plays h3, preventing Bg4. This is a common move in the Closed Ruy Lopez.
notes.teaches: Small prophylactic moves like h3 can prevent pins and maintain flexibility.
notes.plans: Black can play Na5, c5, or Re8. The game continues in a strategic manner.

notes.explains: Black's b5 is a dubious pawn sacrifice, not a standard Benko Gambit (which requires a6). White is simply up a pawn with no compensation for Black.
notes.teaches: Against offbeat openings, don't overthink—develop naturally and trust your extra material. The simplest response is often best.
notes.plans: Take the pawn with cxb5, then develop knights (Nc3, Nf3) and bishops (Bf4, Bd3) while protecting the b5 pawn.

notes.explains: Nc3 is flexible: it protects the b5 pawn and prepares e4. Bf4 is better than Bg5 because Bg5 would allow a quick trade with Be7, while Bf4 pressures c7.
notes.teaches: When choosing a developing square for the bishop, consider which pawns it pressures and whether the opponent can easily trade it off.
notes.plans: Play e3, Bd3, Nf3, and h3 to prevent ...Nh5 harassing the bishop.

notes.explains: White plays Nc3, which can lead to a Grand Prix Attack or a Closed Sicilian, but also keeps the option of transposing into an Open Sicilian with d4 later. Black's response depends on which Sicilian variation they play against Nf3.
notes.teaches: Against Nc3, choose your move based on your preferred Sicilian setup against Nf3. For Najdorf players, d6 is recommended; for Sveshnikov or Accelerated Dragon players, Nc6; for Kan or Taimanov players, e6.
notes.plans: Black should develop harmoniously, aiming for a flexible setup.

notes.explains: Black plays a6, preparing b5 to expand on the queenside and fianchetto the light-squared bishop. This is an underrated response that works well against the Grand Prix Attack and the Closed Sicilian.
notes.teaches: Early queenside expansion with b5 can be a good way to counter White's setup, gaining space and activating the bishop on b7.
notes.plans: Follow up with b5, Bb7, and then develop kingside pieces, keeping the center flexible with d6 and e6.

notes.explains: Black builds a hedgehog-like structure with pawns on d6 and e6, controlling central squares. The queen on c7 connects rooks, controls e5, and prepares for action. The knight on d7 is preferable to c6 as it doesn't block the bishop.
notes.teaches: In such setups, the queen often goes to c7 to support the center and connect rooks. The knight belongs on d7 to keep the c-file open for the bishop and to avoid blocking the bishop's diagonal.
notes.plans: Castle kingside or keep the king in the center if both flanks are dangerous. Prepare to counter White's kingside expansion with h5 if needed.

notes.explains: Black plays h5 to prevent White's g4 expansion, keeping the kingside closed. This is risky because it weakens the kingside, but it forces White to reconsider their plans. The king remains in the center for now.
notes.teaches: Sometimes it's better to prevent the opponent's expansion even at the cost of weakening your own pawn structure. Keeping the king in the center can be safer than castling into an attack.
notes.plans: If White plays a4, respond with b4 to keep the queenside closed. Consider castling queenside if the center remains closed.

notes.explains: White plays c3, weakening the d3 pawn. Black notices that the pawn on d3 is now vulnerable to undermining with c4, rather than direct attack.
notes.teaches: A weak pawn can be exploited not only by attacking it with pieces but also by using your own pawns to undermine the opponent's pawn structure. Here, c4 attacks the base of White's pawn chain.
notes.plans: Play bxc3 first to avoid dropping the b4 pawn, then play c4 to attack d3. Follow up with Nc5 to put more pressure on d3.

notes.explains: White plays f3 with the immediate idea of playing e4, challenging Black's control of the center. The battle revolves around whether White can successfully push e4 under favorable conditions.
notes.teaches: In the Sämisch Variation, White's entire setup is directed at preparing e4. Development should prioritize king safety (castling) and piece coordination over gaining space for its own sake.
notes.plans: Develop with e3, Bd3, Nge2, O-O, then prepare e4. Once e4 is played, White will have a powerful kingside attack.

notes.explains: White's last move Nd2 is awkward because it blocks the bishop and does nothing to prevent ...Bg4. The immediate threat is ...Bg4 attacking the queen and threatening to sink into f3.
notes.teaches: When your opponent makes a move that doesn't address the main threats, you should punish it by executing your plan immediately.
notes.plans: Play ...Bg4 to pin the knight and create pressure on f3.

notes.explains: White played f3, which weakens the g3 pawn and creates a typical tactical pattern. The pawn on g3 becomes a weak link, and sacrificing the bishop on g3 is low-risk because Black has a perpetual check in reserve.
notes.teaches: When evaluating a sacrifice, if you spot at least a perpetual check, the risk is greatly reduced. You can then try to find a win, knowing a draw is guaranteed.
notes.plans: Play ...Bxg3, forcing hxg3 (or else checkmate), then ...Qxg3 with perpetual check. Black may have more than a perpetual, such as winning material (e.g., the rook on e1).

notes.explains: After the sacrifice, Black brings the rook to e8, defending the bishop and preparing to bring it into the attack. The rook can later go to e4 to attack g4 or support a pawn push.
notes.teaches: In attacking positions, bring all available pieces into the attack. The rook on e8 is well-placed to support further advances like ...f5 to open the f-file.
notes.plans: Play ...f5 to open the f-file and accelerate the attack. If White plays g5, Black has a passed pawn on f5 and can continue the pressure.

notes.explains: Black accepts the gambit but plans to return the extra piece to avoid deep theory. By playing Ng6 and then sacrificing the knight back, Black gains development and a solid position.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit you haven't studied, returning the material can simplify the position and reduce White's attacking chances. Development and activity can compensate for the sacrificed piece.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, castle, and aim for a solid middlegame with equal chances.

notes.explains: After d4 exd4, Black castles. White can play Nxe4 (Max Lange) or d6 (solid but passive). Here Black chooses the principled Nxe4.
notes.teaches: In the Max Lange, Black can accept the pawn on e4. White gets compensation with pressure on the e-file and a lead in development.
notes.plans: After Nxe4, White plays Re1, forcing d5. Black must be careful: the knight on e4 is pinned, and the queen must move after Bxd5 Nxd5 Nc3.

notes.explains: After dxe5, Black can play Bg4, developing actively without rushing to recapture on d4. The bishop pins the knight and supports future pressure.
notes.teaches: Don't rush to recapture in the center if you can improve your pieces first; timing matters.
notes.plans: Black will eventually take on d4 and castle, maintaining pressure on the d4 pawn.

notes.explains: If White plays Nf3 instead of the main line e3, Black can immediately play e5, challenging the center and gaining active play.
notes.teaches: In the Chigorin, Nf3 is less accurate because it allows Black to play e5 with tempo, leading to a good position.
notes.plans: Black will continue with Bb4 or other developing moves, putting pressure on White's center.

notes.explains: After cxd5 Qxd5, White can play Nc3 attacking the queen. Black should take on d4, not retreat. The queen trade leads to a queenless middlegame where Black's activity compensates for the pawn deficit.
notes.teaches: Don't be afraid to trade queens when you have compensation in piece activity and king safety. The extra pawn is often temporary and Black gets quick development and attacking chances.
notes.plans: Black will develop with Bg4, threatening to win back the pawn, and exploit White's weak king.

notes.explains: After e3, Black plays Nb4, threatening Nc2+ forking queen and rook. White must find the only move e4 to block the bishop's diagonal and prevent the fork.
notes.teaches: When your opponent has a threat like Nb4, look for a move that addresses multiple threats at once. e4 blocks the bishop and opens lines for White's pieces.
notes.plans: Black will take on e4 and then play g5 to attack the knight on f3, creating further complications.

notes.explains: Black's bishop g4 is a mistake because it leaves b7 and f7 vulnerable. Qb3 hits both targets and is more forcing than Bxf7.
notes.teaches: When attacking f7, consider queen checks or queen attacks that also target other weaknesses. The queen can often create more threats than a piece sacrifice.
notes.plans: After Qb3, if Black plays Bh5, White has Qb5+ exploiting the a4-e8 diagonal; if Black plays Bb6, White trades queens and wins a pawn.

notes.explains: Bg4 develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before Black closes with e6, following the Trompowsky idea.
notes.teaches: Get the bishop outside the pawn chain before it gets locked in.
notes.plans: Prepare e5 to open the center, exploiting White's many pawn moves near his king.

notes.explains: Black puts the knight on d7 instead of c6 to meet Bb5 with c6, blunting the bishop and enhancing central control.
notes.teaches: Choose knight development squares that anticipate and neutralize opponent's pinning moves.
notes.plans: Continue developing, keep central tension, and look for holes like g3 after h3.

notes.explains: h3 creates a hole on g3. Black can exploit it by centralizing a knight to g3, threatening Qh4 and forcing a fork on f1 after castling.
notes.teaches: When developing, look for holes in the opponent's position; moving a piece twice is fine if it exploits a weakness.
notes.plans: Play Ng3, threatening Qh4. If White castles, Nxf1 wins the exchange.

notes.explains: After h6, White prepares d4 with c3, ignoring Black's early flank move and focusing on center control.
notes.teaches: Against early flank moves, prioritize central control with moves like c3 preparing d4.
notes.plans: Play d4, then develop naturally. If Black attacks e4, consider sacrificing it to open the e-file.

notes.explains: Black's Na5 is premature here because White can trap the knight with Bb5+ c6 Bd3, then b4.
notes.teaches: Knights on the rim are vulnerable; look for ways to trap them by cutting off retreat squares.
notes.plans: After Bd3, aim for b4 to trap the knight; if Black avoids it, White still gains time and pressure.

notes.explains: Black took on d4, giving White a piece for two pawns. The extra piece is far more valuable than the pawns with many pieces on the board.
notes.teaches: A piece is worth more than three pawns in the middlegame; don't trade down to a pawn-up endgame when you have a winning attack.
notes.plans: Develop rapidly, target the weak d4 pawn, and open the center before Black can castle.

notes.explains: Black's c5 weakens the d5 square and opens lines for White's attack. White can now play e5 to break open the center.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development, open the center to exploit the opponent's uncastled king.
notes.plans: Play e5 immediately, recapture on e5 with a piece, and continue the attack against Black's king.

notes.explains: Black plays d5 to counter e5, a typical idea in the Bowdler Attack. White's queen is misplaced on f3.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen comes out early, look for ways to gain time by attacking it with pawns and pieces.
notes.plans: After d5, Black can develop with ...Bc5 or ...Be7, and later ...b5 to gain space on the queenside.

notes.explains: White has sacrificed a pawn for development and an open g-file. Black's king is stuck in the center.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development and open lines, a pawn sacrifice can be justified to maintain the initiative.
notes.plans: Black should aim to castle queenside and use the light-squared bishop on the long diagonal.

notes.explains: Black has castled queenside, but White's pieces are active. The g7 pawn is a target.
notes.teaches: In opposite-side castling positions, attack with pawns and pieces; every tempo counts.
notes.plans: White can play h4-h5 to open the h-file, or target the d5 square with Ne4.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Accelerated Grand Prix Attack
notes.explains: White's early f4 is met by d5, which undermines the center and leaves White's setup toothless. Black should not play e6, which would give a French structure with the bishop inside the pawn chain; instead, ...Nc6 is flexible, waiting for Nf3 to pin with ...Bg4.
notes.teaches: When facing an early f4 in the Sicilian, ...d5 is a strong equalizer. Avoid ...e6 unless you want a French—here you can get the bishop outside the pawn chain.
notes.plans: After ...Nc6 Nf3, play ...Bg4, then ...e6, and if h3, capture on f3 to exploit White's weakened kingside and center.

notes.opening: Sicilian Defense, Accelerated Grand Prix Attack
notes.explains: If White plays Bb5, Black's ...Qb6 attacks the bishop and prepares to recapture with the queen, keeping the queenside pawn structure intact.
notes.teaches: When White pins your knight with Bb5, ...Qb6 is a strong multipurpose move: it attacks the bishop and avoids doubled pawns.
notes.plans: Follow up with ...e6 and ...Be7, then castle kingside and prepare ...h5 to control the kingside dark squares.

notes.explains: After e4 e5 Nf3 d6 Bc4 Be7 d4, Black often plays c5, which weakens d5 and creates a backward pawn on d6. The automatic retreat Nf3 is not best; instead Bb5+ exploits the exposed king and prepares Nf5.
notes.teaches: When the opponent weakens a key square like d5, look for forcing moves that trade off their best defender and plant a knight on the outpost.
notes.plans: Play Bb5+ to exchange light-squared bishops, then Nf5 hitting the weak d6 pawn and eyeing g7. If Black plays c5, punish with Bb5+ and Nf5.

notes.explains: After c5, Bb5+ forces Black to block with Bd7 or Nc6. If Bd7, Bxd7+ Qxd7 and Nf5 gives White a dominating knight. If Black plays c5, the move Bb5+ is a key resource.
notes.teaches: In positions with a weak d5 square, an intermediate check to trade bishops can open the door for a knight to occupy the outpost.
notes.plans: Follow Bb5+ with Nf5, then target the d6 pawn and prepare an attack on the kingside.

notes.explains: White's c4 is a mistake, allowing Black to play e5 with tempo. After Bg3, Black can play Bb4+ and develop rapidly, exploiting White's lagging development.
notes.teaches: When the opponent makes a weakening pawn move, strike immediately with e5 to open the center and gain time.
notes.plans: Play e5, then Bb4+ to force a concession. Follow with Qa5 and Nc6, piling on the pressure.

notes.explains: Black has a huge lead in development. White's king is stuck in the center. Black can play d5 to open lines, or even Qxa2 winning a pawn.
notes.teaches: With a big development lead, open the center to expose the enemy king. Every piece becomes a threat.
notes.plans: Play d5, opening the center. After cxd5, Nxd5 threatens to win the rook on c1. White is helpless.

notes.explains: After d5, White's position collapses. The knight on d5 is a monster, and Black's queen and bishops dominate. White's king is stuck in the center.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development, don't hesitate to sacrifice a pawn to open lines. The initiative is worth more.
notes.plans: Play d5, then after cxd5, Nxd5 threatens Nxc3 and the rook. White's best is to give up material to survive.

notes.explains: If White plays a3, Black should retreat the bishop to e7, maintaining the pin on the knight. The pawn on a3 is weak and will fall.
notes.teaches: In a double pin, retreating one piece while maintaining the pin with the other is a powerful idea. Don't rush to capture; consolidate.
notes.plans: Play Be7, then after b4, Bxb4+ wins the pawn and keeps the initiative. The bishop can re-enter the attack with devastating effect.

notes.explains: White has a strong attack with the semi-open f-file. The key move is e5, clamping down on Black's queenside development and preparing Nf5 or Ng5.
notes.teaches: In the Fantasy Variation, the f-file is a highway to the king. Use e5 to restrict Black's pieces and then launch a kingside attack.
notes.plans: Play e5, then Ne4 to control the center. Follow with Ng5 and Qh5, threatening mate on h7.

notes.explains: Black's best defense is to play e5 before castling, preventing White's e5 clamp. If Black castles prematurely, White gets a strong attack.
notes.teaches: In the Fantasy, Black must be careful about castling too early. The move e5 is a key defensive resource to blunt White's attack.
notes.plans: If Black plays e5, White should play Kh1 to avoid tricks, then continue with Ng5 and Qh5, but the attack is less potent.

notes.explains: Black plays e5, and White closes the center with d5. This is standard when attacking on the flank: you want to keep the center closed to limit Black's counterplay.
notes.teaches: When launching a flank attack, close the center to prevent the opponent from opening lines for counterplay.
notes.plans: White continues with Qd2, O-O-O, and then prepares h4-h5 and g4.

notes.explains: White plays Bh6 to trade off Black's fianchettoed bishop, the main defender of the kingside. This is a standard idea in the Sämisch to weaken Black's king.
notes.teaches: Trading off the opponent's fianchettoed bishop is often a key step in a kingside attack, as it removes a crucial defender.
notes.plans: After Bh6, White aims to follow up with h4-h5 and g4, opening the h-file for the rooks.

notes.explains: White played Be3, a waste of tempo (likely a mouse slip). Black should not immediately lash out with Ng4; instead, castle and then strike the center with c5. This is a typical King's Indian pawn break, attacking white's center before white can complete development.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, be flexible with your pawn breaks. If white's setup is passive, c5 can be more effective than the traditional e5 because it attacks the center immediately and opens lines for the queen.
notes.plans: After c5, play Na6 and Qa5, threatening to take on c5. If white plays a3, then Ne4 is strong, hitting c3 and threatening Bxc3+ if white captures. The idea is to create chaos and exploit white's lack of development.

notes.explains: Nf6 is inaccurate because it forces Black to ruin his pawn structure after Nxf6+ gxf6. White gets a lead in development and Black's kingside is weakened.
notes.teaches: In the Rubinstein French, Black should prefer Nbd7 to recapture with the knight, keeping the pawn structure intact and avoiding weaknesses.
notes.plans: White develops naturally (Nf3, Bd3) and aims to challenge Black's only strong piece, the bishop on b7, with ideas like Qe2 and Bg5 or Be4.

notes.explains: Qe2 prepares both Bg5 and Be4 to trade off Black's strong bishop on b7. The immediate Bg5? would allow ...Bxf3 and Black's bishop pair becomes annoying.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has a single strong piece, consider ways to exchange it or neutralize it, even if it requires preparatory moves.
notes.plans: After Qe2, White can play Bg5 followed by 0-0-0, or Be4 to trade bishops. The queen also eyes the a6-square for a potential fork.

notes.explains: White's d3 is passive, blocking the bishop. Black can strike in the center with d5, which is principled and beneficial if trades occur.
notes.teaches: When White plays passively, Black should challenge the center immediately with d5.
notes.plans: Play d5, and if White takes, recapture with the knight, then develop naturally.

notes.explains: After Nxd5, Black should not take on c3, as that pawn structure is not bad for White. Instead, develop the knight to c6.
notes.teaches: Avoid releasing tension with captures that improve the opponent's pawn structure; develop pieces first.
notes.plans: Continue development, aiming to place bishops on safe squares.

notes.explains: After d4 d5 c4 c6 Nf3 Nf6 Nc3 a6, Black prepares b5. White's g3 fianchetto is a Catalan-style approach, often sacrificing the c4 pawn for dynamic play.
notes.teaches: In the Slav, g3 can lead to rich, imbalanced positions where piece activity compensates for a pawn deficit.
notes.plans: White develops with Bg2 and may play Qb3 to pressure Black's queenside, or simply complete development and open the center.

notes.explains: Black's Bg4 is dubious because White can immediately play h3, forcing the bishop to retreat to h5, after which Qb3 creates strong pressure on b7 and d5.
notes.teaches: When an opponent's bishop pins a knight on f3, look for h3 to gain a tempo and follow up with Qb3 to attack the center and queenside.
notes.plans: After Bg4, White plays h3, then Qb3, targeting b7 and d5, forcing Black to defend passively.

notes.explains: White plays e4 to blast open the center. Black's underdevelopment makes this aggressive push especially strong, as White's pieces are more active.
notes.teaches: When you have a lead in development, opening the center with pawn breaks like e4 can expose the opponent's king and create tactical opportunities.
notes.plans: White aims to open lines for the bishops and rooks, while Black struggles to catch up in development.

notes.explains: Black's early e5 weakens the d5 square, giving White total control over it.
notes.teaches: Avoid weakening key central squares like d5 without good reason, especially in gambit lines where development and square control matter most.
notes.plans: Develop normally with Bc4, then put pressure on f7 with Qb3.

notes.explains: Qb3 is better than Bxf7+ because after Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qb3+ Black can play d5, using the tempo to push the pawn and gain counterplay. Qb3 keeps the pressure on f7 and avoids giving Black time.
notes.teaches: When attacking, prefer moves that maintain pressure and force concessions over flashy sacrifices that give the opponent counterplay.
notes.plans: After Qb3, if Qd7, take on b4 with the pawn to keep the battery on f7 and prepare Ba3+.

notes.explains: After dxc5, Black plays Na6, which both attacks the c5 pawn and develops a piece. This is preferable to Qa5+ (which brings the queen out early and makes it vulnerable) or e6 (which allows White to control d6 with a bishop).
notes.teaches: When recapturing a pawn in the opening, prioritize developing a piece over winning the pawn immediately with the queen. Na6 checks both boxes: it attacks the pawn and develops.
notes.plans: After Nxc5, Black will have equal material and a good central presence. Next, develop the kingside and castle, while keeping an eye on the d5 square.

notes.explains: White plays Nb5, threatening a fork on c7 that would win the queen. Black can neutralize this with Qa5+, forcing the knight back to c3. This is a common tactical pattern: a check on a5 often chases away a piece on b5.
notes.teaches: When a knight lands on b5 threatening a fork, a queen check to a5 is a standard defensive resource that forces the knight to retreat, often to its original square.
notes.plans: After the knight retreats to c3, Black has a lead in development and can look to exploit the pin on the knight on c3.

notes.explains: With the knight back on c3 and the queen on a5 pinning it, Black has a brief window to exploit the pin. The most effective way is to attack the pinned knight with another piece. Na4 is strong because it also attacks the b2 pawn.
notes.teaches: When a piece is pinned, look to attack it with a minor piece. Attacking from the side (like Na4) can be just as effective as the more conventional Ne4, and may create additional threats.
notes.plans: Black plays Na4, threatening Nxb2. If White defends b2, Black can capture on c3 or continue pressuring the pinned knight.

notes.explains: White plays Be5, a creative defensive move that connects the bishop to the knight on c3. Black can simply capture the b2 pawn with Nxb2, as the knight on c3 loses its defender and White's queenside collapses.
notes.teaches: When a pinned piece is defended only by a bishop, capturing the defender's pawn can be decisive. The b2 pawn is often a weakness in the London System.
notes.plans: After Nxb2, Black is up a pawn and White's position is on the verge of collapse. Black can then target the bishop on e5 or continue to exploit the pin.

notes.explains: White plays Qd2, a blunder that allows Black to capture the bishop on e5. However, the best way to take the bishop is with Nc4, maintaining the pin on the knight on c3. This is stronger than Qxe5 because it keeps the pressure on.
notes.teaches: When converting an advantage, prefer moves that maintain the opponent's weaknesses. Here, Nc4 keeps the pin, whereas Qxe5 would relieve the pressure on the knight.
notes.plans: After Nc4, the queen must move, and Black captures the bishop with the knight, still pinning the knight on c3. Black will likely win that knight as well.

notes.explains: Black captures the bishop and White resigns. The game is a miniature illustrating the dangers of the London System when met with the c5 variation.
notes.teaches: A quick victory in the opening often results from exploiting a pinned piece and attacking weak pawns like b2.

notes.explains: After the game, the teacher shows a similar pattern from his own tournament game: a knight on c3 undefended and an uncastled king. Black played Qa5, forcing the rook to b1, then won material.
notes.teaches: Whenever the knight on c3 is undefended and the king is uncastled, look for queen attacks on the queenside (Qa5 or Qb6) to exploit the weakness.
notes.plans: In the example, Black played Qa5, then Nc6, forcing the rook to move, and eventually won a piece.

notes.explains: After e3, Black plays e5, attacking the bishop on f4 with tempo. The bishop must move, and Bb4+ follows, exploiting the weakened dark squares. White is in huge trouble.
notes.teaches: In the c5 variation, the move e5 is a powerful tempo-gainer that highlights the awkwardness of the London bishop on f4. It often leads to a quick collapse of White's position.
notes.plans: After Bb4+, White must block with Nd2 (Ke2 is even worse). Then Black can play Ne4, and later g5 to further harass the bishop, eventually winning material.

notes.explains: If White plays e3, Black again plays Qb6, attacking b2. White's best is Nc3, sacrificing the pawn, but this requires deep knowledge. Black can play a6 to reinforce the threat.
notes.teaches: Even in the main line e3, the queen sortie to b6 is the key idea. White often has to make concessions to defend b2.
notes.plans: After Qb6, if White plays Nc3, Black plays a6 to cover b5 and maintain the threat of Qxb2. Black gets good play.

notes.explains: After c5, White often plays e3 or c3. e3 is a solid, 'Londony' move. Black can play Nc6 and Nf6, leading to theoretical lines.
notes.teaches: In the London, e3 is a common response to c5, aiming for a solid pawn structure. Black should continue developing naturally.
notes.plans: Black can play Nc6, Nf6, and later consider Qb6 to pressure b2, or play d5 to transpose to a French-type structure.

notes.explains: Even if White plays a developing move like e3 instead of Nb5, Black is still slightly better. Black should avoid d5 (which allows Nb5) and instead play d6, then fianchetto the dark-squared bishop with g6.
notes.teaches: In the c5 variation, Black's setup often resembles a King's Indian or Dragon: d6, g6, Bg7, with excellent piece activity and pressure on the center.
notes.plans: Play d6, then g6, Bg7, O-O, and bring the rook to c8. Black has a very comfortable position with active pieces.

notes.explains: After Qxd4, Black develops with Nc6. White can play Bb5, pinning the knight. If Black plays Bd7, White trades bishops, leaving Black with a bad bishop on e7 and a weak d6 pawn.
notes.teaches: In the Philidor, trading the light-squared bishops is often favorable for White because it leaves Black with a passive dark-squared bishop and a weak d6 pawn.
notes.plans: Trade on d7, then focus on pressuring the d6 pawn and controlling the d5 outpost.

notes.explains: White has played the Scotch Gambit. Black can choose sharp theory (Nf6 or Bc5) or a quieter approach.
notes.teaches: When you sense your opponent knows the main line better than you, you can play a solid, slightly passive move to avoid being blown off the board.
notes.plans: Play d3 to prevent White from building a dominant center, accepting a slightly worse but safe position.

notes.explains: After d3, White can play c3, threatening to take the d-pawn. Black cannot recapture with dxc3 due to Qd5 threatening mate on f7.
notes.teaches: When a pawn capture leads to a tactical disaster, consider sacrificing the pawn back on your own terms to complete development.
notes.plans: Play Nf6, allowing e5, then d3 to force White to capture, or play d3 immediately to keep the pawn.

notes.explains: Black played Nf6 and d5, entering main line theory. White now has a strong center and attacking chances.
notes.teaches: The Scotch Gambit is dangerous for Black if you don't know the theory; White gets a pawn on e5 and active pieces.
notes.plans: Black should aim to complete development and challenge White's center with ...c6 or ...d6.

notes.explains: Black's Bb4 is a passive move that doesn't challenge the Vienna setup. It resembles an inverted Trompowsky, but the natural response Nd5 is unstable because Black can chase it with c6.
notes.teaches: When facing an unfamiliar move, stay calm and ask what your opponent wants. Here, Bb4 doesn't interfere with f4, so keep the opening's spirit.
notes.plans: Play f4 anyway, maintaining the aggressive Vienna structure.

notes.explains: Black's h6 reveals his plan: g5 to build a pawn chain and keep the f4 pawn. If White plays d4 now, Black replies g5 and White gains nothing. The correct response is to ignore the pawn and develop rapidly, punishing Black's slow play.
notes.teaches: Read your opponent's intentions. When they waste time on pawn moves, accelerate your development rather than reacting mechanically.
notes.plans: Play Bc4, a calm developing move, and see how Black arranges his pieces before deciding on further action.

notes.explains: Black plays Nf6, a solid move. White should not play e5 immediately because Black replies d5, opening the center and exploiting the pin on the c3-knight. Instead, castle first to safeguard the king.
notes.teaches: When in doubt, develop and castle. Premature central pushes can backfire if your king is still exposed.
notes.plans: Castle, then consider e5 after Black's king is committed.

notes.explains: After Nxc6, Black plays Qf6, attacking the knight on c6 and threatening the scholar's mate. This is an in-between move that develops the queen with tempo.
notes.teaches: When your opponent moves a piece twice in the opening, you can often gain time by developing your pieces while attacking theirs. This is called 'developing with tempo.'
notes.plans: Black intends to recapture on c6 with the d-pawn, opening the diagonal for the bishop on c5.

notes.explains: White plays Bf4, attacking the pawn on c7 but ignoring the queen on f6. This is tunnel vision: White only sees the pawn and misses that the queen can capture on f2 with check, winning a piece.
notes.teaches: Tunnel vision is a common mistake where a player focuses on one threat and misses a more important one. Always consider all your opponent's threats, especially checks.
notes.plans: Black plays Qxf2+ winning a pawn and forcing the king to move, then can continue attacking.

notes.explains: White's setup with Nc3 and exd5 blocks the c-pawn, preventing c3 or c4. This makes d4 a static weakness rather than a dynamic center.
notes.teaches: In the Caro-Kann, White's ideal is to maintain tension with c3 or c4. Blocking the c-pawn with Nc3 after exd5 is a common inaccuracy.
notes.plans: Black develops naturally (Nc6, Nf6, Bg4/Bf5) and aims to keep the pawn chain intact.

notes.explains: Black is not worried about Bxf6 because the doubled f-pawns can actually strengthen the center, and White loses time.
notes.teaches: Don't fear doubled pawns if they come at the cost of opponent's development; they can be a structural asset.
notes.plans: If Bxf6, recapture with gxf6 and maintain the center.

notes.explains: Black develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain (Bg4) rather than locking it in with e6. This is a luxury because White hasn't played c3 or c4.
notes.teaches: When White's center is not dynamic, you can often develop the bishop outside the pawn chain for more activity.
notes.plans: Continue development, possibly with e6 later, but keep the bishop active.

notes.explains: Black plays Bc5, which prevents d4 but has a flaw: the fork trick Nxe5. If Black takes on f2, White gets central control and king safety despite losing castling.
notes.teaches: When facing Bc5 in the Four Knights, Nxe5 is a strong reply because Black's bishop is vulnerable and the fork trick can be dangerous if Black takes on f2.
notes.plans: After Nxe5, if Black plays Bxf2+, respond with Kxf2, then play d4 to control the center. The king will hide on g1, and White's development advantage compensates for the exposed king.

notes.explains: Black plays d6, which loses a queen to Bg5! because the bishop on c4 guards the only escape square. This is a tactical trick that arises from natural development.
notes.teaches: Play moves that are good in themselves but also contain a threat. Here, Bc4 is a strong developing move that also sets up a trap. Always look for such dual-purpose moves.
notes.plans: Play Bg5, trapping the queen. After winning the queen, convert the extra material without unnecessary complications. Simplify only when convenient; don't give up your best pieces.

notes.explains: The correct response to Nxe5 is Bd6, not Bxf2+. Bd6 wins back the pawn and keeps the bishop pair. Black is slightly worse due to White's center control and development lead, but it's much better than the losing line with Bxf2+.
notes.teaches: In the fork trick position, don't give up your bishop for a pawn. Play Bd6 to regain the pawn and maintain piece activity. Giving up the dark-squared bishop early is a major concession.
notes.plans: After Bd6, White can play f4 or Bd3 to maintain an advantage. Black should aim to complete development and challenge White's center.

notes.explains: Retreating the bishop to e2 (instead of a4) avoids being chased by b5 and then Nc5, which would trap the bishop. From e2, the bishop is safe and can later go to f3.
notes.teaches: Don't automatically retreat a bishop to a4 after a6; consider the opponent's counterplay. Preserve your active pieces by retreating to a square where they remain useful.
notes.plans: Black will likely play Nb6 to attack the d5 pawn. White should complete development with Nf3 or Ne2 and d4.

notes.explains: Playing d4 controls the center and prepares to develop the knight. Black's knight on b6 attacks d5, but White can defend or trade.
notes.teaches: In the opening, central control is paramount. Even when behind in material, completing development and controlling the center gives compensation.
notes.plans: After Black recaptures on d5 (e.g., Nxd5 or Qxd5), White can develop with Nf3 or Ne2 and Bf3, aiming for a slight advantage.

notes.explains: After Qxd5, White has a choice: develop the knight to f3 or play Bf3. Bf3 puts the bishop on the long diagonal, eyeing b7, and then the knight can go to e2.
notes.teaches: Be flexible with knight development. Ne2 is a legitimate square; the knight can later go to g3 or c3. Don't be afraid to put knights on non-standard squares to improve other pieces.
notes.plans: Play Bf3, then Ne2, castle, and aim to pressure b7. Black will struggle to develop the c8-bishop without losing the b7 pawn.

notes.explains: Black's queen on b5 defends b7 and threatens to develop the bishop. White should not play a4 immediately because the queen can drop back to b6, and the threat is not meaningful. Instead, continue development with Ne2.
notes.teaches: Don't make a move just because it creates a threat. The threat must be meaningful; if the opponent can easily sidestep it, you may waste time. Focus on your own plans.
notes.plans: Play Ne2, castle, and later consider a4 when the king is safe and the bishop on f3 pressures b7.

notes.explains: After castling, the situation changes: the king is safe, and the bishop on f3 pressures b7. Now a4 becomes a meaningful threat because the queen is the only defender of b7, and it can be chased away.
notes.teaches: Re-evaluate tactical ideas as the position evolves. A move that was bad earlier (a4) can become good later when conditions change (king safety, piece placement).
notes.plans: Play a4, then a5, then Nc3 to chase the queen and win the b7 pawn.

notes.explains: Black plays e6, heading for the French Defense. White intends to play the Gionatus Variation but Black plays a6, an unusual move.
notes.teaches: When facing unusual early pawn moves, simply develop your pieces. Don't try to punish immediately; principled development is best.
notes.plans: Develop with Nf3, preparing to play c3 later if needed.

notes.explains: After e4 d5 e5 d4, Black's d-pawn counterattacks the knight on c3, which is the cleanest path to equality.
notes.teaches: Counterattacking the opponent's pieces is often more effective than simply retreating.
notes.plans: After …d4, White may capture on d4, leading to mutual destruction with ...Qxd2+ allowing Black to survive.

notes.explains: White starts with b3, a hypermodern opening that avoids occupying the center with pawns, instead fianchettoing the bishop to attack the center from a distance.
notes.teaches: In hypermodern openings, you don't need to occupy the center immediately; you can control it with pieces and later strike with pawns.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to b2, then play e3 or c4 to support the center, and eventually d4 to open lines.

notes.explains: White fianchettoes the queen's bishop, aiming to pressure Black's center hypermodernly. The idea is to attack Black's e5 pawn without building a pawn center.
notes.teaches: In hypermodern openings, you don't occupy the center with pawns but attack it with pieces from a distance. The bishop on b2 targets e5.
notes.plans: Play Bb5 to pin the knight and threaten the e5 pawn. Develop knights to e2 instead of f3 to avoid e4 with tempo, and prepare f4 to open lines.

notes.explains: Black's h5 is an unusual move that weakens the kingside, especially the g6 square. White should not react to such provocation but instead continue with solid development.
notes.teaches: When your opponent plays dubious moves, focus on your own development and central control rather than reacting to threats.
notes.plans: Play e3, then develop the knight to f3, and later occupy the center with d4.

notes.explains: Black's a5 aims to undermine White's pawn structure with a4. White can neutralize this with a3, preparing b4 if Black plays a4.
notes.teaches: Against a5, a3 is a good prophylactic move that keeps the pawn structure flexible and prevents Black from gaining space on the queenside.
notes.plans: After a3, continue development with Nf3, then d4, and later consider c4 if needed.

notes.explains: Black played d6 instead of the critical d5, leaving White with a full center and the c3 square for the knight. White's position is already very pleasant.
notes.teaches: In the Alapin, Black must play d5 to fight for the center; otherwise White gets a dominant center and easy development.
notes.plans: Develop naturally, keeping the center intact. Consider h3 to restrict Black's light-squared bishop.

notes.explains: White develops the knight to c3 first. Nf3 would allow Bg4, giving Black extra options. By playing Nc3 first, White can follow with h3 to restrict the bishop.
notes.teaches: When two moves are equally good, choose the one that limits the opponent's options. Here, Nc3 avoids Bg4 and allows h3 to force Black's bishop to a passive square.
notes.plans: Play h3, then Nf3, developing with the bishop on e3 or d3, keeping the center solid.

notes.explains: After h3 and Nf3, Black has fianchettoed. White considers d5 but prefers simpler development. d5 would open the fianchetto bishop and require precise follow-up like Bg5 to neutralize the dark-squared bishop.
notes.teaches: Don't overextend the center unnecessarily. Simple development (Be3, Bd3) keeps the position solid and avoids creating weaknesses.
notes.plans: Play Be3 (not Bf4, which is vulnerable to e5 or Nh5), then Bd3, castle, and prepare queenside or kingside play.

notes.explains: White develops the bishop to d3 instead of c4. Bc4 is tactically bad because of Nxe4! d5 winning back the piece, and positionally bad because b5 can chase it away. Bd3 reinforces the center and is safe.
notes.teaches: Avoid placing bishops on c4 in the Alapin when Black has a knight on c6; the tactical trick Nxe4 is a common pitfall. Prefer d3 for solidity.
notes.plans: Complete development with O-O, then consider queenside expansion with a4 or kingside play.

notes.explains: White plays a4 to provoke b4, creating a weakness on b4 and a hole on b5. This restricts Black's queenside counterplay and gives White freedom to operate on the kingside. The knight can later maneuver to g3 via c3-e2-g3.
notes.teaches: Provoking pawn weaknesses can be a strategic tool. a4 forces b4, which becomes a target and gives White the b5 square for a bishop or knight.
notes.plans: After b4, maneuver the knight to g3, then play Qd2 and Bh6 to trade Black's fianchetto bishop, followed by kingside attack.

notes.explains: In a similar position, a4 is not always correct. Playing a4 automatically can create a hole on b4 for Black's knight. It's often better to allow b5 and keep the queenside solid.
notes.teaches: Don't play a4 automatically to prevent b5. Consider the downsides: it weakens b4, which can become an outpost for Black's knight. Sometimes allowing b5 is safer.
notes.plans: If Black plays b5, consider maneuvers like Nc3-e2-g3 to attack on the kingside, or simply continue development and wait for Black to overextend.

notes.explains: Black voluntarily ruins his pawn structure with Nf6, leading to the Tartakower after exf6 exf6. This opens the bishop on c8 and gives Black dynamic chances.
notes.teaches: Accepting a compromised pawn structure can be worthwhile if it activates your pieces and creates attacking chances.
notes.plans: Develop naturally with Bd6, O-O, and then pin White's knight with Bg4 to create pressure.

notes.explains: Black recaptures with the e-pawn, creating a 'pawn cube' on f6, g7, h7. This structure is solid defensively and allows Black to push f- and g-pawns for attack without exposing the king.
notes.teaches: The pawn cube (three pawns on f6, g7, h7) provides king safety and attacking potential; pushing two pawns leaves the king still well-protected.
notes.plans: Develop the knight to d7, then consider rerouting it to f8 or b6 to reach d5 or e6.

notes.explains: Black pins the knight with Bg4, a very annoying move for White. White's typical responses (h3 or Be2) are either weakening or passive.
notes.teaches: Pinning a knight to the queen or king can be a powerful developing move that disrupts the opponent's plans.
notes.plans: Complete development with Nd7, then consider Bh5 to maintain the pin, or trade on f3 if beneficial.

notes.explains: Black's f6 is a serious mistake because it weakens the kingside and allows White to play Nxc3, winning a rook after Bxf7+ Kxf7 Qd5+ and Qxa8.
notes.teaches: In open gambits, accepting material and then exploiting the opponent's weakened king safety is often decisive.
notes.plans: After Bxf7+ Kxf7, Qd5+ followed by Qxa8 leaves White with a rook and pawn for a bishop and knight, a winning material advantage.

notes.explains: In the Nimzo-Indian, Black pins the knight on c3 to prevent e4 and control the center from a distance. White's e4 is a mistake because it allows Black to take on c3 and win a pawn.
notes.teaches: The Nimzo-Indian is a hypermodern opening where Black controls the center with pieces rather than pawns, and the pin on the knight is a key idea.
notes.plans: After e4, take the pawn on e4 with the knight, then later take on c3 with the knight to win a pawn and ruin White's structure.

notes.explains: When White plays Nf3 in the Caro-Kann, Black has the extra option of Bg4 instead of the usual Bf5, because the queen no longer controls g4. This pins the knight and puts pressure on d4.
notes.teaches: In the Caro-Kann, if White plays Nf3 early, consider Bg4 to pin the knight and create pressure, as the queen no longer defends that square.
notes.plans: Play Bg4, then e6, c5, and Nc6 to develop and challenge the center.

notes.explains: After c5, White may play d5, closing the center. Black's knight can go to a5, seemingly on the rim, but it supports the b5 break and opens the diagonal for the bishop on g7.
notes.teaches: Knights on the rim can be useful when they serve a specific plan, like pressuring c4 and preparing b5. General principles can be violated for concrete positional gains.
notes.plans: Black aims for a6 and b5 to undermine White's pawn chain and create queenside play.

notes.explains: White fianchettoes both bishops, creating pressure on the center. The bishop on b2 is particularly strong, eyeing the long diagonal.
notes.teaches: In the Sicilian, fianchettoing the light-squared bishop can be a flexible setup, avoiding early commitments and keeping the bishop active.
notes.plans: White can aim for Nd5, exploiting the undefended bishop on g7 and the queen's position.

notes.explains: Nd5 is a powerful move, threatening to capture on e7 and exploiting the undefended bishop on g7. The knight sacrifice on b5 is a thematic idea to open lines.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's bishop is undefended, look for tactical shots like Nd5 that create threats and force concessions.
notes.plans: After Nd5, Black may capture, leading to a sacrifice on b5 that destroys Black's kingside.

notes.explains: The Carlsbad pawn structure arises after White captures on d5 early, releasing central tension. White gets an e-pawn versus Black's c-pawn, creating a structural imbalance that defines the middlegame.
notes.teaches: Releasing central tension early can create a fixed pawn structure with clear strategic plans for both sides.
notes.plans: White aims for a minority attack on the queenside (b4-b5) or a central break with f3 and e4, depending on piece placement.

notes.explains: Playing Qc2 early prevents Black's bishop from coming to f5, which can be annoying. It's a useful prophylactic move with no downside.
notes.teaches: Prophylactic moves that prevent opponent's active options are often worth including, even if they seem slow.
notes.plans: Continue development with Nf3 or Ne2, then castle and decide on the minority attack or central break.

notes.explains: In the Carlsbad, White can develop the knight to f3 or e2. Here Nf3 is chosen because Ne2 runs into the tricky idea ...Bxh2+ and ...Ng4+ after castling, which is messy.
notes.teaches: Knight development in the Carlsbad depends on specific tactical nuances; both f3 and e2 are viable but have different pros and cons.
notes.plans: Prepare to play Ne5 (Pillsbury knight) supported by f4, or go for the f3-e4 central break if the knight is on e2.

notes.explains: Black's bishop on d6 is less accurate than e7 because it doesn't address the pin on the knight and weakens control over e5.
notes.teaches: In the Carlsbad, Black's dark-squared bishop is usually best on e7 to support the kingside and avoid weakening key squares.
notes.plans: White can now aim for Ne5 (Pillsbury knight) since Black's bishop doesn't contest e5.

notes.explains: White establishes a Pillsbury knight on e5, supported by pawns on d4 and f4. This knight is very strong and hard to dislodge.
notes.teaches: The Pillsbury knight (knight on e5 supported by f4) is a powerful attacking formation in the Carlsbad, often leading to a kingside crush.
notes.plans: Play f4 to entrench the knight, then decide on castling direction. If Black plays ...Nbd7, push f4 immediately.

notes.explains: White's bishop on g5 pins the knight on f6, but Black can break the pin with ...h6, forcing the bishop to retreat or trade.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, Black often accepts a space disadvantage to later strike in the center with ...e5 or ...c5, using tactical tricks to regain the pawn.
notes.plans: Black should play ...h6, then ...Nbd7 and ...c6, preparing ...d5 to challenge White's center.

notes.explains: After the exchange on f6, Black has the bishop pair and a solid pawn structure. White's knight on d4 is a strong outpost, but Black can challenge it with ...c5 or ...Nc6.
notes.teaches: When you have the bishop pair, avoid trading one off without compensation. The knight on d4 is a blockader; if Black opens the center, the knight loses value.
notes.plans: Black should play ...c6 and ...Nc6, aiming to trade the knight on d4. If White recaptures with the pawn, Black gets a semi-open b-file and a passed d-pawn.

notes.explains: White has a space advantage and a strong pawn on c5. Black's bishop on c7 is passive, and Black's rooks are active on the a-file. White's knight is well-placed on c3, and White can consider pushing b5 to create a passed pawn.
notes.teaches: In the Caro-Kann, White often gets a space advantage and a queenside majority. Black should aim to trade off White's active pieces and create counterplay on the kingside or with ...b5.
notes.plans: White can play b5 to create a passed pawn, then support it with the rook and knight. Black should try to block the pawn with ...Ra4 and ...Bc6, then seek counterplay with ...f6 or ...g5.

notes.explains: White pushes b5, creating a passed pawn. Black's rook on a2 is active, but Black's bishop on c7 is stuck. White's knight on c3 is well-placed, and White can support the pawn with the rook.
notes.teaches: A passed pawn on the queenside can be a decisive advantage if supported properly. Black must find counterplay or block the pawn before it advances.
notes.plans: White should continue with b6, then Rc1-c3 and Rb3 to support the pawn. Black can try ...Ra4 and ...Bc6 to block, or create kingside threats with ...f6 and ...g5.

notes.explains: Black's passive development and h6 are serious weaknesses. White has a space advantage and can now consider opening the center.
notes.teaches: When your opponent plays passively, look for the right moment to open the center and exploit their lack of development.
notes.plans: Consider Bb5+ to force a pin on the bishop, then take on e6 to leave Black's bishop pinned and vulnerable.

notes.explains: Black's h6 is a serious mistake. Instead, Black should have played e5 to close the center and limit White's development advantage.
notes.teaches: When underdeveloped, closing the center with e5 can reduce the opponent's attacking chances. Avoid weakening pawn moves like h6.
notes.plans: If Black plays e5, White is still better but the advantage is smaller. White can reroute the knight to c4 and prepare f4.

notes.explains: White's f3 is premature and weakens the kingside. Black should focus on development rather than immediately exploiting the weakness.
notes.teaches: Don't rush to exploit a weakness if it means neglecting development. The weakness will remain; develop first and exploit later.
notes.plans: Black plays Bf5, developing with pressure on the knight. Later, the weakness of f3 can be targeted.

notes.explains: White plays c4 to contest the d5 square immediately, but Black should still play d5. This often transposes into the Panov-Botvinnik Attack or an IQP position.
notes.teaches: When White plays c4 in the Caro-Kann, Black should not be deterred from playing d5. The resulting structures often lead to an isolated queen's pawn (IQP) position, which is comfortable for Black.
notes.plans: Black will develop naturally, aiming for an ideal French setup with the bishop outside the pawn chain.

notes.explains: Black plays a6, a rare move. White should continue developing with Nf3, not Nc3, to keep the option of c3.
notes.teaches: Avoid committing your knight to c3 if you want to play c3 later. Keep flexibility.
notes.plans: Develop naturally and wait for Black to reveal more intentions.

notes.explains: White plays f3 to maintain the center and prevent Black's light-squared bishop from developing to f5. This line is underrated but dangerous if handled correctly.
notes.teaches: In the Fantasy Variation, White's main idea is to keep the center intact and not allow Black easy development. Flexibility is key—be ready to adapt your plans.
notes.plans: Develop naturally with Nc3, Be3, and consider castling queenside to exploit Black's potential overextension.

notes.explains: Black plays ...d5 and White advances e5, gaining space and kicking the knight. Black's knight on f6 is vulnerable, and White can now build a strong attack.
notes.teaches: When Black plays ...Nf6 in the Fantasy, e5 is a strong reply—it's not like the Advance Variation; here Black is nearly busted if he doesn't respond accurately.
notes.plans: After e5, if Black retreats to d7, play e6 with a gambit. If Black plays ...Nh5, continue with g4 or other aggressive moves.

notes.explains: c6 is a rare but tricky move, preparing d5 after Nf3, similar to the Caro-Kann idea. Black is slightly worse if White knows how to respond, but often Black gets good practical chances.
notes.teaches: In sharp openings, unusual moves can create confusion and steer the game into less theoretical territory.
notes.plans: After Nf3, play d5, striking in the center.

notes.explains: After d5 exd5, pushing e4 gains space and attacks the knight on f3. White should take on e4, trade queens, and force the white king to d1, leaving it vulnerable.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, trading queens can leave the king in a dangerous central position even without queens on the board.
notes.plans: Take on e4, trade queens, and exploit the king on d1.

notes.explains: After d4 d5 c4 dxc4, the most ambitious response is e4, leaving the d4 and e4 pawns exposed but aiming for a powerful center if White recovers the pawn.
notes.teaches: In the Queen's Gambit Accepted, e4 is the most challenging move; Black must immediately attack the center pawns to avoid being overrun.
notes.plans: White intends to recapture on c4 and build a strong pawn center with space advantage.

notes.explains: After e4 Nf6, the old move Nc3 allows …e5 with comfortable equality for Black. Instead, e5 forces the knight to d5, and White recovers the pawn with Bxc4.
notes.teaches: Avoid automatic developing moves like Nc3 when a pawn push (e5) disrupts Black's plans and maintains the initiative.
notes.plans: White will follow up with Nf3 or Ne2, aiming to control d5.

notes.explains: Black's Bf5 is inaccurate; the correct move is Nb6, which prepares to meet Qb3 with e6 and then Nd7, offering a pawn for development.
notes.teaches: When facing Qb3 in such positions, Black should not fear the pawn grab but instead aim for rapid development to compensate.
notes.plans: White should not grab the b7 pawn but instead focus on controlling d5 with Ne2 and Nbc3.

notes.explains: White plays Ne2 instead of Nf3 to avoid a potential Bg4 pin and to support the knight on c3, reinforcing control over d5.
notes.teaches: Ne2 is not inferior to Nf3; it has specific pros: avoiding pins and supporting the c3 knight. Choose development based on positional needs.
notes.plans: White will follow with Nbc3, castle, and then consider Qb3 to pressure Black's position.

notes.explains: Ng3 appears to blunder a pawn because of Nxc3 bxc3 Bxc3, trapping the rook. However, White has a powerful tactical idea: Nxf5, and if Black takes the rook, Nd6 gives devastating compensation.
notes.teaches: When a move looks like a blunder, calculate deeper. Here, the trapped rook is irrelevant because White's attack on the uncastled king is overwhelming.
notes.plans: After Nxf5, White threatens Nd6, and if Black takes the rook, the knight on d6 is crushing.

notes.explains: Black plays Qe7, counter-attacking the e5 pawn. White must decide how to defend.
notes.teaches: In gambit lines, accepting the pawn and then defending with natural developing moves is often best.
notes.plans: White should play Bf4 or Bg5, transposing into the main line.

notes.explains: Black forks king and bishop with Qb4+. White blocks with Bd2, but Black captures on b2, threatening the rook.
notes.teaches: Falling into the 'trap' is correct; Black's queen becomes overextended and White gains a development lead.
notes.plans: Play Bd2, then Nc3 (not Bc3, which allows Bb4 pinning the bishop).

notes.explains: Black plays Qa3 instead of the main line Qxc3. White can play Nd5, attacking c7 and threatening the bishop on b4.
notes.teaches: When the opponent's queen is deep in your position, target weak pawns and force trades to exploit the development advantage.
notes.plans: Play Nd5, offering a bishop trade; after Qxd2, the threat to c7 is devastating.

notes.explains: Black plays d6, a more solid try. White can play Bg5, forcing f6 or trading bishops to soften the d6 pawn.
notes.teaches: Against the Englund, even 'better' lines leave Black with a poor position due to weak pawns and lagging development.
notes.plans: Play Bg5, then exd6, leaving Black with an isolated d-pawn and no compensation.

notes.explains: Black plays the main line Qxc3, sacrificing the queen for two pieces and a rook. White must know the correct response.
notes.teaches: In queen sacrifice lines, precise play is needed to exploit Black's lack of development and the exposed king.
notes.plans: Play Rxb4, then target the bishop on c3 with Rb3, Qa1, and eventually push e3 or e4.

notes.explains: Black plays Nxe5, which loses quickly. White can target the bishop on c3 with Rb3, then Qa1 attacking the knight.
notes.teaches: When the opponent has two pieces for a rook, look to harass the more vulnerable piece with rook lifts and queen maneuvers.
notes.plans: Play Rb3, then Qa1; if Nc4, take on g7; if d6, play Rb5 hunting the bishop.

notes.explains: After the sequence e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 Nf3 Qb6 Bd3 cxd4 Nxd4 Nc6, White has a comfortable position. The pawn structure is favorable for White, and Black's dark-squared bishop is bad because its counterpart on light squares is hemmed in.
notes.teaches: In the French Advance, the knight often goes to d2 and then b3, but here Nc3 is also strong because it threatens Na4 to eliminate Black's important dark-squared bishop. The Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh7+) is a tactical idea if Black castles kingside.
notes.plans: Develop with Nc3, aiming for Na4 or Nb5 to pressure d6. If Black plays Qc7, Nb5 is a good option to target d6.

notes.explains: Black's d6 is passive; White can trade on favorable terms. The key is to force Black to capture on e5, leading to a queen trade that leaves White up a pawn with a passive Black position.
notes.teaches: When facing a gambit, look to trade queens if you come out ahead materially and the opponent's position is passive. Force the trade on your terms.
notes.plans: Develop the bishop to f4, inviting Black to take on e5. After the queen trade, White is up a pawn with a solid position.

notes.explains: Bf4 is the best move; it pressures e5 and forces Black to decide. If Black takes on e5, White recaptures with the queen and trades queens favorably.
notes.teaches: Develop with threats. Bf4 both develops and creates a tactical threat that simplifies to a favorable endgame.
notes.plans: After the queen trade, continue developing with Nc3 and e3, maintaining the extra pawn.

notes.explains: Black's Bg4 pins the knight. White can ignore the pin and continue developing; the bishop on g4 is not dangerous.
notes.teaches: Don't fear pins in the opening if you have a lead in development or a material advantage. Just continue with your plan.
notes.plans: Play e3, developing the knight to c3, and castle kingside.

notes.explains: Black plays d5, but being down a pawn, this doesn't equalize. White should anticipate Black's desire to play Bb4 and prevent it with a3.
notes.teaches: When you have a material advantage, you can spend a tempo to prevent the opponent's counterplay. a3 stops Bb4 and preserves your pawn structure.
notes.plans: Play a3, then continue development with Nc3, and castle.

notes.explains: a3 is a judgment call: it delays development but is safe because Black is underdeveloped and cannot exploit the tempo loss. White is only two moves from completing development.
notes.teaches: Sometimes you can afford a 'luxury' move like a3 when the opponent has no active counterplay. Evaluate whether your lead in development or material allows such a move.
notes.plans: After a3, play Nc3 and Be2, then castle.

notes.explains: White plays a passive system (the KIA setup). Black can prepare the e5 pawn break. The knight goes to c6 instead of d7 because White's setup is so passive that Black can afford this more aggressive development.
notes.teaches: Against passive setups, you can deviate from standard move orders to pursue your plans more aggressively. The e5 break is the thematic King's Indian pawn break.
notes.plans: Play Re8, then prepare e5 with ...d6 and ...Nbd7 or ...Nc6. After e5, open the center if White allows.

notes.explains: Black plays Nc6, preparing e5. If White plays b5 attacking the knight, Black can sacrifice the pawn because White's lack of development will be exposed if the center opens.
notes.teaches: In the King's Indian, be ready to sacrifice a pawn for initiative if the opponent is underdeveloped. The center opening favors the better-developed side.
notes.plans: Play e5, and if White takes, open the center with ...dxe5 or ...exd4, exploiting White's undeveloped pieces.

notes.explains: Black improves the rook to e8, supporting the e5 pawn and preparing potential tactics. White's bishop on b5 pins the knight, but Black can unpin with Bd7.
notes.teaches: Improve your pieces before committing to tactical operations. Re8 is a useful prophylactic move that also supports the center.
notes.plans: Play Bd7 to unpin, then consider the tactical shot Nxd4 if White's bishop is undefended.

notes.explains: Black unpins with Bd7. Now the bishop on b5 is undefended, creating a standoff. Black can consider Nxd4, exploiting the undefended bishop.
notes.teaches: Always be alert to undefended pieces. A bishop on b5 is a common tactical target; look for ways to exploit the pin or the lack of defenders.
notes.plans: If White plays exd5, Black can recapture with the knight and win a pawn due to the undefended bishop. Otherwise, continue with ...a6 or ...b5.
